The fixtures mean it is difficult for Maresca to get training time as he tries to instil his style. “We try and do what we can on the pitch to go through a few things and tactics before the games,” the defender Marc Guéhi said. “It’s just a lot of recovery, sleep, to make sure the body is right for the next game,. It’s been enjoyable, to be honest; not to train, just playing games, which is fun.”

Sports.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action
Sports.content:
1 In-form Calvert-Lewin causes a ‘ruckus’

Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s physicality overpowering Bryan Mbeumo in Manchester United’s area at a corner grabbed him a fifth goal in 10 outings for Leeds: a pretty respectable ratio. “I just tried to cause a ruckus,” said Leeds’ No 9. “I make it difficult for the defender. I read the flight of the ball and was quickest to react. I feel really comfortable [here]. I feel the support from the club and the fans and it is a great feeling stepping on to the pitch, particularly at Elland Road.” Of the contenders to be understudy to Harry Kane as England’s centre-forward, Calvert-Lewin may be the lead act – if he can stay injury-free, which has been a difficulty throughout his career. Jamie Jackson

2 Baleba adds fresh energy to United

After the defeat to Atlético Madrid last Tuesday, Manchester United’s director of football, Jason Wilcox, could at least sit a bit more comfortably watching Michael Carrick’s side battle to a draw at Elland Road. Lisandro Martínez bemoaned, among other things, the lack of squad depth at United in his post-match comments in Madrid, but one area Wilcox did strengthen over the summer was United’s midfield. Carlos Baleba, a £65m arrival from Brighton, started his first game for the club alongside Andrey Santos, a £50m signing from Chelsea, and the pair held their own against Leeds’ combative midfield three. “They’re both young players adapting to life at this football club and I thought both of them were terrific today,” Carrick said. “That’s a massive positive for us.” As for Martínez, he was taken off at half-time with a tight thigh. Billy Munday

View image in fullscreen Carlos Baleba made his mark for Manchester United in midfield. Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty Images

3 Wirtz grows into role of Liverpool creator

Florian Wirtz created nine chances during Liverpool’s comeback win against Brentford. The German’s effectiveness grew when Brentford were reduced to 10 men but it was still one of Wirtz’s better games in a Liverpool shirt. The playmaker took on responsibility in the second half. Andoni Iraola was happy and perhaps sees a connection growing between Wirtz and Víctor Muñoz. Both of Wirtz’s assists in the league this season have been for Muñoz, a £34.5m summer signing from Osasuna who hugs the touchline and stretches the play with speed and directness. Iraola plays positive, vertical football. Wirtz could be more dangerous if his passes are hitting speedy wingers such as Muñoz and Bradley Barcola. Jacob Steinberg

4 Bouaddi belies his years in assured display

Ayyoub Bouaddi made his first league start for Manchester City in the win against Ipswich but anyone watching would have thought he was an old hand. The teenager belied his years with a mature performance at the base of midfield, controlling the tempo while keeping things simple in possession and spotting danger when required. The Moroccan cost £85m in the summer from Lille to battle for a place in Enzo Maresca’s revamped side, fighting Enzo Fernández and Elliot Anderson for a spot in the team – and he is looking their equal. “Not bad, yeah?” Maresca joked about Bouaddi’s performance. “I think that the manager is always looking to find minutes and space for good players. Ayyoub is very good. He is very young, coming from France, so we need to help him, not put him under pressure every game. I think he is doing well.” Will Unwin

View image in fullscreen Ayyoub Bouaddi has made a promising start in England. Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/EPA

5 Arbeloa claims ‘sky is the limit’ for King

If you were at Craven Cottage on Saturday and didn’t know which three players Álvaro Arbeloa had brought with him from the Real Madrid setup, you would have assumed one of them was Josh King. The 19-year-old has started every league game this season ahead of Emile Smith Rowe in the No 10 position and has already taken on the role of chief creator. King has been in Fulham’s academy since under-nine level and became a regular in the first team under Marco Silva last season. Arbeloa has spoken of wanting to help the youngster raise his level, to help him kick on. “He’s a top talent,” said Arbeloa after King’s all-action performance against Hull that helped Fulham to their first league win of the campaign. “The sky is his limit. He has the talent, the mentality, the character – he has everything to become a top, top player.” BM

6 Moyes aggrieved after Rogers escapes red

David Moyes claimed Chelsea got the rub of the green with the two goals that condemned Everton to a first defeat of the season but there was no question it was deserved on the basis of their respective second-half performances. Everton’s response to Pedro Neto’s opener was nonexistent, with Moyes’s decision to introduce a seemingly unfit Christian Nørgaard instead of Hayden Hackney a contributory factor, but they could feel aggrieved about Morgan Rogers avoiding a second yellow card in the 44th minute for leaping into James Garner. With Harrison Armstrong booked for what the referee, Paul Tierney, deemed a reckless challenge on Josh Acheampong earlier in the game, his inconsistency on the Chelsea forward’s tackle was a key moment. “I would love to speak on the referees but I would probably get fined,” said Garner. “All this camera stuff on their heads, you need to keep out of the game. Just let referees ref it and stop making it about them. That’s all I’ve got to say.” Andy Hunter

View image in fullscreen Morgan Rogers (centre) was not the most popular man on Merseyside at the weekend. Photograph: Mike Egerton/PA

7 Time for Jaissle to switch up defence?

Sven Botman was extremely fortunate not to be sent off for a nasty tackle on Nicolas Jackson as Newcastle lost 1-0 at home to Aston Villa, with the excellent Johan Manzambi heading the first-half winner. The rash, high way Botman lunged in on Jackson seemed emblematic of the centre-back’s decline since he suffered a serious knee injury three years ago. The moment has surely arrived for the now under pressure Matthias Jaissle to drop Botman and recall not merely Dan Burn but Fabian Schär, too, in a switch to a more stabilising back three. Newcastle’s failure to keep a clean sheet in their last 13 Premier League games at home – a run stretching back into last season under Eddie Howe – emphasises the need for defensive fortification. Moreover Schär’s ball-playing ability, and particularly his dangerous long diagonal passes, would enhance Newcastle’s pretty dismal threat as an attacking force. Tellingly, Jaissle’s team registered only one shot on target on Saturday, paving the way for Unai Emery’s 100th Premier League win as a manager. Louise Taylor

8 Madueke upstages struggling Eze

When Arsenal signed Eberechi Eze, it was hard not to be a little suspicious. Though he started his top-level career relatively late, it is rare a player steps up levels at 27 – all the more so given Mikel Arteta is not exactly in love with mavericks and risk. Ultimately, Eze looks better suited to being the main man in a mid-ranking team rather than a cog in a top one which prioritises shape and system above all else. He was anonymous against Nottingham Forest prior to his removal at half-time. Though Arsenal did not explode thereafter, Noni Madueke did offer greater threat, his speed challenging defenders inside and out before scoring a winning goal that, though fortuitous, also reflected the difference he made. There is surely little chance Eze is picked to start Arsenal’s next game, at Bayern Munich, and he is running out of time to establish himself at the club. Daniel Harris

View image in fullscreen Eberechi Eze (right) made little impact against Nottingham Forest. Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty Images

9 Sage on thin ice after grim trip to seaside

Pierre Sage is treading on very thin ice at Crystal Palace after another disastrous defensive display allowed Brighton to equal their biggest win against their arch rivals. A poor start to the season has been marked by Palace conceding 17 goals in seven league matches – the worst in the division. The chair, Steve Parish, admitted during the international break that the Frenchman’s position remains on “high alert” and, judging by the angry reaction of some Palace fans to the 5-0 thrashing at the Amex Stadium, Sage could be in big trouble. But there must be some sympathy given the failure to adequately replace the influential Maxence Lacroix in central defence after he was sold to Chelsea. That is believed to have led to disagreements with Parish, who has shown a tendency to act quickly if things aren’t going his way. It could be a nerve-racking few days for Sage before Thursday’s trip to face Besiktas in the Europa League. Ed Aarons

10 Sunderland’s squad buckles under strain

Sunderland’s problems are stacking up. Brian Brobbey’s continued absence with an injury sustained while playing for the Netherlands is beyond Régis Le Bris’ control but defeat at Bournemouth was self-inflicted. The swift journey from the Championship to the Europa League has become a stumble. Kevin Danso’s red card was by no means the only error committed during a performance where cross words were exchanged between befuddled defenders. Granit Xhaka found himself incapable of exerting anything like the influence he showed last season. Instead, Tyler Adams and Lewis Cook dominated midfield. Trips to Poznan, Milan and Anderlecht await for Sunderland but Le Bris’ squad is struggling to straddle two fronts. A horrible performance at the Vitality Stadium came despite five purported first-team players being rested against Torreense. Play like they did on Sunday and a struggle in the bottom half surely awaits. Just about everything that went right last season has taken a turn for the worse. John Brewin

Sports.title: Elite-level incompetence is Manchester United’s problem – not Michael Carrick | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
At the final whistle at Elland Road the TV cameras cut to a lingering shot of the Manchester United chief executive, Omar Berrada, looking down pensively from the stands, deciding, it is to be hoped, on a little clemency, a re-sheathing of the managerial shotgun.

Here we have the man who hired the man. The man who fires the man. The man who also hired or rehired the previous two men he had to fire. Berrada was poached from Manchester City on the basis of his ability to grow commercial revenue (yes, OK, stop laughing), and appears, like everyone else with any actual reach around here, to exist in a strangely consequence-free bubble.

How do you solve what is, on revenue versus results, the worst-run club in world football? By changing the name of the latest patsy on the touchline, of course. For now a hard-fought point is perhaps enough to stave off that pre-programmed emergency response.

Stand down the cowboy cops. Call off the blue and white saloons. Although with a run of Bournemouth, Chelsea, Aston Villa and Liverpool next up in the league it will no doubt soon be time to go out there and arrest Lee Harvey Oswald again. What’s that you say? OK, well, dig him up again. Re-arrest him. Whatever it takes. Someone has to stop these lone gunmen, these managerial magic bullet merchants from derailing the Manchester United supremacy.

This was a dual-track football match between Leeds and Manchester United, on the face of it a good, even game between two teams of well-matched players. A 1-1 draw was fair in the end, although Leeds played well and probably should have won. But of course they won’t be the story.

Instead this game had already been billed as that familiar thing, a referendum on the future of Michael Carrick. A stay of execution for a week or two. Or another livestreamed firing squad for the Super Sunday cameras.

There has been a predictable sense of low comedy about Carrick’s own transformation in the United dugout this season. It was always going to be the case that his widely praised qualities in victory, blazer, T-shirt, jawline, inscrutable sense of calm, would become his fatal flaws in defeat.

Where’s the passion, the whirling arms, the range of tailored collars? At Elland Road Carrick simply looked drained in the second half as United were pegged back and overrun at times, the beard a little more ragged, the hair unkempt but still sweeping, the look of a brave, doomed tugboat captain resigned now to the approaching tsunami wave on the horizon.

A point leaves United 13th in the league and still struggling to reverse a dreadful start to the season. But it was a good game for two people. First for Carrick, who remains a million miles away from creating the problems afflicting this club, even if you accept that his presence as head coach is one of them.

Michael Carrick did not hire Michael Carrick. Getting rid of Michael Carrick is, by definition, not going to solve the problems that led to his appointment. But it might just help to prolong them. Whatever his ultimate ceiling, it is surely worth keeping him just to try, for once, to do something different.

View image in fullscreen The Manchester United director of football, Jason Wilcox (centre), and chief executive officer Omar Berrada (right) watch on at Elland Road. Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA

This was also a good game for Lisandro Martínez, who went off injured at half-time with United 1-0 up, and who was also vindicated in his allegedly controversial (translation: entirely correct) comments on the club hierarchy in midweek.

United’s energetic first-half performance clarified one half of this. The players are committed in support of the manager, at least to the best of their ability. The second half made the other half of the argument, that this remains a mismatched, lopsided, cut-and-paste squad, always likely to be pulled apart by opponents as urgent as this Leeds team, which fully deserves its current seventh place in the table.

The problems are so obvious it is barely worth repeating them. But here goes. The third-richest club in the world played a second half with three of its back four out of position. Harry Maguire, signed under Ole Gunnar Solskjær, remains the best straight defender. But Maguire is also essentially a man-shaped solid wood armoire in a pair of shorts at this stage in his career, always the slowest person on any pitch, which means you will not be able to cover space, play a high line or counterattack without leaving yourself exposed to the counter-counter.

So good luck, guys. And remember Omar, who gave you this whisky bottle and loaded pistol of a squad, will be watching.

This was made painfully clear after half-time as Martínez went off and Noussair Mazraoui came on. Leeds scored an equaliser that felt structurally inevitable. They found space down their right side repeatedly. At times they seemed to be constantly peppering the seats behind the United goal, like a group of kids hammering a ball against a garage door. By the end Leeds had more possession, more shots on target and just looked a happier, better structured entity than the travelling heritage exhibit at the other end.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The key point here is to accept that all of this is entirely logical. This is not a mystery, a haunted house, a place of bad voodoo. Why do we talk about Manchester United so much? For obvious reasons. It’s a massive part of the English football landscape. Mainly, though, because this is a story of mind-bending waste, real-time elite-level incompetence played out on a weekly basis.

Yes, you could sack Michael Carrick. It won’t change much. Let’s destroy Eddie Howe for a bit instead. But the available evidence suggests every single person making executive decisions here is outmatched and outmanoeuvred.

There is a reason Manchester United feels like one of those high street legacy chain shops just before it collapses, piles of Quality Street by the door, a rat in the lingerie department, destined to become a pop-up vape shop run by Albanian money launderers. There’s a reason it feels so badly run. This is because: it is.

View image in fullscreen Lisandro Martínez, who criticised the Manchester United hierarchy in midweek, went off injured at half-time against Leeds. Photograph: Phil Noble/Reuters

We know the Glazer ownership has zero interest in minding the details, that this has been a wonderful acquisition whatever the performance on the pitch, an asset supremely sweated. We know also that Sir Jim Ratcliffe is pub-level incoherent on the details he promised to fix. Remember when he was going to sit down and decide what the “style of football” would be? How’s that working out?

Instead Carrick is left shuffling a first XI acquired by endlessly revolving administrations. Here United had four defenders signed under Erik ten Hag, two Ruben Amorim recruits, two from the mist-shrouded age of Solskjær. No players were recruited under Ralf Rangnick, of course. But then Rangnick wanted to sign Erling Haaland, Luis Díaz, and Julian Álvarez, which all sounds far too sensible.

An organisation can be built with many hands. But not when so many of those hands appear to be so far from best in class it’s hard to work out which class they’re supposed to be attending. John Murtough, the former Manchester United football director, is currently director of global development at Atalanta, who have a 24,000-seat stadium and almost zero global presence. Meanwhile Berrada, the axeman, seems entirely invulnerable from the axe himself, despite the fact his job seems to orbit around resolving the consequences of his own mistakes.

United probably will sack their current manager before the year is out. This is the way this machine has to operate, always looking to buy itself, and those in the executive seats, a little more time on the payroll, an entity that has been hollowed out and allowed to rust, run on buzzwords and brown paper and string. Meanwhile, over to you Michael. We’ll see you next week, and maybe even the week after that, for more of exactly the same.

Sports.title: Another unremarkable win shows Arsenal’s strength is in depth rather than creativity | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
Pass. Pass. Pass. Pass. Sideways. Square. Backwards. Pass. Pass. Recycle. Pass. It wasn’t much of a spectacle. But in the end, for the second week running, thanks in no small part of their bench, Arsenal won. Fireworks in the autumn are for Bonfire Night; titles require relentless accumulation. Since the international break, Arsenal have won three games out of three despite not being in the lead at half-time in any of them.

Hammered at Brighton and having endured a drab first hour at home to Leeds last week, there has been a rare sense, for the first time really since Manchester City dropped points at Everton at the beginning of May, of Arsenal not being quite at their best, needing to reassert their quality. This was not a performance that would terrify any opponent, but it did highlight Arsenal’s consistency and it did demonstrate just how deep their squad now runs.

There were long periods when they were extremely flat. In the first half the ball was moved too slowly, too risk-aversely, for Bukayo Saka and Eberechi Eze consistently to isolate their full-backs. There were very few attempts to play the ball in behind an admittedly well-organised Forest backline. It was all very safe, seemingly predicated more on waiting for Forest to make a mistake than on trying to break the game open with a moment of genius.

View image in fullscreen Mikel Arteta has employed a creativity coach to help the players. Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty Images

The breakthrough, ultimately, was delivered by Noni Madueke who, when he got a run at Daniel Múñoz, took full advantage, albeit with a substantial deflection off the thigh of Jair Cunha. It was Arsenal’s only shot on target – and it wasn’t even on the bit of the target it ended up going in.

Arsenal may have been working with Germán Castaños, a creativity coach who has worked in handball, in designing TV gameshows and with his local council. By challenging the players and presenting them with unusual situations during the week, the theory goes, he can help them to come up with innovative solutions at the weekend. It must take a lot of creativity to make a team as unremarkable as this.

Mikel Arteta is a great believer in the sort of team-building techniques that to outsiders might look like high-performance gimmicks but you dread to think how hard a watch his side would be if their collective imagination wasn’t constantly being stimulated.

Castaños got a boxer to fight two opponents and a Japanese football team to play against a side with 16 men. You wonder how a team might prepare to face an Oliver Glasner side in full stifle mode. Running headfirst into a line of three brick walls, perhaps? Or rather, given how Arsenal played for the first two-thirds of the game, running parallel to three walls looking suspiciously at them? For an hour, this was about patience and risk aversion, the only occasional flurries of something approaching unpredictability coming via Saka on the right.

The England winger perhaps suffers the curse of those who emerge young, that consistent excellence seems somehow not quite enough, a betrayal of that teenage potential. Familiarity in football often breeds, if not quite contempt, then at least a sense that there could be more. He is certainly not playing badly, and he has scored three league goals, but equally, at 25, he is not the exhilarating presence he was at 21.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Noni Madueke provided the breakthrough but Arsenal offered little else in attack. Photograph: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC/Getty Images

Perhaps that is simply how Arteta wants his wide players to play, prioritising consistency and efficiency over the spectacular. Perhaps the fears of those who felt Saka was being played too consistently are being realised and he is experiencing an element of fatigue. Or perhaps this is just what regular mature performances look like in the modern Premier League.

There was one delightful early turn that drew Neco Williams into a trip that earned him a yellow card, which it might have been thought would encourage Saka to run at the wing-back, but the pattern remained the patient sideways passing. Saka, though, did at least offer more than Eze on the other flank, and it was no great surprise when the former Crystal Palace man was withdrawn at half-time for Madueke. Staying wider more consistently, Madueke did perhaps offer a greater threat but he did have more space for him to exploit as an encouraged Forest began to push forward more.

That, in fact, for a long time seemed Arsenal’s best chance, playing with such an absence of threat that it lured Forest into the thought that there was more for them in the game than a worthy clean sheet and a notable point. Leeds, perhaps, might argue they were suckered by something similar last week. As in that game, what turned things Arsenal’s way was a triple substitution midway through the second half.

The arrival of Jurriën Timber, Mikel Merino and Viktor Gyökeres gave Arsenal legs and purpose that Forest could not match. Even as Forest were forced out of their defensive shape to chase an equaliser, the bulk of the game was played in their half. It may not have been especially thrilling, but it was enough and it was, in its own understated way, an expression of Arsenal’s strength. Thrills can come later.

Sports.title: Enzo Maresca confirms huge Antoine Semenyo injury blow and gives Erling Haaland update
Sports.content:
Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca revealed Antoine Semenyo faces up to eight weeks on the sidelines with a knee injury.

Semenyo sustained the injury in the later stages of City's 3-2 win over Ipswich Town on Saturday.

3 Semenyo has two goals and three assists for City this season Credit: Getty

Enzo Maresca gives update on Antoine Semenyo's knee injury

“In the first moment we expected an even worse injury so we were more worried," Maresca said.

“After yesterday’s [Sunday] scan we feel much better because it’s not so big like we expected.

“It could be eight weeks. Now in this moment the most important thing for him is his recovery.

"When he is back around December it will be like a new player in terms of energy.”

In brighter news, Maresca confirmed superstar striker Erling Haaland would be available for City's Champions League clash against AEK Athens on Tuesday.

Haaland, who scored twice against Ipswich, was seen limping off the field at full-time.

Is Erling Haaland available to play against AEK Athens?

"He can be available," Maresca said.

"We'll see. We have a session now and we have some doubts after Saturday's game.

"He was quite good yesterday. Better. So we'll see today.

"Replacing Erling is always difficult. We have some different options and we'll see tomorrow.

3 Haaland's potential absence against AEK leaves a serious hole in City's starting lineup Credit: Getty

“It depends a little bit on the gameplan and also there is a chance he can be available tomorrow.”

Erling Haaland's relentless workload

The timing of Semenyo's injury is particularly unfortunate given Maresca had identified him as a possible option to give Haaland a breather.

Haaland has started all but one of City's 11 fixtures in all competitions this term.

The superstar striker's high volume of minutes comes after he played a key role in helping Norway reach the quarter-finals of the World Cup, where they were eliminated by England.

“First of all, to lose Antoine or any player for us is not good,” Maresca added.

“In terms of Erling, we said we can use Antoine as a nine but we have different players that we are going to try to find a new solution. We will see.

3 Maresca is hoping City can bounce back from a 4-2 loss against PSG last Wednesday Credit: AFP

“At the moment it’s Erling. Why do we need to think about a different nine when Erling is there? If something happens and we need a different plan or different nine, we will see.”

City's Champions League clash against AEK takes place at the Etihad Stadium and gets underway at 8pm.

Sports.title: Man United warned they face major fight for top target if Michael Carrick is sacked
Sports.content:
Man United warned they face major fight for top target if Michael Carrick is sacked

Manchester United might have to battle against Juventus to appoint Antonio Conte should they sack Michael Carrick.

That's the impression of Italian football journalist Daniele Fisichella as Carrick remains up against at in the Old Trafford gig.

3 Carrick is facing the sack at United just five months after taking the job full-time as United maintained their winless run against Leeds Credit: Getty

United drew 1-1 away to rivals Leeds United on Sunday and confirmed their worst start to a season since the 1986/87 campaign.

They have one win from seven Premier League matches, are 13th on just seven points and closer to relegation than the top four.

Carrick landed the permanent head coach job in the summer after he secured Champions League qualification by finishing third during the second half of last season.

But with no victories in their last six across all competitions, the ex-midfielder faces increased pressure to generate some winning form.

talkSPORT understands Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler is an option to potentially succeed Carrick, whilst the former Chelsea and Tottenham manager Conte would be prepared to take the job.

However, Fisichella has warned that the Italian's local club Juventus may stand in United's way if they decide to dismiss Luciano Spalletti.

United vs Juve for Conte

"I think if Manchester United comes knocking, Conte would feel ready to take on the challenge," he said on Trans Europe Express. "Although, I do feel that his favourite solution would still be Juventus.

"Following tonight's result (3-0 defeat against Lazio), maybe he's a step closer to going back to Turin, or staying in Turin because that's where he lives and likes to live.

"But, after leaving Spurs a couple of years ago, the family circumstances, his personal circumstances have changed - his family would be more ready for him to move back to England again.

"He really likes to stay close to his family, but now his daughter has grown and going to university, there is not such a need for him to stay in Italy.

3 Conte would be willing to take the reins at United, but his former club Juventus could stand in their way Credit: Getty

"He's got very strong family ties but he also feels that, by going back to England, it's the place where he would be more likely to win a Champions League anytime soon, rather than in Italy.

"That's what he really needs to do to complete his career. So, if Manchester United come asking, I think he would feel ready to do that, and I think it would be a brilliant appointment for United.

"A short-term one, no doubt about it, but a quick fix, a good fix for a team that's underperforming."

Conte success at Juventus and beyond

A former midfielder, Conte made over 400 appearances for Juventus, won five Serie A titles and the 1995/96 Champions League.

He remained in Italy to begin his coaching career and returned to The Old Lady in 2011 for a spell as their head coach, during which he won three consecutive Serie A honours until 2014.

Conte also delivered two Supercoppa Italiana triumphs before leaving to take charge of the Italian national team.

3 Conte has won six top flight league titles during his managerial career, three of which have come at Juventus Credit: AFP

An appointment at Chelsea followed in 2016 and he won the Premier League in the first of two seasons at the club, and then Inter Milan brought him back to Italy.

Yet another Serie A title was lifted at San Siro, although Conte then had a difficult one-and-a-half year stint at Spurs.

Napoli are the 57-year-old's most recent club, where he won a tenth Serie A title of his playing and managerial career.

Sports.title: Spurs have unmatched record in Premier League and EFL – but are they ‘playing the best football?’
Sports.content:
Spurs have unmatched record in Premier League and EFL – but are they ‘playing the best football?’

If you peek at every table from the Premier League down to the National League, one team stands out for all the wrong reasons.

That team would be Tottenham Hotspur.

3 Spurs' £300m summer spending spree is yet to translate into any Premier League joy Credit: PA

Remarkably, Spurs are the only club across the top five divisions yet to win a league fixture this season.

Yep, Roberto De Zerbi's side is the lone soldier among those 116 clubs yet to enjoy the sweet, sweet taste of three points.

Spurs have proved they are capable of winning matches this season, albeit their sole victory came against Championship outfit Charlton Athletic in the second round of the EFL Cup.

Brutal numbers behind Tottenham's woes this season

But outside of that fixture, their form this term makes for grim reading.

Spurs' record reads three draws and three defeats from their first six league games.

It could have looked even worse if not for Dominic Solanke rescuing a 1-1 draw in the 92nd minute against Manchester United.

In that run, De Zerbi's side have scored three goals and conceded nine.

Even then, Spurs' first league goal of the campaign didn't arrive until the 86th minute of their match against Aston Villa.

For those playing at home, the defeat to Villa was Spurs' fifth league game of the season, meaning they'd gone four games without scoring.

Now that Spurs know where the back of the net is, they need to prove they can win, too.

3 De Zerbi has won just four games from 15 since his appointment last season Credit: Getty

The next opportunity to pick up their first three points of the season comes on Monday at home against Coventry City.

Tottenham's bleak record at home since 2024/25 season

Home games have not exactly provided many happy memories for Spurs fans from the 2024/25 season onwards.

In that period, Spurs have won nine, drawn 10 and lost 22 of their 41 league fixtures at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

Unsurprisingly, the 22 home defeats is the most among the ever-present Premier League teams since the start of the 2024/25 campaign.

But there's no time like the present for Spurs to change the narrative regarding their home woes.

That won't be an easy feat, though, as Coventry enter the contest on the back of a 4-1 win over Newcastle.

3 Monday's contest is the first time Coventry and Spurs have met in league competition since March 2001

Encouraging signs for Spurs?

One customer who will nervously watch Monday's game is ex-Spurs midfielder Jamie O'Hara.

And, in a massive boost for talkSPORT fans - perhaps less so for O'Hara - the Sports Bar co-host's reactions to the match will be available for all to see on a special live watchalong, beginning at 8pm, to help launch the new Sports Bar: Lock In channel on YouTube.

As ever, O'Hara will be joined by fellow Sports Bar co-host Jason Cundy, who will no doubt have the iconic Ange Postecoglou mask ready to go should Spurs fail to beat Frank Lampard's outfit.

Cundy will certainly have plenty to say about Spurs if their winless run continues, especially since O'Hara made a rather staggering proclamation on the Sports Bar last week.

"I think we're actually playing the best football in the Premier League, I do," O'Hara said.

"We just haven't got the wins, we haven't got the results. I'm being serious.

"The problem we've got is we concede goals. Spurs aren't taking our chances."

Those may be encouraging signs, but time is of the essence for those signs to morph into something more tangible.

Sports.title: How Jadon Sancho could line up at surprise La Liga side alongside two Real Madrid icons
Sports.content:
How Jadon Sancho could line up at surprise La Liga side alongside two Real Madrid icons

Getafe president Ángel Torres has confirmed his ambitious plot to rescue his side from relegation with heavyweight reinforcements.

'Azulones' qualified for the UEFA Conference League after finishing seventh last season but now sit just one point above the drop zone.

5 Getafe has been remarkably ambitious in recent weeks and have just unveiled a former Madrid captain Credit: Getty

José Bordalás' men only scored 32 goals in 38 La Liga fixtures in 2025/26 (only bottom club Real Oviedo managed less in total).

That lack of firepower has taken its toll this campaign, with Getafe now the lowest scorers in the entire division with just four goals.

The club have won just two out of their opening eight games in La Liga and are only one point above Elche in the relegation zone.

Understandably, Getafe are now looking to strengthen in the free agent market - with Jadon Sancho among their targets.

Sancho interest from Getafe

The former England winger is still without a club after leaving Manchester United at the end of June.

The 26-year-old won the Europa League while on loan at Aston Villa last season but scored once in 39 appearances across all competitions.

Asked about reports that Getafe are interested in Sancho, club president Torres told Cadena Cope radio on Thursday: "That's absolutely true; I've been working on this for four months.

"He's now a free agent. We've made him a final offer."

"He's 26 years old; he's very good, so this [signing] is a bit trickier," Torres added on Sancho.

5 Sancho won the Europa League on loan at Villa last season Credit: Getty

"He's previously played for Manchester [United] and Aston Villa, so it's not as if he's coming from anywhere. I know he's got offers from Qatar and from a number of other places.

"We need to be patient, not put pressure on him, and let him decide for himself."

It comes after Getafe signed six-time Champions League winner Dani Carvajal following his Real Madrid release earlier this month.

The defender, who has penned a deal until the end of the season, would likely line-up directly behind Sancho on his new team's right side.

The latter is capable of playing on either flank, but left-winger Ramon Terrats has been among Getafe's rare shining lights this year.

The Spaniard has scored one of the club's only four league goals and tops the charts for shots per 90 (with 2.9 per game).

5 Carvajal was a key component of Real Madrid's Champions League three-peat Credit: Getty

Sancho and Terrats would then help support Enes Unal as part of Getafe's new-look attack.

Unal, who rejoined the Spanish outfit from Bournemouth in August, has scored once in seven games but has been nursing a muscle injury.

Carvajal, meanwhile, may be reunited with his ex-Real Madrid teammate Sergio Ramos, who has also been linked with Getafe.

The 40-year-old, who was last on the books at Mexican side Monterrey, has had his brother and agent Rene speak to Torres.

5 Ramos could be heading back to Madrid...but at Getafe Credit: Getty - Contributor

“We have been pursuing this for some time, but it was not the priority. The priority was to get wingers,” Getafe's president explained via Marca.

Should Ramos arrive at Getafe, he would likely be deployed as the central centre-back in the club's five-at-the-back system due to his age, with captain Djené Dakonam in between him and Carvajal.

Sports.title: Arsenal held secret talks with Mauricio Pochettino as surprise shortlist before hiring Mikel Arteta revealed
Sports.content:
Arsenal held secret talks with Mauricio Pochettino as surprise shortlist before hiring Mikel Arteta revealed

In a parallel universe, it is not Mikel Arteta in charge of Arsenal.

Instead, it's Mauricio Pochettino.

2 Arteta has brought success back to Arsenal, but things could have been very different in 2019 Credit: Getty

As part of a new book charting Arsenal's journey to becoming Premier League champions for the first time in 22 years, the Telegraph's Sam Dean revealed Pochettino was among several candidates who the Gunners spoke with following Unai Emery's sacking in November 2019.



How close did Mauricio Pochettino come to joining Arsenal?

Pochettino was, at the time, available as he'd been axed by Tottenham only 10 days before Emery's departure.

According to Dean, Arsenal held 'serious conversations' with Pochettino, who 'showed willingness to engage' with the Gunners.

Had such an appointment transpired, it would have taken the iconic north London rivalry to a different stratosphere.

No player has moved from Arsenal to Spurs or vice-versa since William Gallas in 2010.



Before Gallas, the last high-profile move involving the two clubs was Sol Campbell, who left Tottenham to join Arsenal in 2001.

The scarcity of moves between Arsenal and Spurs in the following years underlines the deep roots of the rivalry, which is why Pochettino being appointed the new Gunners boss would have sent shockwaves through football.



Pochettino was far from the only intriguing name on Arsenal's shortlist following Emery's departure.

Who else was on Arsenal's list to replace Unai Emery?

It is claimed Gunners great Patrick Vieira had admirers at the Emirates thanks to his work at Ligue 1 side Nice.



Roberto Martinez, who was in charge of Belgium at the time, was another and even 'advanced a long way in the process'.

2 Pochettino got Spurs to a Champions League final and EFL Cup final Credit: Getty

Also on the list was ex-Nottingham Forest and Wolves boss Vitor Pereira.

Other managers eyed by the Gunners included Carlo Ancelotti, Julian Nagelsmann and Massimiliano Allegri.



Despite the vast managerial backgrounds of all the candidates, especially the trophy-laden CVs of Ancelotti and Allegri, then-Arsenal technical director Edu boldly handed the reins to Arteta.

The Spaniard had only worked as an assistant to Pep Guardiola at Manchester City prior to his appointment, making it a risky roll of the dice from Arsenal.

Luckily for the Gunners, the decision has proved to be a masterstroke.

Arteta won the FA Cup in his first season at the helm and helped the Gunners end their 22-year wait for a Premier League title last season, having finished runners-up in the three campaigns prior.



And the Spaniard won't be leaving the Emirates any time soon having inked a bumper new deal to remain as Arsenal boss until 2030.

Sports.title: Martin Keown reveals sources have told him when to expert Man City punishment – ‘won’t be as bad as we think’
Sports.content:
Martin Keown reveals sources have told him when to expert Man City punishment – ‘won’t be as bad as we think’

Manchester City will learn the outcome of their appeal in around six weeks' time.

That's according to Martin Keown, although his talkSPORT colleague Simon Jordan has suggested that the process will take even longer.

3 City have been found guilty on financial charges, but have expressed their innocence and launched an appeal Credit: Getty

On September 29, it was announced that City were found guilty on all charges relating to Premier League financial rule breaches from 2009 to 2018.

The club used 'sham' contracts to artificially inflate their revenue by more than £900million, broke spending limits and did not show full cooperation during the investigation.

City launched an appeal on October 2, and claim they are backed by a 'comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence'.

As per new Premier League rules, the appeal hearing must take place within 12 weeks of it being made, last just five days and then reveal a decision within 30 days of it ending.

David Kogan, the head of the Independent Football Regulator, says an outcome is expected in the early part of 2027.

However, Arsenal legend Keown told White and Jordan on talkSPORT that he has heard speculation of the decision being revealed before the end of 2026.

When could City learn appeal outcome?

"They're resolute, they believe that they're right, and their owners are giving them that firm message, 'irrefutable evidence' will be revealed, so they're holding onto that," he said on the City fans.

"There is a feeling... I'm hearing rumours that this will all be over in a number of weeks."

Jordan dismissed this idea, but Keown responded: "I'm just telling you what I'm hearing. In six weeks or so, we'll see what's going to happen, and it won't be nearly as bad as we think it might be.

"Maybe they get off with huge fines and we return to the football pitch again."

3 Keown has heard rumours that the outcome of City's appeal and their sanctions could come within the next six weeks Credit: PA

As Keown mentioned, hefty fines are among possible sanctions for City if their appeal fails, as well as points deductions, stripped titles and relegation.

Premier League clubs are understood to want the case to be resolved this season, inclusive of appeals, with City top of the table thanks to seven wins from seven matches.

But former Crystal Palace owner Jordan believes that the appeal process will not follow its new rules and take longer than it should do.

Hold owners more to account rather than blindly following them?

"Well, not until the final nail has been whacked in their disingenuous coffin, no," he said on whether City fans should hold the owners more to account. "They are convincing those that want to be convinced that there is a conspiracy against them....

"They're playing it through the press, they've done a lot of stuff in the media this weekend with The Telegraph, they will convince people that they've been poorly treated, that a panel of independent experts are rather simple and disingenuous, and partisan.

3 Jordan believes that City will challenge the new rules on appeals and the hearing will last longer than expected Credit: Getty

"That's what they're being able to convince those that are willing to listen to it. The interesting thing is, how will they be able to circumvent it? I don't know, because they've got witnesses that have given evidence, basically said that they're liars, that they had an intention of lying, and went into independent commissions and lied.

"They're going to play this game, they're probably going to win their little arguments about how long the appeal should take, because the Premier League probably won't have the courage to turn around and say, 'We've changed the appeal process, we want this to be a five-day hearing'.

"Man City will argue that they shouldn't have that rule, because the rule wasn't in place when the charges were originally brought, and the Premier League will probably cower away from it thinking, 'We don't want to give them an opportunity to say they weren't fairly treated, so we'll probably go back to the longer appeal process'.

"None of this, of course, is in the area of irrefutable evidence and integrity to clear up the position as quickly as possible. What we're going to see is a litany of arguments being run by very sophisticated lawyers that could argue with anything."

Sports.title: Man City to face HUGE points deduction which will guarantee relegation - and more could come next season - but they won't be sent down to League Two, insiders tell OLIVER HOLT
Sports.content:
Man City to face HUGE points deduction which will guarantee relegation - and more could come next season - but they won't be sent down to League Two, insiders tell OLIVER HOLT

Oliver Holt Chief Sports Writer

Several times over the weekend, the same refrain escaped from the lips of various football broadcasters and analysts, who suggested that the struggle for the Premier League title this season has already become a ‘two-horse race’.

The comfort of denial, especially in a multi-billion-pound industry, is a powerful coping mechanism.

Maybe those broadcasters were talking about Arsenal and Brighton as the leading contenders for honours and, if that is the case, I apologise for my mistaken assumptions. Because if there is going to be a two-horse race for the title, neither of those horses should be carrying the colours of Manchester City.

City have indeed started the season in stunning form. Even by their own exalted recent standards, winning their opening seven league games, with Pep Guardiola gone and a new manager in Enzo Maresca at the helm, is an impressive feat. But it does not remove the shadow that hangs over the club. If anything, it lengthens it.

Perhaps it has been obscured by the wall of whataboutery, obfuscation and risible petro-state propaganda about a ‘red cartel’, but late last month, City were found guilty by an independent commission of the vast majority of 115 charges of financial wrongdoing levelled against them by the Premier League.

In any vaguely functional sports league, that would remove City from consideration for challenging for the title this season. Their punishment should have been handed down already and, given the scale of their cheating, that punishment would inevitably have taken them out of the race for the title.

In any vaguely functional sports league, the guilty verdicts against Manchester City would remove them from consideration for challenging for this season's Premier League title

Their punishment should have been handed down already and, given the scale of their cheating, that punishment would inevitably have taken them out of the race for the title

The timeline of the case against City has been so tortuous and protracted that there is already uncertainty and pessimism about quite how long the rest of football will have to wait for the decision about what sanctions City will face and how long it will take to reach a judgment on the appeal they have launched.

It is unlikely, sources close to the process have told me, that City will face a doomsday scenario of being expelled from the Premier League and forced to start again in League Two at the beginning of next season.

Expulsion would plunge both the Premier League and the EFL into an unprecedented kind of chaos. It would be self-defeating.

It is thought that the Premier League are pressing for City’s punishment to be announced before the result of their appeal, which is unlikely to be decided before the end of January. Soundings from insiders suggest the most likely punishment is a swingeing points deduction which will ensure City’s relegation to the Championship, plus a huge fine.

It is also possible that the punishment would include a further points deduction that would effectively confine City to the Championship for at least one more season. The EFL would not be obliged to accept that sanction for one of their clubs but it is probable that they would.

From there, City should be allowed to rebuild. The intransigence and arrogance of City’s owners have hardened opinion against them but they are already facing the kind of ignominy that will stain them for many years to come.

It is time for those imposing the punishment to try to find a solution that represents middle ground.

There is very little point in pursuing a Treaty of Versailles-type punishment. The desire to humiliate the defeated might satisfy a base instinct but it does very little for the future well-being of the body politic. City must be punished, of course, but they must also be given a pathway towards rehabilitation.

Soundings from insiders suggest the most likely punishment is a swingeing points deduction which will ensure City’s relegation to the Championship, plus a huge fine

Yes, there is a blood-lust among some for City to be cast into the outer reaches of the football pyramid, but if that were done mid-season it would effectively void this campaign

Yes, there is a blood lust among some for City to be cast into the outer reaches of the football pyramid – Steven Gerrard, the former Liverpool captain, was candid in his hope that City be made to ‘suffer’ for what they have taken away from other teams and their supporters – but if that were done mid-season, it would effectively void this campaign.

If City were expelled from the Premier League, where would they play for the rest of the season? Would the club just be put into hibernation for six months? All their results preceding their expulsion would have to be made null and void. It would satisfy a desire for vengeance but at the cost of the wider health of the league.

It would also punish City’s supporters a disproportionate amount. This should not be about punishing City’s fans. It is about punishing the club’s ownership, which, the independent commission decided, was the author of the sustained period of cheating that gave City an unfair advantage over its rivals.

It is in that realm – and not in relegation to the Championship – that the most serious threat to the future of the club exists. Because, if City’s appeal fails, it is hard to see how a regime found guilty of such egregious deception could possibly be allowed to remain as custodians of the club.

If they did remain, it would fatally undermine the authority and purpose of the Independent Football Regulator. There is already some scepticism about quite how much power the regulator really wields.

If Sheikh Mansour and his cronies were allowed to continue, the credibility of its chairman, David Kogan, would be shot to pieces.

But then how do City survive without the Abu Dhabi United Group? How do they survive without the hundreds of millions in revenue that City now insist came directly from the Abu Dhabi government? Would another buyer step forward to rescue a club whose image has been so badly tainted?

The only clear answer to that is that the longer it takes to punish City, and the longer it takes for the result of their appeal to be decided, the more damage it does to a league paralysed by uncertainty and denial.

Arsenal should take criticism as a compliment

No team plays well every week and on Sunday, Arsenal did what they had to do and got out of Nottingham with the three points they came for

Arsenal did not play well against Nottingham Forest on Sunday afternoon. But they won the game at the City Ground 1-0 and moved back to within three points of Manchester City at the head of the table. Given the guilty verdicts returned against City recently, that effectively puts Arsenal top.

So I don’t agree with the feast of hand-wringing and the wail of lamentations about the quality of their football. No team plays well every week and at Forest, Arsenal did what they had to do and got out of there with the three points they came for. That is sometimes what the best teams do.

I saw them against Lille in the Champions League at the Emirates last week and some of the football they played in the second half of their 3-0 victory made the heart sing.

We grow bored quickly with a team that wins and wins: Arsenal should take the criticism coming their way as a compliment.

Sports.title: Revealed: How Geri Halliwell 'went silent and told husband Christian Horner "just tell your truth"' when his sex texts scandal story broke - before predicting his £67m Red Bull sacking
Sports.content:
Revealed: How Geri Halliwell 'went silent and told husband Christian Horner "just tell your truth"' when his sex texts scandal story broke - before predicting his £67m Red Bull sacking

Christian Horner has detailed the support he received from his wife Geri Halliwell following the ‘sex texts’ scandal that led to his departure from the Red Bull F1 team.

The 52-year-old was sacked as chief executive and team principal in July 2025 after 20 years following an internal power struggle and a decline in form.

Horner received a £67million severance payment, as Daily Mail Sport reported earlier this month, with his exit coming a year after he was cleared of misconduct over a texting scandal with a female employee.

He has always denied the claims and was twice cleared of any wrongdoing in internal investigations at Red Bull.

A tranche of supposedly intimate text exchanges between the pair – including messages and photographs – were made public in an explosive email sent to F1 figures before the 2024 Bahrain Grand Prix.

Horner’s sacking was unrelated to the scandal but in his upcoming autobiography Drive, he has revealed how his wife reacted when news of the scandal broke – and predicted his sacking.

The former Red Bull boss wrote: 'What was going on? The lawyer, presumably aware that a wrecking ball was being aimed at my life, explained the situation as my sense of bewilderment rose.

Christian Horner has opened up on wife Geri Halliwell's support during his 'sex texts' scandal

Horner was embroiled in the saga in 2024, but he was cleared of any impropriety in two internal investigations and has always denied the claims

'Geri knew by my face that something was very wrong. She fell silent as she listened. We both understood the implications immediately. She looked at me: "Just tell your truth", she said.

'‘That’s all I can do’, I replied. She reassured me that everything would be all right. Her resilience was remarkable.'

Horner continued: 'Our lives had been turned upside down, yet she found the strength and conviction to support me through an immensely difficult period, one that was undoubtedly challenging for her as well.

'Her belief in me gave me the determination to move forward. At a time when my confidence was being tested, Geri provided the perspective and stability that I needed most.

'Without her support, I’m not sure I could have navigated those months in the same way.'

Horner's time at Red Bull saw the team win six constructors' championships, while drivers Sebastian Vettel and Max Verstappen both won four titles in a row.

Despite that success, things became more difficult after the death of Red Bull founder Dietrich Mateschitz in 2022.

The Austrian had always been a big supporter of Horner, but the 52-year-old then appeared to be regularly undermined by Helmut Marko, a key consultant for Red Bull, and Jos Verstappen, father of Max, as the team was plunged into a power struggle, with Horner's fate eventually sealed in July 2025.

And, in an interview with BBC Radio 5 Live, Horner opened up on his wife's backing at that time and how she 'called' his sacking.

Horner also revealed that his wife could sense that his sacking was coming in July 2025

'Well she's sensitive to all of these things,' he said. 'You know, a woman's intuition and I think your partner perhaps always has a bit more subjectiveness, being in it but slightly removed.

'And she could see the dynamics were changing and she could see that things were different for me.

'And so yeah, she called it. Obviously it (the sacking) felt pretty brutal at the time but life goes on.'

Sports.title: Former England footballer Steven Caulker pleads for work on LinkedIn as he says he's now stuck unemployed and 'can't even get an interview'
Sports.content:
Former England footballer Steven Caulker pleads for work on LinkedIn as he says he's now stuck unemployed and 'can't even get an interview'

Former England defender Steven Caulker has taken to social media to share his struggles with unemployment.

Caulker, who made one cap for England in 2012, retired as a footballer last year and has since pursued a career in coaching.

The former Tottenham and QPR man spent eight months as Turkish club Konyaspor Kulubu Dernegi's assistant manager until his departure in September, but now he is struggling in his search for a new opportunity.

'Being unemployed is stressful,' Caulker wrote on social media platform LinkedIn. 'I've been here many times before, I'm used to the rollercoaster of emotions, but it doesn't make it easier.

'Applying for jobs for which I have all the qualifications yet am unable to get even an interview hurts, but that does not mean I should panic.'

Caulker, 34, vowed to stay positive through the challenging period, highlighting the importance of routine as he shared a photo of himself out on a sweat-inducing run.

Stephen Caulker has taken to social media to share his struggles with unemployment

The unemployed former England defender admitted it 'hurts' not being able to get an interview

'Walt Disney was rejected over 300 times; rejection is part of most people's stories. The bit I find difficult is turning down the jobs that do come my way which are not aligned with my goals,' he continued.

'Staying calm and composed during these times is important, and adding some kind of structure to my day certainly helps. I've just finished my morning run and feeling pretty good after releasing some endorphins. Have a great Sunday!'

As shown in the experience section of Caulker's LinkedIn page, he was a player-manager for Malaga City Academy in 2024 and also took on the role of assistant manager at Icelandic outfit Stjarnan between July and November 2025.

Alongside his experience in the dugout, Caulker was a founder at Behind the White Lines until October 2025 and is currently a founder at his own wellbeing consultancy.

Caulker officially announced his retirement as a player in December 2025, calling an end to his storied 16-year career.

During his playing days, the centre-half starred for a remarkable 17 different clubs including Spurs, Swansea, Cardiff, Southampton, Liverpool, QPR and Turkish giants Fenerbahce.

The crowning moment of Caulker's career came in 2012, when he scored on his England debut against Sweden under Roy Hodgson.

Despite the goal-scoring debut, Caulker never represented England again at senior level and instead carved out a second international career with Sierra Leone, chalking up 18 caps until his retirement in 2024.

Sports.title: England star Marc Guehi suggests taking the knee may have 'lost its meaning' and questions its significance as he leads Premier League stars in rejecting the anti-racism gesture
Sports.content:
England star Marc Guehi suggests taking the knee may have 'lost its meaning' and questions its significance as he leads Premier League stars in rejecting the anti-racism gesture

Manchester City and England defender Marc Guehi has suggested that taking the knee as an anti-racism gesture may have lost its meaning after choosing to remain standing at kick-off on Saturday.

Premier League players were invited to take the knee before matches this weekend as part of the top flight's 'No Room for Racism' campaign, which aims to combat discrimination.

Guehi was one of six players to stay on his feet across the weekend, with Dominic Calvert-Lewin, Ainsley Maitland-Niles, Rayan, Tyler Adams and Issa Diop also doing the same.

Asked why he chose not to take the knee on the eve of Manchester City's Champions League clash with AEK Athens, Guehi said: 'I'm not sure to be honest. The campaign's still there, which is great.

'The message is still there, which is great. Whether more can be done? More can always be done. So I think we have to see how we can move the campaign along.

'I don't think it's necessarily a football issue, it's a wider societal issue and football is just that beacon of, I guess, hope, to try to get the message out. But whether more can be done - we'll try, hopefully with the PFA, with the league, we'll see what can be done.'

Marc Guehi fears that taking the knee as an anti-racism gesture may have lost its meaning

Guehi did not perform the gesture while his Man City team-mates took the knee on Saturday

Guehi was then asked if he believes the gesture has lost its meaning.

'Maybe. I haven't been taking the knee for a while now,' he admitted. 'I'd always clap just because of what that actually signifies but in terms of if something can be done, hopefully.

'I hope we can do a bit more but we'll just see. Hopefully the message is getting out there which is the most important thing.'

Leeds United manager Daniel Farke has also explained why his striker Calvert-Lewin chose not to take the knee ahead of Sunday's 1-1 draw with Manchester United.

'Dom is more or less like, "No, I don't go down. I show my respect by standing up." Every individual is different and shows respect for this campaign in a different way,' he said, defending the forward after his goal earned Leeds a 1-1 draw at Elland Road.

'It's definitely a good campaign and a good topic that football and sports, in general, support situations like this because a dressing room is a perfect example of how we should all live together.

'Different passports, different languages, different religions, but they are all together as human beings and friends who work together toward one target. This is how the world should be.'

Parts of Elland Road loudly booed as players took the knee ahead of Leeds' clash with Manchester United, amid fears the gesture has lost its impact since its introduction during the Covid-19 pandemic.

It is not the first time players have refused to take the knee. Last year Calvert-Lewin did so in Burnley's fixture with Leeds, while Crysencio Summerville has been known to take the same action.

Former Premier League star Wilfried Zaha previously explained why he objected to the gesture in 2021, saying: 'I feel like taking the knee is degrading, because growing up my parents just let me know that I should be proud to be black no matter what and I feel like we should just stand tall.'

When Marcos Alonso was at Chelsea, he opted to point to the Premier League's 'No Room For Racism' badge on his arm rather than join his fellow players.

Two Bournemouth players stood while their team-mates took the knee against Sunderland

Ahead of the 2021-22 season, Luton indicated that they would not be taking the knee and instead all stood in the centre circle.

At that stage, players were still taking the knee ahead of every game – but that policy was stopped in August 2022. Instead, a decision was made to limit the gesture to match rounds falling during the No Room For Racism initiative.

It was agreed ahead of the season among Premier League captains that they would continue to perform the gesture twice per season.

Players and staff have the opportunity to perform the pre-match gesture for the next two gameweeks in October, with the Premier League reiterating 'the commitment to tackling discrimination and highlight the importance of diversity in football'.

The move started in the UK in 2020 following the death of George Floyd in US police custody, which sparked the Black Lives Matter movement.

Sports.title: Reclusive poppy protest footballer James McClean says he 'supports the IRA' - and their 'bloodshed' - as he reveals he mutes the TV whenever 'God Save The King' is played
Sports.content:
Reclusive poppy protest footballer James McClean says he 'supports the IRA' - and their 'bloodshed' - as he reveals he mutes the TV whenever 'God Save The King' is played

Controversial footballer James McClean has opened up on his refusal to wear the poppy and revealed what it was like growing up in a 'staunch Republican community' in Northern Ireland.

McClean, 37, won 103 caps for Republic of Ireland between 2012 and 2023 and represented the likes of Stoke, Sunderland, West Brom and Wigan in England, yet he has rarely been far from the news.

That stems from his refusal to wear the poppy on his shirt on Remembrance weekend, while he often stands away from team-mates during pre-match commemorations.

McClean has regularly defended his stance, saying it is because the poppy symbol honours all British military personnel, including soldiers who operated in Northern Ireland during the Troubles, insisting he would have no problem if it just represented those who died in World War One and Two.

The winger grew up on the Creggan estate in Londonderry, an area that was directly affected by the Bloody Sunday massacre in 1972 when British soldiers shot 26 unarmed civilians during a protest march, with 14 killed.

McClean was born in 1989, but in an interview with the Irish Independent, he reflected on his childhood and 'growing up listening to all the old war stories from men who had been there and done it'.

James McClean has opened up on his refusal to wear the poppy and revealed what it was like growing up in a 'staunch Republican community'

McClean pictured in action for West Brom against Huddersfield in 2017 not wearing the poppy

He said: 'Walk around and you’ll see it on every second wall: "Join the IRA... Free Prisoners of War... RUC f***ing out". So you’re surrounded by it.

'And people say, "he won’t wear the poppy because of Bloody Sunday, but he didn’t have Bloody Sunday". No, I didn’t. And I didn’t have the Troubles either, but I grew up in the aftermath and the pain was still there.'

Creggan was a Republican stronghold with strong support for the IRA, and McClean revealed he actually grew up in the house where 15-year-old Daniel Hegarty, who was killed during a British army operation in 1972, used to live.

Meanwhile, a quote in the 37-year-old's upcoming biography The Walls also talked about the IRA.

It reads: 'I’m not claiming that every action was justified. Obviously, I don’t support anyone innocent being killed. But I am saying that I supported the original end goal, even if that involved bloodshed '

After being asked about those comments in this interview, McClean added: 'When you grow up listening to the stories there’s a part of you thinking: "These are heroes. I wish I was part of that or born a decade earlier". I’d be a hypocrite if I sat here and said I didn’t support their cause.

'Don’t get me wrong; I don’t believe that anybody innocent deserved to be killed, right? Unfortunately, it was a dirty war, and there were a lot of casualties on both sides.'

McClean was then pressed on the particular example of Jean McConville, a 38-year-old widowed mother of ten who was horrifically abducted, murdered and secretly buried by the IRA after they wrongly believed her to be an informant for the British army.

McClean also revealed that he mutes the TV when he hears God Save the King being played

'Do I agree with that? Absolutely not,' he replied. 'I support the IRA’s cause. Do I support what happened to people like Jean McConville? No, because not everything the IRA did was justifiable, even in terms of... like, I had a very strong relationship with Martin McGuinness. Do I believe that him meeting the Queen was right? Absolutely not.'

On his opposition to the British army and government's historical actions, McClean spoke about the 'backlash' when he refused to look at the flag when God Save the Queen was played during a pre-season friendly in the US while he played for West Brom.

He added: 'When I’m watching England matches, or the FA Cup final, I’ll mute the TV when the national anthem comes on. And I’m not the only one - you can ask anyone in Derry and they’ll say the same.'

Sports.title: 'Completely unaware Paris is in ruins': England keeper Jordan Pickford and wife Megan's romantic 24-hour private jet break is derailed by rioting - and they had no idea it was happening!
Sports.content:
'Completely unaware Paris is in ruins': England keeper Jordan Pickford and wife Megan's romantic 24-hour private jet break is derailed by rioting - and they had no idea it was happening!

Jordan Pickford and his partner Megan saw a romantic trip to Paris slightly disrupted by the ongoing riots in the French capital.

A weekend of widespread violence took place in the city after an initial peaceful protest on Saturday against rising living costs and poor public services turned nasty.

Reports suggested around 1,500 shops and businesses were looted and destroyed as riot police were called in, with tear gas and water cannons used on crowds.

Officials claimed around 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday alone.

In a TikTok post titled '24 hours in Paris with a twist', Megan documented her trip with Jordan to see legendary singer Celine Dion in concert.

Showing the couple travelling on a private jet, the first caption of the video said: 'Come to Paris with me and my husband. Completely unaware the capital was in ruins.'

Jordan Pickford and his partner Megan embarked on a romantic trip to Paris at the weekend

Megan shared several insights from their trip as they travelled to see Celine Dion in concert

But their trip to the French capital to see the Canadian singer coincided with the ongoing riots

Over the clip, the couple looked loved up as they visited various famous venues as Megan highlighted her 'love' of the city.

After making their way to the concert, Megan shared a couple of snippets of Dion singing.

She said she was left in 'tears' given how impressive the Canadian performer was, before she provided the first insight of the troubles.

At the end of Dion's performance, she said: 'Then when our driver picked us up he advised us to go straight to the hotel.'

That setback didn't appear to disrupt the pair too much though as they went on to spend time in their hotel lobby, where someone was playing the harp.

Following a visit to the Notre Dame the following morning, Megan shared a snippet from their taxi ride, presumably back to the airport, before she added: 'Thinking of all those affected.'

Earlier in the video she had mentioned that they were attending the final night of Dion's performances in Paris.

Given this was on Saturday night, it appears the quick trip took place after Everton's defeat by Chelsea on Saturday lunchtime, before they returned to the UK on Sunday.

Reports suggested around 1,500 shops and businesses were looted and destroyed as riot police were called in

Megan revealed they were 'advised to go straight to the hotel' after the concert finished

Amid the chaos in France, the country's interior minister Laurent Nunez admitted the police had 'lost control' in some cities.

That came despite President Emmanuel Macron's pleas for calm as rioting and looting also spread to Milan.

In a national address following emergency talks with senior ministers, Macron made an impassioned plea 'for unity' and insisted everything would be done to bring thugs to justice.

The French leader pledged that 'all the necessary lessons' would be drawn from the 'intelligence failures' that ultimately led to almost 2,400 arrests over the weekend.

The Minister for Urban Affairs Vincent Jeanbrun, meanwhile, described the violence as 'a form of insurrection'.

He said: 'You have young people and older people who are perfectly trained in this kind of violence, this kind of urban guerrilla warfare, and this isn't taught in school. So where is it learned?

'In the streets of certain neighbourhoods, with shadowy forces of drug traffickers who teach our youth very early on to attack the police and to hate them.'

'It's a minority,' the minister added. 'Investigations will determine where these individuals come from.'

Sports.title: No wonder there is frantic hype around Carlos Baleba - desperate Man United know his £70m move HAS to work... and did Man City sell the wrong goalkeeper this summer? IAN LADYMAN on My Football Weekend
Sports.content:
No wonder there is frantic hype around Carlos Baleba - desperate Man United know his £70m move HAS to work... and did Man City sell the wrong goalkeeper this summer? IAN LADYMAN on My Football Weekend

In football desperation can lead to exaggeration. Straws are clung on to and early conclusions drawn. That is why in and around Manchester United so much is being made of new midfielder Carlos Baleba.

The 22-year-old has played less than two hours of Premier League football since his move from Brighton in the summer.

He is clearly a very good player. He has a lovely first touch, can pass and seems to have the kind of awareness of time and space that no coach can really teach.

But United manager Michael Carrick got lost a little in exaggeration when describing his midfield as ‘terrific’ and ‘fantastic’ after the draw at Leeds. He is not alone.

Baleba has been hailed as some kind of shape-shifting saviour since leaving behind some early-season injury worries to come off the bench against Tottenham nine days ago.

But all the frantic hype is understandable because Baleba’s £70million switch from Brighton simply has to work. If it doesn’t, United are in even more trouble than they would appear after taking only seven points from their opening seven Premier League games.

This was the summer of the United midfield rebuild. There was £70m for Baleba, £50m for Andrey Santos from Chelsea and £35m for Youri Tielemans from Aston Villa. The club have spent upwards of £150m on a new central platform for their team and if it doesn’t work there will be no cavalry coming to sort it all out next year.

United are trying to rebuild a squad like people spruce up a house. Bathroom, kitchen, bedroom.

Carlos Baleba started his first Premier League game for Manchester United at Leeds

The intelligence from inside Old Trafford is that next summer the transfer budget will be spent on the defence.

So the midfield has been ticked off yet still we sat at Elland Road and watched Leeds take 61 per cent of the possession.

That’s a huge number when you are playing a supposed top-six team and it shows where United are.

Carrick’s players can’t control games. Not with the ball anyway. United haven’t been able to do for years and until they do they will continue to live or die on the strength of their counter-attack.

Carrick spoke of having witnessed a ‘fresh start’ at Elland Road yesterday and that was a huge stretch.

For Baleba, the weight on a young man’s shoulders already looks rather heavy.

United bringing their own noise

Carrick also spoke yesterday of having metaphorical headphones on as he looks to find a way round his current problems. The insinuation was that the noise about United’s predicament doesn’t bother him.

I wonder how he really feels, though, about the presence in the background of an Amazon film crew and also a journalist still trying to fulfil a Jim Ratcliffe brief to write a book chronicling United’s return to eminence.

United are said to be getting in the region of £20m for allowing access to Amazon. That’s about a quarter of what a club gets for qualifying for the Champions League.

Carrick will hope that one doesn’t get in the way of the other.

Why is Farke in limbo?

At Leeds Daniel Farke is threatening to be the club’s most successful manager since David O’Leary 25 years ago.

Outside Elland Road there is a mural tribute to a real Leeds hero, Marcelo Bielsa – who brought Leeds up in 2020 but couldn’t sustain it.

Maybe Farke will get one of those, too, but what the German deserves more than anything is a new contract.

Daniel Farke's Leeds sit seventh in the table having lost just one of their first seven games

Farke had it all on to prove himself a Premier League boss after a yo-yo spell with Norwich but that journey of validation now seems complete.

The 49-year-old’s current deal with the club expires at the end of this season. It’s said a new one has been tentatively agreed.

Leeds fans will feel better when they hear news of a signature.

Did City sell the wrong goalkeeper?

The FA coaching network have been convinced for two or three years that James Trafford would get past Dean Henderson to become Jordan Pickford’s successor as England No1.

For a while that looked fanciful but national coach Thomas Tuchel agrees and with maybe good reason.

The last time we saw the Leeds goalkeeper playing regularly in the Premier League was for Burnley two seasons ago and he looked like a boy in a man’s outfit, bullied at set-pieces and unable to command his penalty area.

Here we are in 2026 – less than two years out from a home European Championship – and the Cumbrian, signed from Manchester City for £40m in the summer, looks like a different goalkeeper.

The more I watch him play this season and the more I watch Gianluigi Donnarumma at City, the more I wonder if the Manchester club sold the wrong one.

Not all City numbers are bad

City’s start to the season has been overshadowed by numbers – 115 of them to be precise – but there has been no disguising the leaps forward they have made on the field under Enzo Maresca.

The Premier League leaders have now racked up exactly 100 shots in seven games – a figure skewed a little by the fact they only managed six when playing against United with ten men before the international break.

At this time last year – at the start of Pep Guardiola’s final campaign – City had taken 84 shots on goal so the uptick is clear.

The squad depth available to Maresca also became startlingly clear on Saturday as the Italian rested his first-choice midfielders Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernandez against Ipswich and still saw his team win comfortably.

How many other teams could do that?

Enzo Maresca rested Enzo Fernandez, Elliot Anderson and Rayan Cherki but a goal from Phil Foden and two from Erling Haaland was enough to secure a 3-2 win over Ipswich

Red Cartel jibe won't go away

Anger at the media’s coverage of City’s fight with the Premier League has been clear on social platforms and has spilled over a little on matchday.
