World.title: French protest violence: A ‘Christmas present’ for Le Pen’s far right?
World.content:
Le Pen is positioning her party as more capable than centrist or left-wing forces ahead of the presidential election in April 2027.

As massive protests swept through cities across France over the weekend, degenerating into riots in many places, far-right politician Marine Le Pen has attempted to profit from the crisis ahead of the presidential election in April 2027.

On Sunday, the leader of the National Rally party, or RN by its French initials, railed against President Emmanuel Macron’s handling of the crisis in a video statement, saying the outgoing centre-right leader no longer has any “credibility or authority” and that the country’s people were caught between his austerity “hammering” them on the one hand and “insurrectionary activists” on the left on the other.

School protests in France erupted on September 21 in a poor borough of Paris as pupils demonstrated against dilapidated infrastructure, teacher shortages and tight class schedules. The demonstrations quickly spread across the country and coincided with a nationwide public sector strike against the government’s plans to cut public spending.

Le Pen blamed the political left and “decades of immigration” to France for the looting and destruction that trailed the demonstrations, and presented her party as capable of restoring order — without offering any firm evidence to back up assertions that the rioting was led by immigrants.

The politician is already far ahead in recent polls, and some say she is likely to be the next leader. Here’s what we know:

What happened over the weekend?

Scenes of burned cars, vandalised and looted shops and defaced public buildings emerged from across France.



Some 550,000 people demonstrated on Saturday, according to the Ministry of the Interior, although protest organisers put the figure at 800,000. Protesters included students, union groups and supporters of the “yellow vests” movement, which protested against inflation back in 2018, at the start of Macron’s presidency.

Although most marched peacefully, masked groups attacked city halls in several cities on Saturday, including the 19th-century City Hall in the city of Limoges, which was badly damaged.

In Lyon, a tourist office was set ablaze.

In Marseille, hooded individuals attacked a police station. The city has since banned protests.

Looters also targeted hundreds of shops in several locations.

In Paris, storefronts were shattered and broken glass littered the Place de la Republique. The Marianne statue, an important symbol of France, was partially dismantled. Paris police said one person died of a heart attack, but did not provide more details.

Protesters and rights groups have accused police of using disproportionate force throughout the protests. Some 2,400 people were arrested by Sunday, officials said. Several police officers were injured.

In a national address, Macron condemned rioters and accused far-left groups of attacking police and public buildings. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Monday that partial curfews would be imposed in some areas.

How could the far right gain?

Peter McPhee, a professor emeritus at the University of Melbourne, described the protests as a “Christmas present” for Le Pen’s National Rally ahead of the presidential election.

Le Pen said in a video statement protesters have “legitimate social grievances” but that Macron’s government was “exhausted, disoriented and seemingly incapable” of addressing them.

She criticised the administration’s controversial budget plans and promised to free the French from “Macronist toxic policies” while failing to mention that her party has also proposed strict spending cuts to bring down rising public debt.

The politician, who is far ahead of other candidates in the polls, fuelled right-wing narratives spreading online that immigrants, not the French people, are instigating the protests, even as the grievances driving the agitation have intersected, with flag-carrying pro-Palestinian, environmental, feminist and anticolonial movements joining in.

McPhee called Le Pen’s move “profoundly worrying”.

“It is easy for Le Pen to make the link between the violent attacks on buildings and shops with African migrants because of the Palestinian and Algerian flags,” the professor said. “People in many parts of the world are attracted to simplistic, often racist, answers to economic and social problems.”



Analysts add that far-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon of the France Unbowed party, or LFI, who has joined the protests, could also face backlash if anger grows over the destruction, further handing Le Pen a stronger platform.

How did the far right gain ground after previous protests?

Right-wing and centrist parties have historically gained after mass protests and disorder as people, fearing anarchy, vote for them.

In May 1968, similar student-led protests erupted after millions of students and striking workers rallied against poor schooling conditions, increasing economic inequalities and stagnant wages.

Left-wing communist and socialist political parties joined the protests and called for a revolution. Then-President Charles de Gaulle’s conservative government initially struggled to control the demonstrations, even escaping to a French base in West Germany for a few days as violence spiralled and the country ground to a standstill.

However, the protest soon lost momentum amid the shutdown of public services. De Gaulle dissolved parliament and called for snap elections in June 1968, blaming the left for the violence and promising to restore order. His conservative Union for the Defence of the Republic party went on to win in an astounding landslide while left-wing parties lost more than half their seats.

Again, during the 2018 “yellow vest” demonstrations, working-class protesters rallying against Macron’s government’s decision to raise taxes found support among Le Pen’s party, although the left wing also tried to ingratiate itself with the movement.

Many of the movement’s supporters ended up voting for Le Pen’s party in the 2022 legislative elections to punish the Macron government, a move that still shapes the deeply divided parliament.

World.title: Doctors describe hospitals shattered by Israel’s genocide in Gaza
World.content:
Doctors describe hospitals shattered by Israel’s genocide in Gaza

Doctors who volunteered in Gaza have described working during Israel’s genocidal war on the strip, treating critically wounded patients without essential equipment, as damaged hospitals and a collapsing healthcare system continue to turn treatable conditions deadly.

World.title: Russia’s Lavrov discusses US war and regional security in Tehran visit
World.content:
GCC states have pressed Moscow to help halt Iranian attacks and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Tehran, Iran – Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has met his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Tehran, to discuss the war with the United States and efforts to end it.

Lavrov landed in the Iranian capital on Monday afternoon on his first visit to Iran since February 2025. Araghchi said talks with Lavrov had focused on regional developments, including the US-Israeli war on Iran.

“Regarding the Gulf and West Asia, we have had talks, and also on Ukraine and the Iranian-American negotiations,” Araghchi said in a press briefing.

He also called out Israel’s “dangerous expansion” in the region, which he blamed for the current hostilities.

“The lack of security in the Gulf and in the Strait of Hormuz … this is due to the Israeli-American aggression,” he said.

Lavrov said Russia is committed to a 20-year strategic partnership agreement with Iran, which officially came into force on October 2, 2026.

He is scheduled to hold talks with President Masoud Pezeshkian later on Monday.

Moscow said the trip was part of efforts to ease months of tension, since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran on February 28.

On Sunday, Lavrov was in Bahrain, which was heavily targeted by Iran during the war, to participate in a strategic dialogue session between Russia and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC).

He was urged by GCC members to use Moscow’s influence with Tehran to press for “serious dialogue” and restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been severely disrupted by attacks on commercial vessels.



GCC chief Jasem Al-Budaiwi said member states had faced more than 7,000 Iranian missiles and drones since the start of the war.

In the council’s closing statement, the six Arab countries said they wanted Iran’s nuclear and missile programmes, as well as its support for regional armed groups, to be included in future talks to end the war.

Nikita Smagin, an analyst and researcher on Iran and Russia’s role in the Middle East, said Lavrov’s trip reflects Moscow’s efforts to maintain working relations with all countries in the region.

He said Lavrov also wants to maintain Russia’s status as a mediator, despite the impact of the Ukraine war on its global reputation.

“The timing of visits to the Gulf monarchies and Iran, taking place almost simultaneously, is a deliberate signal: Moscow wants to show that it approaches relations with all these countries on broadly equal terms and is equally interested in cooperation with each of them,” Smagin said.

How does Russia fit in?

Lavrov told GCC ministers in Manama that the region was once again teetering on the brink of a full-scale war and Russia wanted to establish a regional architecture for “collective security”.

He said this could include combining initiatives from countries in the region, along with those put forward by Russia and China, with the aim of restoring maritime traffic and achieving lasting peace. The Russian foreign minister urged other regional states such as Iraq and Jordan, which have also been hit by Iranian strikes, to participate.

Lavrov expressed support for the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed between Iran and the US in June, which later collapsed, as a framework for reducing tension.

Iran has said it wants a return to that agreement, and for Washington to honour a finalised bilateral deal between Iran and Oman to manage territorial waters in the Strait of Hormuz. This has been opposed by the US, which has established its own route in the waterway for shipping.

Intelligence reports cited by US media said that Russia and China are providing military support to Iran in the form of satellite imagery for targeting purposes and components for weapons.

But US President Donald Trump contradicted those reports last week, saying Moscow and Beijing would have “too much to lose” if they helped Iran.

Washington has also issued sanctions waivers for Russia in a bid to lower fuel prices driven up by the war against Iran.

Mixed intentions

Russia’s position on the Iran war is somewhat unusual, said Smagin. It has a partial interest in the conflict continuing, as higher oil prices and the severe restrictions on Iranian oil reaching China all benefit Moscow.



“Russia and Iran have been competing primarily for the Chinese market, so China is now effectively forced to buy Russian oil at higher prices because Iranian supplies are largely unavailable,” he said.

Smagin added that Russia does not want the conflict to escalate further, as the consequences could be unpredictable, but its leverage over either Iran or the US to influence the course of the conflict remains limited.

Russia will continue to expand relations with Tehran, Smagin said, including through Caspian Sea trade, and limited military cooperation with Iran.

“These efforts appear to be aimed less at generating economic returns than at expanding Russia’s political influence over Iran and the course of events,” he said.

Military strikes by Iran and the US to wrest control of the waterway have continued, with the US midterm elections approaching on November 3 .

In comments to the media, Trump threatened to “soon finish the job” with Iran, to which Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi replied: “We have unfinished jobs too.”

World.title: ‘Weight of responsibility’: Promise and perils of covering Ethiopia’s war
World.content:
Al Jazeera correspondent shares his experience of covering the latest fighting between government forces and Tigray rebels.

Addis Ababa, Ethiopia – On September 23, fighting erupted in Ethiopia’s northern region of Tigray, shattering the peace agreement between the Ethiopian government and Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) signed nearly four years ago.

The latest fighting between the federal government-backed Tigray Peace Force (TPF) and TPLF started in the Erbeti area of Ethiopia’s Afar region after the 2022 peace deal unravelled over disarmament and territorial claims.

For me, the latest war is more than a story unfolding on television. It brought back painful memories of what I had experienced during my reporting in November 2021. The previous episode of fighting killed more than half a million people and displaced about 2 million others by the time the rival sides signed a deal to end the war in 2022.

After I was assigned to cover the fighting, I was once again faced with the challenge any war correspondent faces: how to stand in the midst of active fighting as a witness to the truth.

Soon, our team set off from the capital, Addis Ababa, to the Afar region and then to Mekelle, the capital of the Tigray region, covering the journey by road.

When I reached Erbeti, about 900km (560 miles) northeast of Addis Ababa, I hoped to catch my breath for a few hours and organise our coverage. Instead, events overtook us immediately.

Residents were leaving the town, which, until the previous day, had seemed safe. Small trucks and cars were piled with belongings. Men hurried to load whatever they could carry as families tried to get away before the fighting drew closer.



As we were still figuring out what to do next, loud sounds of shelling shook us. We decided to leave Erbeti only hours after arriving as staying would put the team’s lives at risk.

That had not been the plan. But war pays little attention to a correspondent’s plans.

We withdrew towards Afdera, about 100km (60 miles) to the east via unpaved roads. Afdera is a small town that serves as the administrative centre for the district of the same name in the Afar region, known for its salt mining.

We spent the night inside our car in the middle of the desert with the temperature hovering above 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit).

Intensified fighting

The next day, we started early to review information, make calls, prepare footage for reports and coordinate with the newsroom in Doha, Qatar.

Meanwhile, the heat and humidity drained our remaining energy as the mercury hit 50C (122F). As we lay in the car trying to catch some sleep, my thoughts were still in Erbeti.

Early the next morning, we headed for Afdera. After arriving there at 7am, we found that breakfast choices were limited.

The town followed a different rhythm: Many residents ate breakfast after dawn prayers, then headed to work. It was part of a correspondent’s daily reality – arriving somewhere unfamiliar and learning its routines.

We headed north towards Erbeti again, only to find the fighting intensifying in the mountains between the government-backed forces and TPLF.

I couldn’t see the clashes directly, but their sounds filled the area. The sound of artillery firing became louder as we got closer. At one point, we were barely 3km (almost 2 miles) from the front line.

We put on body armour and helmets, picked up our cameras and approached the government troops stationed on the front line.

We managed to film some footage and record brief accounts from soldiers. Then the assignment ended abruptly when the soldiers ordered us to evacuate immediately.

There was no time to argue or capture a final shot. We gathered our equipment and left with the shelling still echoing through the mountains behind us.

For days, we travelled difficult mountain routes through the regions of Afar, Amhara and Tigray. Roads we travelled on in the morning couldn’t be used by evening. Reports received before noon needed checking again before sunset.

In villages near the front lines, fear was visible in the faces we encountered as mothers packed small bags and children watched the road with anxious eyes.



I made a point of listening with sensitivity, respecting their suffering without exploiting their emotions for the camera.

Journey to Mekelle

As our coverage continued, the journey led us towards Mekelle, Tigray’s capital. We arrived the day after Ethiopian federal forces and their allies entered the city. The TPLF forces had retreated.

But Mekelle was a different city. I had expected it to be alive with unfolding events. It looked exhausted, with the usual police and security presence absent. It seemed to be trying to absorb what had happened in the hours before.

Daily life continued cautiously. Cars moved quietly through the streets, and shops had reopened in some neighbourhoods.

We saw soldiers welcomed in some streets while others remained silent, fearful of what might come next.

Many people declined to speak on camera because they didn’t know how events would unfold. There was no disorder in the conventional sense, but apprehension was everywhere. It was difficult to establish who was maintaining order or what the coming hours might bring.

We had no assurances about what might lie ahead. The possibility that our exit routes might close weighed on every decision.

Still, we had to keep working. Our audience was waiting for pictures and news. As far as we knew, we were the only media team in Mekelle.

I felt the weight of that responsibility. When you are alone in a place like this, every word matters. You must distinguish between what you have witnessed, what residents tell you and what the warring parties announce.

In a city that has only just emerged from battle, verifying information becomes harder than obtaining it.

We maintained as normal a routine as possible, filming in the morning, returning to prepare reports and following developments hour by hour.

Preserving impartiality

The challenges extended beyond security. We also faced the demanding ethical task of preserving impartiality and professional distance in a deeply polarised war.

People in the Tigray region have historic grievances against the federal government. After coming to power in 2018, President Abiy Ahmed reformed political institutions, lifted media censorship and freed thousands of political prisoners. But ethnic tensions have since erupted in this diverse nation of 139 million people.

Documenting residents welcoming incoming government-backed troops without presenting those scenes as universal or reporting fears about withdrawing TPLF fighters without drawing definitive conclusions could expose us to accusations of bias from any party that wanted us to see the battlefield exclusively through its own eyes.

That’s why I went beyond what the camera captured, talking to residents and listening to those who preferred to speak off camera. I understood that our task involved listening not only to what people said but also to what remained unspoken.

Their accounts helped us understand the situation. With each hour in the city, we tried to weigh the different narratives, recognising that our observations and residents’ accounts offered distinct perspectives.



The exhaustion of days on the road had accumulated, but my mind stayed on the day just ended and the one ahead. Which road would we take? Where would we go? Would the events of the coming hours allow us to complete our plans?

After two weeks of moving between front lines, fatigue had become a constant companion.

While we kept reporting, rumours that we were arrested or trapped inside the city kept our colleagues and family members anxious. They searched for the smallest piece of information confirming we were safe.

Only after I appeared live on TV did I understand that it carried another meaning. For many who had been trying to reach us, it was more than a live report. It was an unintended reassurance that we were still there – and still alive.

I later learned that some Mekelle residents had discovered that government forces had taken control of their city from our broadcast.

With communications disrupted and information scarce, television was bringing people news of events unfolding close to their homes.

After three days of reporting, we left Mekelle, carrying testimonies and documented facts.

On the return journey, looking through the car window at the roads we had travelled over the previous two weeks, I reflected that memories of war are not confined to battlefields.

What remained were the faces of the people I had met along the way, the anxiety in people’s eyes and the persistent sense that life seeks to continue, even in the places closest to war.

World.title: At least 18 killed in Houthi attack on military camp in Yemen’s Shabwa
World.content:
Houthis launch ballistic missiles at camp in southern governorate during training exercise, government forces spokesman says.

Share At least 18 killed in Houthi attack on military camp in Yemen’s Shabwa on social media

Dozens of people have been killed and wounded in a Houthi missile attack on the al-AIam military camp in southern Yemen, authorities say.

The Houthis launched three ballistic missiles on Monday at the camp in Shabwa governorate during a training exercise, a spokesperson for the Yemeni government forces said.

Officials in the internationally recognised government and medical sources said at least 18 people were killed and more than 30 wounded in the attack. The deputy governor of Shabwa said there were at least 40 casualties without giving a breakdown of those killed and injured.

The attack was carried out as fighting continued to rage across Yemen. The civil war has escalated sharply since the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized strategic territory from forces loyal to the government along the Red Sea coast last month.

Government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, responded to the losses with a counteroffensive and then launched the “Dawn of Yemen” operation, which aims to recapture Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the Iran-aligned group seized in 2014.

Rashad al-Alimi, the head of the Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council, said those killed were new recruits and promised a “firm response”.

“Targeting recruits reflects the Houthi militia’s approach of resorting to terrorist attacks when under pressure,” he said.

Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said the Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack.



“The Houthis said the attack targeted what they called a ‘Saudi-backed’ military base, referring to Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces who are stationed at military camps across the country,” he said.

“The Houthis say they will continue to target those bases. Spokesperson Yahya Saree says anywhere with a Saudi-backed military presence will be considered a legitimate target.”

Earlier, Yemeni government forces said they targeted Houthi gatherings, vehicles and weapons in al-Aqroudh, al-Shaqab and al-Sarari, south of Taiz, which is suffering from fuel shortages and soaring prices.

World.title: The night watch: Palestinians protecting their homes from settler pogroms
World.content:
Palestinians in the occupied West Bank are organising to protect themselves from settler attacks.

The life of 32-year-old Abdul Rahman Jabr changed more than a year ago when his home in the village of al-Mughayyir, east of Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank was targeted by Israeli settlers. After the attack, he put up barbed wire in an attempt to fend off future settler pogroms.

The house, built by Abdul Rahman in early 2023 before his marriage, is located on the outskirts of the village in an area with a long history of settler violence. He now lives there with his wife and their two-year-old daughter, but settler attacks on his home and his neighbours have intensified over the past year.

His vehicle was set on fire by settlers in April 2024, and his home’s windows were smashed with stones. He cannot count the number of times his home has been targeted. In the past week alone, settlers reached his property seven times, which forced him to miss work to stay at home to protect his wife and child.

“I thought about my wife and child. How could I protect them from the settlers when there is no protection for us? I began surrounding the house with barbed wire and an iron fence. This isn’t a sufficient measure, but it’s the only thing I can do on my own,” he told Al Jazeera.

“All the neighbouring households have had to install these fences to protect themselves. We’ve made countless appeals, but no one listens, so we had to take this step. At the very least, it has helped keep their livestock away from our yards.”

Night guard

Abdul Rahman’s experiences are not unique. They are part of a rapid rise in settler activity across the West Bank since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023.



Settlers carried out 14,742 attacks against Palestinians, their land or properties from October 7, 2023, to October 4, 2026, according to the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, which is part of the PLO.

In the first seven months of 2026 alone, the commission recorded 4,113 attacks, ranging from assaults on people to vandalism of orchards. This was a 63 percent increase compared with the same period in 2025, and this month saw a spate of attacks on Palestinian farmers as they harvested olives.

Palestinians are now beginning to organise to protect their families and homes from settler attacks.

In the town of Sinjil, north of Ramallah, a group of young Palestinian men have repelled several settler attacks in recent months. Basel Awad, a pseudonym used for security reasons, told Al Jazeera that the village’s guard committee, which he is a member of, is unofficial and intended to protect the homes of residents.

Each night, 20 to 30 unarmed people gather at key locations that settlers have used as staging posts for their raids into Sinjil.

They have paid a high price for their efforts. The Israeli army has arrested six members of the guard and at least 10 have been injured in an apparent bid by Israel to dismantle this neighbourhood watch.

“We had set up a tent in the Jabal al-Batin area, which is frequently targeted by attacks. Soldiers arrived last winter and fired tear gas canisters inside. We all suffered from suffocation, and then they demolished the tent and confiscated it,” Basel told Al Jazeera.

Protecting communities

Despite the dangers, Palestinians are refusing to leave their homes and have their land seized by settlers.

Nasr Radwan, 53, is one of the landowners in the village of Beitillu, west of Ramallah, whose property is frequently raided by settlers. The land owned by Nasr, his brothers and their relatives spans 1,500 dunums (1,000sq metres or a quarter of an acre) and contains more than 100 springs.

He has been beaten by settlers on several occasions, but he and his brothers insist on being present on the land every single day.

In June, settlers established an outpost near his land, which is being used as a base to attack his crops and assault his family, he said.

“The most recent attack took place last Saturday. We were on our land harvesting olives when settlers attacked us, smashed the windows of our vehicles and beat my brother. Even so, we continue to go there every day,” he added.

For the past three years, settlers have tried to seize the family’s land, blocking an access road to prevent Nasr and his relatives from reaching it by car. Family members persist, travelling 5km (3 miles) on foot to reach their land.



“We know that being on our land means facing constant attacks. It could even cost us our lives. But we also know that if we abandon it, it will be lost forever,” he said.

“This is not just land or a source of livelihood; it is our soul, our memory and our very life.”

Violation of international law

With the settler raids sanctioned by Israeli authorities, Palestinian residents have no real protection or recourse for legal action when they are attacked. This has left West Bank villages exposed to continual assault with no penalties for settlers who destroy, assault or sometimes kill.

Human Rights Watch in August reported that Israeli authorities have failed to prosecute settlers for acts of violence committed against Palestinians. By the end of 2025, the Israeli human rights organisation Yesh Din reported that out of hundreds of cases it has documented since 2005, only 3 percent have resulted in convictions. The village watch scheme is an attempt by Palestinians to mitigate these risks.

Omar Rahhal, director of the Ramallah-based SHAMS Center for Human Rights, told Al Jazeera that the fact that Palestinians resort to self-protection measures against settler attacks doesn’t absolve Israel as an occupying power of its legal responsibility under the Fourth Geneva Convention to protect civilians.

He said such measures are merely a stopgap solution to the settler dilemma for Palestinians, who are faced with a profound power imbalance. An illustration of this is the presence of Israeli soldiers as settlers attack their families and raze their lands.

“Impunity, the arming of settlers, the allocation of funds to settlements and policies adopted by ministers in the Israeli government are factors that contribute to the continuation of attacks and the resulting increase in the number of victims,” he said.

World.title: Kenya pastor accused of ordering parents to starve their children to death faces verdict
World.content:
A Kenyan judge has started to deliver a verdict in a mass murder case involving doomsday preacher Paul Mackenzie.

Mackenzie and 29 of his followers are being charged with the murder of 191 people, all but one of them children.

His cult is alleged to have forced children to starve to death so that they could "meet Jesus". His doomsday doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was considered "evil".

Mackenzie and the 29 others have all pleaded not guilty to murder, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die.

Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but then entered a plea deal and became a witness for the prosecution.

Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult also face a raft of other legal cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children.

But this is the first time the pastor will face a verdict on the most serious charges of murder.

Authorities said over 400 bodies were found in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast, where Mackenzie led his followers from across the country.

Seventeen men were hired from the nearby town for the horrifying task of digging up the shallow graves. Some were paid just $8 (Â£6) a day.

"Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old."

"We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another."

Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".

World.title: Alberta heads to polls to decide whether to hold vote on separation from Canada
World.content:
People in the province of Alberta head to the polls on Monday to decide whether to hold a binding referendum at a later date on separating from Canada.

The vote was called earlier this year by the leader of the province, Danielle Smith, after a grassroots group gathered about 300,000 signatures on a petition that asked for a binding referendum on separation.

Many of those who support separation say the oil-rich province's economic growth has been stifled by the environmental policies of Canada's central government in Ottawa.

But those who want Alberta to remain part of Canada - who include Prime Minister Mark Carney - have called for the country to show unity in the face of external pressures.

Polls have suggested that the majority of Albertans would vote to remain in Canada, though the pre-vote debate alone has proven divisive.

Another group collected signatures for its own petition that opposed separation, which was signed by more than 400,000 people. The province's population is about five million people.

If Albertans do vote on Monday to move ahead with a binding referendum, that could happen as soon as 2027, Smith has said.

Smith's decision to allow Monday's vote came in spite of the fact that a court blocked the pro-separation petition, saying it failed to consult indigenous First Nations whose land would be affected if the province separated from Canada.

Following the judge's ruling, First Nations groups have branded Smith's decision to allow the voting process to play out as "undemocratic" and "authoritarian".

Smith, the leader of the United Conservative Party of Alberta (UCP), has defended her decision to put the issue to voters. She opposes separation herself, but says the process gives the province's residents a chance to have their say on the issue.

The key question on the voting paper will ask: "Should Alberta remain a province of Canada or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?"

World.title: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table.

"I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table".

Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia on Friday night, two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened.

Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake".

Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment". He said the sanctions, which were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the US president in September, would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described the suspension of the sanctions as a 60-day pause during which their potential impact on the US and global economies would be analysed.

In his Truth Social post, Trump also said Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now".

Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week.

Despite the international sanctions, Russia has still been able to export oil, much of it to China and India - often at attractive discounts. According to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), China has taken about half of Russia's crude exports, with India accounting for about 37%.

In remarks to a European Union summit, after Trump announced the deal to buy diesel from Russia and said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin, Zelensky said it was nice to be among "real leaders".

World.title: Personal attacks fire up debate before Brazil's run-off vote
World.content:
Brazil's left-wing President, Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva, and his right-wing rival, Senator FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, have clashed in a debate held one week before the run-off presidential election.

Polls suggest the two candidates are neck and neck and the televised debate was hailed as a chance for both to sway undecided voters.

But the showdown was marked by personal attacks and analysts have warned that its aggressive tone may increase the abstention rate further.

In the first round of voting, held on 4 October, Bolsonaro defied opinion polls by securing a narrow lead over Lula.

Sunday's debate was the first of two before the vote. The second is planned for Friday, just two days before polls open.

FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro is standing for the Liberal Party after his father, Jair Bolsonaro - who governed from 2018 to 2022 - was sentenced to more than 20 years in prison for plotting to overthrow Lula after the latter beat him in the 2022 election.

The younger Bolsonaro won 47% of the vote in the first round, compared with Lula's 45.2%, with both falling short of the 50% of the valid votes needed to stave off a decisive second round.

Since the return to democracy in 1988, there has been no instance in which the candidate who lost in the first round went on to win in the second but Lula has told his supporters that he will "win in extra time".

Analysts consulted by BBC News Brasil were struck by how much the debate was dominated not by issues but personal attacks.

Yuri Sanches from pollsters AtlasIntel said it was a debate in which no policies were discussed and there were no rational arguments.

"The independent voter, who is sometimes against Bolsonaro and sometimes against the Workers' Party [of Lula], came out of it with a very negative impression."

Lucas AragÃ£o from political analysis firm Arko Advice said Bolsonaro had appeared calmer during the debate and seemed to have managed to "get under Lula's skin".

Rafael Cortez from consulting firm da TendÃªncias Consultoria, however, argued that Lula had managed to score a goal when he said he would open up his financial and phone records and those of his family to judicial scrutiny, and challenged his rival to do the same before Sunday's run-off.

Many observers criticised the format of the debate, which was described as chaotic at times, with each of the candidates pacing around the TV studio as the other was speaking.

One heated exchange saw Bolsonaro telling Lula he should come stand next to him so that the two could talk.

Referring to alleged links between the senator and paramilitary vigilante groups, Lula said "I don't want to be close to you", and that he wanted to maintain "distance from the Bolsonaro family" and "the militia".

Bolsonaro, who has dismissed the allegations as fake news, in turn tried to bait Lula by saying, "On second thoughts, maybe it's better to keep my distance so that my wallet isn't stolen."

He also accused the Workers' Party of being corrupt, holding up the palm of his hand on which he had scribbled "CORRUPTO" (Portuguese for "corrupt).

World.title: Catalonia's former rebel president can return to Spain, court rules
World.content:
Spain's Supreme Court has ruled the former president of Catalonia, Carles Puigdemont, can return without fear of arrest nearly a decade after going into self-imposed exile having led a failed independence bid.

The court upheld a decision to lift an arrest warrant for him linked to the referendum his regional government organised in 2017, in defiance of Madrid.

Direct rule was imposed on the region soon after the vote and Puigdemont fled to Belgium, where he has been based ever since - with a surprise appearance in Barcelona in 2024 prompting a police manhunt.

But the Spain to which he may return is much different from a decade ago, with Catalan independence now a marginal political issue.

Monday's ruling brings to an end a lengthy legal wrangle between the Spanish judiciary and the former Catalan president.

In 2024, Spain's socialist government introduced a controversial amnesty for dozens of Catalan politicians and activists who were involved in the secession drive, but the Supreme Court said Puigdemont and several of his colleagues should be excluded.

It argued this was because of the charges against them of alleged financial crimes around staging the referendum.

The Constitutional Court overruled that interpretation earlier this month, and on Monday the Supreme Court rejected an appeal by the far-right Vox party against lifting national arrest warrants for Puigdemont, as well as his former ministers LluÃ­s Puig and Toni ComÃ­n, paving the way for their return to Spain.

World.title: Meloni calls emergency meeting after weekend of violent clashes
World.content:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is set to hold an emergency security meeting on Monday after protests over the rising cost of living broke out into violent clashes in Milan.

More than 5,000 people gathered over the weekend. Police deployed tear gas and water cannons after protesters - many in masks - threw paving stones, bins and chairs at officers.

"To demonstrate is a right. To lay our cities to waste is not," Meloni said on Saturday, adding that "hooligans" had exploited the protests to "sow chaos".

Rioting and violence have broken out on the sidelines of mostly peaceful youth-led protests in other European countries including France, Spain and Albania.

Milanese Mayor Giuseppe Sala said he was worried it was a "new phenomenon" that "originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself".

Speaking to Italian news agency Ansa, he said he witnessed "smashed shop windows, looted stores, and frightened citizens", adding that "what happened here is what we are seeing in many cities around the world".

Clashes began on Saturday and continued into Sunday in Milan. More than 200 people were detained, 80% of whom were minors, Ansa reported.

The city's prosecutor's office has requested prison sentences for five adults arrested for looting, vandalism and resisting arrest, according to Italian news agency AGI.

Italian media reported that people - including police officers - were injured.

Violence between protesters and police also rippled into other cities in the north.

Meloni said people in Turin were detained while "carrying cobblestones and window-breaking hammers", while a train station in Bologna was closed as a precaution after similar disorder.

The prime minister - who is facing an election next year - also called on her political opponents to condemn the rioting.

"Do not be ambiguous about this," she said on X, explaining that condemnation must be "unanimous" because "any hesitation becomes justification".

Democratic Party leader Elly Schlein said her party had always condemned violence and that the rioting should not be used to stifle the voices of peaceful protesters across the country who are struggling to make a living, Ansa reported.

The violent disorder followed anti-government protests held by students in various Italian cities on Friday, and echoed similar unrest in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands took to the streets.

World.title: Possible wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane likely to be trees, say researchers
World.content:
Researchers inspecting an object that some thought could have been the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane on a remote Pacific island say it is likely to be washed up trees.

The team travelled to a lagoon in the Taraia Peninsula on Nikumaroro, Kiribati, to confirm whether a shiny object first spotted on satellite imagery in 2020 solved the decades-long mystery of the pioneering pilot's disappearance.

But Purdue University, which has a leading role in the study, said the so-called Taraia Object "was likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula's sandspit".

By the time the team arrived at the site a good portion of the debris had fragmented and washed away, leaving only a single Y-shaped segment, the university said.

World.title: Bangladesh says it was not informed of its citizens' execution by Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Bangladeshi authorities say they were not informed of the recent execution of two Bangladeshi nationals in the holy city of Mecca until after it had taken place, local media reports.

A Bangladeshi man and woman were executed last Wednesday after being convicted of committing an "indecent act" inside a mosque, according to the Saudi interior ministry. The ministry did not specify the nature of the offending act.

Bangladesh says it has reached out to the Saudi Arabian government to ask for more details about the case.

The two Muslim countries share a close relationship due to their religious affinity and strong economic ties.

More than three million Bangladeshis work and live in Saudi Arabia, mostly in low-paying jobs, and news of the double execution has raised public concern in Bangladesh.

According to the Saudi interior ministry, the two Bangladeshi nationals were convicted and sentenced to death under "tazir", which in Islamic law refers to punishments left to the discretion of the judge.

The ministry statement said they were handed the sentences because of the severity of the offence, and the fact that they violated the "sanctity" of the mosque.

Bangladesh has reached out to the Saudi government about the offences involved and legal proceedings in the case, said state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam.

The government would consider next steps, such as the repatriation of the bodies, after getting information from Saudi authorities, Islam said.

She added that the government was committed to safeguarding the welfare and interests of Bangladeshis abroad.

The two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh, upon a request from the Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah - but that list did not indicate that the pair had been sentenced to death, the Daily Star reported.

This is not the first time that foreign nationals have been executed by Saudi authorities.

According to Amnesty International, the country has executed around 100 people this year, many of whom are foreigners convicted of drug offences.

In 2011, eight Bangladeshi men were publicly executed in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh after they were found guilty of killing an Egyptian.

Earlier this month, Saudi Arabia overturned a death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan man over a comment he had made on Facebook, which had led to him being convicted of blasphemy. That decision came after the case sparked public outcry in Sri Lanka and spurred diplomatic efforts to seek clemency for the man.

World.title: Cross River PDP chairman resigns after five years, gives reasons
World.content:
Venatius Ikem, the chairman of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in Cross River State, has resigned from the position, citing a crisis of direction and leadership coherence within the opposition party.

Mr Ikem announced his resignation in a letter posted on his Facebook page on Friday, saying his decision followed a period of reflection on the party’s internal dynamics and his ability to continue leading the state chapter.

The resignation takes immediate effect, according to the letter addressed to the PDP national secretary and the state secretary of the party in Cross River.

“As we enter a critical electoral season, I have found it increasingly difficult to reconcile my responsibilities as State Chairman with the prevailing internal dynamics and divergent positions that continue to weaken the party’s ability to pursue a clear and united course,” he wrote.

Mr Ikem said the party was grappling with a crisis of direction and leadership coherence, warning that the challenges could undermine the sacrifices and aspirations of members who had worked for its success.

He described the decision as difficult but necessary, given what he called circumstances that increasingly challenged the principles, cohesion and sense of purpose that should guide the party.

Despite his concerns, Mr Ikem expressed gratitude for the opportunity to serve the PDP for five years, acknowledging party leaders and supporters who stood by him during his tenure.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He specifically thanked Senator Sandy Onor and Senator Jarigbe Jarigbe for their encouragement and support during difficult moments in his political journey.

He also acknowledged Nyesom Wike, the minister of the Federal Capital Territory and a prominent PDP figure, describing his contribution to their collective political efforts as indelible.

Mr Ikem thanked his supporters across Cross River, particularly the people of Obudu, his immediate constituency, for their loyalty and commitment.

Possible new political direction

Although Mr Ikem did not announce his next political move, his resignation letter suggested that he was considering a new direction.

“Life and leadership often require periods of reassessment and renewal. I believe I have reached a moment where a clearer vision and a new pathway are necessary, both for myself and for those who have entrusted me with their confidence and support,” he said.

He added that future choices should be guided by purpose, clarity and a commitment to advancing the interests of the people.

Mr Ikem, however, did not expressly state that he was leaving the PDP or identify another political party he intended to join.

His resignation follows persistent internal divisions within the PDP, which has faced competing leadership claims and disagreements over the party’s direction ahead of future elections.

Mr Ikem has been associated with Wike’s faction within the PDP, based on his previously documented political positioning. However, his resignation leaves his current political alignment uncertain.

He ended his letter by reaffirming his commitment to the progress, stability and development of Cross River and Nigeria, while wishing the PDP success in its future endeavours.

World.title: Cross River bans roadside workshops, street trading in Calabar metropolis
World.content:
The Cross River State Government has banned the activities of roadside mechanics and street traders in Calabar metropolis effective 31 October.

The Commissioner for Environment, Bassey Mensah, disclosed this during an on-the-spot inspection of business areas, erosion sites, and other locations in Calabar on Monday.

Mr Mensah said roadside technicians and traders were obstructing pedestrian and vehicular movement in the city.

The commissioner also said their activities had caused serious environmental degradation in Calabar City.

The News Agency of Nigeria reports that during the inspection, Mr Mensah visited Kings Street, White House, Bedwell, Punch, Victor Akan and adjoining streets.

He told roadside mechanics and traders in the area to relocate their operations to designated places.

“There is the possibility of exposure to harmful chemicals; we need to collectively protect public health and restore environmental order,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Mensah said improved sanitation is critical to creating a safe environment for residents.

The commissioner expressed the government’s commitment to address environmental degradation triggered by roadside workshops and street trading.

He said the state government would collaborate with the Nigeria Climate Adaptation–Erosion and Watershed Project to tackle the matter.

He said the inspection was part of the ministry’s ongoing efforts to restore a clean, healthy environment in the state through improved sanitation, enforcement of environmental regulations, and sustained public sensitisation.

Ndem Effiong, the senior special assistant to Governor Bassey Otu on the Automobile Technician Regulatory Department, said vehicle sales and mechanic operations need to be separated.

He expressed concern about increasing environmental degradation caused by mechanics operating on the streets.

World.title: Students threaten university with lawsuit over expulsion
World.content:
Seven students expelled by the Federal University Dutse (FUD), Jigawa State, have served the institution a pre-action notice, demanding their immediate reinstatement and N200 million in damages.

The notice, issued on 15 October, was signed by their counsel, Garba Umaru.

The students are Emmanuel Anenechukwu, Mubarak Usman, Divine Inuwa, Yusuf Lawal, Ismail Idris, Ayomide Kayode, and Miracle Kayode.

According to official correspondence dated 8 September, the university expelled the students after a police report indicted them and they were subsequently arraigned before Chief Magistrate Courts II and III in Dutse for alleged criminal conspiracy and armed robbery.

In the letter addressed to the the university’s vice-chancellor, Ahmad Gumel, the counsel described their expulsion as hasty, uninformed, and a breach of the Nigerian constitution.

Mr Umaru said the police report relied upon by the university is merely investigative and that no competent court has convicted the students of any crime.

Denial of fair hearing

Mr Umaru said the university’s disciplinary committee did not invite or afford the students an opportunity to defend themselves before reaching a “guilty verdict” and recommending their expulsion under Section 31 of the student handbook.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The lawyer noted that the charges against the students in court differ from the armed robbery allegations cited by the university.

He further pointed out that chief magistrate courts lack jurisdiction to try capital offences such as armed robbery.

The lawyer decried the publication of the students’ names, photographs, and academic records across various news and online platforms, stating that depicting them as “petty criminals” has inflicted severe psychological trauma and irreparable damage on their reputations and family standing.

The solicitor gave the university management two weeks to unconditionally reverse the expulsion and reinstate the students with full access to university facilities, student privileges, and the return of their ID cards.

He further demanded:

“Special arrangements enabling the affected students to write the examinations they were barred from taking.

“A formal letter of apology published in the University’s internal newsletter, on its official Facebook page, across three national daily newspapers, and on online news platforms.

“Payment of N200,000,000 (Two Hundred Million Naira) in damages for public ridicule, defamation, embarrassment, and psychological trauma,” the expelled students demanded.

The university’s spokesperson, Abdullahi Bello, could not be reached through his known phone number for his comments on the development.

The expulsion

On 16 September, the Federal University Dutse published the names and photographs of seven students in its internal bulletin, which announced their expulsion.

Their alleged offences included criminal conspiracy, armed robbery, cultism, drug abuse, cyberbullying, and attempted sexual assault.

​According to the publication, 12 students were expelled, and five others were rusticated.

It said the decisions were approved at the 20th Students’ Disciplinary Committee.

​It said Emmanuel Anenechukwu, Ayomide Peter, Idris Ismail, Miracle Pelumi, Yazi Saleh, and Yusuf Abdurrazak were expelled for criminal conspiracy and armed robbery.

Also, Mubarak Usman and Divine Inuwa were expelled over allegations of robbery and cult-related activities, while Ahmed Bashir was expelled following allegations of phone theft.

​In addition, drug abuse allegations on campus led to the expulsion of Ismail Muhammad, Aisha Yakubu, and Fatima Muhammad.

​Five other students were rusticated for alleged offences relating to cyberbullying and attempted sexual assault.

Four of them received a two-semester suspension, while one was suspended for one semester.

World.title: Nigerian emerges West Africa chair for IUCN Snake Specialist Group
World.content:
Nigerian conservationist Edem Eniang has emerged as the West Africa regional chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Snake Specialist Group, placing him in a regional leadership role in efforts to strengthen snake conservation and coordinate research across the sub-region.

His emergence comes as the group works to establish its regional structures, membership lists and specialist working groups, alongside a revised process for admitting members.

In a message of appointment shared with PREMIUM TIMES by Mr Eniang, the organisation said they had gained momentum following recent engagements at a meeting of the Wildlife Conservation Society, with encouraging responses during and after the conference.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that Mr Eniang a professor and executive director of the Biodiversity Preservation Centre, Uyo, Akwa Ibom State, was Nigeria’s only representative at the first World Congress on Snakes held from 1 to 4 October in Sri Lanka.

The organisation said it was developing documents and strategies, including terms of reference for regional chairs, membership lists, working groups and a clearer organisational structure.

The proposed arrangements are intended to improve coordination among regional teams, exchange ideas and reduce duplication of conservation activities.

The proposed coordination framework would include online meetings of regional chairs three times a year, with separate quarterly meetings between each regional chair and members in their respective regions.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

IUCN stated that the meetings would help specialists share updates on the group’s priorities and exchange ideas without duplicating ongoing work. They also proposed holding a brief introductory meeting for regional chairs before the end of 2026.

Global conservation network

The IUCN Snake Specialist Group is part of the IUCN Species Survival Commission, a global network of experts that provides scientific advice on species conservation and supports efforts to address threats to wildlife.

According to the group’s official website, its work covers knowledge of snake populations, conservation planning, analysis of threats, policy guidance and public education aimed at reducing conflict between people and snakes.

The group focuses on thousands of snake species worldwide, although some groups, including vipers and sea snakes in the subfamily Hydrophiinae, fall under separate specialist groups.

Mr Eniang’s appointment gives Nigeria representation in the group’s emerging regional leadership structure at a time when coordination among researchers and conservation practitioners is being strengthened.

Other regional chairs listed in the message include Tim Colston and Adriaan Jordaan for East and Southern Africa; Chifundera Kusamba for Central Africa; Steven Allain for Europe; Evan Quah and Justin Bernstein for East and South-East Asia; and Melissa Bruton for Australia, Oceania and Melanesia.

The message also listed regional representatives for South Asia, North America, Central America and the Caribbean.

The group said it would circulate further information on its organisational arrangements and membership once the relevant documents and strategies were ready.

World.title: NBBF Election: Oyedeji challenges Abdullahi’s emergence, demands fresh poll
World.content:
Former D’Tigers captain Olumide Oyedeji has asked the Nigeria Basketball Federation (NBBF) Electoral Appeals Committee to nullify the federation’s recently concluded board elections and order a fresh exercise over alleged constitutional violations and electoral irregularities.

In an appeal addressed to the committee, chaired by lawyer Emmanuel Okibe, Mr Oyedeji challenged aspects of the electoral process, including his initial exclusion from the list of candidates, the expulsion of eight board members, and the accreditation of delegates.

He also questioned the emergence of Mustapha Abdullahi as NBBF president and Babatunde Ogunade as the South-West representative, alleging that irregularities affected the process through which they secured their positions.

Mr Oyedeji said his appeal was not merely about the election outcome or his personal ambition, but about protecting the federation’s constitution and the integrity of basketball administration in Nigeria.

Disputed election

Mr Abdullahi, Director-General of the Energy Commission of Nigeria, won the presidency with 40 votes, defeating Mr Oyedeji, who received eight votes, at the Bola Ahmed Tinubu International Conference Centre in Abuja.

Former Nigerian international Ejike Ugboaja received no votes. Meanwhile, another presidential aspirant, Igoche Mark, withdrew from the contest a day before the election, citing concerns about the process’s credibility.

Mr Ugboaja also walked out after voting began, alleging that the election had been hijacked in favour of Mr Abdullahi.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The election proceeded despite protests by some aspirants and a pending court case challenging the legality of the federation’s electoral process.

In his latest appeal, Mr Oyedeji said his initial exclusion from the list of candidates for the South-West representative position disadvantaged him, despite meeting the requirements.

He argued that his eventual inclusion, after the electoral committee led by Lanre Glover widely publicised his exclusion, violated the NBBF constitution and electoral guidelines.

Expulsion of board members

Mr Oyedeji also challenged the Musa Kida-led NBBF board’s expulsion of eight board members, describing the decision as unconstitutional.

He argued that their removal prevented duly elected members from participating in the processes leading to the Extraordinary Congress and Elective Congress, thereby undermining the legitimacy of the proceedings.

The former captain further alleged that the former NBBF president and secretary circumvented the electoral process.

He also raised concerns about the removal of state basketball association chairmen and the accreditation of individuals he said did not satisfy the eligibility requirements under the federation’s constitution.

The allegations form part of broader complaints about the election. In a petition dated 12 October, Mr Mark, Mr Oyedeji and Mr Ugboaja had asked President Bola Tinubu to direct the National Sports Commission (NSC) to halt the exercise and investigate alleged breaches of the NBBF constitution.

They alleged that the National Sports Commission (NSC) removed and replaced more than 15 chairmen and representatives of state basketball associations shortly before the election.

The allegations have not been independently established. Mr Kida and Mr Abdullahi did not respond to the claims in the earlier petition.

Court case and calls for unity

The election also proceeded while a Federal High Court in Abuja was considering a suit challenging the legality of the NBBF elective congress. The court adjourned the case until 3 November.

The suit was filed by former D’Tigers coach Ayodele Bakare against the NBBF and the NSC. Mr Bakare, who was disqualified from contesting the presidency after submitting his nomination forms after the deadline, is challenging the validity of the Extraordinary Congress held in Yola, Adamawa State.

The election was also held against the backdrop of a directive from the International Basketball Federation (FIBA) that the NBBF conclude its board election by 15 October.

NSC Chairman Shehu Dikko had urged candidates and basketball officials to put their differences aside after the election and work together to advance the sport.

“Today is the day to show that we are for basketball. Whatever it is, let’s put the ball to a stop here and see how we can move forward together as one family,” Mr Dikko said.

Mr Oyedeji is seeking to nullify the election and hold a fresh poll, arguing that the allegations must be addressed to protect the NBBF constitution and restore confidence in the federation’s electoral process.

World.title: 2027: Wike, Rivers Assembly members, council chairpersons meet Fubara
World.content:
The FCT Minister, Nyesom Wike, members of the Rivers State House of Assembly, and the 23 local government chairpersons in Rivers State met with Governor Siminalayi Fubara at his private residence in Port Harcourt on Sunday.

The meeting comes about a fortnight after Mr Wike led members of the Rainbow Coalition in Rivers, including Kingsley Chinda, the 2027 Rivers APC governorship candidate, to meet with the governor.

Although details of Sunday’s meeting were not made public, Punch newspaper reported that it was part of efforts to accommodate Mr Fubara’s camp in the emerging political structure in the state ahead of the 2027 elections.

The meeting is significant because Mr Wike and the state lawmakers had been at loggerheads with Mr Fubara amid a prolonged political crisis that disrupted governance in the oil-rich state.

Reconciliation ahead of 2027

Mr Wike, a former governor of Rivers, has intensified political engagements across the state ahead of the 2027 elections. He has held rallies and visited traditional rulers to consolidate support for President Bola Tinubu and the APC.

The minister has repeatedly vowed to deliver victories for Mr Tinubu in Rivers and the FCT.

The renewed reconciliation efforts come as political alignments ahead of the 2027 elections gather momentum, with former Rivers governor Rotimi Amaechi emerging as the African Democratic Congress’s vice-presidential candidate.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Although some of Mr Fubara’s supporters appear reluctant to embrace the reconciliation efforts, Sunday’s meeting could signal a further attempt to bring the governor’s camp into the emerging political arrangement.

However, it remains unclear how much influence Mr Fubara and his loyalists would have in the proposed arrangement.

Background to Rivers political crisis

The meeting comes against the backdrop of a protracted power struggle between Mr Fubara and Mr Wike, which extended to the state legislature and local government administration.

The crisis escalated in March 2025 when President Tinubu declared a state of emergency in Rivers, suspended Mr Fubara and his deputy, Ngozi Odu, as well as the state House of Assembly, and appointed a retired naval chief, Ibok-Ete Ibas, as sole administrator.

During the emergency rule, Mr Ibas dissolved boards and parastatals constituted under Mr Fubara’s administration and appointed new officials, many of whom were described as loyal to Mr Wike.

His administration also conducted local government elections in which Mr Wike-aligned candidates emerged as chairpersons in the state’s 23 local government areas.

The emergency rule was lifted in September 2025, paving the way for Mr Fubara and other suspended elected officials to return to office.

Despite the governor’s return, tensions over political control and the state government’s composition have continued to shape relations between the two camps.

Uncertainty over power-sharing

Sunday’s meeting was also significant because of the strained relationship between Mr Fubara and lawmakers who had rejected some of his commissioner nominees during screening.

Mr Fubara’s cabinet remains incomplete, and he has yet to submit additional nominees to the state assembly for screening, leaving key ministries such as information without a commissioner.

The reported reconciliation effort is expected to test whether the governor’s loyalists can secure a place in the state’s evolving political structure ahead of the next general elections.

However, neither the details of the discussions nor the terms of any proposed political arrangement were disclosed.

For now, it remains unclear whether the meeting will bring a lasting resolution to the rivalry or mark another phase in negotiations over political control in Rivers State.

World.title: Ex-Governor Uduaghan is dead
World.content:
Former Governor Emmanuel Uduaghan of Delta State, South-south Nigeria, is dead.

Mr Uduaghan passed away on the morning of Monday, 19 October, according to a press statement by Toju Uduaghan, on behalf of the family.

The statement did not disclose details about the former governor’s passing.

“His passing is an immeasurable loss to our family, the people of Delta State, and Nigeria at large.

“Beyond his public service, he was a beloved father, brother, uncle, and respected patriarch whose presence enriched our lives. We will deeply miss him and forever cherish his memory and enduring legacy,” the family said in the statement.

See full statement below:

ANNOUNCEMENT OF THE PASSING OF HIS EXCELLENCY, THE DR. CHIEF EMMANUEL EWETA UDUAGHAN CON

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

It is with profound sorrow and heavy hearts that we announce the passing to glory of our beloved Father, Brother, Uncle, and Patriarch, His Excellency, Dr. Emmanuel Eweta Uduaghan, former Governor of Delta State, who departed this world on the morning of 19th October 2026.

He served Delta State with distinction as Commissioner for Health from 1999 to 2003, Secretary to the State Government from 2003 to 2007, and Governor from 2007 to 2015. Throughout his years of public service, he demonstrated a commitment to the human and infrastructural development of the state.

His passing is an immeasurable loss to our family, the people of Delta State, and Nigeria at large. Beyond his public service, he was a beloved father, brother, uncle, and respected patriarch whose presence enriched our lives. We will deeply miss him and forever cherish his memory and enduring legacy.

We thank Almighty God for his life and pray that He grants his soul eternal rest and comforts our family, friends, associates, and all who mourn this painful loss.

Rest well, our beloved Father, grandfather, Brother, and Uncle. Your memory will forever remain in our hearts.

Asamaigor, may your gentle soul rest in perfect peace. Amen.

Signed Toju Uduaghan on behalf of the Uduaghan Family.

World.title: Police rescue eight kidnap victims, arrest two suspects
World.content:
The Benue State Police Command says it has rescued eight kidnapped victims and arrested two suspects following an abduction along the Ugbokolo-Ajegbe-Awume Road in Ohimini Local Government Area.

The victims were abducted on Tuesday, 13 October, at about 8:15 p.m. by armed men who intercepted a group of people returning from a village market before Ipiga village, the police said in a statement on Monday.

The statement, signed by the police spokesperson, Peter Aondongu, said two victims were rescued on 16 October and six others on 18 October.

The victims were taken to the Federal University of Health Sciences Teaching Hospital, Otukpo, for medical examinations and treatment.

The police said officers from the command, the Police Mobile Force, and the Benue State Civil Protection Guards were involved.

The statement said officers arrested two suspects, identified as Echefu Emmanuel and Obonyilor Emmanuel, during the operation, who are assisting with investigations.

The police said efforts were ongoing to arrest other members of the suspected gang.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The Commissioner of Police in Benue, Cletus Nwadiogbu, commended the officers involved and said the command would sustain intelligence-led operations against kidnapping and other violent crimes.

He also urged residents to provide security agencies with credible information and report suspicious activities.

Catholic priest among abductees

The police announcement follows the kidnapping of John Otache, the priest in charge of St Margaret’s Parish, Ajegbe-Awume, in Ohimini LGA.

PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that the Catholic Diocese of Otukpo confirmed the priest’s abduction on 13 October while he was returning from Otukpo.

The police spokesperson, Mr Aondongu, had confirmed the incident, saying efforts were underway to rescue the priest.

In a statement, the Bishop of the Catholic Diocese of Otukpo, Michael Ekwoyi Apochi, appealed to Christians and other people of goodwill to pray for the priest’s safe release.

The latest police statement did not identify the eight rescued victims or confirm whether Father Otache was among them. His status therefore remains unclear from the information provided by the command.

READ ALSO: Benue Catholic school relocates students over security concerns

Police deny withdrawal of officers from Ayilamo

The rescue announcement also comes days after the police command dismissed reports that Mobile Police personnel had withdrawn from Ayilamo in Logo LGA, another area affected by insecurity.

In a statement dated 16 October, the command described the report as false and said Mobile Police personnel, the divisional police team and other tactical units remained in the community.

The report claimed the officers left with their belongings, including an armoured personnel carrier, raising residents’ concerns about security in the area.

Mr Nwadiogbu urged residents to remain calm and verify information before sharing it, warning against circulating unconfirmed reports that could cause panic.

The command said security personnel remained deployed in Ayilamo to protect lives and property.

The police have urged residents across Benue to cooperate with security agencies by providing credible information that could assist operations against criminal groups.

World.title: Ogoni Oil Resumption: Tinubu misled on true situation — SSRG
World.content:
Group demands 50,000bpd crude allocation for coastal highway

By Daniel Abia, Port Harcourt

The Convener of the South-South Reawakening Group (SSRG), Joseph Ambakaderimo, has said President Bola Tinubu may not be receiving adequate information about the situation in Ogoniland, a development he believes could be delaying the planned resumption of oil production in the area.

Ambakaderimo called on the Federal Government to address the concerns of the Ogoni people before proceeding with oil exploration, insisting that their interests and demands must be given priority in ongoing negotiations.

Speaking on efforts to restore oil production in Ogoniland, he said the President needed accurate information on developments in the area to enable him to make informed decisions.

“I think Mr President is not being properly informed of what is going on in Ogoniland. Therefore, it will be difficult for him to make very sound pronouncements and determine the proper way forward,” he said.

He urged the Federal Government, through the Office of the National Security Adviser, NSA, to examine the Ogoni Bill of Rights and identify and implement the demands considered most important to the people.

“The interest of Ogoni people is paramount to oil extraction. What does the Federal Government have for the Ogoni people? That should be the most important thing before the planned oil resumption,” he said.

Ambakaderimo argued that Nigeria had abundant oil and gas resources that could be harnessed to drive economic development and fund critical infrastructure.

On the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, he dismissed concerns that difficult terrain in parts of the South-South could make construction impracticable, insisting that modern engineering and technology could overcome such challenges.

“I don’t want to hear it. I don’t like it, because I know with engineering, with modern technology, you can build on any kind of environment and make progress for your people,” he said.

He called for a review of the project’s feasibility studies where necessary, rather than abandoning or altering the original route.

“I believe the feasibility of that road has been done. We know the processes of building roads, infrastructure, all over the world. Proper and concrete feasibility would have been done. So let the engineers go back to the drawing board,” he said.

The SSRG convener said the coastal highway had remained on the drawing board for decades, adding that the Federal Government should seize the opportunity to complete the project in line with the expectations of communities along its route.

He called on the government to allocate 50,000 barrels of crude oil per day to finance the multi-billion-dollar project, arguing that Nigeria had sufficient resources to fund the infrastructure without diverting it from its original alignment.

“Who said we don’t have the money? Nigeria has the money. Allocate 50,000 barrels of crude oil every day. And pay. And get it done,” he said.

Ambakaderimo insisted that the highway must extend to Calabar, Cross River State, traversing all the states in the South-South geopolitical zone as originally conceived.

“I think that project should go on, should progress as per the original design, to having it at the Calabar end, traversing all the states in the South-South geopolitical zone. There shouldn’t be any form of diversion, negotiation,” he said.

He opposed any attempt to realign the coastal highway with the existing East-West Road, insisting that both routes should be maintained.

“We want to see the coastal road side-by-side the East-West Road. We want to see that happen. Not to do any alignment. Alignment of what? Where? We need that coastal road,” he said.

To support his proposal, Ambakaderimo cited the Third Mainland Bridge in Lagos as an example of major infrastructure allegedly financed through crude oil proceeds.

“The Third Mainland Bridge was paid with crude oil,” he said, adding that part of the payment was made to the construction company involved in the project.

He questioned why the Federal Government could not adopt a similar financing arrangement for the coastal highway, given the country’s oil and gas resources.

World.title: NMA president condemns attacks on doctors, demands safe workplaces
World.content:
By Dayo Johnson, Akure

The President of the Nigerian Medical Association (NMA), Prof. Afekhide Ernest Omoti, has condemned the rising cases of threats, intimidation and physical assaults against healthcare workers in the country, calling for stronger measures to guarantee their safety in the workplace.

Omoti also warned that poor working conditions, inadequate remuneration and insecurity were worsening the migration of Nigerian doctors, stressing that patriotism alone could not persuade medical professionals to remain in the country.

He spoke in his address to mark the 2026 Physicians’ Week, themed “Securing the Future of Medicine in Nigeria,” delivered on his behalf in Akure by the Ondo State NMA Chairman, Dr. Roland Bola Arohunmolase.

According to him, the wellbeing of physicians is inseparable from their working environment, adding that doctors cannot provide compassionate care while living in fear.

“A doctor cannot provide compassionate care while constantly worrying about personal safety.

“The increasing incidents of threats, intimidation, assault and other forms of violence against healthcare workers are unacceptable. Hospitals must be places of healing — not theatres of violence,” he said.

Omoti said the NMA would continue to demand safe workplaces, adequate protection, appropriate equipment, decent accommodation where necessary and improved conditions of service that reflect the responsibilities of the medical profession.

“The safety of doctors is not negotiable. And when doctors are safe, patients are safer,” he declared.

He said the association would engage governments, employers, hospital administrators, security agencies and other stakeholders to develop enforceable mechanisms for protecting healthcare workers.
