World.title: Africa: Every Story Is Unique, Every Journey Matters for Women's Cancers
World.content:
Raising awareness of early detection of breast cancer, at the WHO regional office for Africa.

guest column

Addis Ababa and Geneva — Leaders of the Organization of African First Ladies for Development, the African Union and the World Health Organization issue a call to accelerate action on women's cancers in Africa in this AllAfrica guest column during Breast Cancer Awareness Month

Across Africa, too many women are dying prematurely from breast and cervical cancers. In 2024 alone, 350,000 women across the continent died from these diseases, often because prevention, early detection, diagnosis and treatment came too late or were inaccessible.

Behind every statistic is a woman, a family and a community. A mother waiting too long for a diagnosis. A daughter unable to access preventive care. A family struggling to afford treatment.

These stories are unique but the responsibility to respond is shared.



Our message to governments, policymakers and partners is clear: the time has come to accelerate action on women's cancers and move them from the margins of health policy to the centre of Africa's health, development and financing agendas.

The African Union is leading the way by placing the health and wellbeing of Africa's people at the heart of the continent's development agenda. This leadership provides an important platform for Member States to translate continental commitments on women's health, noncommunicable diseases and universal health coverage into measurable results.

Through the Organization of African First Ladies for Development (OAFLAD), African First Ladies are bringing a complementary and powerful form of leadership. They are using their voices and platforms to mobilize political attention, engage communities, challenge stigma and keep the experiences of women and families visible in national and continental discussions.

WHO, through its initiatives on breast and cervical cancer, is supporting governments and communities with the evidence, technical approaches and implementation support needed to translate political commitment into effective services.

The challenge is substantial.

Breast and cervical cancer burdens are increasing across Africa. Women still face barriers to vaccination, screening, diagnosis, referral, treatment, palliative care and survivorship support. Diagnosis frequently occurs at advanced stages, when treatment becomes more difficult, more costly and less likely to succeed. WHO's latest Global Status Report on Cancer, issued this year, provided the first global estimates of breast cancer survival and cervical cancer screening coverage. It showed that the African continent is lagging behind the progress happening elsewhere.

Yet there is hope. WHO's Global Breast Cancer Initiative and Cervical Cancer Elimination Initiative provide governments with a practical pathway to improve outcomes. Through multi-sectoral partnerships, WHO is bringing resources to implement new global standards in the prevention and care of breast and cervical cancers, already benefiting millions of women on the continent.

Current efforts alone are not enough.

Governments must integrate women's cancers into national health strategies, primary health care, essential benefit packages and domestic financing priorities. Development partners must align behind country-led priorities and invest in sustainable systems rather than fragmented interventions. Parliamentarians must support enabling legislation, adequate budgets and accountability. Survivors, civil society and communities must have a meaningful voice in shaping policies and assessing progress. Political champions must keep women's cancers visible at the highest levels of decision-making.

The respective strengths of our institutions must be pooled.

OAFLAD uses advocacy and mobilizes political attention. The African Union provides continental leadership and policy direction. WHO brings evidence, standards and technical and implementation support. Governments translate commitments into national policies, budgets and services. Partners bring catalytic financing, innovation and implementation capacity.

Together, these contributions can turn awareness into policy, policy into investment and investment into services that women can actually access.

The steps to expand this access are clear.

We must expand HPV vaccination, cervical cancer screening and breast health awareness. We must shorten the time from detection to diagnosis and treatment. We must strengthen pathology, imaging, referral pathways, surgery, radiotherapy, access to medicines, palliative care and survivorship support. We must also protect families from financial hardship caused by cancer care.

These investments can do more than strengthen cancer care for women. They will reinforce primary health care and accelerate progress towards universal health coverage.

The time is ripe to make these investments and deliver results. Africa stands at a defining moment. Through the African Union, OAFLAD, WHO, governments and many committed partners, there is today a growing momentum to advance a stronger continental agenda for women's cancers and other noncommunicable diseases.

During October's Breast Cancer Awareness Month, the theme "Every Story is Unique, Every Journey Matters" reminds us that every woman experiences cancer differently. But the need is universal for sustained leadership, financing, investment in research and accountability to deliver these solutions at scale. possible thanks to the leadership, knowledge and capacity that Africa possesses to protect women's futures from the threat of cancer. What will make these advances possible is the leadership, knowledge and capacity that Africa possesses to protect women's futures from the threat of cancer.

Access to prevention and care should never depend on geography, income or circumstance.

We call for greater investment in the prevention and care of women's cancers. We call for women-centred policies that place equity, dignity and access at the heart of cancer care. We call for reliable domestic financing, aligned partner support and stronger accountability for results. We call for greater protections from the social, physical and economic hardship that cancer can bring.

Close 

This is not only a call for greater awareness. It is a call to governments, political leaders, partners and communities to act with urgency.

Because every woman deserves the opportunity to live a healthy and productive life.

Because every family deserves more time with its mothers, daughters and sisters. And because Africa's development depends on the health of its women and girls.

For Africa, tackling women's cancers is not only a health imperative; it is a question of equity, dignity and development, and a measure of whether our health systems serve every woman.

The measure of our commitment will not be the declarations we make, but whether women can access prevention, screening, timely diagnosis and quality treatment when and where they need them.

H.E. Dr Fatima Maada Bio is President of the Organization of African First Ladies for Development; H.E. Amb. Amma Twum-Amoa is African Union Commissioner for Health, Humanitarian Affairs and Social Development; Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus is Director-General of the World Health Organization

The authors acknowledge the WHO Liaison Office to the African Union and UNECA, the UN Economic Commission for Africa, for coordinating this joint contribution.

World.title: Zimbabwe: Zimbabwe's Women Cotton Farmers Stitch More Value From Their White Gold
World.content:
Women cotton farmers in Zimbabwe’s Shamva district are turning to sewing and collective savings to diversify their incomes and adapt to a changing climate. Making school uniforms and taking clothing orders, they are creating earning opportunities beyond the crop they call their “white gold”.

For Brenda Dzuda, cotton is “white gold” that helps support her household in a community where, she says, women have few alternatives for earning a living.

But the 48-year-old widow who farms four hectares in Shamva, Mashonaland Central, says unpredictable weather, poor seed and disappointing prices are making it harder to realise the value in her gold.

“Shamva is a very dry region, and most men survive on illegal gold mining. But for us as women, cotton is our white gold,” she said.

Dzuda and other women farmers say cultural expectations and traditional restrictions limit their participation in mining. Cotton offers a way to earn, but increasingly, they are looking beyond the fields to sustain their households.

Through sewing and collective savings, women in Shamva are creating another source of income when harvests disappoint, or cotton payments arrive late.



When the Weather Becomes an Economic Burden

Across the fields, dry stalks remain where cotton plants once stood. The harvest has been packed into sacks, some already sold by farmers hoping to turn a season’s labour into household income.

But returns have not always matched expectations. Seed, fertiliser, chemicals and labour demand investment before farmers know what the harvest will bring. Unpredictable rainfall, prolonged dry spells and high temperatures add to the uncertainty.

“Cotton does not require much water, but the rains are no longer reliable. Sometimes they come earlier than expected or heavier, and sometimes the dry spells last longer than cotton can withstand. We are worried because our livelihoods depend on this crop,” said Dzuda.

Zimbabwe’s Meteorological Services Department had forecast an erratic start to the 2025–26 rainfall season, followed by improved rainfall prospects from December. For farmers such as Dzuda, the timing and distribution of rain shape planting decisions and crop development.

Dzuda said she was selling her cotton for US$0.24 a kilogram, questioning both the price and the quality of seed supplied to farmers.

“The money we are selling per kilogram versus the world market price is very upsetting. We are also not getting the best seed, then our cotton is sold as a third grade; then on the other side we are constantly attacked by the shift in weather patterns. This is a double blow for us,” she said.

For her, adapting means getting the crop through the season and earning enough to justify the investment. She also wants support for women to turn cotton into products beyond the raw crop.

“We had an exchange with women cotton farmers in Malawi, and they are doing value addition. As Zimbabwe Women in Cotton, we also wish to have backyard industries because in cotton we get toilet paper, cooking oil, stock feed and many others. We can do that on our own,” she said.

Seventy-four and Still Waiting

About 60 kilometres from Dzuda’s farming area, 74-year-old widow Getrude Motsi faces another part of the struggle.

At her home, sacks of harvested cotton remain stored, waiting to be sold. The crop represents months of work and money that could meet household needs or help finance another season.

“I have been growing cotton since 2014, and for the past seasons everything seemed to be going well; weather conditions are worsening, and the severity of it is the most scariest,” she said.

Motsi said delayed payments compounded the difficulties caused by the weather, weakening the economic security she had relied on cotton to provide.

Her experience shows how uncertainty can continue after the work in the fields is complete. A farmer must grow and protect the crop, harvest it, find a buyer and then receive payment.

Until then, the value of that work remains tied up in the cotton.

How Cotton is Priced and Paid For

Responding to farmers’ concerns about prices, grading and payments, the Cotton Company of Zimbabwe (COTTCO) said producer prices were benchmarked against international market fundamentals in consultation with regulators.

A company representative said cotton was graded from A to D based on fibre maturity, cleanliness, colour and trash content.

Farmers initially receive a base payment at the lowest grade, D, paid 70% in US dollars and 30% in Zimbabwe Gold, or ZiG. COTTCO said these initial payments had been made in full for the past season.

The company said it was completing laboratory grading and raising funds for additional payments to farmers whose cotton qualified for Grades A, B or C.

COTTCO also said it worked with the government’s Presidential Input Programme to provide subsidised seed, fertiliser, chemicals, herbicides and mechanised tillage services.

Addressing concerns about seed quality and weather risks, it said it supplied certified seed, including drought-tolerant, early-maturing varieties. Extension officers trained farmers in moisture conservation, input placement, weed control and integrated pest management.

For farmers, payment timing and the income remaining after production costs help determine whether they can support their households and plant again.

Another Way to Earn

Patience Zhakata, national chairperson of Zimbabwe Women in Cotton, said the restrictions women described around mining reflected wider questions about their ability to make economic decisions, own productive assets and control the proceeds of their labour.

“So as an organisation, cotton is white gold because that is the only field we can mine without restrictions,” she said.

Cotton has offered women a route into agricultural enterprise. Now, they are working to create income beyond the crop.

In 2022, the group approached Zimbabwe’s First Lady, Auxillia Mnangagwa, who assisted them with sewing machines, to which they started a sewing project in February 2023. Women are using the machines to make clothes and mend garments for people in their communities.

Close 

Happiness Marape, a trainer in the sewing project, said 60 women in Shamva participated, meeting on different days so everyone could use the machines.

“The initiative has 60 women in Shamva who meet weekly but on different days so that we all get access to the sewing machines. The sewing machines initiative came as an idea to counter climate shocks which are always attacking women, cotton farmers.”

The group takes orders for school uniforms and other garments, as well as repairs. Members also save together, creating a fund they can draw on for household needs and farming expenses.

“We also do savings as a group to assist each other financially or loan when we want to buy farming inputs,” Marape said.

The sewing work provides income beyond the agricultural season and another source of earnings when farming falls short.

“The sewing initiative is helping us a lot. When the fields fail to produce, we then rely on sewing, telling people that we work from cotton to the fabric. We get money from there and put it in our savings, and we all benefit,” she said.

Sewing does not resolve the problems of cotton prices, production costs, or delayed payments. But it gives the women another way to earn while they continue farming.

Back in Shamva, Dzuda’s description of cotton as women’s “white gold” still carries hope. For the women building savings from stitches as well as harvests, its value is measured in what their work can provide: money for their households and a way to begin the next season.

World.title: East Africa: Ghana Set to Overtake Ethiopia As Africa's Eighth-Largest Economy After Kenya Takes East Africa Lead
World.content:
Addis Abeba — Ghana is projected to overtake Ethiopia as Africa's eighth-largest economy in 2026, with its gross domestic product (GDP) forecast to reach US$128.64 billion, exceeding Ethiopia's projected US$127.15 billion by US$1.49 billion, according to the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) October 2026 World Economic Outlook (WEO), as reported by African Business Insider on 17 October.

The projected shift comes after Kenya overtook Ethiopia as East Africa's largest economy in nominal US dollar terms, marking another change in the continent's economic rankings driven partly by exchange-rate movements rather than differences in real economic growth.

The IMF's latest estimates place Ghana eighth among Africa's largest economies, ahead of Ethiopia in ninth place and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), whose economy is projected at US$122.28 billion. While Ghana's nominal GDP is expected to edge ahead of Ethiopia's, the two countries have markedly different growth forecasts.

Ethiopia's economy is projected to expand by 9.2% in real terms in 2026, compared with Ghana's forecast growth of 5.7%. However, the depreciation of the Ethiopian birr following the government's July 2024 foreign-exchange reforms has reduced the dollar value of the country's economic output, narrowing its position in nominal GDP rankings despite strong projected domestic growth.



Ghana's recovery and economic position

Ghana's projected rise comes as the West African country continues to recover from a severe financial crisis marked by currency depreciation, high inflation, mounting public debt and pressure on government finances.

In 2023, Ghana secured a US$3 billion IMF support programme aimed at restoring macroeconomic stability, addressing debt vulnerabilities and rebuilding investor confidence. The government subsequently pursued fiscal reforms, debt restructuring and measures to stabilise prices and the national currency.

The country's economic position is also supported by exports of gold, cocoa, oil and gas, alongside financial services and a growing consumer market. Gold remains a major source of export earnings and foreign exchange, with higher international prices providing additional support to inflows.

However, an improved position in nominal GDP rankings does not necessarily translate into higher living standards or stronger productive capacity. Sustaining the recovery will depend on Ghana's ability to attract long-term investment, create employment and expand industrial production.

Ethiopia's growth versus dollar-denominated output

Ethiopia's projected position reflects the distinction between real economic growth and nominal GDP measured in US dollars. While real GDP growth captures changes in domestic production after accounting for price changes, nominal GDP expressed in dollars is also affected by inflation and movements in the exchange rate.

The depreciation of the birr following Ethiopia's July 2024 shift toward a more market-determined foreign-exchange system substantially reduced the dollar valuation of its output. The reform formed part of the government's broader economic programme, supported by an approximately US$3.4 billion IMF Extended Credit Facility.

As Addis Standard reported last week, Kenya's emergence as East Africa's largest economy in dollar terms was similarly shaped by exchange-rate movements, with the comparatively stronger performance of the Kenyan shilling increasing the dollar value of its economic output.

The IMF's October projections indicate that Ethiopia's economy is expected to grow by 9.2% in 2026 and 7.8% in 2027, while Kenya's growth is forecast at 4.5% and 4.7%, respectively. The figures highlight how an economy can record faster real growth without maintaining a higher ranking when GDP is measured in US dollars.

The projected shift involving Ghana therefore does not, by itself, establish that its underlying economy is growing faster than Ethiopia's. Rather, it underscores the influence of exchange-rate movements and macroeconomic conditions on the relative dollar value of African economies.

Close 

The IMF projects Sub-Saharan Africa's economy to grow by 4.5% in both 2026 and 2027. However, its October WEO, titled Resilience Under Strain, Urgent Choices, warns that high debt-servicing costs, limited foreign-exchange reserves and declining aid are constraining governments' ability to respond to economic shocks.

For Ethiopia, the projected change in Africa's economic rankings highlights the challenge of sustaining rapid domestic growth while managing currency pressures, inflation and foreign-exchange constraints. For Ghana, moving ahead in nominal GDP terms would mark a recovery in its relative economic position, but translating that ranking into lasting gains in investment, employment and industrial development remains a separate challenge.

World.title: Tanzania: Anaesthesia Fears Delay Surgeries At Bugando
World.content:
Mwanza — FEAR of anaesthesia, fuelled by misconceptions about its safety, is among the challenges facing Bugando Zonal Referral Hospital, with some patients postponing or abandoning surgical procedures until their conditions become more complicated.

Head of the hospital's Anaesthesia Department, Dr Rebecca Shija, said initial assessments had identified misconceptions surrounding anaesthesia as one of the reasons some patients were reluctant to undergo surgery.

Speaking during the commemoration of World Anaesthesia Day at the hospital yesterday, Dr Shija said some people wrongly believed that anaesthesia was equivalent to half-death, creating unnecessary fear about undergoing surgical procedures.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

She said others feared that spinal anaesthesia, which involves administering medication into the fluid-filled space surrounding the spinal cord, could cause permanent back pain.

"These misconceptions have made some patients avoid surgery, with others returning for treatment only when their conditions have advanced, making their recovery more difficult to predict," she said. Dr Shija added that some patients abandoned the process altogether and never returned to the hospital for the recommended procedures.

To address the challenge, she said Bugando was intensifying public education to explain the role of anaesthesia in surgery and reassure patients about the safety measures used by trained specialists.

She emphasised that modern equipment, qualified personnel and careful monitoring were essential components of safe anaesthesia services.

"Medical teams monitor patients before, during and after surgery to assess their condition and identify potential complications, allowing them to respond promptly, when necessary," she said.

Dr Shija further said patients with serious non-communicable diseases, including hypertension, diabetes, cancer, kidney disease and heart conditions, required careful assessment before anaesthesia and surgery to identify risks and determine appropriate management.

She also called on stakeholders to support government efforts to increase the number of anaesthesia specialists at the hospital, saying the department needed to expand its workforce to meet growing demand.

According to Dr Shija, the hospital's anaesthesia services handled at least 500 patients a week, while the department had six specialists, highlighting the need for additional trained personnel.

She said Bugando was also working with stakeholders to strengthen the capacity of healthcare providers in other hospitals across the Lake Zone, particularly in the use of modern anaesthesia machines and related medical equipment.

The initiative aims to improve the quality of anaesthesia services and bring appropriate care closer to communities outside major referral centres.

Close 

Dr Shija further proposed the introduction of degree programmes in anaesthesia at the Catholic University of Health and Allied Sciences (CUHAS) in Mwanza as part of efforts to address the shortage of specialists.

Bugando Director General, Dr Alicia Massenga, thanked the government for supporting improvements at the hospital, including the provision of modern medical equipment and medicines, as well as sponsorship for staff training to strengthen their anaesthesia skills.

Dr Massenga said the hospital had five anaesthesia specialists and 46 non-physician anaesthesia providers, underscoring the importance of continued investment in the workforce.

"The commemoration served as a reminder to the public of the critical role anaesthesia plays in surgical care. Safe surgery depends on safe anaesthesia," she said.

World.title: Nigeria: Dangote Group Didn't Advertise Thousands of Jobs At Kenyan Refinery - Ads Circulating On Facebook Fake
World.content:
Dangote Group didn't advertise thousands of jobs at Kenyan refinery - ads circulating on Facebook fake

IN SHORT: Job ads circulating on Facebook claim Dangote Group is recruiting thousands of workers for its planned refinery in Lamu, Kenya. But be warned: the advertised vacancies don't appear on the company's official careers portal, and the ads direct applicants to unverified email addresses.

On 30 September 2026, construction of the Dangote oil refinery began in Lamu county, northeastern Kenya, as Kenyan president William Ruto and Dangote Group founder Aiko Dangote broke ground.

The refinery is expected to process 700,000 barrels of crude oil per day and create thousands of jobs, making recruitment claims bearing the Dangote name particularly attractive to job seekers in Kenya.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

In this context, an advert started circulating on Facebook, claiming that Dangote Group had thousands of vacancies for the Lamu plant.

The listed positions include 412 electricians, 221 plumbers, 750 brick masons, 142 iron workers, 110 carpenters, 179 tile setters/flooring installers, 65 excavator/equipment operators, 157 welders, and 1,870 general labourers.

It asks interested users to send applications to the provided email address by 14 October 2026 and warns them to apply for only one position, saying multiple applications will result in disqualification.

This job ad and a similar version have also been posted here, here, here, here and here.

But can they be trusted? We checked.

Fake job ad

We searched Dangote Group's official careers portal, as well as its Facebook and X accounts, but found no announcement confirming the advertised vacancies.

The adverts direct applicants to email addresses that do not match the official Dangote Group email domain, @dangote.com. One lists an Outlook address, while the other provides a Gmail address. They also don't link to the company's recruitment portal. These are major red flags.

The adverts also provide limited information about the vacancies. Although they list numerous positions across different departments, they lack detailed job descriptions and responsibilities. Some posts don't even specify the application deadline.

All signs point to fake job adverts using the group's name.

Remember, do not send your personal or banking information to unverified email addresses. Follow official channels for genuine vacancies.

World.title: Africa: A New SAPS Oath Could Help Restore Police Pride and Public Trust
World.content:
analysis

Building a professional police identity based on a strong ethical commitment is as important as discipline and accountability.

There is no question that the South African Police Service (SAPS) is in trouble. Whether measured by low public trust or the evidence of organised criminal infiltration presented to the Madlanga Commission, it is clear that serious steps must be taken to turn the SAPS into a trusted, credible police service. But what should these steps be?

A critical issue is police integrity. Many reforms currently envisaged involve subjecting members to greater scrutiny in order to expose those involved in wrongdoing and remove criminally oriented staff.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia's 'police reset agenda' includes measures to improve the SAPS disciplinary system and encourage the reporting of crime committed by members. Those convicted of offences involving dishonesty, corruption or violent crime, including rape, should face mandatory dismissal, he said.

The Madlanga Commission report, to be submitted to President Cyril Ramaphosa in January 2027, will likely also call for stronger scrutiny of SAPS personnel through better vetting, financial disclosures and lifestyle audits.

Cachalia says the main purpose of the reset agenda is to 'build a disciplined, professional and ethical police service that commands public confidence and supports honest police officers in carrying out their duties effectively.'

Considering the current allegations it faces, turning the SAPS into a trusted and respected service requires engagement with the foundations of policing. As much as it needs more scrutiny, the SAPS - and members of metro and other policing formations - also need strong moral leadership.

The SAPS Code of Conduct was adopted in 1997, making it nearly 30 years old and out of date. In its 2024 report on strengthening policing in South Africa, the Institute for Security Studies (ISS) recommended measures to build 'a more positive and professional police identity' that restores pride in wearing the SAPS insignia and uniform. The ISS said 'building greater self-respect within the SAPS' was an 'essential element of building public trust in the SAPS.'

The ISS motivated for 'a succinct new SAPS oath or declaration' to which members should commit. This should convey core principles that are meaningful to honest police officers. It should be clear that only police who are true to these principles are worthy of wearing the SAPS uniform and badge.

The International Association of Chiefs of Police model Code of Ethics emphasises a similar point. It requires officers to recognise that only if they are 'true to the ethics of police service' should they be entitled to wear the badge.

How a new oath or declaration is written may be as important as what it says. It should be concise and easy to understand. Police codes of conduct often refer vaguely to upholding the law. An exception is the 74-word statement of ethical policing principles published by Britain's College of Policing, which foregrounds courage, respect, empathy and public service.

Alongside the 1997 Code of Conduct, the SAPS Code of Ethics, first published in 2011, should also be interrogated. For instance, it narrows down the principle of respect to respect for diversity. Britain's College of Policing, by contrast, defines respect more broadly, linking it to empathy. It calls for police to understand the views of others and 'recognise and respond to the physical, mental and emotional challenges that we and other people may face.'

This is not to say that South Africa should replicate codes adopted in other countries. The ISS recommended that the new oath or declaration emphasise 'dignity and respect.' SAPS members should conduct themselves, it said, 'in a manner that is based on treating members of the public with respect, and that promotes respect for the SAPS.'

Building respect for the SAPS is connected to questions of integrity. The British College of Policing embeds integrity in an ethic of 'courage' that asks police to be accountable for decisions and stand 'against anything that could bring our profession into disrepute.'

In South African policing, courage and integrity are also intertwined. The physical courage required to help people in danger must be combined with the moral courage to withstand pressure from corrupt colleagues to stay silent about their wrongdoing.

Studies show that police often see loyalty to colleagues as a moral duty. But the positive solidarity involved in defending colleagues who are in danger must be distinguished from the unethical solidarity of the code of silence that conceals police criminality. Recognising that providing support to colleagues is fundamental to policing, ISS recommended that police commit to 'support their colleagues, but not at the expense of professional policing standards.'

Close 

Ideally, supporting colleagues should include being attentive to other situations in which police need help, considering that officers face a high risk of stress-related mental and physical ill-health. The duty of care that SAPS members carry towards the public should also extend to their colleagues and themselves.

A new oath will work best if used by police commanders in their day-to-day engagement with officers. It will not get corrupt and dishonest police to change their ways. But it can help honourable members embed the ethics of policing within the work, and reputation, of the SAPS. Rather than a burdensome obligation, a well-considered, concise new code can inspire police to uphold high standards.

Honest, committed officers are the most important asset that South Africa has for building an honourable and trusted SAPS. To win public respect, the SAPS should help such members maintain clarity about the standards they must uphold.

David Bruce, Independent Researcher and ISS Consultant

NEWSOM-BACKED LAW LETS ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHILD RAPIST SEEK EARLY RELEASE AGAIN AS DA URGES 'STOP THE MADNESS'

He was originally sentenced to 124 years in prison. He has now been released from State prison and is reportedly residing in our community. This is unacceptable."

Luster was convicted in 2003 of 86 felony counts stemming from the drugging and sexual assault of three women at his beachfront home in Ventura County.

Prosecutors said he used the drug GHB to render the women unconscious before sexually assaulting them.

Luster fled to Mexico in January 2003 while free on $1 million bail during his trial. He was convicted in his absence and later captured by celebrity bounty hunter Duane "Dog" Chapman in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico.

The Max Factor heir was originally sentenced to 124 years in prison, but a California judge set aside the sentence in March 2013 after finding that the trial court failed to adequately explain its reasons for imposing consecutive sentences, as Fox News Digital previously reported.

CALIFORNIA SUED OVER POLICY THAT COULD FREE SERIAL KILLERS AS LACI PETERSON'S FRIEND SOUNDS ALARM

NEWSOM BLASTED BY SHERIFF IN HIS OWN BACKYARD OVER CALIFORNIA CRIME AS VICTIMS CRY FOUL

CHARLES MANSON FOLLOWER TIED TO SHARON TATE MURDERS GETS RECOMMENDED FOR PAROLE AFTER 55 YEARS IN PRISON

Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon defended the Trump administration's investigation into noncitizen voters ahead of the midterm elections during CBS' "60 Minutes" on Sunday.

"There are people who feel that the point is to sow distrust about the whole election system. There are very few people who are noncitizens who end up voting — very, very few. And so, therefore, what's the purpose?" Lesley Stahl, host of "60 Minutes" asked Dhillon.

ELECTION CRIME ARRESTS KEEP PILING UP AS DEMS INSIST IT 'JUST DOESN'T HAPPEN'

Dhillon responded, "The point is actually the opposite of what you were saying. It's not to sow distrust. The distrust is there. And so, all of these kinds of crimes are being prosecuted now for the first time really, in volume. And look, even the Biden administration prosecuted 13 people for noncitizen voting."

Stahl interrupted and said the numbers were tiny.

"So Lesley, we've been in office for less than two years. We've had investigations ongoing for over a year, and it takes time. There are literally thousands of them out there that we are looking at," Dhillion responded.

DEMOCRAT NEW JERSEY GOVERNOR SAYS THOUSANDS OF NONCITIZENS DISCOVERED ON VOTER ROLLS, PURGED

Dhillon pledged in July that the Trump administration will pursue every provable case of illegal voting under what she described as a "broken windows" enforcement strategy, marking a sharp shift from prior administrations as the DOJ intensifies scrutiny of voter rolls following revelations that noncitizens were registered to vote in New Jersey.

Dhillon told Fox News Digital at the time the department's approach is to investigate every credible lead and prosecute every case supported by the evidence, rejecting what she described as the prior view that only widespread fraud or election-altering misconduct warranted federal action.

Her statement came after Democratic New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill revealed that thousands of noncitizens ended up on the state's voter rolls through the motor-voter system.

The "60 Minutes" host asked if there were plans to send Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to polling locations.

Dhillon said there were "no plans" to do so.

Dhillon dismissed concerns that President Donald Trump would challenge the results of the midterms as "paranoia," Stahl said during a voice-over moment in the segment.

The "60 Minutes" host asked Dhillon, "So would you consider a noncitizen voting an irregularity that would lead to a challenge of the vote?"

Stahl went on to ask if Dhillon could rule out a challenge to a state vote.

World.title: Alberta holds non-binding separation vote as independence fight grips Canada
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

OTTAWA: Residents of Alberta began voting Monday in a non-binding referendum that will determine whether the western-Canadian province should pursue separation from Canada.

The vote comes at a time when the province is mourning the deaths of four soldiers, while dozens of others were injured from a fast-moving fire that burned through a military base in Alberta.

While the results of a poll involving 1,021 respondents released by Abacus Data on Saturday showed that 74% of decided voters favor Alberta remaining within the Canadian Confederation, the independence issue won’t disappear for the nearly 30% (26%) who want Alberta’s government to begin the process to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether Alberta should separate from Canada, according to veteran separatist organizer Cory Morgan, who leads a group called Pathway to Independence.

"It will say that about one in three Albertans have had it," Morgan told Fox News Digital. "There is a big rift within Alberta and if things don’t change, it will be a growing faction in this province – so this vote is an important one."

EXCLUSIVE: ‘BROKEN COUNTRY’ FILMMAKER WARNS CANADA’S SLOW DECLINE OFFERS CAUTIONARY TALE FOR AMERICANS

About three million Albertans are eligible to vote in the referendum.

Another recent Abacus poll found that 61% of the 1,021 eligible voters surveyed expect Albertans will vote again on separation, even if most will choose to remain in Canada.

On Friday, the Angus Reid Institute released the results of its poll that found 62% of 1,010 Albertans surveyed believe "there will never be an end to the separatist movement" in the province.

Morgan, who led the short-lived Alberta Independence Party from 2000 to 2001, said that while "a vocal minority" within the separatist movement favor Alberta becoming the 51st state, most pro-independence Albertans "don’t want to become a small fish in an even bigger pond." He added that "Albertans in general are not too thrilled with President Trump right now and that makes them less inclined to leave the federation."

At a "Forever Canadian" rally on Friday in Edmonton, where he was raised, Prime Minister Mark Carney told a crowd of over 5,000 people that "this referendum comes at the worst possible time." He said that "the world is becoming more dangerous and divided [and] some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us," making an indirect reference to Trump’s trade war against and annexation talk about Canada.

Alberta-born and raised, 55-year-old Morgan said that his home province is "politically and culturally different" than eastern Canada. "There’s a lot more focus on individual freedoms and property rights," he noted, acknowledging that those values are traditionally viewed as American.

"Most Albertans are going to feel much more comfortable sitting down for a beer with people from Great Falls, Montana than they would in Ottawa," said Morgan. He explained that when Alberta became a Canadian province in 1905, its population grew largely from a migration of Montanans, and when oil was discovered in the 1940s, U.S. companies Chevron and Mobil helped develop what became Alberta’s biggest industry.

Also earlier this year during an appearance on Real America’s Voice at Davos, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent described Alberta as "a natural partner for the U.S." and described Albertans as "very independent people."

In response, Carney said that he "expect[ed] the U.S. administration to respect Canadian sovereignty."

Earlier this month, The Globe and Mail reported that Alberta separatist leaders met with Republican strategists in Calgary in January to look at software designed to identify and mobilize supporters. Separatist leaders also reportedly suggested exchanging water and oil for U.S. support when they met with State Department officials in Washington last year.

CANADIAN PM TELLS TRUMP TO 'STOP TRYING TO BE TOUGH' IN TRADE FIGHT

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith told CBC News that if most Albertans support staying in Canada, she would not hold another referendum on the matter as long as she heads the provincial government.

However, on Oct. 18, 2027, residents of the province will vote again in a general election, and Smith could be out of her job by then, warned Morgan, a founding member of the former conservative Wildrose Party, for which Smith served as leader.

That party merged with the then-Progressive Conservative Party of Alberta in 2020 to form the United Conservative Party (UCP) that Smith heads. But Morgan explained that more than half of the UCP’s nearly 55,000 members support Alberta’s independence. The premier has said that she will vote to keep the province in Canada.

Angus Reid, founder and chairman of the Angus Reid Institute, told Fox News Digital that in his firm’s recent polling, 67% of the 293 UCP voters who support a future binding referendum on separation, said that they would either "definitely support" or "consider" supporting the creation of a separatist provincial political party – not unlike the Parti Québécois, which won the recent election in Quebec.

The emergence of an independence party in Alberta "would probably spell the death of the UCP since it is so badly divided between separatists and non-separatists, and it would likely end the career of Danielle Smith because of the amount of breakage in her party," said Reid, whose firm’s survey found that 60% of the respondents who support a future binding referendum are "more likely sending a message to Ottawa" about the Canadian government’s often fractious relationship with Alberta.

"Separatist types are looking at how much leverage Quebec has been able to achieve in Canada as a result of its threats of exiting, and saying ‘Hold it, we can pay that game too,’" explained Reid.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

As of Saturday, more than 1.2 million Albertans had cast a ballot on the referendum, which, in addition to the question on separation, has nine others, five focusing on immigration, such as one asking voters whether their province should take more control "for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities."

World.title: Top tourist destination in the world shuts down amid violent protests

The Louvre, the globe's most visited and prominent museum, has closed its doors as turmoil sweeps across Paris.

The institution, which houses renowned masterpieces like the "Mona Lisa," announced on Monday that it has shut down due to protesters barricading the entrances, pushing the disruption past a weekend of nationwide riots and demonstrations, according to local newspaper Le Monde.

"Dear visitors, due to student strikes, the museum is currently closed. We apologize for the inconvenience," the Louvre said in a post on X.

FURIOUS CROWDS PROTEST SKY-HIGH HOUSING COSTS AND MASS TOURISM IN MAJOR CITY

No reopening time was provided at the time of publication.

Visitors arriving for a Monday morning visit found the iconic glass pyramid, as well as the Carrousel du Louvre and Passage Richelieu entrances, barricaded by protesters from the École du Louvre, according to Agence France-Presse (AFP).

The blockade — organized in solidarity with nationwide protests over the rising cost of living and recent police actions — forced management to turn away crowds at a site that normally draws up to 20,000 visitors on its busiest days, French media reported.

CLICK HERE TO 

The disruption extends far beyond the Louvre's courtyards.

Following a weekend of violent street clashes that left hundreds of businesses damaged and led to nearly 2,400 arrests across the country, other top Paris destinations, including the Eiffel Tower and major central shopping districts, have been heavily affected as international travelers navigate a city gripped by mass demonstrations and heightened security cordons, according to The Associated Press (AP).

The Eiffel Tower was recently forced to turn away visitors and close its operations for a full day after staff initiated a sudden strike, AP reported.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

The monument's unionized employees organized the walkout to protest limitations placed on female staff members during a private delegation's visit, completely halting public access to the world-famous iron structure, according to several French media outlets.

Outside the immediate city center, the Château de Versailles has also faced abrupt closures that have derailed tourists' itineraries.

The sprawling palace had to close its interior doors to the public on Oct. 6 following a severe power outage in the surrounding area, Xinhua News Agency reported.

Operational hurdles have historically impacted several prominent cultural sites across the French capital.

In September 2025, major institutions, including the Musee d'Orsay and the Arc de Triomphe experienced temporary closures due to staff shortages amid strikes over proposed government spending cuts, Artforum reported.

World.title: Chris Janson has a message for hunting critics as country stars face social media backlash
World.content:
Chris Janson isn't losing any sleep over people who get upset when he posts photos from his hunting trips.

And if you've spent any time on social media lately, you know those people aren't particularly hard to find.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

Anti-hunters always seem to find their way into the comments section when someone posts a photo of a successful hunt. But the trolls really come out of the woodwork when that hunter happens to be a country music star.

Just ask Cody Johnson, who faced backlash over a grizzly bear hunt in Alaska earlier this year. Johnson defended the hunt as a conservation effort, explaining the role of predator management in protecting other wildlife, including moose and caribou.

Then there was Jordan Davis, who caught heat for harvesting an axis deer in Hawaii. Never mind that axis deer are an invasive species that can wreak havoc on the islands' native ecosystems.

And most recently, old hunting photos of Ella Langley resurfaced online, prompting some critics to call for the "Choosin' Texas" singer to be canceled.

So, what does Janson think about all of this?

Well, not much, actually. Because unlike the rest of us, the "Buy Me a Boat" singer has figured out the secret to a happier existence: Stay off social media and don't read the comments.

"I don't watch much internet. I don't watch much TV," Janson told OutKick OutDoors. "I hunt and fish and raise kids and love my wife."

Amen to that.

Watch Chris Janson's entire interview with OutKick OutDoors here:

Janson said he hadn't seen the controversy involving Langley, but he's certainly familiar with the criticism that comes with being a hunter in the public eye.

"If you're in the public spotlight, no matter if it's me, Jordan, Cody, it doesn't matter who it is, you better be ready for arrows to come against you and just build your shield up," he said.

"I don't really care what people think. I want them to like me. I think everybody wants someone to like them, but if they don't, that's okay too."

Janson said his wife, Kelly, and his team handle much of his social media, allowing him to steer clear of the negativity. And frankly, he figures people will find something to complain about no matter what he does.

Post a photo of a Ford truck, and the Chevy fans are upset. Drive a Chevy, and the Dodge guys have something to say.

You get the idea.

Hunting for more than a trophy photo

While Janson isn't particularly concerned about what strangers on the internet think of his hunting habits, he does wish more people understood everything that goes into responsible hunting.

"Who doesn't love a big rack on a great big elk or a big whitetail? And who doesn't love holding up a big fish in a picture?" he said. "But I'm also a conservation guy."

For starters, Janson hunts for food, and much of that food actually ends up on someone else's dinner table.

"Every animal that I've harvested, at least this year, at least 50% of it has gone to someone else to help somebody," he said. "And that's a big part of why I hunt."

Regulated hunting also plays an important role in wildlife management across the United States. Hunting license fees and federal excise taxes on firearms, ammunition and archery equipment help fund habitat restoration, wildlife research and conservation programs. And in some areas, hunting is an important tool for managing animal populations and reducing damage to native ecosystems.

In other words, there's often a whole lot more to that grip-and-grin photo than meets the eye.

Giving back beyond the hunt

Janson's commitment to conservation extends beyond his own time in the woods.

Since 2019, he's partnered with Bass Pro Shops founder Johnny Morris on a signature conservation hat, with proceeds benefiting three nonprofit organizations: Tennessee Hunters for the Hungry, Tennessee Riverkeeper and the Harpeth Conservancy.

Through the Tennessee Wildlife Federation's Hunters for the Hungry program, hunters can donate harvested deer to participating processors, who prepare the venison for distribution to food banks and other organizations serving people in need.

The other two organizations focus on protecting waterways and aquatic ecosystems, including the Harpeth River, where Janson lives.

"I have a very close connection with it," Janson said of the Harpeth. "Lots of Native American history there, and just the best hunting grounds you could ever imagine."

EVA SHOCKEY SAYS SHE RECEIVED 'THOUSANDS AND THOUSANDS' OF DEATH THREATS FROM ANTI-HUNTING ACTIVISTS

And he's taken that same give-back approach into other business partnerships.

Through Crav'n Flavor, Janson helps recognize peer-nominated hometown heroes with grocery assistance and gift cards. He's also teamed up with agricultural seed company Pioneer on its "Hats Off to Farmers" initiative, which raises money for Rural Minds, a nonprofit providing mental health resources to farmers and rural communities.

The partnerships may support different causes, but Janson sees them as part of the same commitment to giving back.

For him, hunting and conservation aren't just about what happens in the woods. They're about taking care of the land, the wildlife and the people who depend on both.

As for the critics, Janson isn't interested in arguing with them.

"For any haters out there on social media, I would just encourage them to try it," he said. "If you haven't, you can't knock it."

"The hunting thing may not be your thing, and I understand that. But the fishing thing, you can throw a fish back, and there's nothing like catching a great big fish or even a small fish. It's fun."



"If you think you hate it, you might find something that you love."

Sure beats griping at strangers on the internet.

World.title: Russians locked out of bank accounts and apartments as Ukraine hits data centers
World.content:
While most Yandex services have been coming back online, three people told NBC News they had been left locked out of their disposable cash and savings for days after disruptions to Yandex Pay, a digital payment service that many Russians use.

Irina, 21, said that in the future she will diversify her deposits across different banks and have a “substantial cash reserve” just in case.

Yandex said Oct. 9 that no employees were hurt and that the company is working to restore service.

“Data centers are the iron heart of Yandex,” the statement said. “Their operation is critical for services that have become part of people’s everyday lives.”

Anastasiya Mityaeva, 25, who splits her time between the southern city of Krasnodar and Moscow, said she was “shocked” by the outages, which initially left her family worried about being able to pay down their mortgage after her account, her mother’s account and her grandmother’s account were all inaccessible.

“The uncertainty was scary,” said Mityaeva, who has two million followers on TikTok and is originally from Russian-annexed Crimea. “We realized just how much hangs on Yandex. We did not quite appreciate it before,” she added.

Mityaeva, who regained access to her money after several days, also had issues calling a taxi on the first day of the outages, and encountered problems with the system to enter her apartment building. Her Yandex home voice assistant, equivalent to an Amazon Echo, stopped responding to requests to play music and turn off the lights.

She did not blame the company, saying Yandex was a “hostage of the situation,” adding: “I understand that this was not up to them, this came from the outside.”

Others were more critical of the company. Viktoria, a 30-year-old barista from Moscow, said she plans to stop using Yandex completely after being unable to access her money during the outages, describing it as the last straw after other recent issues.

She said Saturday that she once again had access to her money through Yandex Pay, but said the service was displaying the wrong balance on her account.

Three taxi drivers in Moscow, who use Yandex’s taxi application to take orders and get paid, all told NBC News they couldn’t see how much money they were making and could not withdraw their earnings during the outage. One of the drivers said he has stopped working altogether until the problem gets fixed. He was originally from Kyrgyzstan and did not know why the outages were happening.

World.title: Ukraine claims world’s first drone evacuation of wounded soldier
World.content:
Ukraine has shared a video showing what it says is the world’s first evacuation of an injured soldier from the frontlines by drone.

The “historic” mission comes just as Kyiv faces a dire turn in its relationship with Washington over the withdrawal of support in its fight against Russia.

Shared by the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade on Monday, the video shows the soldier strapping himself into a large drone and being flown at what appears to be relatively low altitude over blurred-out territory. The drone carefully lowers him down and the drone operator greets him with “Welcome back to the ground!” The video also showed blurred faces of drone operators who carried out the mission.

The post said the unidentified infantryman was wounded while at his position. “Due to intense enemy drone activity and the presence of landmines, evacuation using conventional unmanned ground vehicles was impossible,” the brigade said.

“At that point, the specialists in our unit took it upon themselves to attempt something that had never been done before: evacuating a serviceman using an aerial drone,” it added.

The craft used was a heavy-lift hexacopter, it said, originally designed as a bomber by a Ukrainian manufacturer. It looks about twice the size of the soldier in the video.

The specialists working on the mission had to ensure the drone could carry a human being without flipping over or swaying excessively, according to the unit.

The unidentified infantryman was wounded while at his position, before he lifted out in a drone rescue mission. Ukraine's 92nd Separate Assault Brigade

The rescued soldier is currently undergoing treatment and rehabilitation, the brigade added. The squad leader and programmer with the brigade, only identified by his call sign Napalm, called the soldier a “hero” for agreeing to the mission, “having seen and heard the kind of machine that had arrived to get him.”

In a separate statement, Ukraine’s Ground Forces said its drone units are already conducting operations “that were recently considered science fiction.”

The war has increasingly become a technological arms race, with both Ukraine and Russia relying on drones to reduce human casualties.

The conflict has taken a severe toll on both armies, although neither side reports up-to-date numbers of those killed, injured or missing. Ukraine in particular has faced a severe shortage of manpower as it has tried to ramp up recruitment.

Ukraine had a major leap in drone technology this year, allowing it to limit Russian logistics in occupied territories as well as strike deeper inside Russia to target Russian oil refineries, commercial warehouses and data centers.

Fires at an oil refinery in Moscow, following a reported Ukrainian drone strike, on Sept. 20. Reuters

“This mission proves once again that Ukrainian service members, working in tandem with Ukrainian manufacturers, are setting global trends in the conduct of warfare,” the brigade’s statement added.

Despite hoping that its drone innovation would give it the upper hand at the negotiating table, Kyiv has faced pressure from the U.S. to halt its strikes on Russian oil sites after President Donald Trump signed a diesel deal with the Kremlin earlier this month.

Kyiv has since also reported gaps in intelligence sharing and restrictions on Elon Musk’s Starlink service that is crucial for its drone missions, battlefield communications and air defense.

A Russian missile strike on an apartment building in Kyiv on Tuesday, following Genya Savilov/AFP; Yan Dobronosov/Global Images Ukraine / via Getty

The drone evacuation comes just days after Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced the Ukrainian government had approved an “experimental project” to use drones for medical logistics. Koretskyi said flights would require coordination with the military, and drones would be given a special status and would be identifiable in the air.

“During the war, moving medical cargo by road can cost critical time, especially for transplants,” he said. “Drones will be able to carry medicines, medical products, blood samples, and donor organs between hospitals, including from remote areas.”

World.title: Supreme Court rejects alleged 9/11 mastermind’s attempt to revive plea deal
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday rejected an appeal brought by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two other alleged 9/11 plotters seeking to hold the government to a plea deal it later withdrew.

The court action removes one barrier to Mohammed standing trial before a military commission in 2028, where the death penalty is a possible punishment. He has been held at the U.S. base in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, since 2006.

Mohammed is accused of being the ringleader of the plot to crash hijacked planes into the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon on Sept. 11, 2001. A fourth plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania.

The other two men who appealed to the Supreme Court were Mustafa Ahmed al-Hawsawi and Walid bin Attash, who are also held at Guantanamo and set to face trial.

The three men had agreed to a plea deal with military prosecutors in 2024, signed off on by a military commission judge, that would have given them life sentences.

But days later, then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin rejected the proposal, saying he had the authority to override the deal.

Military courts said he had no such authority but, in an August ruling, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit ruled in favor of the government, prompting the men to appeal to the Supreme Court.

They argued, among other things, that the appeals court had no authority to intervene in the case.

The long delay in Mohammed facing trial was caused partly by concerns about evidence obtained via CIA torture.

A fourth alleged plotter earmarked for trial, Ali Abdul Aziz Ali, was not involved in the appeal.

World.title: NFL Week 6: The return of Caleb Williams, and life gets worse for the Rams
World.content:
Week 6 of the NFL season featured a star player returning from one the season’s most dramatic injuries, an important game across the pond, and another devastating loss for a Super Bowl contender.

Here’s all the action you need to know about from Sunday.

Caleb Williams picked up where he left off

Chicago Bears starting quarterback Caleb Williams played Sunday for the first time since sustaining a hamstring injury in Week 2, and he was spectacular in a 31-23 victory over the Atlanta Falcons. Williams completed 30 of 36 passes for 305 yards and one touchdown, improving his completion percentage to 72.5% for the season.

Williams was especially efficient when not facing pressure. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, Williams completed all 24 of his passes from a clean pocket, the most attempts without an incompletion under such circumstances since 2018.

After going 2-1 without their starter, the Bears improved to 4-2 with the win. The offense has been humming with Williams under center, averaging 31.0 points per game in his three starts. Chicago will now enter a spotlighted stretch of its season, as the team’s next three games will all be played in primetime.

The Rams are still searching for answers

Six weeks after entering the season as a heavy favorite to win the Super Bowl, the Los Angeles Rams (2-4) are in last place in the NFC West after Sunday’s 18-16 home loss to the Arizona Cardinals.

After a frustrating day with little offense, the Rams had finally pieced together a productive drive to tie the game at 15-all in the fourth-quarter’s final minute. The point-after was no foregone conclusion. The team cut kicker Harrison Mevis after a miss in last week’s loss to Buffalo, only to see his replacement, Blake Grupe, get hurt trying to make a tackle early Sunday. That left Rams punter Ethan Evans to step up to attempt his first point-after since college — which he made to give Los Angeles a one-point lead with 47 seconds left.

It was a different kicker who ended up the hero, though. A controversial penalty on the Rams for unnecessary roughness — a penalty that increased the Cardinals’ win probability from 26% to 74% — helped Arizona’s final drive move downfield in position for Chad Ryland to attempt a game-winning kick from 43 yards. He nailed it to keep the Rams still looking for any consistency. By the way: The Rams and Chargers have one win combined inside their home stadium, SoFi Stadium, this season. The Cardinals are 2-0 there.

The Texans’ season isn’t over just yet

The Houston Texans are winners of two straight after a 34-31 victory over the Jacksonville Jaguars in London. This was the first game of the day on Sunday, and perhaps the best. Quarterbacks C.J. Stroud and Trevor Lawrence combined for 618 yards, seven touchdowns and two interceptions. Stroud was nearly perfect, posting a quarterback rating of 96.9 (out of a possible 100).

After the Texans opened up a 10-point lead in the final minute of the third quarter, the Jaguars stormed back. First, Lawrence led a nine-play, 61-yard touchdown drive to cut the score to 31-28 early in the fourth. Then, after a Travis Hunter interception, Lawrence led a 38-yard drive that culminated in a 60-yard field goal from Cam Little.

But Houston got the last laugh. After Little’s kick, the Texans quickly marched into Jacksonville territory on their ensuing possession. Ka’imi Fairbairn hit a 49-yard field goal as time expired, securing Houston’s second win of the season.

The Texans are now 2-4, and while their climb into playoff position will be an arduous one, Houston did make the postseason after an 0-3 start a year ago. If Stroud maintains his current level of play — he’s thrown nine touchdowns and only one interception so far this season — the Texans won’t be a pushover.

The Titans rose from the ranks of the winless

Tennessee’s season-long nightmare is finally over. The Titans finally won a game, knocking off their divisional rival the Indianapolis Colts 26-20. Tennessee stormed back in the second half, scoring all of its points in the final 30 minutes, including 20 in the final quarter.

The Colts aided the cause with a litany of mistakes. Quarterback Daniel Jones threw two interceptions, running back Jonathan Taylor had a fumble, the special teams had a punt blocked for a touchdown, and the offense also had a turnover on downs for good measure.

The Titans are now 1-5. Indianapolis, meanwhile, entered this season with high expectations from ownership, but fell to 2-4 after the loss.

World.title: Can making two credit card payments a month save you money?
World.content:
We may receive commissions from some links to products on this page. Promotions are subject to availability and retailer terms.

Splitting your monthly credit card payments into two can be useful, but will it help you save money on your bill? Getty Images/iStockphoto

For the millions of Americans carrying credit card debt, making progress on their balances feels increasingly difficult in today's landscape. Part of the issue is that the interest rate on the average credit card is above 22% currently, meaning that if you're carrying a balance from month to month, a significant portion of each monthly credit card payment goes toward interest rather than reducing what's owed. But with everyday expenses continuing to strain household budgets, finding extra money to put toward those balances isn't always realistic.

Case in point? A recent Freedom Debt Relief study shows that of the borrowers with substantial debt, 28% can only afford to make the minimum-required payments, while 20% are behind on at least one account. In turn, it's particularly important for borrowers to find ways to reduce borrowing costs right now. While transferring a balance to a lower-rate card or consolidating debt with a personal loan may help, those approaches aren't necessarily accessible to everyone.

Fortunately, changing how you approach your existing credit card payments is another option to consider. One strategy that could be worth examining is making two payments each month instead of one. But can making two card payments every month really save you money on interest charges? That's what we'll examine below.

Find out how Freedom Debt Relief can help with your debt today.

Can making two credit card payments a month save you money?

Making two credit card payments per month can potentially save you money on interest. Still, the amount depends on your balance, interest rate, payment timing and whether you're paying more than the required minimum. Here's what to know:

You may reduce your interest charges

Most credit card issuers calculate the interest charges you owe each month using your average daily balance. That means the amount you owe throughout your billing cycle, rather than just on your payment due date, helps determine how much interest accrues.

Making an additional payment earlier in the billing cycle can lower your balance sooner, potentially reducing the interest charged. For example, if you typically make a $400 payment at the end of the month, paying $200 halfway through the month and another $200 on your regular payment date could reduce your average daily balance.

The savings from changing the timing alone may be modest, however. And if you're already paying your statement balance in full each month and maintaining your purchase grace period, splitting payments generally won't provide additional savings.

Learn about the debt help Freedom Debt Relief can offer you here.

You could pay off your debt faster

Making two payments can also accelerate debt repayment, particularly if the strategy encourages you to contribute more than you otherwise would. For example, someone who typically pays $250 monthly might instead make two $150 payments. That increases their total monthly contribution to $300, putting an additional $600 toward their debt over a year.

Those extra payments can reduce the principal credit card balance faster, which also lowers future interest charges. Over time, that combination could shorten the repayment period and reduce the total cost of carrying the debt.

Your credit score could benefit

Another potential advantage of making two credit card payments each month involves your credit utilization ratio, which measures how much of your available revolving credit you're using. Lower utilization can help your credit score.

Credit card issuers typically report account balances to credit bureaus around the statement closing date, though reporting schedules vary. Making an additional payment before that date could reduce the balance reported, potentially improving your utilization ratio.

That benefit isn't guaranteed, however, and, as noted, it doesn't necessarily translate into immediate interest savings, either. Payment history and other factors also influence credit scores, so it's important to keep that in mind if you're relying on this approach to improve your credit.

How to make two monthly credit card payments work for you

While splitting your credit card payments into two each month can be useful, getting the most from the strategy requires more than simply sending money to your issuer twice a month.

To start, try to time your payments strategically. Consider making one payment shortly after receiving your paycheck and another before your credit card statement closes. Paying earlier can help reduce your average daily balance, while paying before the closing date may lower your reported utilization.

You may also want to pay more on what's owed whenever possible. Splitting your usual payment into two installments may produce limited savings, but increasing the total amount you pay each month can have a much greater impact on your balance and interest costs.

Don't overlook your due date, either. Making an early payment doesn't necessarily eliminate your obligation to satisfy the minimum payment by the due date. So, check your account to ensure you've met the card issuer's requirements and avoid late fees.

In some cases, it may also make sense to consider other debt repayment options instead. If your balances remain difficult to manage despite making frequent payments, a balance transfer card, debt consolidation loan or even working with a credit counselor or debt relief expert may provide more meaningful relief. Each option has different costs, eligibility requirements and potential drawbacks to consider, though.

The bottom line

Making two credit card payments each month can help reduce interest charges, support faster debt repayment and potentially improve credit utilization. However, the biggest savings generally come from paying down your balance earlier and contributing more money toward your debt, not simply increasing the number of payments.

Before changing your payment schedule, also make sure to review your credit card's billing cycle, interest rate and minimum payment requirements. A strategy that fits your cash flow and consistently reduces what you owe is ultimately more valuable than the number of payments you make each month.

World.title: Expedition to find Amelia Earhart's missing plane comes up empty
World.content:
A mysterious object discovered near a remote Pacific island is not the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's missing plane, researchers said after an expedition to the site, dealing another setback to efforts to solve one of aviation's greatest mysteries nearly 90 years after the pilot disappeared.

"Evidence gathered at the Taraia Peninsula on Nikumaroro confirmed that the visual anomaly first seen in satellite imagery in 2020 was likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula's sandspit," the researchers said. "By the time the team arrived at the site, a good portion of the debris had fragmented and washed away, leaving only a single Y-shaped segment," which they said is what they had initially hoped was the plane.

The researchers said the reflective surface of the anomaly, which had led them to believe it could be metal, was the result of a carbonate veneer, noting other items found nearby were "similarly coated with a shiny concretized amalgam of coral sand."

On Oct. 14, a 17-member expedition team led by Purdue University's Steve Schultz and the Archaeological Legacy Institute's Richard Pettigrew launched an expedition to investigate a mysterious object that in aerial photos appeared to resemble possible wreckage of Earhart's Lockheed Electra 10-E plane.

Severe weather kept the research team aboard their ship for three of the five days allotted for the search, while limited fuel and supplies prevented them from extending the expedition. The search area was so remote, it took the team five days at sea to reach it.

The expedition focused on a lagoon off Nikumaroro, where researchers examined the Taraia Object, an anomaly spotted by a Navy veteran in satellite imagery during the COVID pandemic. Although visible in aerial photos dating back to 1938, the object went unnoticed until 2020. Pettigrew said before reaching it that they believed it could be metal rather than a tree, but further investigation was needed to confirm its identity.

A satellite image shows the Taraia Object in a lagoon on Nikumaroro Island. Rick Pettigrew, Archaeological Legacy Institute

"Amelia Earhart's spirit of courage and curiosity drove every step of the search," Pettigrew said Sunday. "We accomplished our goal to determine what the Taraia Object was, and we're deeply grateful to the private donors who shared our vision and made this journey possible. Our team remains in great spirits and proud of what was accomplished."

The team had developed plans to photograph and film the lagoon and Taraia Object before using magnetometers and sonar equipment to survey the area. Researchers then planned to retrieve the object for identification. The Archaeology Channel documented the expedition through short video updates on its Heritage Broadcasting Service streaming platform.

The research team previously said in a news release that there was "very strong" evidence that the object is Earhart's lost plane.

Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, disappeared on July 2, 1937, roughly 22,000 miles into their trip. Earhart was attempting to become the first female pilot to circle the world, and the first pilot to do so around the equator, Earth's widest point.

American aviator Amelia Earhart at a refueling stop in Khartoum, Sudan, with the Lockheed Electra 10E in which she was attempting to circumnavigate the world with navigator Fred Noonan, on June 13, 1937. Getty Images

Recently, President Trump ordered the declassification of records related to Earhart.

Nikumaroro is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, located roughly halfway between Australia and Hawaii. The island lies about 400 miles southeast of Howland Island, where Earhart and Noonan were headed when they disappeared during their attempted flight around the world.

Pettigrew believes Earhart and Noonan landed on Nikumaroro and survived there for some time. He points to relics dating to the 1930s and to human remains discovered on the island, which were later lost as possible evidence. However, several competing theories about the aviator's disappearance have emerged over the decades, many of which lack conclusive evidence.

Researchers have spent decades searching for Earhart's plane, hoping its discovery could shed light on her disappearance. In 2024, an expedition team captured a sonar image of what appeared to be an aircraft on the ocean floor, but the object was later identified as a rock formation.

World.title: Supreme Court turns away appeal from alleged 9/11 mastermind
World.content:
Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday rebuffed a bid from accused Sept. 11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two alleged accomplices to revive plea agreements that they reached with military prosecutors before being revoked by the Biden administration.

In an unsigned order, the high court turned away the appeals from Mohammed, Mustafa al Hawsawi and Walid bin 'Atash of a lower court decision that prevented a military judge from enforcing pretrial agreements they reached with military prosecutors in 2024, which were withdrawn by then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin.

In rejecting their case, the government's withdrawal of the plea deals remains in place. Justice Brett Kavanaugh did not participate in the court's consideration of the appeal.

Mohammed, Hawsawi and bin 'Atash, were captured in 2003 and charged before a military commission with several crimes for their alleged roles in crafting and perpetrating the Sept. 11 attacks, five of which carry the death penalty.

But their cases have been mired in lengthy legal delays over whether evidence extracted during their interrogations could be used in court. The defendants were held at secret CIA prisons, where they were subjected to "enhanced interrogation techniques," or torture, before they were moved to Guantanamo Bay in 2006. They were formally charged in 2008.

In 2023, following the appointment of retired Brigadier General Susan Escallier as the Convening Authority for military commissions, military lawyers began discussing plea deals with the defendants. Agreements were subsequently reached in 2024 and approved by Escallier, who oversees the military court at Guantanamo Bay.

Under the terms of the deals, the defendants would plead guilty to all charges arising from their alleged roles in the 9/11 terror attacks and serve life sentences, avoiding the death penalty. But shortly after the agreements were announced, Austin said he was revoking them.

But a military judge ruled in November 2024 that Austin's nullification of the deals was unlawful, rendering the agreements valid and enforceable. A military appeals court then said Austin couldn't rescind the plea deals because the defendants had begun to perform one of the terms.

The Justice Department then asked the D.C. Circuit to step in and find that Austin validly withdrew from the pretrial agreements. The D.C. Circuit sided with the government in a decision last year and ruled that the defense secretary "indisputably" had the authority to withdraw from the plea deals.

"The Secretary acted within the bounds of his legal authority, and we decline to second-guess his judgment," the D.C. Circuit panel found.
