World.title: U.S. lauds Israel for arresting 10 over West Bank settler attacks
World.content:
Tel Aviv — Israeli police announced on Monday the arrest of 10 people suspected to have taken part in recent violent attacks on Palestinians, an American photojournalist and European diplomats in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.

The arrests come amid an avalanche of criticism, including from some senior U.S. officials, directed at Israel over repeated violent attacks by groups of mostly young Israeli settlers targeting Palestinians and others in the West Bank.

The announcement of the arrests came as more violence against Palestinians in the occupied territory was reported Monday.

Israeli police said officers working in conjunction with the Shin Bet domestic security and intelligence agency conducted a pre-dawn raid in the West Bank to locate individuals suspected of involvement in the violence and of violating a military commander's order declaring a closed military zone.

Israeli soldiers survey the scene as Israeli settlers gather while Palestinian farmers harvest their olives in the Israeli-occupied West Bank village of Deir Abu Mashal, Oct. 19, 2026. ilia YEFIMOVICH/AFP/Getty

The arrests, dubbed Operation Olive Leaf by the police, came in the wake of multiple reported attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians as they worked on the annual olive harvest.

"Items linking the suspects to the alleged offenses were seized, and several vehicles were confiscated," the police said in a statement after the arrests.

On Friday, several Palestinians and Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine were injured when a group of masked Israeli men attacked Palestinians harvesting olives in the West Bank, according to videos, eyewitnesses and Palestinian authorities.

On Saturday, European officials and the Israeli military said a diplomatic convoy with representatives from France, Belgium and Poland was assaulted by masked individuals near the Palestinian village of Taybeh.

U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, in a social media post on Monday, called the arrests "a very positive development in finding & punishing those who severely attacked and beat Heidi Levine an unarmed journalist."

Over the weekend, Huckabee called the attack on Levine an "act of terror carried out by masked cowards."

Heidi Levine, a photojournalist with the Washington Post, speaks to journalists at the hospital after sustaining multiple injuries during an attack by Israeli militant settlers on Palestinians harvesting olives, in Ramallah in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, Oct. 16, 2026. Ali Sawafta/REUTERS

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also condemned the attack on Levine Saturday, saying President Trump didn't want to see a crisis in the West Bank.

"We've asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff," Rubio said.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office, in a statement on Saturday, urged people to exercise caution before drawing conclusions about the reported attacks on the European diplomats.

Netanyahu's office noted that video published online of the incident appeared to show masked individuals confronting a diplomatic vehicle and others showed a smashed car window and someone lying on the ground, but it said those images alone did "not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility."

Israel's military said the diplomatic convoy was not coordinated with the defense forces, and that such coordination would've provided more safety, but it did not deny that the convoy came under attack by settlers.

On Monday, new attacks on Palestinians by Israel settlers were reported by WAFA, the official media arm of the Palestinian Authority, which governs most Palestinians in the West Bank but has limited control over security in the occupied territory.

Two Palestinians were injured in the villages of Turmus Ayya and Deir Abu Mash'al, northwest of Ramallah, amid attempts by individuals to set homes on fire by torching vehicles in front of the buildings, WAFA reported.

A Palestinian resident looks at the shattered glass of his home following a reported attack by Israeli settlers in the Israeli-occupied West Bank village of Turmus Ayya, Oct. 19, 2026. ilia YEFIMOVICH/AFP/Getty

On Sunday night, Israel's military said several Israeli civilians entered the Palestinian village of Wadi a-Rahim in the West Bank, sprayed graffiti and set fire to a storage shed. The military said it had begun dismantling an illegal Israeli settler outpost in the area.

Violence by Israeli settlers targeting Palestinians in the West Bank has surged in recent years.

Statistics released by the United Nations humanitarian office show that it started ramping up after Netanyahu took office in 2022 at the head of Israel's most far-right-wing coalition government in modern history in late 2022.

The attacks have intensified in the wake of the war in Gaza, and amid strong support from some members of Netanyahu's cabinet for settlement expansion, and even for the West Bank to be completely annexed by Israel.

World.title: Australian prime minister says lawmaker critically injured by car is 'no accident'
World.content:
Australian prime minister says lawmaker critically injured by car is 'no accident'

toggle caption i Mick Tsikas/AAP Image via AP

MELBOURNE, Australia — A car hit an Australian federal independent lawmaker on Monday, critically injuring her in an apparent deliberate attack, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said. The driver was arrested.

Helen Haines, 65, was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV outside her electoral district office mid afternoon in the city of Wangaratta in Victoria state, a police said.

Albanese said the national counterterrorism team, incorporating police and intelligence agencies, was investigating.

"This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear. We don't know what the motivation is," Albanese told Australian Broadcasting Corp.

toggle caption i Lukas Coch/AAPIMAGE via AP

The 43-year-old driver was arrested at the scene by a passerby. He will be interviewed in relation to the incident, police said.

Sponsor Message

"A knife was located by police and seized from inside the Toyota," police said.

"At this stage, police are investigating as to whether this was an intentional act," police added.

Haines, who was first elected to the Parliament in 2019, was taken to a hospital with critical injuries, police said.

The episode has renewed safety concerns for Australian lawmakers, in a country where politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security officers present. But public incitement against officials is growing.

Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett said in 2025 that threats against parliamentarians had doubled over the past three years. Police data showed more than 1,000 such threats against politicians in the 2025-2026 financial year, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Monday.

Albanese told the ABC it was "unfortunate" that an increasingly polarized political climate had already led to security changes for Australia's lawmakers.

"I think there has been a rise in temperature and there has been too much shouting, not enough discourse, not enough polite conversation and disagreement," he said Monday. There was "no question" that social media played a part, Albanese added.

In Britain, murders of politicians have prompted bolstered security. Labour lawmaker Jo Cox was shot and stabbed in 2016 by a far-right extremist, and Conservative David Amess was stabbed in 2021 by an attacker inspired by the Islamic State group.

Sponsor Message

In July, the former politician and reality TV contestant Ann Widdecombe was found slain with a hammer at her home. A man has been charged with murder and terrorism-related offenses.

Today's top stories

The 2026 midterm elections are set to become the most expensive on record. More than $15 billion has been raised to influence the outcome and control of Congress.

🎧 Democratic nominees in House and Senate races are raking in incredible amounts of donations, even though the Democratic Party remains unpopular, NPR's Stephen Fowler says. Republicans are also unpopular, largely due to issues like the war in Iran, gas prices and the economy. At least one person died and more than a dozen were injured in a major Ukrainian drone strike yesterday on Saint Petersburg, Russia's former imperial capital. The attack targeted strategic sites, including a key port oil terminal. Over the weekend, Russian missile strikes in Ukraine killed at least 11 people. This conflict continues as President Trump says that relieving pressure on Russia is the best way to end the war.



🎧 The recent attack on Saint Petersburg appears to mark the largest one on the city since Russia's 2022 invasion, NPR's Charles Maynes tells Up First. While it's unclear how many drones struck the city, Russia's Defense Ministry reported intercepting 1,000 drones across various regions that night. Trump seems to be working to protect Russian oil facilities after cutting a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel. The move was aimed at lowering gas prices for U.S. voters before the midterm elections. Trump has called previous Ukrainian strikes a "disgrace," even as Russia continues to strike Ukraine, Maynes says. He adds that the president blames President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for attacks that allegedly raise U.S. fuel prices, despite economists attributing the price increase mainly to Trump's war in Iran.

French President Emmanuel Macron denounced violence over the weekend that he says has overshadowed largely peaceful protests across the country. The unrest began as a student protest for better conditions and has expanded to include public-sector workers protesting high energy prices, the rising cost of living and social inequality. The Interior Ministry reported about 2,300 arrests and nearly 1,000 injured police officers.



Sponsor Message

🎧 NPR's Eleanor Beardsley, who was in the streets of Paris yesterday, witnessed burned bikes, shattered glass and graffiti on looted stores saying things like "tax the rich." She spoke with 23-year-old Sarah Berlia, who says she believes these actions come from a frustrated generation facing dwindling rights and opportunities. Beardsley says the protest culture in France often attracts "troublemakers," but the scale of current events is massive. The protests have had political implications, as France is six months away from a presidential election. Far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon has joined the protesters, while far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls, has condemned the violence and the government.

Living better

toggle caption i Siv Dolmen for NPR

Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America.

Saunas are gaining renewed attention in the wellness world for their potential to improve mental health. This trend reflects the growing interest in the broader wellness movement and social connection, especially post-pandemic. While scientists understand how saunas affect the cardiovascular system, they are just beginning to explore their impact on mental health. Here's what they know so far.

🥵 When our skin detects heat, it sends signals to a primitive brain area that prompts our body to cool down. This pathway also influences mood and pleasure, which is associated with depression.

🥵 Heat triggers an anti-inflammatory response similar to the effects of exercise, which is known to help with depression and other mental health issues.

🥵 Heating people up can act like a "thermoregulatory workout," helping their bodies cool down more efficiently over time.

Picture show

toggle caption i Jennifer Teresa Villanueva

Artist Jennifer Teresa Villanueva has captured her family's everyday life through her lens for eight years, revealing moments of love, care and sacrifice within their Chicago home. The personal project took root in 2018, sparked by her grandmother's hospitalization. It started as a way to better understand her grandmother's daily routines, and soon it blossomed into a heartfelt exploration of the immigrant experience. "I am interested in what happens when the camera enters a home where everyone already knows one another," Villanueva told NPR. "There is no distance between photographer and subject. I am photographing the people who raised me, and I am also photographing the home that raised me." See photos from the project and read more about Villanueva's work.

World.title: The real reason it's going to take a while to know who won in some midterm races
World.content:
The real reason it's going to take a while to know who won in some midterm races

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

Stephen Richer no longer runs elections in the fourth-largest county in the country.

But for the rest of his life, he'll remember the feeling when polls closed on an election night.

More than a million ballots staring at him and his staff. Every moment that passes without them fully counted means another conspiracy theory sprouting online.

"Those days, those were hell for me," said Richer, a Republican who served as the clerk and recorder for Arizona's Maricopa County. "You'd have a limited number of workers, and you'd have a limited amount of space, and you'd be doing everything that you possibly could. … And yet you have everyone blowing up your phone, everyone saying that you're incompetent or corrupt or worse."

Sponsor Message

This midterm year, election officials in competitive congressional districts will face that same pressure.

But they will also face a hard reality: that those races might not be called until days after Election Day.

Here's an FAQ on why that is, and what it could mean this year.

Why do we know the results immediately in some places, and in others it takes days or weeks?

It comes down to the margin of victory.

Which sounds strange, since who wins an election and by how much shouldn't impact how long it takes election officials to count ballots.

But the reality is what most Americans think of as "election results" — the winners announced on election nights across TV networks and social media — are not the result of all ballots being counted, but rather, races being called by news organizations that determine the winners based on a state or district's demographics and initial returns. (NPR relies on The Associated Press for its race calls.)

Those determinations come a lot faster when races aren't close.

"Margins matter," said Richer, who noted that in recent elections, there has been a lot less scrutiny on Utah than there has been on his home state of Arizona, or certain contests in California, despite the states counting votes at similar speeds.

Sponsor Message

"In Utah you can call all the races very quickly because the Republicans there have high margins," Richer said.

That gives the illusion of elections there being complete, but no state is done counting ballots on election night, even if it seems that way because notable races are called early.

Loading...

So you're saying the timing of results isn't at all tied to vote-counting speed?

Not exactly.

The closer the race, the more election analysts need to see before they can make a call. So the faster states count ballots, the faster those determinations can be made.

This is why the longest wait times every election usually come from places that have competitive races and which also count slowly.

Like, California?

Exactly. California has become the poster child for long results times because of both those factors: a bevy of competitive congressional districts, which help determine the balance of power in the U.S. House, and a vote count that's been among the slowest in the nation.

Add in that President Trump, the most prominent purveyor of election misinformation in the country, has long targeted the liberal California, and experts see a perfect storm for false voting narratives.

"It's progressive, it likes mail ballots, it gets [postmarked] mail ballots after Election Day," Richer said. "It just all adds up to a fairly incendiary situation."

Charles Stewart, an elections expert at MIT, put it more simply.

"California just has a big target on its back," said Stewart.

California's slow vote counting caused a lot of conspiracy theorizing during the state's June primary. Is this fall going to be a rerun?

Kim Alexander is cautiously optimistic that won't be the case.

She runs the California Voter Foundation, which has been advocating for ways to speed up California's vote tally without giving up the state's generous voting access policies, like mailing every active registered voter a ballot.

Sponsor Message

"We have all these amazing rights and opportunities that we give to our voters, and the price we're paying is a longer vote count," Alexander told NPR. "But that doesn't mean that it has to be this long."

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

The single biggest cause for California's slow count comes from a phenomenon Alexander calls "the pig in the python" problem: a logjam of millions of vote-by-mail ballots getting returned on Election Day that need to be processed.

Those ballots take longer to count than in-person votes, as officials need to deal with envelopes and verify signatures to make sure mail ballots are cast by the people they're supposed to be cast by.

Some counties see up to 50% of their vote-by-mail ballots turned in on Election Day, Alexander said, which means processing work doesn't even begin until later in the week.

"I can't tell you how many people who are informed and engaged and … when I tell them that the cause for the long vote count is voters holding on to their ballots to Election Day and turning them in, they look at me and they're like, 'That's what I do,'" Alexander said. "And I'm like, 'I know! You're part of the problem!'"

The state allocated $40 million to speeding up its counting this year, and part of that money is going to voter education.

Alexander is optimistic that once voters learn they can play a role in speeding up the process by voting earlier, or by utilizing other voting methods that allow for quicker counting, they will respond.

"California has been beaten up by this president for over a decade over our election process, and it's gotten pretty worrisome," Alexander said. "I think that California voters, if they feel they can do something to respond to that, many will take action."

Sponsor Message

To that point, research conducted earlier this year found that when voters in California's San Joaquin County received postcards urging them to vote earlier, they were more likely to meet the recommended deadline that allowed for election-night counting.

Alexander noted one more change that could mean less spotlight on California this year: fewer competitive House districts.

Ahead of the 2022 elections, the state had nine districts that the Cook Political Report considered competitive. But this year, in part because voters approved a mid-cycle gerrymander to respond to gerrymanders in Republican-controlled states, the state has just three.

That makes it less likely the entire country will be waiting on California to know who controls the House.

OK, anywhere else we should be watching when it comes to results speed?

Using the formula discussed earlier (competitive races + slow vote counting), it's impossible not to look at Alaska.

According to data from the MIT Election Lab, Alaska was the last state in 2024 to reach 95% of its ballots counted.

Election Day was Nov. 5 that year, but the state's lone House race — which Republican Nicholas Begich won by fewer than 10,000 votes — wasn't called by the AP until Nov. 20.

This year, polling shows a tight Alaska Senate race. That means, if results fall a certain way in other states, the entire country could be waiting weeks to know which party will control the U.S. Senate next year.

World.content:
A Kelvin wave raised sea levels on the West Coast. More are coming

toggle caption i Dillon J. Amaya/North Carolina State University

One of the first major signs of this year's "Super El Niño" has reached the U.S. It's called a Kelvin wave – a deep ocean wave that's currently raising sea levels along the West Coast.

Scientists have long known about Kelvin waves, but this year, the phenomena grabbed the public's attention with video explanations receiving thousands of views across TikTok and X .

"It does surprise me – I mean, here it's been around all this time," says Mark Cane, who created one of the first models to forecast and predict El Niño . "I'm sure Lord Kelvin is happy in his grave."

Sponsor Message

(Lord Kelvin, the British physicist who also developed the Kelvin temperature scale, first described the wave back in the late 1800s.)

Kelvin waves can develop along the equator during El Niño years, when a vast region of water in the Pacific Ocean becomes much warmer than usual.

Some of this warm water, in the form of a Kelvin wave that stretches thousands of miles, moves slowly east beneath the ocean's surface until it reaches South America. Then it splits, traveling north along the West Coast and as far south as Chile.

"It's like an enormous bathtub sloshing around," Cane says, professor emeritus of earth and climate sciences at Columbia University. "But the slosh is very peculiar, because it only goes west to east along the equator in a Kelvin wave."

These are not the massive, highly visible waves that crash into shorelines during major storms and hurricanes .

"It's not a wall of water, it's not a tsunami, it's not a wave you can surf," says Dillon Amaya, an assistant professor of atmospheric sciences at North Carolina State University. "It's a planetary-scale wave."

A Kelvin wave's impact is gradual, raising sea levels as it moves up the coast, and bringing with it an elevated risk of floods and warmer water temperatures.

Sponsor Message

What's the impact?

Kelvin waves can increase the risk of flooding and coastal erosion.

By themselves, Kelvin waves don't cause flooding, Amaya says. Instead, they load the dice, making flooding more likely by raising sea levels.

"It makes the background conditions more favorable towards coastal flooding, but what you need are triggering factors," Amaya said, such as a major storm or very high tides.

Josh Willis, a climate scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, says Kelvin waves raise the chances of a "triple whammy" along the California coast: "El Nino, the high tide and the storm surge all coming at once."

That's exactly what some Southern California communities experienced in early October. Sea levels were already higher than normal because of the Kelvin wave – about six to eight inches, Amaya says. Then, when Tropical Storm Rachel hit, a storm surge flooded neighborhoods and left oceanfront homes partially submerged .

"That storm surge was almost certainly made more devastating because of the Kelvin wave," Amaya says.

Warmer water temperatures

toggle caption i Dillon J. Amaya/North Carolina State University

Kelvin waves also bring warmer water up the coast, which can be disruptive and put stress on marine life .

"We've seen tropical fishes in places that we don't normally see them," Amaya says. "Like a whale shark was spotted off the coast of San Diego."

The Kelvin wave can push down nutrient-dense cold waters that support productive marine ecosystems. Amaya says researchers have already seen evidence of sea birds dying in response to warmer water temperatures along the coast.

When is the next Kelvin wave?

There are usually five to six Kelvin waves during a strong El Niño year, Amaya says.

Amaya predicts the next Kelvin wave will reach San Diego in late October or early November. Several more waves are expected through the fall and early winter, he says. Kelvin waves usually subside before the peak of El Niño.

World.title: Alberta voters weigh future in Canada
World.content:
Alberta voters weigh future in Canada

toggle caption i John Diep/Bloomberg via Getty Images





EDMONTON, Alberta — For decades, Alberta separatism remained on the political margins. Now, voters in the oil-rich Canadian province are deciding whether to take the first step toward a future referendum on independence.

The nonbinding referendum vote on Monday is the first time the province has put the question of separation to a public vote, in what Elections Alberta has described as the largest electoral event in the province's history.

Polls indicate that Alberta voters will overwhelmingly reject the option of beginning the legal process toward a referendum on separation.

Pollsters generally estimate that about one in five Albertans support separation from Canada. But the vote has brought the question of Alberta's place in the Canadian federation to the forefront of public debate.

Sponsor Message

The questions on the ballot

Essentially, this is a referendum about whether to hold another referendum on separation.

There are 10 questions in total. The first nine address immigration, access to provincial services such as health care, education and other social services, and potential changes to the Canadian Constitution. Voters can answer yes or no to each of these questions.

Question 10 offers voters two options. Option 1 asks whether Alberta should remain part of Canada, while option 2 asks whether the province should begin the legal process toward holding a referendum on separation.

Western alienation and grievances against Ottawa date back decades, including to the administrations of Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau, Justin Trudeau's father, during the 1970s and 1980s.

"I feel the Canadian system is broken. I know we aren't living in hell on earth. But it's the trajectory we're worried about and where things are going," says Cory Morgan.

Morgan founded the Alberta Independence Party in 2000 and is also the founder of Pathway to Independence, a third-party advertising group that advocates for an independent Alberta.

toggle caption i Megan Albu/AFP via Getty Images

"Even if we don't get over the line on Monday, I would hope that some people understand that something large is brewing here and if we don't get some change, it's going to continue to grow," Morgan told NPR.

Sponsor Message

Support for separation intensified among some Albertans following COVID-19 lockdowns and vaccine mandates. Premier Danielle Smith said in May that it was "time to have a vote, understand the will of Albertans on this subject, and move on."

The referendum campaign brought Prime Minister Mark Carney back to his hometown of Edmonton on Friday, where he urged Albertans to keep their province in Canada ahead of the vote.

"A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians," Carney told the rally.

What's at stake?

Alberta is one of Canada's wealthiest provinces and is home to the world's fourth-largest known oil reserves. The province contributes to Canada's equalization system, which provides federal funding to provinces with lower fiscal capacity. Some Albertans argue that the province should retain more of its revenue rather than see funds redistributed elsewhere in the country.

"We want to make a new country where we can stop sending our money 1,000 kilometers away in Ottawa," says Jeremy Clive, a 23-year-old pilot and university student from rural Alberta.

Leaving the Canadian federation would not be as simple as holding a referendum.

"It requires negotiating your way out," says Jared Wesley, a political scientist at the University of Alberta. "The Supreme Court has stated clearly that in order to leave, a province must negotiate with nine other provinces and the federal government to secure an amendment to the Constitution to remove themselves."

In 1995, Quebec held a referendum on sovereignty that narrowly rejected independence. The vote helped set the stage for Canada's Clarity Act, which Parliament passed in 2000.

The act states that secession negotiations can begin only after a referendum question and its result meet standards of clarity. It does not specify a fixed percentage that constitutes a clear majority. Any separation would also require constitutional negotiations involving provincial and federal governments.

Sponsor Message

"It's a bit ironic that separatists are a bit frustrated with the inability to change the constitution and they are using that as a pretext to leave, but, in order to leave, they need to change the same constitution with a much higher threshold for agreement," says Wesley.

toggle caption i Megan Albu/

AFP via Getty Images





What happens if Albertans vote for a separation Referendum?

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has said she will respect the result and begin the process of holding a legally binding referendum, subject to the applicable legal requirements. That would not happen immediately.

The province would also need to consult with First Nations. Treaties between First Nations and the Crown predate Canadian Confederation, and First Nations groups have objected to the idea of an independent Alberta.

In May, an Alberta court ruled that a separatist petition seeking to trigger the referendum violated Indigenous rights because the province had failed to consult First Nations. The province has appealed the decision.

The economic cost of Alberta independence

A government-commissioned report by the University of Calgary's School of Public Policy estimated that separating Alberta from Canada could cost as much as $170 billion Canadian dollars over five years. The report examined two scenarios involving a relatively smooth transition.

Under both scenarios, Alberta's debt would rise substantially as the province assumed a share of Canada's federal debt. The report projected that costs could range from $324 billion to $442.3 billion Canadian dollars.

An independent Alberta would also face billions of dollars in additional interest payments compared with what it currently pays as part of Canada.

Thomas Lukaszak, founder of Forever Canadian, a pro-unity movement, and a former deputy premier of Alberta, has spent 18 months campaigning across the province for Alberta to remain in Canada. He points to Quebec's 1995 referendum as a warning about the potential economic effects of separation.

"Several hundred thousand Canadians moved out of the province of Quebec and moved to other provinces," says Lukaszak. "And until today, the province of Quebec hasn't recovered economically from that because industry and investment has left Montreal and I'm fearing that the same thing would happen to the province of Alberta."

Sponsor Message

When will the referendum results be available?

According to Elections Alberta, unofficial results for referendums with this many questions will be posted 48 hours after polls close. Recruiting enough staff for the vote has been a challenge, and Elections Alberta staff are expected to work around the clock to tally the results.

"This story won't end once the ballots are counted," says Wesley.

The referendum has highlighted deep divisions among Albertans. The question of separation is likely to remain prominent in the lead-up to the provincial election next year.

World.title: It’s referendum day in Alberta. Here’s what you need to know
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Albertans will cast their ballots in a historic referendum Monday, weighing in on 10 questions about the future of the province.

Already, Elections Alberta says 1.3 million people across the province have voted either by special ballot or in advance polls.

The referendum features 10 questions. Questions one through nine centre around immigration and the Constitution.

Question 10 asks if voters support Alberta remaining a province of Canada, or if they support the provincial government beginning the process of holding a second, binding referendum on separation.

If you are voting on referendum day, here is what you need to know.

Where to vote and what to bring

Polls are open across the province from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Unlike in advance voting, on referendum day voters are required to vote at their designated polling station. If you’re not sure where that is, you can enter your address on Elections Alberta’s website to find it.

Voters must be over 18, and a resident of Alberta.

To vote, bring a piece of government-issued photo ID with your address on it, like a driver’s licence, or two pieces of ID including at least one with an address. An attestation form from an authorized signatory will also be accepted.

What if lines are long?

While polling stations are set to close at 8 p.m., if voters are in line before 8 p.m., they will still be allowed to cast their ballots.

“The location will stay open until everyone in that line has had the opportunity to vote,” said Elections Alberta spokesperson Maia Hanrahan.

What if you’re not sure your special ballot’s been counted?

Elections Alberta received requests for more than 600,000 special ballots, and encouraged Albertans to post them in by Oct. 9 in order to meet the Oct. 16 deadline.

If your mail-in ballot was not received by the deadline, or if you applied for a special ballot but never mailed it in, you can still vote on referendum day.

After marking their ballots, voters place each of their 10 ballots in its corresponding box. (Janet French/CBC)

“I'd encourage [voters] to first have a look at that link that they received when they applied for that special ballot. They will be able to see there if it's marked as received and that they've cast their ballots,” said Hanrahan.

“If they're not marked as received, they can go and attend in person to vote.”

Do you have to vote on all 10 questions?

No, says Hanrahan. Voters can vote on all 10 questions, just one, or however many of the 10 questions they would like. She suggests voters familiarize themselves with the questions to speed up the process.

Each referendum question is on a separate, colour-coded ballot. After marking an X on their ballots, voters fold them and place each one in its corresponding box. The ballot will be counted no matter how it is folded, Hanrahan said.

Voters can also request a replacement ballot at the station if they mark an option they don’t want, or if they accidentally tear or rip a ballot.

Can you wear pro-Canada or pro-Alberta apparel?

“People can wear what they'd like to the voting locations. The only rule there is that they can't be wearing something that would be classified as referendum advertising,” said Hanrahan.

That means wearing an Alberta flag baseball cap or a T-shirt with the Maple Leaf is fine, but wearing a campaign slogan, or a message on how to vote on any of the questions, would not be.

When will we know results?

Election officers will count the ballots by hand and the count must be completed within 48 hours under provincial rules.

Question 10, the ballot related to separation, will be counted first. Then counters will deal with the other questions in order, starting with the first question.

Hanrahan says workers will not wait for all polling stations to finish their count of the 10th ballot before moving on, meaning results may start coming in for the other nine questions before the 10th question has been declared.

For live results and analysis on referendum night, watch Alberta Votes: Referendum Night starting at 7 p.m. MT on CBC TV in both Calgary and Edmonton, CBC Gem, CBC News YouTube, CBC News App, CBC News Network and listen live on CBC Radio One.

Referendum results will also be covered live on the CBC Edmonton and CBC Calgary websites.

Then, tune into Alberta Morning on Oct. 20 starting at 5:30 a.m. MT on CBC Radio One and CBC TV in both Calgary and Edmonton.

World.title: Inflation rises to 3.1% in September, as fuel prices push higher: StatsCan
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's annual inflation rate rose to 3.1 per cent in September, Statistics Canada said on Monday, as war in the Middle East caused gasoline prices to accelerate again.

The agency says the switch to less expensive winter blends of gasoline provided some relief last month, even as pump prices jumped 27.8 per cent year-over-year, following a 22.8 per cent annualized increase in August. Statistics Canada says ongoing conflict in the Middle East has pushed benchmark oil prices to their highest level since May.

Grocery prices also rose, by 1.7 per cent year over year, though this was down from the 2.8 per cent increase in August. September marked the smallest yearly increase since May 2024, the agency said.

The reduced food inflation was due to cheaper fresh vegetables, and a decline in the "sugar and confectionary" category.

"Despite the year-over-year slowdown in prices for groceries, prices have increased 33.0 per cent since September 2020," StatCan said.

Shelter prices rose 1.8 per cent year over year, up from 1.5 per cent in August.

WATCH | Why diesel prices are high: Here’s why you’re paying more for diesel | Duration closed caption 6:06 Crude oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz are slowly recovering, so why is the price of diesel skyrocketing? The National's Eli Glasner breaks down what’s causing the increase, and why diesel prices likely won't drop anytime soon.

Statistics Canada's core inflation measures eased slightly on a monthly basis in September. These metrics, which strip out extreme price swings, are closely watched by the Bank of Canada.

Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem recently warned that persistently high global energy prices due to ongoing conflict in the Middle East could drive up the central bank's inflation outlook ahead of its Oct. 28 rate announcement.

Ahead of Monday’s release, a Bloomberg survey of 12 economists predicted the September consumer price index would rise 3.18 per cent year over year.

The national inflation rate held still at three per cent in August, according to a prior report.

World.title: Bank fraud victims ask: Why aren't Canadian banks held more liable?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Over 10 months, Ralph Moore lost $450,000 to an online investment scam — drawn in, in May 2025, by a deepfake video of Prime Minister Mark Carney, heralding a new government investment platform where people could safely grow their savings.

The 88-year-old did transactions online and made multiple trips to his local TD Bank to arrange transfers, bank drafts and payments to other people's credit cards.

Now, Moore and his family are asking why the bank didn't do more to stop the transactions — and won't reimburse him.

" I don't think they protected me," he told Go Public from his home in Qualicum Beach, B.C.

His daughter Leslie Herrndorf, who lives in another city, says she was incredulous when she learned what happened.

Got a story you want investigated? Contact Erica and the Go Public team gopublic@cbc.ca

"How could $450,000 be allowed to be given away by a bank who'd been dealing with my dad for decades?" she asked. "They knew this was unusual behaviour."

Shortly after discovering the bank fraud, Herrndorf had her father's mental capacity tested. He failed.

When Ralph Moore tallied up the money he'd withdrawn from TD Bank, it totalled more than $450,000. (Mike McArthur/CBC)

Early on, the bank recognized that Moore was falling victim to a scam. It took some steps — questioning several of Moore's transactions and warning him and his wife about scams. It also alerted its fraud and anti-scam teams and at one point placed temporary restrictions on his account.

But Herrndorf wonders why the transactions weren't permanently blocked, her father's account frozen, or why the bank didn't make an effort to reach out to its client's adult children or possibly contact the police.

They are among the more than three dozen victims of bank fraud contacted by Go Public for this story who want to know: why doesn't Ottawa hold banks more liable for fraud, like some other countries do?

"It is outrageous, with the known number of frauds happening, that a bank has decided that this is the level of customer service that's acceptable," said Herrndorf.

Moore's daughter Leslie Herrndorf only learned her father was the victim of bank fraud when it was too late. Her father, a longtime TD Bank customer, had lost $450,000. (Michael McArthur/CBC)

Bank fraud is a massive and growing problem, according to the government's Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre. It reports people lost more than $700 million to all fraud in 2025 — and estimates only five per cent of victims report when it happens. Banking-specific numbers were not available.

Go Public receives emails almost daily from people who've suffered fraud losses: from e-transfer fraud to the bank impersonator scam to investment scams and credit card fraud.

In almost all cases, financial institutions hold their customers accountable – issuing similarly worded denial letters, in which people are accused of sharing passwords and account information or blamed for co-operating with scammers posing as investment experts, bank employees or other authorities.

"These are not negligent people, not stupid people," said Alexandre Plourde, a lawyer and analyst at Option consommateurs, a Montreal consumer advocacy organization that also regularly hears from bank fraud victims.

"I don't think the law does enough to protect consumers."

Go Public requested interviews with TD, Royal Bank, the Bank of Montreal, Scotiabank and CIBC after submitting inquiries about various customer losses at all five banks. All declined.

See statements from the big five banks

In February 2026, after Moore had lost virtually all of his money, TD shut down his account.

In a letter to Herrndorf written July 31, 2026, TD said it decided to "exit the client relationship" to "prevent further financial harm."

In a written statement to Go Public, a TD spokesperson did not answer any questions about Moore's case, citing client confidentiality. He said that protecting customers "remains a top priority through robust security, monitoring and education resources" and encouraged victims of fraud and scams to file reports with authorities.

'Zero responsibility'

Scotiabank customer Karla Zwicker says hackers stole over $13,000 from her accounts and line of credit last year. The bank said there was no evidence her account was compromised and declined to reimburse her.

"They've got to stop blaming the customers," said Zwicker, of Edmonton. "We need the government to do more."

Ivanka Bubic believed she was co-operating with RBC's fraud department last year, when scammers spoofed the bank's phone number and convinced her to withdraw money from her line of credit and approve charges on her credit card.

Moore was misled by a video like this that he saw online – a deepfake of Prime Minister Mark Carney, encouraging Canadians to invest in an online platform. (Michael McArthur/CBC)

RBC reimbursed its Montreal customer about $26,000 in credit card charges, but said she was responsible for $15,000 taken from her line of credit.

"It's crazy that they have zero responsibility when fraud happens," she said.

Deepak Kadaba of Mississauga, Ont., lost $3,400 to unauthorized withdrawals and debit transactions. BMO said the withdrawals were completed using his banking information, and the bank is therefore not liable.

"They're hanging customers out to dry," said Kadaba. "Where are the protections?"

'Big incentive' for Canadian banks

Cases like this often have very different outcomes in the U.K.

Since October 2024, the U.K. makes financial institutions shoulder the responsibility for fraud losses, except in cases of extreme negligence.

"The bank must reimburse consumers when they're a victim of fraud … unless the consumer has been grossly negligent," said Plourde, the lawyer. "That's a very high threshold for the banks to prove."

He says Moore's $450,000 loss is "unacceptable" and when customers are clearly being scammed, banks "should have protocols to go deeper, ask more questions."

Go Public requested interviews with TD, Royal Bank, the Bank of Montreal, Scotiabank and CIBC after submitting inquiries about various customer losses at all five banks. All declined. (CBC)

Other jurisdictions, like the E.U. and Australia, have also introduced laws that can force banks to reimburse fraud victims in many cases — though none have gone as far as the U.K.

"Putting more liability on Canadian banks would be a big incentive for banks to develop better security measures," said Plourde.

The Canadian Bankers Association, a trade group, told Go Public that "placing further liability on financial institutions alone will not prevent scams" and could "unintentionally have a negative impact" on bank customers and the economy.

Calls for liability laws

Consumer advocates like Plourde, some MPs and the Ombudsman for Banking Services and Investments have called on Ottawa to make the banks pay for fraud losses for several years.

But when the federal government introduced changes to the Bank Act on March 26, 2026, there was nothing about holding the banks responsible.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne recently told CBC News that he takes bank fraud seriously, and outlined several new measures the government is taking, including working on a national anti-fraud strategy.

"We're acting. We're not waiting, we're acting," said Champagne.

He did not commit to holding financial institutions accountable for fraud.

Meanwhile, a new survey released Oct. 13 by Option consommateurs found that Canadians overwhelmingly (87 per cent) believe that banks should reimburse victims of banking fraud, except when the customer has been grossly negligent.

The survey was conducted by Léger earlier this month, and involved just over 1,500 Canadians.

"The survey results show a public consensus on the need to strengthen banks' obligations," said Plourde.

"We're reaching record highs of fraud every year," he added. "It's time to act."

World.title: For thousands of workers, lifelong time-zone math will go out the window when B.C. stops changing clocks
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On any given workday, Nathan Fehr calculates time zone differences without much of a thought. He works in sales remotely from his home in British Columbia for a biotech company headquartered in Boston, Mass., supporting customers across North America as part of a unit based in the United Kingdom.

At the moment, that means accounting for Pacific time, eastern time, British Summer Time and other time zones spanning North America.

"These things are just kind of second nature to me," Fehr, 43, said from his home in Coquitlam, B.C.

Workers across B.C. who have colleagues or customers in other parts of Canada often organize their days around eastern time, given Ontario is the country's major hub for business, finance and government.

But that second nature will soon have to change to avoid scheduling mistakes and missed connections. As of Nov. 1, B.C. will adopt a year-round time zone, ending the twice-annual ritual of changing clocks for summer and winter.

For thousands of people working out west for federal government departments, Crown corporations, airports and other agencies, it means changing their shift times entirely to stay in line with eastern time or with B.C.'s neighbours in Washington state.

"The challenge around this will be remembering what the time zones are for everyone now because, right now, it's pretty ingrained in me," said Fehr, who's worked in North American sales for more than a decade.

"I'm going to be in the habit of probably just Googling it quickly before a meeting."

Thousands of public sector workers must adjust: union

When B.C. permanently adopts a year-round time zone on Nov. 1, the province will be:

Two hours behind most of Ontario.

One hour behind Alberta.

On the same time as Yukon.

One hour ahead of Washington state.

Two hours ahead of Alaska.

The union representing more than a quarter-million public sector employees in Canada said the new time structure affects thousands of workers in B.C., from border agents and call-takers to fisheries officers and park wardens.

The Public Service Alliance of Canada (PSAC) said more than 100 call-centre employees working for the Canada Revenue Agency will have to adjust their schedules to work until 6 p.m. instead of 5 p.m., equal to 8 p.m. ET.

An hour might not sound like much, a representative said, but the later schedule can throw a wrench in family scheduling that's already adjusting to return-to-office mandates.

"It's going to mean that folks are going to need to have child care for an hour later … elder care as well," said Jamey Mills, the regional executive vice-president for PSAC.

"It's just compounding on our members."

Some border agents will also be bumping schedules because the Canada Border Services Agency adjusted its opening hours at nine land crossings to align with neighbouring U.S. ports of entry, which will be an hour out of time with B.C. as of next month.

Mills said fisheries officers, Parks Canada wardens and staff with the Canadian Food Inspection Agency will all be adjusting to commuting and working through darker mornings. Airport workers will likely face "confusion in the early days" of the change, he added.

Vancouver International Airport said in a statement that passengers should "b e mindful that some destinations, which previously were in the same time zone as Vancouver, may now be different" after the shift.

WATCH | Manitoba becomes latest province to stop changing clocks: Confused about Canada's new time zones? It's about to get complicated | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration closed caption 8:15



On permanent daylight time, skies could stay dark until as late as 9 a.m. in Vancouver and 9:30 a.m. in communities further north, like Prince George.

The change does not affect B.C.'s Peace Region or the Kootenay town of Creston, which have never changed clocks for daylight time. It would also not affect the East Kootenay region, which is aligned with the time in Alberta.

The repercussions go beyond the public sector. The association representing construction workers in B.C. expressed concern around later sunrises for crews who already work well before dawn. Several scientists, including a Stanford professor whose work was cited by B.C.'s government, said the shift could be detrimental to public health .

Alberta, Manitoba, parts of northern Ontario and the Northwest Territories adopted similar measures this year, while Yukon did the same in 2020. Saskatchewan has had permanent standard time since 1966.

"I grew up in Saskatchewan and the time never changed," said Mills, the union representative. "Moving to B.C., it was always weird when it did. I think, obviously, there is going to be some hazards, but I think British Columbians will eventually just adapt."

WATCH | Scientists say they worry new time zone will do more harm than good: Why some scientists don't support B.C.'s switch to permanent daylight time | Duration closed caption 2:17



A 2019 public survey in B.C. found 93 per cent out of a "record" 223,000 people polled supported year-round daylight time, according to officials, and "across all industry groups and nearly all occupational groups, support for year-round [daylight time] observance was higher than 90 per cent."

Fehr said the new schedule will make his job easier because he'll have an extra hour of overlap in the workday with his colleagues out east. He said it will also make his life better, personally, as the father of a boy in elementary school.

"I'm happy with it, not having to have my son go through the whole time change, which can really mess with their internal clock and to make bedtime a little less fun and in the morning time as well," said Fehr.

"It's nice that we'll not have to do that again."

World.title: NATO's race against time: Senior commander warns alliance must adapt faster to deter Russia
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There's a nightmare that keeps one of NATO's most senior military commanders up at night and it's not what you might think.

It isn't the idea of Russian tanks rolling into the Baltic states or Poland. Nor is it a sudden military confrontation in the Arctic.

The scenario that keeps NATO Supreme Allied Commander Transformation Pierre Vandier up at night is the notion of the Western military alliance being caught unprepared and unable to keep up with the pace of technological innovation that's happening on the modern battlefield.

"Being late is really my nightmare," Vandier, a French admiral, told CBC News in an exclusive interview.

"When I see people chatting, delaying some important decisions, not committing the money, using some … old-fashioned process, then it keeps me [up] at night."

Vandier met Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Jennie Carignan and other high-ranking defence leaders for an up-close look at some of Canada's defence innovation plans during his recent low-key trip to Ottawa.

His warning about keeping pace comes at a particularly uncomfortable moment for the 32-member alliance.

WATCH | NATO commander on his biggest concern: 'Being late is really my nightmare,' says NATO commander | Duration closed caption 3:26 French Admiral Pierre Vandier, NATO's Supreme Commander of Transformation, says delays in upgrading the military alliance's technology keep him up at night. 'If you need five years to buy a software, it's totally irrelevant,' Vandier says.

Russia's war against Ukraine is approaching its fifth anniversary. Moscow has been accused of escalating a campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions in Europe along NATO's eastern flank. And Western governments are scrambling to rebuild military capabilities and defence industrial production lines that were allowed to shrink following the end of the Cold War more than three decades ago.

The danger, according to Vandier, is that the alliance is trying to prepare for tomorrow's war using institutions, procurement systems and assumptions inherited from yesterday.

"We thought that time was our friend," he said. "Now time is not our friend. It's the enemy's friend. The agenda is built on the other side."

During four years of grinding combat in Ukraine, Russia has suffered an enormous number of casualties. According to the British Ministry of Defence, as of mid-September, the Russian military has suffered 1.3 million casualties in the Ukraine war, including over 500,000 dead.

And there is a paradox at the heart of NATO's current security dilemma. While there have been devastating casualties and an enormous amount of equipment lost, the Russian Army that stumbled into Ukraine four years ago is not the same one on the battlefield today.

Vandier argued that Moscow has become more innovative, more adaptable and, in certain areas, more dangerous.

"The enemy is not the same as the one we had in 2022," he said.

"They learn, they adapt."

WATCH | How NATO is responding to suspected Russian incursions: How NATO is flexing in the face of Russian aggression | Duration closed caption 5:44 NATO is strengthening its air defence and border security in the Baltics in response to escalating Russian sabotage and drone threats. A CBC News team gets an up-close look at the alliance’s readiness and the Canadian military’s contribution.

He pointed specifically to Russia's evolving drone technology, including faster jet-powered attack drones that have complicated Ukraine's ability to defend its cities and critical infrastructure.

According to Vandier, the introduction of more advanced propulsion systems has significantly reduced the effectiveness of some Ukrainian drone-interception methods.

He estimated that interception success rates against certain Russian drones have fallen from approximately 90 per cent earlier this year to roughly 50 per cent as the technology has evolved. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, at the end of September, pegged the interception rate at about 55 per cent.

There's been a significant body of research published over the past year which challenges the assumption that Russia's enormous losses in Ukraine have left its military weaker, less capable or unable to threaten NATO.

Western military analysts increasingly describe a Russian military that has learned to adapt under fire, regenerate formations while fighting, absorb technological innovation and sustain operations despite staggering casualties.

"Russian military institutions reward loyalty over competence," said a study written last July by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies, which argued Russia has become increasingly dependent on Chinese, Iranian and North Korean military assistance.

The authors argue that Russia's military can absorb new technology without developing the capacity to exploit it fully and effectively.

An assessment written last year by the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), based in the United Kingdom, was even more stark. It pointed to how Moscow is rebuilding equipment inventories, expanding units and reorganizing forces near NATO territory.

The think-tank's report said that Russia may restore important elements of its prewar ground-force equipment strength sooner than expected, although newly formed units could remain undermanned.

The IISS report also suggested that equipment shortages throughout the Russian military could potentially be resolved by late 2026 or early 2027. However, the full equipping and expansion of Russian ground forces could take until 2030 or 2035.

"It's a very fast-evolving environment," Vandier said.

WATCH | NATO grapples with 'grey zone' attacks: Why 'grey zone' drone attacks are a problem for NATO | Duration closed caption 5:53 Suspected Russian drones have repeatedly entered NATO airspace on its eastern flank and as far west as Germany, Belgium and France. But responding to incursions by ambiguous drones poses a problem for a defensive alliance such as NATO, says Wendy Gilmour, former NATO assistant secretary general for defence investment.

Russia has the ability to produce enormous quantities of relatively inexpensive drones and missiles. And that has exposed the limitations of Western defence industries designed to manufacture smaller numbers of highly sophisticated weapons.

Vandier believes the alliance has underestimated the scale of the challenge.

"The idea that the war is just a crisis of a few weeks is something that nobody can bet on anymore," he said.

He pointed to the enormous numbers of drones and missiles being employed in Ukraine as evidence that NATO must rethink not only what it buys, but how quickly it can replenish its arsenals.

The problem, Vandier said, is not simply a shortage of weapons. It is a shortage of industrial capacity.

Western economies have spent decades moving manufacturing and critical supply chains overseas, leaving defence industries dependent on materials and components that may not be readily available during a prolonged conflict.

Vandier challenged the suggestion that NATO's combined economic strength automatically translates into an overwhelming industrial advantage over Russia.

"I disagree with the point where we have a good industrial depth," he said.

"The challenge now is to produce what we can produce in mass and rapidly, and not only what we have on a very exquisite and limited quantities."

The implication of that is significant. In a prolonged conflict with Russia, the West would quickly run out of equipment and ammunition.

The U.S-Israeli war with Iran has seen a number of published reports about the scarcity of high-end weapons systems.

For Canada, Vandier's assessment comes as the federal government embarks on an unprecedented expansion of defence spending.

After decades of relatively limited investment, Ottawa has committed billions of additional dollars to modernizing the Canadian Armed Forces and rebuilding the country's defence industrial base.

Vandier said he has been struck by the scale of the change.

"It's very impressive to see how this country, which has spent a limited amount of money focused on NORAD, now is opening eyes on all the NATO [area of responsibility]," Vandier said.

World.title: Where do B.C.'s parties stand on the future of AI data centres?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

AI data centres have become a hot-button political issue the world over, and in British Columbia it's no different.

Earlier this year, the federal government announced backing for "sovereign AI data centre" clusters led by Telus in Vancouver and Kelowna.

That announcement drew support from industry and provincial and municipal leaders, but sparked protests among groups citing concerns about big tech and environmental impacts.

With B.C.'s election day less than a week away, how the province's political parties approach the issue could play a role in who forms the next government.

WATCH | Federal government backs new data centres for B.C.: Ottawa announces funding for AI, new data centres in B.C. | Duration closed caption 3:13

B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson says data centres are something to "contemplate" going forward.

"Obviously the data centres are important, but we've got significant challenges with water in this province, you know, in places that you would never think," he said.

The B.C. Green Party, meanwhile, is calling for a moratorium on the construction of new data centres until stronger regulation and environmental policies are in place.

"We have allowed AI tech companies to charge forward and tell us what's going to be beneficial rather than independently evaluating the cost and benefit to this province," said Green Leader Emily Lowan.

WATCH | B.C. Greens pitch AI data centre moratorium: B.C. Greens calling on province to stop AI data centres, contain water usage | Duration closed caption 4:56

The B.C. NDP pointed to its Energy Statutes Amendment Act as an example of how it has approached the issue.

The policy requires data centre proponents to compete for a limited quantity of electricity, prioritizing those with environmental benefits and First Nations involvement.

"We as a government require them to meet certain hurdles," NDP Leader David Eby said.

"They're going to pay a higher electricity rate. They're going to ensure that they're not wasting water, using water that is closed loop systems and that they're providing employment."

OneBC told CBC News it was not explicitly for or against data centres.

"It will always depend on what the plan is, how it will effect the community and what will allow local residents to live their lives without undue disruption," spokesperson Wyatt Claypool said in a statement.

"Data centres are important for the development of our digital services but like with any project issues around time, place, and manner will always be considered."

CentreBC did not respond to a request for comment.

Public concerns about data centres have often focused on the facilities' potential for heavy water and power consumption, along with air and noise pollution when they use on-site generators.

And while British Columbia has dozens of hydroelectric dams, persistent drought in the province has left the province reliant on power imports from the United States in recent years.

"We're simply getting to the point where there may not be enough electricity to go around in the next few years simply because we haven't been generating enough to make ourselves self-sufficient," said Barry Penner, chair of the Energy Futures Institute.

Telus says the data centres announced in May will run on 98 per cent clean hydro power and recycle enough waste energy to heat 150,000 homes, while using 90 per cent less water than traditional data centres.

But some experts are still recommending a cautious approach to the new industry.

"We need to maybe slow down a little bit and make sure we do it right rather than do it wrong and have to pay later," University of British Columbia economics professor Werner Antweiler said.

In the meantime, construction and planning continues on the Telus clusters, while B.C. Hydro has been reviewing applications for new projects.

British Columbians go to the polls on Saturday, Oct. 24.

World.title: Houthi attack on Yemeni government forces kills 53: officials
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Fifty-three people were killed and 200 were injured in an attack on Monday by the Iran-aligned Houthis on a government security forces training camp in ‌Yemen's Shabwa province, according to the local authority, as fighting in the country intensifies.

Video verified by Reuters from Shabwa province showed injured people and bloodied bodies scattered across the ground.

The ​Houthis and the internationally recognized government, which is ​backed by a Saudi-led coalition, have been trading attacks since the group advanced in September toward territory near the Bab ​el-Mandeb Strait, a shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the ⁠Red Sea.

Local authority ⁠sources who spoke on condition of ‌anonymity said the Houthis had launched three ballistic missiles at security forces during a training exercise.

WATCH | How Yemen plays into the Mideast war: How the Houthi-Saudi Arabia conflict plays into broader Middle East war | Duration closed caption 8:02 Saudi Arabia has recently been rocked by attacks from Yemen's Houthi rebels. The weekend strikes came in response to Saudi's own ongoing attacks on Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen, which resumed in July amid the U.S. and Israel's war with Iran. Analyst Sina Toossi explains how the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis plays into the broader war in West Asia.

Shabwa, an energy-rich province in southcentral coastal Yemen overlooking the Gulf of Aden, is home to the ⁠Balhaf liquefied natural gas facility, Yemen's largest industrial investment.

Government forces this month began a campaign aimed at recapturing areas controlled by the Houthis, recovering ground near the ‌strait, while the group besieges Taiz, the last major urban stronghold of anti-Houthi forces in the southern highland area of Yemen.

The conflict in Yemen has become another frontline in the wider U.S.-Israeli ​war on Iran as the Houthis have escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's largest ⁠crude exporter, targeting Riyadh's international airport and the state oil company Saudi Aramco.

War ⁠broke out in Yemen in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital ⁠Sanaa, ⁠driving the government south. ​A Saudi-led military intervention the following year led to a bloody stalemate until the ​sides agreed a ⁠2022 truce that held until this year.

Yemen is already one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with aid agencies warning of rapidly deteriorating conditions there.

World.title: Report traces alleged Muslim Brotherhood influence in Canada
World.content:
Article content

While the final result of the audit was never publicized, the CRA’s initial 150-page assessment was later released. In that assessment, reviewed by National Post, the CRA drew from financial records and correspondences between 2011 and 2015 that the CRA had indicated some of MAC’s top leaders were actively involved in activities of the Egyptian chapter of the Muslim Brotherhood. It also details how the CRA alleged that members of the Egyptian and other chapters of the Brotherhood could immediately become MAC members upon coming to Canada. In its assessment, the CRA also said the MAC had expanded its real estate property holdings from $12 million in 2006 to more than $51 million by 2015, enough that the federal agency took the position that the expansion was of an unstated or non-charitable purpose.
