World.title: Football Federation of Belize and U15 prepare for team’s trip to Azerbaijan
World.content:
Football Federation of Belize and U15 prepare for team’s trip to Azerbaijan

By Zoila Palma: On October 17, the Football Federation of Belize (FFB) met with parents of the Under-15 (U15) Boys National Football Team as final preparations continued for the FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival 2026 in Azerbaijan, scheduled for October 24–30.

Fourteen young footballers have been selected to represent Belize at the international event, with the team scheduled to depart today for the three-day journey to Azerbaijan.

The meeting was led by Head Coach Wayne Casimiro and the team’s technical staff. FFB General Secretary Ian Jones and Executive Member Shane Orio also attended, reaffirming the federation’s commitment to the safety and well-being of all athletes travelling for the competition.

Presentations were made to help parents understand the team’s travel itinerary and preview the facilities and schedules the players will follow during their stay. The selection process began with more than 30 young footballers from across Belize competing for one of the 14 available spots. The FFB acknowledged the dedication of all participants, including those who did not make the final squad.

FFB noted that for some players, the trip will also mark their first opportunity to travel abroad, exposing them to new cultures and traditions while allowing them to connect with other young athletes.

The FFB noted that football helps young people develop discipline, teamwork, resilience, friendships and confidence.

World.title: Team Belize prepares for 2026 CODICADER Disability games in Guatemala
World.content:
Team Belize prepares for 2026 CODICADER Disability games in Guatemala

By Zoila Palma: The National Sports Council of Belize held a send-off ceremony on October 17 to celebrate athletes preparing to represent the country at the 2026 CODICADER Disability Games, scheduled for October 25–31 in Guatemala.

The ceremony recognized the athletes’ dedication and determination as Belize prepares for its third appearance at the regional competition, which promotes inclusion, equality, friendship and sporting excellence among young athletes with disabilities across Central America.

Belize’s delegation comprises approximately 63 members, including 34 athletes and 29 officials and support personnel.

The athletes will compete in athletics, boccia and goalball. The team includes students from 10 schools across the Belize, Cayo, Toledo and Orange Walk districts, representing athletes with various disabilities, subject to the Games’ eligibility requirements.

Minister of Tourism, Youth, Sports and Diaspora Relations Anthony Mahler and Minister of State in the Ministry of Youth and Sports Devin Daly attended the ceremony, where they handed over gear and flags to the delegation, shared words of encouragement and wished Team Belize success at the Games.

The National Sports Council also recognized the contributions of coaches, teachers, parents, chaperones and support personnel, as well as organizations supporting the delegation, including Special Olympics Belize, The Inspiration Center, the Belize Council for the Visually Impaired and the Special Education Unit.

World.title: DFC stands in pink for Breast Cancer Awareness Month
World.content:
DFC stands in pink for Breast Cancer Awareness Month

By Zoila Palma: The Development Finance Corporation (DFC) is standing in solidarity with individuals and families affected by breast cancer throughout Belize as part of Breast Cancer Awareness Month this October.

DFC says its pink campaign honors the strength and resilience of breast cancer survivors while showing support for everyone whose life has been touched by the disease.

DFC is also encouraging the public to look beyond wearing pink by promoting early detection, regular screenings, and awareness of breast cancer signs and symptoms.

DFC reminds Belizeans that support and care are important for those affected by breast cancer.

World.title: Barton Creek Archaeological Reserve open; Nohoch Ch’een remains closed
World.content:
Barton Creek Archaeological Reserve open; Nohoch Ch’een remains closed

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Institute of Archeology informed that Barton Creek Archaeological Reserve is now OPEN for visitations.

The Nohoch Ch’een Archaeological Reserve remains CLOSED until further notice.

All other archaeological reserves, including Actun Tunichil Mucnal (ATM) are OPEN for visitations.

Tour operators and tour guides are advised to exercise caution, especially during water-based activities.

World.title: Help needed to recover bag with passport, US cash and visa left at Western Border
World.content:
Help needed to recover bag with passport, US cash and visa left at Western Border

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A San Ignacio family is asking the public for help to recover a bag left behind at the Belize Western Border.

According to the family, a woman forgot her black Michael Kors tote bag on a bench outside the money exchange booth near the taxi stand on the night of Monday, October 12, while waiting for her ride.

The bag contained US cash, her passport with an American visa, a credit card and other personal belongings.

The family says video footage appears to show a woman in red shorts and a black blouse picking up the bag and getting into a red car.

They are asking anyone who can help identify the person or vehicle to come forward. A reward is being offered.

If you have information, please call or WhatsApp 610 8117.

World.title: 24 live rounds and suspected cocaine found hidden under cement block in Orange Walk
World.content:
24 live rounds and suspected cocaine found hidden under cement block in Orange Walk

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Orange Walk police have recovered live ammunition and suspected cocaine hidden in an empty lot in Orange Walk Town.

Police say that around 8:00pm on Friday, October 16, officers from the Orange Walk GI3 Unit acted on information that someone had hidden something in a bushy lot at the corner of Chips Alley and Cabbage Street.

During checks, an officer found a green plastic bag tucked under a cement block.

Inside were 24 live 9mm rounds, 13 Luger brand and 11 S&B brand, along with a small plastic bag of white powder suspected to be cocaine.

The suspected cocaine weighed 7.3 grams.

No one was in the area at the time, and both the ammunition and drugs were sealed and logged as found property.

World.title: Teen reports being beaten with belt by stepfather in Orange Walk
World.content:
Teen reports being beaten with belt by stepfather in Orange Walk

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 13 year old boy from Orange Walk District has reported to police that he was struck with a belt by his stepfather.

The boy visited the Orange Walk Police Station on Friday, October 16, accompanied by his biological father.

He told police that earlier that afternoon, his stepfather became upset after seeing his younger sibling walking with some boys the teen knew from school. He said his stepfather then lashed him with a belt on his hand and lower back.

According to the report, the boy was then told to pack his belongings and leave to stay with relatives. He later made his way to his father’s home, and his father took him to the police station.

A medico legal form was issued. The boy has been placed in the care of his father, and both parents have been instructed to report to the Human Services Department on Monday, October 19, for a follow up.

World.title: ATM Cave and Barton Creek closed as river levels rise
World.content:
ATM Cave and Barton Creek closed as river levels rise

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Actun Tunichil Muknal (ATM) and Barton Creek Archaeological Reserves are closed to visitors today because of elevated river levels.

The Institute of Archaeology of the National Institute of Culture and History (IA/NICH) made the announcement early Sunday morning, October 18.

All water related tour activities have also been suspended at the Nohoch Che’en Archaeological Reserve, a popular cave tubing destination.

All other archaeological reserves remain open for visitors.

The IA/NICH says it is monitoring conditions and will provide updates as necessary.

The closures come after days of heavy rain across the country, with an excessive rainfall warning issued by the National Meteorological Service.

World.title: ‘Cherish our heritage’
World.content:
Opposition Leader Mark Golding (right) shares a word with Minister of Culture Olivia Grange at the National Heritage Week Thanksgiving Service at Church of the Open Bible on Washington Boulevard, in St Andrew, on Sunday. At left is state minister in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce Delano Seiveright. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

PASTOR of Lakes Pen Apostolic Church, Overseer Cassel Dunkley is urging Jamaicans to reclaim the everyday acts of kindness and respect that once brought communities together.

He argued that the country’s heritage is found not only in its national heroes, anthem, and history books, but also in the values passed down through generations as Jamaica confronts mounting challenges.

Dunkley, who was addressing the National Heritage Week Thanksgiving Church Service on Sunday at Church of the Open Bible on Washington Boulevard, in St Andrew, said Jamaica must preserve the traditions that taught people to care for their neighbours, help grieving families, and treat other people’s children as their own.

He recalled a time when a family experiencing a death could expect relatives and neighbours to arrive with food and other assistance, contrasting that tradition with what he described as a loss of community spirit.

“When somebody died in the country, granny came with a bunch of bananas, auntie came with something, cousin came with something.

Nowadays, when somebody dies, it becomes a party. We want beer, we want Red Stripe, and black stripe, and white stripe.

But I come from a heritage that when something happens, your neighbour is going to look out for you — [and] those are the things we want to get back to,” Dunkley said.

He also called for a return to the close community relationships in which neighbours shared responsibility for children and looked out for one another, regardless of whether they expected anything in return.

“We want to get back and cherish the heritage where your tears become my tears, when I try to do something to help you more than try to do something to belittle you,” he said.

Dunkley said Jamaica’s heritage must also be reflected in how people treat others. “We must cherish respect for all, irrespective of your belief.

We must learn to love, forgive, and respect each other. But sometimes we allow material things to shift our focus, and we judge people by the car they drive, we judge them by the place they live.

But remember… we are one blood,” he said. “Love those who can’t buy you a shirt.

Love those who can’t give you nothing in return. Because sometimes we only give to those who can give back to us, we only are kind to those who can be kind back to us.

But somebody around the corner is looking for your love, somebody who hurt you is looking and waiting for your forgiveness,” Dunkley said.

He argued that preserving the country’s heritage requires Jamaicans to remember the lessons taught by previous generations, including honesty, respect for others, and responsibility for the wider community.

Dunkley recalled how children were expected to return items they found if those items did not belong to them, saying such lessons should not be lost as the country develops.

“Do you remember the time in Jamaica when if you brought home a pen, your mother says, ‘Where did you get it from?’ and granny tied her head and said, ‘We are going to school with you in the morning because you have to give it back’? We couldn’t say ‘finders keepers’; we were taught to return the things that do not belong to us.

We cannot afford to lose that heritage,” he said. Beyond these everyday customs, Dunkley reminded the congregation of the sacrifices made by Jamaica’s national heroes and other leaders in shaping the country’s history.

Dunkley said Jamaicans have much to be thankful for, including the country’s educational institutions and the role the Church played and continues to play in society.

He urged Jamaicans not to allow negative news and the country’s problems to overshadow its achievements.

“But I borrow the words of [Governor General] Sir Patrick Allen. He said, ‘We can use what is right about Jamaica to fix what is not right,’ ” Dunkley said.

He also called for greater civic pride, including respect for the environment, and recalled school lessons that encouraged children to pick up litter and keep their surroundings clean.

Dunkley also called for Jamaica’s national anthem and pledge to be given greater prominence at public gatherings, arguing that the words and values they represent should remain part of the country’s everyday life.

He said Jamaica’s history and traditions should help guide the country through its present difficulties, adding that people must understand their past if they are to make sound decisions about the future.

“We must cherish our heritage! We might have different theological beliefs… but, brothers and sisters, we must embrace and understand where we are coming from — because if we don’t know where we are coming from we will not know where we are going,” said Dunkley.

World.title: PM wants security forces to get tougher on criminals
World.content:
HOLNESS...we must stop making excuses for men who carry illegal guns, terrorise communities, and prey upon the vulnerable.

PRIME Minister Dr Andrew Holness has urged the leadership of the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) to intensify its efforts to go after criminal gangs and the people who support them.

Holness, who returned to the island on Saturday, was immediately briefed by Police Commissioner Dr Kevin Blake about the developments in the Five Miles area off the Sligoville main road in St Catherine which left five men — JCF members Corporal Trevoy Shaw, and Constable Devoney Rose; and civilians Errol Hussey, his son Malique Hussey, and nephew Javoun Cogle — dead, and a 10-year-old girl nursing a gunshot wound.

In his response Holness offered condolence to the families of the dead cops, the hope for the full recovery of the injured child, and expressed relief that other civilians who were in the house escaped unharmed.

The prime minister said the reports on the incident provide a stark reminder that Jamaica cannot let its guard down or relax the laws.

“We must maintain our resolute posture against organised criminal violence. The emerging accounts of this incident point to a disturbing level of planning and coordination. You reported that there was misdirection, diversionary gunfire from outside, [and] there was support and prearranged transport. All of this must be fully investigated.

“We must uncover and dismantle every person, every network, every resource, every facilitator who enabled this violence,” added Holness.

He said the police account also reveals something even more chilling, that the gunmen were willing to use members of their own households as shields to protect themselves.

“This is the kind of evil that we are confronted with in our society. These men had a choice, they could have put down their weapons, they could have surrendered and had their day in court. Instead they chose lethal violence,” Holness said.

“But let me be blunt, we must separate these evil men from our society. We must stop making excuses for men who carry illegal guns, terrorise communities, and prey upon the vulnerable. They are not protectors; they are not justified by poverty, exclusion, or social injustice. They are not freedom fighters, they are not Robin Hoods, they are not rebels or misunderstood victims. They are parasites and pestilence upon our society,” declared Holness.

According to the prime minister, these criminals are obstructions to the progress of the society, which is better off without them.

“They must be identified, disarmed, arrested, prosecuted, and removed from our communities through the full force and uncompromising force of the law. There can be no moral equivalency. There can be no romanticising of guns; no glorifying of gunmen; and no tolerance for those who shelter finance, arm, and celebrate them. We must never comfort ourselves with the illusion that organised terror cannot exist in our communities,” said Holness.

He said the attack on the security forces on Friday has shaken members but it has not diluted the resolve of both the JCF and the Jamaica Defence Force.

Holness said the National Security Council will have its regular monthly meeting this week during which it we will review the situation.

“But I can tell you from now, commissioner… the policy direction is that you should intensify the operations that you have planned to target the criminals, the gang leaders, those who you have been pursuing with intelligence.

“Bring them forward. Intensify it. Because what this has shown is a new level of criminal organisation that is a threat to our national security. Whatever resources you need, we will discuss it but you should make a big push now to get as many of these who are just lying in wait to confront and challenge the security of the country,” added Holness.

He argued that Friday’s incident in Five Miles must be used as a watershed and a turning point as it underscored that there are people with criminal intent and the capability and wherewithal to unleash terror on the society.

“And we must meet them head on. We must meet them head on and maintain our civility and the rule of law. So the word to all gunman: ‘Tek weh unnuself!’ ” declared Holness.

World.title: Police step up hunt for alleged killer ‘Papa’
World.content:
Alleged gang enforcer Kenroy “Papa” Williams who has been linked to at least five murders.

AN islandwide manhunt is now on for Kenroy “Papa” Willis who the police have described as a “high-risk target” linked to at least five murders committed across sections of St Andrew between May 2024 and May 2025.

Jamaica Observer sources say 25-year-old Willis was the main target of an early morning operation last Friday in the Five Miles area, off the Sligoville main road in St Catherine, which left five men dead and a 10-year-old girl nursing gunshot wounds.

The dead men have since been identified as Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) members Corporal Trevoy Shaw and Constable Devoney Rose; and civilians Errol Hussey, his son Malique Hussey, and nephew Javoun Cogle.

According to the Observer sources, Malique Hussey, otherwise called Mal Boss, is a known associate of Willis who is of a Rose Hall District, Lawrence Tavern, St Andrew, address.

Willis has been identified in the JCF’s Violence Producers Workbook as an alleged enforcer of the Rose Hall gang and a suspect in several serious violent crimes, including murder, shootings and robberies.

He is specifically wanted in connection with the October 26, 2024 murder of Verne Ewan Joseph along Essex Hall Main Road.

Willis has also been linked to the killing of Alexian Daley in Mahoney District, Lawrence Tavern, on May 26, 2024; Matthew Williams, who was killed at Lawrence Tavern Square on June 14, 2024; Oshane Blackwood, who was killed along Brooks Level Road, Stony Hill, on May 11, 2025.

Three of the five killings occurred within approximately five weeks in 2024, all in communities in and around Lawrence Tavern. The sources say the police are now targeting several locations where Willis may have sought refuge or maintained connections, including Golden Spring, Lawrence Tavern, Glengoffe in St Catherine, and Bull Bay and Clarks Hill in St Andrew. The police have previously conducted targeted raids as part of their efforts to locate Willis, and Friday’s operation was believed to be the latest move by the cops to nab him. The sources say there was gunfire in areas outside the zone the police had cordoned off during the operation, and they suspect this was an effort by Willis, or his cronies, to distract them while they were being fired on from inside the house. Willis has remained the subject of police interest throughout 2026, with published reports identifying him as wanted for murder and under investigation in connection with other violent crimes. “Willis’s reported gang affiliation, alleged involvement in multiple murders, and associations with other suspected violent offenders have made him a subject of sustained police interest,” added the Observer source.

World.title: NUFF offers more than enough
World.content:
From left: Nadean Rawlings, director, NUFF; Alisa Jones, production assistant, NUFF; and Jesse Royal, recording artiste (Aceion Cunningham)

Negril Universal Film Festival (NUFF), formerly known as the Skylark Film Festival, brought four days of Jamaican and international storytelling from Thursday, October 8, to Sunday, October 11.

The weekend paired film screenings with conversations, industry sessions, culture and hands-on learning, creating a gathering for audiences and emerging film-makers alike.

The festival, now in its 7th staging, opened with a special 25th-anniversary screening of Stephanie Black’s landmark documentary

Life and Debt. The film’s examination of Jamaica and the forces shaping its economy provided a fitting starting point for a conversation about the issues it raised and how they resonate a quarter-century later.

On Friday, the programme shifted from film-maker development by day to a celebration of Jamaican storytelling in the evening. The WES Studios-sponsored Vertical Film-making Masterclass, led by Richard Lawson of Hyperlens Studios, offered practical insight into a changing screen format. Documentary shorts and opportunities to learn, connect, and exchange ideas rounded out the daytime programme.

Friday night’s Jamaican Film Block gave way to a special Jimmy Cliff tribute featuring his daughter Odessa Chambers. Storm Saulter then presented the first two episodes of his new

SKY-TV series,

Possession. An in-depth conversation and question-and-answer session invited the audience to explore the series and its creative vision with the film-maker.

World.title: 149 outstanding Jamaicans to be honoured today
World.content:
Members of the Jamaica Defence Force in rehearsal on Saturday for today’s Ceremony of Investiture and Presentation of National Honours and Awards at King’s House. (Photos: Naphtali Junior)

Six Jamaicans will receive the nation’s fifth highest honour, the Order of Jamaica (OJ), at the 2026 Ceremony of Investiture and Presentation of National Honours and Awards today at King’s House.

They are the former Bank of Jamaica Governor Richard Byles; Minister of Energy, Transport and Telecommunications Daryl Vaz; Chief Executive Officer of Sagicor Group Jamaica Christopher Zacca; philanthropist Donette Chin-Loy Chang; former Government minister Maxine Henry-Wilson; and former Government minister Derrick Smith.

They will be among the 140 Jamaicans who will be recognised for their sterling contribution to nation-building. The ceremony is scheduled to take place on the lawns of King’s House, starting at 9:00 am.

Twenty-five people will be conferred with the Order of Distinction in the rank of Commander; 41 with the Order of Distinction in the rank of Officer; 33 with the Badge of Honour for Meritorious Service; and 30 with the Badge of Honour for Long and Faithful Service.

Three civilians will receive the Badge of Honour for Gallantry. They are Danielle Anna-Marie Barnswell and her husband, Councillor Scean Barnswell, as well as Susan Annmarie Higgins.

As customary, several members of the unformed groups will be awarded with the Medal of Honour for Meritorious Service — 25 from the Jamaica Constabulary Force; 13 from the Department of Correctional Service; 15 from the Jamaica Fire Brigade; and 12 from the Jamaica Defence Force.

The ceremony will be presided over by Governor General Sir Patrick Allen. Under the National Honours and Awards Act, promulgated on July 18, 1969, provision is made for those outstanding Jamaicans to be conferred with one of the honours of the Orders of the six Societies of Honour.

The six honours by rank are Order of National Hero, Order of the Nation, Order of Excellence, Order of Merit, Order of Jamaica, and the Order of Distinction. There is also the Medal of Honour and Badge of Honour, which recognises gallantry and meritorious service.

World.title: Unfair playing field
World.content:
West Indies bowler Kemar Roach (second left) celebrates with teammates (from left) Roston Chase, Amir Jangoo and Shamar Joseph after the dismissal of Asitha Fernando of Sri Lanka during the fourth day of the first cricket Test match at Sir Vivian Richards Stadium in North Sound, Antigua and Barbuda, on June 28, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

With Cricket West Indies (CWI) set to earn nothing from the men’s team’s tour of India, CWI CEO, Jamaica’s Chris Dehring, is urging the International Cricket Council (ICC) to reconsider its revenue distribution model which he believes is placing further strain on cricket in the Caribbean.

CWI has been under the global eye over the past month after revealing their significant financial struggles which has resulted in an array of changes in the set-up, highlighted by the 25 per cent reduction in retainer fees for internationally contracted players.

The deadline for the players to accept the contracts was last week and the names of those who have done so are expected to be revealed in the coming days. The Jamaica Observer reported earlier this month that Jamaicans Rovman Powell, John Campbell, and Vitel Lawes are among the players who were offered international contracts.

The trio were part of the West Indies who recently completed its white ball tour of India. The Caribbean side recovered from losing the One-Day International (ODI) series 1-2 by earning a 2-2 draw in the five-match Twenty20 (T20) series which ended on Saturday.

While it was deemed a thrilling contest on the pitch, Dehring revealed a darker reality of it, with CWI set to receive no financial benefit from the eight-match series.

“That is one of the great anomalies of world cricket where we play against India in India and the West Indies cricket gets nothing when a match that probably has a value and a revenue generation capacity of probably 20, 30 million dollars a series and we’re getting nothing,” he told The Scoop.

Dehring’s comments come days after fellow Jamaican and former CWI President Dave Cameron blasted the ICC’s revenue distribution model, which he believes unfairly favours cricket’s wealthiest nations, particularly India.

Under the ICC’s 2024-2027 financial distribution model, India receives a reported 38.5 per cent of the governing body’s annual revenue believed to be US $600 million, compared with 4.58 per cent for Cricket West Indies (CWI), while the host board generally retains the domestic broadcast revenue generated by bilateral series.

While Cameron, who served as CWI president from 2013-2019, has raised concerns about the financial imbalance during his stint, Dehring believes the roots of the problem stretch back nearly three decades to a 1997 vote by ICC members.

“West Indies were very attractive as a team and everybody wanted us to tour, and so we would be paid a touring fee and essentially that touring fee was more than what we could make in the Caribbean hosting series, so we would make our revenues from the international tours that we would take to Australia, India, and England and that revenue helped to sustain West Indies cricket,” he said.

“[But] all the countries recognised where television rights were going and they decided, ‘well, we don’t want to pay anybody our domestic television rights so we will keep it all to ourselves’. So India gets to keep the revenues based on a billion and a half people and the West Indies gets to keep all the revenues that it can generate on Antigua that has 100,000 people or St Kitts that has 30,000 people. It was just palpably unfair and we were outvoted nine to one by the member countries of the ICC, and from that moment, and I said it then, when that vote was taken, you’ve just signed the demise of West Indies cricket because you’ve taken away our main earning source.”

Dehring believes the current financial model does not account for the economic realities of each member nation, particularly the varying costs of hosting international cricket.

“Nobody has done any kind of economic study to understand or appreciate that to host a Test match in the Caribbean is far more expensive than to hold a Test match in England or in India simply because of the logistical costs which are all well documented,” he said.

“When ECB [England and Wales Cricket Board] decides to hold a Test match at Lord’s one week and then the following week at Manchester, the ECB doesn’t have to move 21 tons of television equipment, TV crew, teams, and so on and fly them all up to Manchester — everybody goes on a bus or a train, and it’s maybe a £1,200 expenditure. For us, it’s a US$250,000 to $300,000 expenditure because we have to charter planes because we don’t have the sort of regular air schedule that we can simply use regular scheduled flights so we have to charter flights in order to meet the tour dates and so on. So it’s a totally different economic formula. I talk about a sort of purchasing power parity [and] there must be a cricketing equivalent to that in terms of the economic costs of hosting these tournaments or matches under the Future Tours programme that needs to be taken into consideration.”

Despite his criticism of the ICC’s distribution system, Dehring doesn’t believe CWI can afford to wait for a change in approach.

“We’re not going to rely on the ICC to change its financial distribution model, [although it] obviously would go a long way in solving the issue,” he said.

“We have started on these initiatives to grow the game and grow our commercial revenues from outside of the ICC distribution, outside of bilateral tours, which we’ve seen now the cricket is evolving in that way and television rights isn’t what it used to be for bilateral tours, but we’re not going to rely on the ICC to change their distribution model even though we know it should be done.”

World.title: AFJ Hummingbird Gala raises more than US$900,000
World.content:
Outgoing AFJ President Wendy Hart participates in the live auction at the 2026 Hummingbird Gala, which raised funds to support the entity’s work in Jamaica. Sharing the table are (from left) Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness, Sandals Resorts Executive Chairman Adam Stewart, and and Emmy Award-winning actress Sheryl Lee Ralph, who has a chat with former US ambassador to Jamaica Nick Perry.

THE American Friends of Jamaica (AFJ) raised more than US$900,000 ($143 million) in total donor support at its 2026 Hummingbird Gala on Friday, surpassing its fund-raising target as supporters gathered in New York to celebrate two distinguished Jamaicans and contribute to the organisation’s work across the island.

Held at The Plaza, the annual gala brought together diplomats, business leaders, philanthropists, members of the Jamaican Diaspora, and friends of Jamaica.

Among those attending were Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness and Minister of Tourism Edmund Bartlett.

Executive chairman of Sandals Resort International and the Jamaica Observer Adam Stewart, and Emmy Award-winning actress Sheryl Lee Ralph, were honoured during the evening which also featured performances by reggae and dancehall pioneers Sister Nancy and Brigadier Jerry.

Stewart received the International Achievement Award, presented by Holness, in recognition of his leadership in Caribbean tourism, business and philanthropy. In accepting the award he reflected on the legacy of his father, Sandals founder Gordon “Butch” Stewart, who started the company with a 99-room hotel in Montego Bay in 1981.

“It is the greatest honour for my family, for myself, [and] my father before me, to be able to get up every day and tell the world about the magic and the gift that is Jamaica land,” Stewart said.

Ralph received the International Humanitarian Award from Bartlett in recognition of her career in entertainment and her advocacy through the DIVA Foundation, particularly in HIV/AIDS awareness.

Recalling learning Jamaica’s national anthem as a child, she urged those attending to look beyond the island’s appeal as a holiday destination.

“Don’t just love Jamaica for your vacation.

Love Jamaica for the people.

Love Jamaica for our culture.

Love Jamaica for our food.

Love Jamaica for our music,” said Ralph.

The Hummingbird Gala is AFJ’s principal annual fund-raising event, with proceeds supporting its work in Jamaica.

This year’s event took place as the organisation continues to assist communities affected by Hurricane Melissa while maintaining its wider programmes.

Mark Newman, AFJ board director and incoming president, said the organisation works closely with Jamaican partners to ensure donations are used where they are most needed.

“The unique aspect about AFJ is that we provide a great platform to take US donations and connect them with Jamaican NGOs and business partners so as not to duplicate efforts but employ resources in the most efficient way so every donor dollar has the highest impact on the ground in Jamaica,” Newman said.

Since Hurricane Melissa hit Jamaica in October 2025, AFJ has mobilised nearly US$12 million in cash and in-kind contributions for relief and recovery, with more than 60 per cent of funds raised for hurricane relief already deployed.

Working with local partners, the organisation has helped families repair damaged roofs, supported the restoration of schools and health clinics, and helped farmers restart production.

AFJ President Wendy Hart and Executive Director Caron Chung spoke about donor response and the importan of working with organisations in Jamaica that understand their communities’ needs.

Hart, who was attending her final Hummingbird Gala as president after 11 years in the role, thanked supporters for their contributions over the years and welcomed Newman as her successor.

Holness commended AFJ for its work in Jamaica, particularly its assistance to communities recovering from Hurricane Melissa.

“For more than four decades AFJ has turned affection for our country into action for our people.

Behind every contribution is a human possibility — a child with a better chance to learn, a patient with access to care, a family finding its way,” he said.

“I want to express, therefore, on behalf of the Government of Jamaica and the people of Jamaica, our sincere appreciation to the American Friends of Jamaica,” added Holness.

The evening also included a live auction and pledge drive, along with the launch of ‘To Jamaica, With Love’, AFJ’s year-end fund-raising campaign.

Running through to December 31, 2026, the campaign will use personal stories, letters and postcards from Jamaica to encourage continued giving from the Diaspora and international supporters.

World.title: Boosting the battle against breast cancer
World.content:
THOMPSON...across this country our buildings, our offices, and our churches are turning pink. And that is good. But I want to say plainly...that pink is not a policy (File photo)

WITH the increasingly high number of Jamaican women affected by breast cancer, and at an earlier age than the global average, Government Senator Dr Elon Thompson has proposed a five-part plan, headed by a national, organised screening programme, to tackle the problem that is devastating families.

Thompson, a trained urologist who is at the forefront of prostate cancer awareness and treatment, unveiled his plan in the Senate last Friday when he rose on the adjournment to talk about an issue that has personally affected him — he revealed that three of his aunts were diagnosed with breast cancer, two of whom have since died.

He told the Senate that, “awareness without capacity breeds frustration. So I respectfully put forward five practical asks”.

The lawmaker said the organised screening programme is not a campaign, but rather “a programme with a defined target population, call and recall, a central register, and published coverage figures each year so this Senate can hold all of us accountable”.

He also proposed a public audit of mammography capacity, asking, “How many machines are there in our public hospitals today? How many are working? What are the waiting times by parish?

“We cannot fix what we do not measure,” he told the Parliament.

Thirdly, Thompson wants an expedited decision on the Jamaica Cancer Society’s grant application for a replacement mammography machine. He also wants a “stable arrangement” so the society, which he noted carries a national burden, is not left to rely on telethons for core equipment.

Significantly, Thompson wants a guaranteed pathway from abnormal result to treatment.

“Clear time standards for biopsy, diagnosis, and the start of treatment, supported by patient navigators, so that no woman with a suspicious finding is lost in the system,” he said.

The fifth plank in the plan is what Thompson called “a strengthened cancer registry and support for local research”. This, he said, would help to explain why Jamaican women present younger and with more aggressive disease, so national guidelines reflect Jamaican realities.

Thompson said his commitment was to see through the creation of a policy paper on cancer screening, remarking, “I do not intend simply to make requests and sit down. I wish to place on record today my intention to support the development of a policy paper to be drafted with colleagues in medicine, public health, and civil society, setting out practical, costed recommendations to improve cancer screening in Jamaica.

“That paper will build on the five points I have outlined. It will look at screening, not only for breast cancer, but for the other cancers we can detect early, among them cervical, prostate, and colorectal cancer. It will examine how we finance screening equipment and keep it working, how we reach rural communities, how we use our health centres and the National Health Fund more effectively, and how we partner with organisations such as NGOs [non-governmental organisations] and private organisations,” he said.

Thompson told his fellow lawmakers that it was his intention, in short order, to seek to move a motion for the establishment of a joint select committee of Parliament to examine and deliberate upon the policy research and its findings, with a view to informing meaningful recommendations for consideration and action.

“I trust that this initiative will receive the support of colleagues on both sides of the aisle in recognition of the importance of the matter before us,” he said.

Despite the increasing numbers and mortality rate, Thompson insisted that “none of this is beyond us. We have the clinicians. We have the civil society partners. What we need is coordination, funding, and political will”.

Pointing out that breast cancer touches nearly every family in Jamaica, Thompson acknowledged the importance of October being observed as Breast Cancer Awareness Month.

“Across this country our buildings, our offices, and our churches are turning pink. And that is good. But I want to say plainly…that pink is not a policy. Ribbons do not read mammograms. Awareness must now become access,” he insisted.

Getting personal, the senator and medical doctor said, “Permit me to speak as a nephew.” He then detailed how his father’s roots are in Cornpiece Settlement, Hayes, Clarendon, where two of his father’s sisters — his aunts — “women who helped to shape the man I am, were diagnosed with breast cancer.

“And on my mother’s side, her youngest sibling, my aunt who made her life in the United States, received that same diagnosis. Three aunts, three women from one family. Two of them are no longer with us.

“I have sat with my family through the waiting, the treatment, and the grief, and I have noticed something that every Jamaican family touched by this disease will recognise: The question is never only ‘Why her?’ It is ‘Could it have been found sooner?’ “ Thompson continued.

Stating that he carries their memory with him in the Senate, Thompson said: “When I speak of statistics…I ask this Senate to remember that behind every number is an aunt, a mother, a sister, a daughter from a district like Cornpiece or a community like yours.”

“Every week I sit across from patients and families receiving news no one wants to hear. The hardest conversations are not about disease that could not be found, they are about disease that was found too late,” he added.

Thompson said the scale of the problem should give senators cause to pause and reflect. He shared that in 2022, according to the Global Cancer Observatory, Jamaica recorded 1,327 new cases of breast cancer among women, about 35 per cent of all cancers in women. In that same period, roughly 684 Jamaican women died of the disease — nearly two women every single day.

“Breast cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death among Jamaican women. And our case fatality rate — the proportion of women diagnosed who go on to die of the disease — has been estimated at between 41 and 51 per cent. In countries with organised screening, that figure is far lower,” Thompson said.

He also noted that younger women are being diagnosed with the debilitating disease, pointing out that the average age at presentation in Jamaica is about 54 years, eight years younger than in the United States.

The senator also shared data from the Kingston Public Hospital, which shows that about 60 per cent of women presenting with breast cancer are between 25 and 59 years old.

“These are women in the prime of their working lives, holding our households, our classrooms, and our businesses together. Perhaps most troubling, approximately 40 per cent of Jamaican women with breast cancer present with locally advanced disease. That is not a biology problem, that is an access problem,” he said.

Thompson said despite the numbers, the uncomfortable truth is that Jamaica still does not have a national, organised breast cancer screening programme.

“We have guidelines, we have dedicated NGOs, we have generous corporate partners, but we do not have a system that invites every eligible woman to be screened, tracks whether she was screened, and ensures that an abnormal result leads quickly to diagnosis and treatment,” he pointed out.

Thompson acknowledged what he said was the the important work of the Ministry of Health and Wellness, the National Health Fund, and civil society partners in improving access to cancer screening and treatment. He cited that initiatives such as the mammography subsidy represent meaningful progress in reducing financial barriers to screening. But, he said, affordability alone does not guarantee access, particularly where the services themselves are unavailable.

He lamented that this October, the gap is not theoretical as the Jamaica Cancer Society, which for 70 years has carried a disproportionate share of the nation’s screening load, entered Breast Cancer Awareness Month without a single functioning mammography machine. Thompson said the society’s only machine has been out of service since August 29 and that replacing it will cost more than $35 million.

“Think about what that means. We are spending this month urging women to get screened while the very institution so many of them rely on has had to turn them away and send them elsewhere. A woman in Hayes, Clarendon, or Westmoreland, or St Thomas should have access to a mammogram,” he said.

Speaking as a urologist, Thompson, who recently used the Senate to urge men to get screened for prostate cancer, noted that breast cancer does occur in men.

“It is rare, but it is real, and because men do not expect it, it is often found late. Any man who finds a lump in the chest, a change in the nipple, or discharge must have it examined,” he said.

And the government lawmaker said there is a further link that families need to understand. He explained that the same inherited gene mutations that raise a woman’s risk of breast cancer — BRCA1 and BRCA2 — also raise a man’s risk of aggressive prostate cancer.

,“A family history of breast cancer, like the one in my own family, is therefore not only the women’s business — it is the whole family’s business. When we talk about cancer at home, the men need to be listening too,” he said.

Thompson closed by urging every woman listening to: “Know your body. Know your family history. If you notice a lump, a change in shape, skin dimpling, nipple changes or discharge, do not wait, and do not let fear or cost stop you from asking for help. Speak to your doctor about when screening is right for you, especially if breast cancer runs in your family.”

To employers, he said: “Give your staff the time to get screened. A morning off for a mammogram is cheaper than losing a valued colleague.

“And I encourage all Jamaicans to support the efforts of our civil society partners this month, including Reach to Recovery’s Pink Run at Emancipation Park on October 25th and the Jamaica Cancer Society’s work to restore its screening services.

“I end by honouring the survivors, the warriors still in treatment,; the families who have lost a mother, a sister, a wife, a daughter, or an aunt; and the nurses, doctors, technicians, and volunteers who stand with them.

World.title: UK and Poland accuse Hegseth of downplaying allies’ role in Afghanistan
World.content:
But he added: “Except there were maybe five that contributed. It was actually closer to one or two that by the end were actually involved in kinetic operations. In fact the patch ISAF, we joked it meant ‘I Saw Americans Fighting’.”

All of NATO’s then-28 members participated in the U.S.-led war in Afghanistan, after the alliance invoked Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty – NATO’s collective defense clause – on September 12, 2001, a day after the terrorist attacks that took place on 9/11.

It remains the only time the article has been invoked in alliance history.

Asked about his comments Monday, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s official spokesperson pointed out that “thousands of British and allied families made huge sacrifices to play their significant part in that war and uphold our values,” while “more than 450 British personnel never returned.”

“Their sacrifice and that of other NATO forces was made in the service of collective security and in response to an attack on our ally,” he continued.

“We are incredibly proud of our armed forces, and their service and sacrifice will never be forgotten. And it is wrong to diminish their role.”

World.title: French PM orders ‘localized’ curfews in response to looting and unrest
World.content:
Those announcements came after an emergency meeting at the French interior ministry following scenes of widespread chaos that played out across France on Saturday. While President Emmanuel Macron attempted to reassure a worried public with a primetime address Sunday night, the speech was widely panned across the political spectrum as insufficient. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez submitted his resignation in the aftermath of the weekend’s unrest, but Macron refused to accept it.

The government is now scrambling to bat down allegations that it has mismanaged the affair and stop it from snowballing into a sustained movement like the Yellow Jackets of 2018 ahead of the spring presidential election, which far-right leader Marine Le Pen is favored to win.

Saturday’s demonstrations saw teachers and students, who have been blockading schools for weeks demanding more funding for schools, join forces with those upset about the rapidly rising cost of living — and while hundreds of thousands of people marched peacefully, violent incidents were observed in some of France’s largest cities, including Paris.

A website claiming to represent the Yellow Jacket movement launched calls for more protests this coming Saturday, and the country’s main unions are organizing strikes and protests on Nov. 5 in opposition to the government’s proposed budget, which includes €43 billion in savings.

While high schools are currently closed for holidays, some students are still protesting. The Louvre museum was closed due to a strike movement from students at an art history university located inside the palace.

Exactly who was responsible for the weekend’s destruction remains a point of debate. While foreign leaders like U.S. President Donald Trump and Hungary’s Péter Magyar have, without evidence, pinned the rioting on immigrants, Lecornu and the government have pointed the finger at so-called “ultra-left” movements, citing analysis by French intelligence services. Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau told TF1 on Monday that she “absolutely [could] not confirm” the government’s analysis based on the profiles of those arrested and placed under investigation in the French capital so far.

World.title: The multiple sclerosis gap Europe cannot afford to ignore
World.content:
As Europe plans its response to the neurological disease burden, a fundamental measurement gap is being overlooked — and the cost of ignoring it is being felt.

A briefing requested earlier this year by the European Parliament’s Committee on Public Health (SANT) put it plainly: neurological diseases are one of Europe’s most urgent and rapidly expanding health, social and economic challenges. Published in February 2026, it calls for a coordinated European plan linking prevention, early diagnosis, research and innovation.1 But before Europe considers what that plan should look like, a foundational question demands attention: are we measuring the right things?

Multiple sclerosis (MS), a chronic, progressive disease of the central nervous system that disrupts communication between the brain and the body, offers a revealing case study. Consider a woman in her mid-30s, working, raising a family, managing what her neurologist calls “stable” MS. She has not slept properly in years, her memory has been slipping and she is cutting her hours at work. Her last clinical note reads: “No change.” On paper, she is stable, but in reality she is anything but.

Her story is not unusual. According to research commissioned by Sanofi*, the gap between what health systems measure and what people with MS experience may be costing individuals, families and economies more than we realize.3

The stakes for Europe

Over 3 million people globally live with MS and Europe has the highest prevalence, at 133 per 100,000 people.2,3 The condition strikes primarily during prime working years, meaning hundreds of thousands of people are navigating a progressive, unpredictable disease at precisely the point when inadequate support is felt most acutely.3

That support begins with measurement. And right now, the tools used to assess MS in clinical practice do not fully capture what people with the disease experience.3

The consequences extend far beyond the clinic: 82 percent of people with severe MS rely on unpaid family caregiving, yet this burden rarely appears in standard health data or policy design.3 When the full impact of disease is not measured, health systems can underestimate need, delay support, and overlook the wider effects on work, welfare and family life.3

The measurement gap

The Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS), the primary tool used to measure MS disability, was developed in 1983 to assess walking ability. We now know that MS affects far more than mobility. Fatigue affects 94 percent of people with MS, while 75 percent report cognitive difficulties, but both are absent in the EDSS assessment.3 In a field where clinical consensus is rare, seven in ten neurologists agree: a more comprehensive approach is needed.3

Growing recognition of smouldering neuroinflammation has made the need for new methods of quantifying MS progression increasingly urgent. This slow, chronic disease activity can persist even when a patient appears clinically stable, with effects that are subtle, cumulative and easy to miss until significant damage has already occurred.4

This is why Sanofi initiated the development of the Smouldering Associated Worsening (SAW) Index+. The SAW Index Study — led by an international steering committee of leading MS clinicians, researchers and patient advocates — is due to complete in 2027. Based on hundreds of hours of in-depth qualitative research with people with MS, the goal of the SAW Index is to provide neurologists with a comprehensive measurement framework that bridges the gap between lived experience and what clinical tools are currently able to detect.

According to the European Multiple Sclerosis Platform, people with MS experience an average of 14 symptoms within the first five years of diagnosis, with fatigue, sensory problems, sleep disturbances, cognitive impairment and balance problems among the most common.5 These are precisely the experiences the SAW Index is designed to surface, replacing static labels like “moderately affected” with measurement metrics grounded in the experience and words of people with MS.

The cost of this gap

These aspects of MS can be challenging to quantify and are associated with substantial societal and economic burdens. Lifetime productivity loss per person with MS ranges from €394,000 in France to €668,000 in Germany.3 The cost profile shifts significantly as the disease progresses: in mild MS, direct healthcare costs dominate; in severe MS, indirect costs become the primary driver.3 Indeed, lost wages, absenteeism, early retirement, disability payments and the growing burden on unpaid carers outweigh medical costs in many countries, placing growing long-term pressure on social insurance and disability systems.3

Early identification of progression could change that trajectory, extending years of employment, preserving household income, and reducing long-term dependence on disability and social benefits.3,6 That is a cost-avoidance opportunity current measurement frameworks are missing.

Progress in motion

There is no single fix, but there is momentum.

MS care has advanced significantly in recent decades: diagnosis is happening earlier, treatment options have expanded and the focus is shifting from relapse control alone to slowing long-term disability progression.7 Furthermore, there is growing recognition of the importance of cognition, mental health, rehabilitation and the day-to-day realities that shape whether people living with MS can remain independent and active.8

The challenge now is to ensure policy keeps pace with that progress, and better measurement is part of the answer. If Europe wants health spending to deliver lasting value, it should see these improvements not as costs to be managed, but as investments in independence, participation, productivity and more sustainable health systems.

Time to act

The European Parliament’s SANT Committee has called for a fully funded European neurological health plan — one with the scale and ambition of Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan, aligning health, research and societal action in a unified framework.1 MS offers a clear and immediate test case for what that ambition looks like in practice.

But ambitious plans require accurate data. If Europe is serious about a coordinated response to neurological disease, getting measurement right is not a secondary concern; it is the foundation on which everything else depends.

The people living with MS across the continent cannot wait for the tools that measure their disease to catch up with the science that understands it. Neither should policymakers.

*Research commissioned by Sanofi. All editorial control retained by Economist Impact.

World.title: Adipositas: Sparen kann für den Staat teuer werden
World.content:
Das deutsche Gesundheitssystem beschränkt sich auf die Behandlung von Folgeerkrankungen der Adipositas, etwa Typ-2-Diabetes oder Herz-Kreislauf-Erkrankungen. Deren Behandlung ist medizinisch notwendig. Die politische Frage lautet jedoch, ob es auf Dauer wirtschaftlich sinnvoll ist, vor allem die Folgen der Adipositas zu finanzieren, anstatt Adipositas direkt zu behandeln. Das ist vor dem Hintergrund des demografischen Wandels und mangelnder Fachkräfte besonders relevant. Eine vom Institut der deutschen Wirtschaft veröffentlichte Prognose geht davon aus, dass Deutschland bis 2036 rund 4,3 Millionen Arbeitskräfte fehlen könnten. Adipositas ist nicht die Ursache des Fachkräftemangels und auch nicht die alleinige Lösung. Sie ist aber ein Faktor, der die Erwerbsfähigkeit beeinträchtigen kann. Eine Gesundheitspolitik, die Menschen länger gesund im Arbeitsleben halten will, muss solche Zusammenhänge berücksichtigen.

Entscheidend ist nicht allein, ob eine Therapie kurzfristig zusätzliche Kosten verursacht.

Der Blick ins Ausland zeigt, dass die politische Debatte über die Versorgung von Adipositas auch anders geführt werden kann. In England hat der staatliche Gesundheitsdienst NHS mit einem stufenweisen Rollout medikamentöser Therapien begonnen. Vorgesehen ist der Zugang zunächst für Erwachsene mit einem Body-Mass-Index von mindestens 35 kg/m2 und mindestens einer Begleiterkrankung. Die Behandlung erfolgt über spezialisierte Dienste und soll zunehmend auch in Hausarztpraxen angeboten werden. Grundlage sind Empfehlungen des englischen Instituts NICE. Nach dessen Schätzungen könnten in England rund 3,4 Millionen Erwachsene grundsätzlich die Kriterien für eine Behandlung erfüllen.

Das englische Modell setzt auf definierte medizinische Kriterien, einen schrittweisen Zugang und die Einbettung in bestehende Versorgungsstrukturen. Gerade darin liegt der gesundheitspolitische Unterschied zu der Debatte in Deutschland. Hierzulande richtet sich der Blick fast reflexartig auf die Kosten moderner Arzneimittel und Therapien. Das ist angesichts knapper Kassen nachvollziehbar, greift aber zu kurz. Entscheidend ist nicht allein, ob eine Therapie kurzfristig zusätzliche Kosten verursacht. Zu berücksichtigen sind ebenso Kosten unbehandelter oder zu spät behandelter Erkrankungen und demgegenüber mögliche Einsparungen durch vermiedene Folgeerkrankungen, weniger Arbeitsausfälle und einen längeren Verbleib im Erwerbsleben. Für Deutschland stellt sich also die grundsätzliche Frage: Soll die medikamentöse Behandlung von Adipositas weiterhin aus der Regelversorgung ausgeschlossen bleiben oder braucht es, ähnlich wie in England, einen zielgerichteten und stufenweisen Zugang für Menschen mit Adipositas?

Gesundheit als Investition

Eine moderne Adipositas-Versorgung ist eine Investition in die Stabilität von Gesundheitswesen, Arbeitsmarkt und Sozialversicherung zugleich. Zugelassene medikamentöse Therapien sollten dort eingesetzt werden können, wo sie medizinisch angezeigt sind. Ernährungs-, Bewegungs- und Verhaltenstherapie bleiben auch weiterhin wichtige Bestandteile, reichen aber in manchen Fällen nicht aus. Notwendig ist ein Versorgungskonzept, das Prävention, Früherkennung und leitliniengerechte Behandlung verbindet.

Wer nur kurzfristige Ausgaben betrachtet, riskiert, langfristig höhere Belastungen zu finanzieren.

Gerade in Zeiten knapper Kassen verlangt ein verantwortungsvoller Haushalt eine vollständige Kostenrechnung. Die entscheidende Frage lautet daher nicht allein, was eine Behandlung kostet, sondern auch, welche Kosten durch Nichtbehandlung entstehen. Wer nur kurzfristige Ausgaben betrachtet, riskiert, langfristig höhere Belastungen zu finanzieren.

World.title: Serbian prosecutor probing Trump Tower in Belgrade targeted with spyware
World.content:
The spyware revelation comes amid mounting controversy over plans to redevelop the former Yugoslav military headquarters in Belgrade into a luxury Trump Tower skyscraper. The project, associated with Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, has faced allegations of political interference and irregularities surrounding the removal of the site's protected heritage status.

Bajić's targeting follows revelations in September that at least 14 people in Serbia, including student activists and opposition figures, had received warnings indicating they may have been targeted with sophisticated spyware. Researchers at Toronto University's Citizen Lab confirmed a Pegasus infection in at least one case.

"In Serbia, spyware surveillance has steadily expanded from civil society and journalists to student activists, politicians and now university and judicial representatives," said Andrijana Ristić, a policy advisor at SHARE Foundation. "This escalation is fueled by perceived impunity and state inaction, even in cases where criminal complaints have been filed."

Another prominent figure caught up in the surveillance scandal is Vladan Đokić, rector of the University of Belgrade, whose phone was infected with Pegasus, according to the same report.

Đokić has emerged as a prominent figure in Serbia's protest movement after refusing to facilitate a government crackdown on student demonstrators. He has faced sustained pressure from authorities, including a police raid on his university offices on March 31, during which computers and servers were reportedly seized.

Until September, Đokić was also frequently mentioned as a potential leader of the student-backed electoral list ahead of Serbia's planned Oct. 25 parliamentary snap elections.

The identity of those responsible for deploying Pegasus against Bajić and Đokić has not been established.

"NSO has spent a decade claiming to turn over a new leaf each time an abuse surfaces. But there is no hiding the truth: Pegasus is a technology for repression," said John Scott-Railton, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab. "It's no accident that people standing up for freedom in the face of corruption keep getting hacked with NSO's products."

World.title: EU eyes Rome for 2027 summit ahead of Italian election
World.content:
Hosting EU leaders in Rome would give Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni a high-profile international stage in an election year.

BRUSSELS — Preparations are underway to hold a March 2027 meeting of EU leaders in Rome, before Italian elections due next year.

World.title: France riots: Presidential hopeful Attal pitches social media blackout
World.content:
Saturday saw hundreds of thousands of protesters take to the streets nationwide across France, with students — who have been blockading schools in recent weeks to call for better study conditions, more teachers and more funding — joining trade unions and members of the public to protest the cost of living. While many protested peacefully, scenes of extreme violence also played out across the country. According to the latest figures from the interior ministry, some 2,000 people were arrested during the turmoil.

During Attal's tenure as prime minister in 2024, France blocked TikTok access to one of its overseas territories, New Caledonia, amid widespread protests there. But France’s highest administrative court ruled that this suspension constituted “a disproportionate infringement of rights and freedoms.”

It’s unclear whether Attal’s latest proposal would survive a judicial review given that over the summer, France’s Constitutional Council, which reviews the constitutionality of French legislation, blocked a bill seeking to ban access to social media for under-15s after finding the legislation disproportionately infringed on minors’ right to freedom of expression and communication.

Such internet restrictions are more commonly associated with countries like China, Iran, Russia and, more recently, India. These countries either have permanent blocks on certain social media platforms or have more recently restricted them during protest movements, with India and Iran going so far as to block internet access completely.

Klara Durand contributed to this report.

World.title: Where’s Burnham really on welfare reform?
World.content:
Having more than a million young people not in education, employment or training is an “economic catastrophe” according to the prime minister. So, what will the government do about it?

With Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review due next month, is Andy Burnham laying the groundwork for tougher benefit conditions in the budget – as ministers look to rein in the spiralling welfare bill?

Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy examine how the report’s findings could complicate the government’s plans for reform.
