World.title: Norway to extend proposed under-16 social media ban to online games and messaging apps
World.content:
Norway is set to introduce a social media ban for children under 16, with the government announcing on Monday that it is finalising legislation to be submitted to parliament by the end of the year.

 

The proposed restrictions will also cover potentially harmful online games and messaging services, beyond conventional social media platforms, the government said in a statement.

TikTok, Snapchat and Roblox, a popular online gaming platform where users can create and play games while interacting with others, would likely fall under the proposed law.

"Children's safety must come first," said Lene Vågslid, Norway's minister for children and families, adding that the legislation was nearly complete.

The restrictions aim to protect children from harmful content, addictive features, illegal advertising and unwanted contact from strangers.

Online games and messaging services were initially expected to receive broad exemptions, but the government has now decided to assess platforms based on their potential risks to children.

This means services considered harmless, such as messaging apps used for school communication, could remain accessible.

Vågslid said the government was also safeguarding children's "right to participate," although Monday's announcement did not explain how this would be ensured under the proposed restrictions.

Technology companies would be responsible for verifying users' ages, with systems required to comply with European data protection rules.

Norway's centre-left Labour government published a draft bill in 2025 proposing a minimum social media age of 15 before revising the threshold to 16 in April this year. The legislation has since undergone public consultation in Norway and the European Economic Area (EEA).

Social media restrictions in Europe

Norway joins a growing number of European countries moving to restrict children's access to social media amid concerns about online safety and addiction.

Denmark has adopted similar restrictions, while Spain is pursuing a ban for pupils under 16.

In September, France attempted to ban social media for children under 15, but its Constitutional Council struck it down over freedom of expression concerns.

At the European Union level, the European Commission proposed the EU Kids Act in September, which would also introduce age-based restrictions on social media, online games and other digital services.

World.title: Could France’s debt troubles tip Italy into recession?
World.content:
The eurozone’s second-largest economy saw its bond yields rise further on Monday, following violent street demonstrations in the country over the weekend.

 

France’s 10-year government bond yield hovered around 4.9% on Monday, near its highest level in more than two decades, as investors demanded a higher premium for holding French debt. Protesters are demanding action on the rising cost of living and declining public services, including education.

The unrest adds to pressure on the government as it battles to get its 2027 budget through a deeply divided National Assembly, the lower house of France’s parliament.

The immediate challenge is to pass a credible budget that reassures investors ahead of the presidential election in spring 2027. But restoring confidence will also depend on whether the next administration can commit to improving public finances over several years.

What is fuelling investors’ concerns?

France is nursing one of the highest public debt ratios in the EU, at 119% of GDP, according to the latest reading from INSEE, the national statistics office. This is coupled with a government forecast for a deficit of 5.4% of GDP in 2026. Public debt stood at €3.596 trillion at the end of June 2026.

The cost of servicing that debt has been rising sharply. The government forecasts public debt interest payments of €91 billion in 2027, up from €79.2 billion this year — an increase of almost €12 billion.

Accelerating inflation and low growth threaten to weaken tax revenues and raise the deficit and debt further.

The current fiscal situation therefore leaves little room for the government to meet protesters’ demands through another large spending package, along the lines of French President Emmanuel Macron’s “whatever it costs” approach when the pandemic hit the country.

The government faces pressure to reduce the deficit and commit to lasting savings to calm nerves on the bond market. If borrowing costs keep rising, France’s debt could become increasingly difficult to control.

And a spiralling crisis could also hit other major eurozone economies, such as Italy.

How France’s debt troubles could hit Italy

Modelling the impact of bond turmoil in France, with some contagion to other high-debt eurozone countries, Oxford Economics found that Italy would be particularly vulnerable because it combines slow growth, high debt and investment that is sensitive to tighter financial conditions.

A key yardstick for measuring market concerns is the gap between a country’s 10-year government bond yield and Germany’s equivalent. The current spread — the extra return investors want to hold French debt instead of German debt — has risen to around 145 basis points (bps). This is still slightly below the peak reached earlier this month, which was the highest since the eurozone debt crisis of 2011–2012.

Oxford Economics sets out a baseline and two adverse scenarios. Its baseline assumes that France’s spread stays below 200bps ahead of the April 2027 presidential election and narrows afterwards. It continues to view a French debt crisis as an unlikely but potentially damaging outcome, rather than its central forecast.

The two adverse scenarios combine higher borrowing costs with a hit to business and consumer confidence. In the moderate scenario, the French spread widens to 250bps from around 140bps when the report was published on 15 October. In the severe scenario, it reaches 400bps.

France and Italy would enter recession in 2027 under the severe scenario. Belgium would also see a jump in its borrowing costs, while Spain, Portugal and Greece would face higher bond yields but less economic damage, with none of the three economies contracting.

Crucially, the eurozone as a whole would avoid recession even under this severe scenario.

According to Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics, a widening of France’s spread to 400bps is a “plausible adverse scenario, (…) which would be comparable to Italy’s spreads in 2012”.

Kenningham agreed that, in that case, there would certainly be a lot of pressure on other high-debt economies, including Italy.

“However, in contrast to the early 2010s, the ECB would be well placed to support countries other than France through its Transmission Protection Instrument,” he said.

With this instrument, the ECB can buy government bonds to help keep borrowing costs under control if the country meets certain conditions.

Kenningham also said that the risks to the banking sector and the risk of a property crash are much lower than in the 2010s.

“So things could get very bad but not as bad as in the 2010s.”

According to Oxford Economics, in its severe scenario, France’s 10-year bond yield would reach 7% in the second quarter of 2027, with the public deficit on track to surpass 6% of GDP. The consultancy warns that yields at such levels could trigger a liquidity crisis.

But expectations of ECB intervention to help France remain low. ECB President Christine Lagarde said last week that the means to stop the surge in French borrowing costs “must first be found in France”, through budget measures to reassure investors.

What France can do to regain investors’ confidence

According to Oxford Economics, the measures needed to calm markets could include gradual spending restraint over several years, accompanied by clear legislative commitments, especially on the retirement age.

But the consultancy warns that “the current minority government will not be able to credibly commit to sustained fiscal consolidation to soothe markets”. Much of the responsibility for carrying out any painful measures could therefore fall to the next administration.

In the meantime, Kenningham said investors are expecting the government to pass a budget that reduces next year’s deficit to around 5% of GDP, “so anything less than that could lead to further loss of confidence in the French bond market”.

Ahead of next spring’s presidential election, far-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading in the polls. In an interview with the Financial Times last week, she promised: “massive reductions in public spending, while reviving the economy”.

She presented her “counter-budget” on 6 October, targeting €140 billion in net savings by 2032 compared with 2026, a deficit below 3% of GDP by 2030 and a constitutional budget rule. Her party proposes cutting administrative and social security spending, immigration-related expenditure and France’s EU contribution.

But economists questioned the figures. Mathieu Plane, deputy director of analysis and forecasting at the French Economic Observatory (OFCE), told Le Monde that more than €80 billion of the proposed savings were questionable, poorly defined and difficult to implement.

In the meantime, France is facing the risk of a vicious circle in which higher borrowing costs force further spending cuts or tax rises, weakening growth and making its debt harder to control.

“France has been heading towards a debt crisis for many years and that moment is now getting closer,” Kenningham concluded.

World.title: Visegrad Four urge Brussels to ease Russian energy phase-out rules
World.content:
Slovakia and Hungary called on Brussels on Monday for greater flexibility in phasing out Russian gas, arguing that their landlocked position and reliance on existing supply routes make diversification more difficult and costly.

 

Bratislava said it had historically served as an entry point for Russian oil and gas but now risks becoming the end of the line, alongside Hungary, as Russian energy supplies to Central Europe are due to end in 2027 under the EU’s plan to phase out imports from Moscow.

“We would like to discuss with the European Commission how the next EU funding period and the availability of EU funds can meet our needs, particularly regarding the expansion of oil and gas infrastructure in the Visegrad Four region,” Slovakia’s Deputy Prime Minister Denisa Saková said on the sidelines of a press conference in Bratislava attended by Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen.

Central European ministers want Brussels to recognise their specific circumstances and take regional needs into account when allocating EU funds for new oil and gas infrastructure and preparing the next EU budget period — another point of contention among member states at the latest European Council summit.

The appeal follows pressure from the Visegrad Group — Hungary, Slovakia, Czechia and Poland — on EU leaders at their 15-16 October summit to reconsider measures to lower electricity bills in the region.

Their demands included greater flexibility in the ongoing review of the bloc’s carbon market, the Emissions Trading System (ETS), and delaying its second phase, ETS2, until 2030.

Related EU leaders demand joint action to tackle soaring energy prices

Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen acknowledged the “serious” situation facing people in Central Europe and reiterated the need for “targeted and temporary measures” that would not undermine the bloc’s goal of reducing its reliance on imported fossil fuels.

“We used to be dependent on Russia. We’re moving out of that. Now, that is good. But the current situation shows that we are now dependent on the global market, and events in the Middle East can affect citizens here in Bratislava,” Jørgensen said.

The four EU countries, traditionally more reliant on fossil fuels, argue that high energy prices make it difficult for their industries to commit to investments in electrification. Prices have been driven higher by the US-Israeli war against Iran.

Central European consumers are facing a significantly heavier financial burden, with wholesale electricity futures more than 60% above pre-crisis levels, according to energy think tank Ember.

Ditching Russian energy is raising economic concerns in both countries.

Bratislava and Budapest argue that they face particular challenges in meeting the EU’s diversification requirements and want funding to expand oil and gas infrastructure in the region.

The Visegrad Group has access to several alternative energy sources and supply routes that bypass Russia, albeit at higher cost, with varying levels of integration across the four countries.

“From 2027, we will not be able to import gas from Russia and would like to sign new diversification contracts. Diversification and energy security mean that we have to have prepared rules for the supplies of oil and gas for the V4 region,” Saková added.

Under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, Hungary challenged the EU’s plan to phase out Russian energy imports, taking the case to an EU court.

Slovakia backed Budapest’s legal challenge, arguing that phasing out Russian energy would put its industrial competitiveness at a significant disadvantage compared with most other EU countries. A first ruling is expected to take months.

World.title: Professional chefs coach amateur cooks in French boxing glove cooking competition
World.content:
Professional chefs swapped their knives for boxing gloves at a food festival in the French Alps, where they had just 20 minutes to coach amateur cooks through making a soufflé omelette.

 

With their hands restricted, the chefs could only give advice while their teammates did all the cooking. The challenge was judged by top chefs, including Éric Frechon, who praised the results despite a few burnt pans.

In the end, Patricia Mathon, who admitted she rarely cooks, took the win.

World.title: French PM Lecornu calls for regional authorities to impose partial curfews
World.content:
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced on Monday that he had instructed regional authorities to bring in "localised and partial" curfews in order to prevent further riots and looting after a weekend of violence across France.

 

Details of the areas that will be subject to curfews are set to be announced later on Monday.

"On Saturday, despite scenes of extreme violence and major material damage, no one was killed, and that is a miracle," the PM said following a meeting of the government's crisis response team.

Lecornu also defended the work of police officers who had confronted groups of rioters.

It comes as French President Emmanuel Macron refused to accept the resignation of Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, citing "the need to ensure the continuity of the command of the security forces given the current situation," the Élysée said in a statement on Monday.

The president has tasked the interior minister "with taking all necessary measures to guarantee full transparency on the failures in planning and intelligence that led to this violence," the statement added.

Macron has also called for the introduction "of new policing tactics on the ground."

Nuñez said that police had "lost control" of the situation in some cities.

"A number of measures to contain and prevent looters and vandals from acting" will be introduced "from this Monday evening," the interior minister announced on Monday, adding that the number of police and gendarme forces on the ground would be further bolstered going into the weekend.

On Sunday evening, some groups again took to the streets to set fire to bins, bicycles, and other objects and looted shops in cities including Paris, Lyon, and Marseille.

Around 2,400 people were arrested across France over the weekend in relation to the protests, according to authorities.

World.title: Protesters block entrances to Paris’s Louvre museum
World.content:
Protesters blocked the entrances to the Louvre museum in Paris on Monday, following a weekend of demonstrations over the cost of living that escalated into violence and looting in several French cities.

 

A sign on the museum gates read “Entrance closed”, while demonstrators handed out leaflets and spoke to passers-by about their action.

The Louvre protest was linked to a wider movement initially led by high school students, but the weekend unrest extended beyond student demonstrations.

A first-year student at the École du Louvre said the action aimed to bring the cultural sector into the movement, citing budget cuts and worsening working conditions at the museum.

She also criticised the police response to Saturday’s protest as repression of a peaceful demonstration.

World.title: 'We won't let this continue': French PM orders local curfews after weekend unrest
World.content:
France will introduce partial, localised curfews in some urban areas following a weekend of rioting and looting, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced on Monday.

 

Speaking after an emergency meeting with government officials in Paris, Lecornu said he had instructed local prefects to coordinate with mayors and business representatives to determine where restrictions would be imposed.

The measures aim to protect residents and businesses after violence damaged public buildings and shops across the country.

Lecornu said a state of emergency had not been ruled out, but that targeted curfews were better suited to the current situation.

World.title: UN food agency to cut aid to 500,000 people in Gaza as funding dries up
World.content:
The World Food Programme will stop monthly assistance to half a million people in Gaza because of a funding shortfall, the UN agency said on Monday.

 

The cuts leave 1.1 million Palestinians, around half of Gaza’s population, receiving food or cash each month. Since the October 2025 ceasefire, the WFP had been reaching between 1.5 million and 1.8 million people a month.

“This has been a lifeline. But now, rather than being able to sustain and scale up that assistance, we’re actually having to reduce it,” Shaun Hughes, the WFP’s country director, told AFP in east Jerusalem.

"And that’s not because we don’t have humanitarian access to deliver food; that’s because we don’t have funding."

The UN estimates 1.2 million people have lost their homes in Gaza. AP Photo

Smaller rations

Families receiving food will now get one parcel instead of two and a smaller bag of wheat flour. The 75,000 families who receive cash will see monthly payments fall from 1,250 to 750 shekels ($400 to $240).

Hughes said conditions had not improved enough to justify the cuts.

“People are not safe. Airstrikes continue on a daily basis. People continue to be displaced,” he said. “Almost everybody remains without a permanent home to live in. And the humanitarian conditions are brutal.”

According to the latest assessments, 1.4 million people, two-thirds of the population, remain “acutely food insecure” and need aid to survive. The WFP warns that needs could rise again with the onset of winter.

In August 2025, the UN-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification declared famine conditions in Gaza, a finding Israel called a lie. The classification was lifted in December, two months after the US-brokered ceasefire, though Israeli strikes have continued.

The WFP’s resources have fallen sharply, partly because US President Donald Trump drastically cut contributions to UN agencies. It needs about $450 million over the next six months for Gaza and the West Bank, but has received only around half its usual funding for the Palestinian territories this year. In September, it halved the number of people it helps in the West Bank to 200,000.

Israel has let more goods into Gaza under the ceasefire but still blocks items it considers to have potential military use, including prosthetic limbs, according to the UN. It also accuses the UN of bias.

“Now is not the time in the history of Palestine and Gaza to turn away from what is happening in Gaza,” Hughes said.

World.title: Shipping attacks threaten Turkey's resolve to keep warships out of Black Sea
World.content:
A wave of deadly attacks on cargo ships in the waters of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania has jolted the alliance into calling an emergency meeting on Black Sea security. Yet any move to send NATO ships hinges on Turkey reversing its steadfast refusal to allow warships into the Black Sea.

Advertising

Thursday saw two chemical tankers struck by drones close to a Romanian port.

It follows two similar attacks in Bulgarian waters in the past week. More than 20 sailors have been killed or remain missing.

“The war has come in full force to the Black Sea now,” said Yoruk Isik, a maritime analyst who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. “With the change in technology compared to the beginning of the war, drones really disrupted maritime traffic.”

According to Isik, the latest attacks underscore the growing spread of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. “Russian ports and Ukrainian ports are heavily targeted, but now even in NATO waters ships are getting hit, in Bulgarian waters, Romanian waters.

“We are at a point where there is no safe place.”

The latest strikes targeted vessels along a key Ukrainian shipping route, casting Russia as NATO’s prime suspect as Moscow intensifies its assault on Ukrainian trade.

After meeting on Thursday with the leaders of Bulgaria and Romania, both NATO members, Secretary-General Mark Rutte said the military alliance would “continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed”.

Romanian President Nicușor Dan said NATO would hold a crisis meeting next week to discuss the situation.

Gatekeeper to the Black Sea

NATO could deploy air defence systems against drones to protect Bulgarian and Romanian waters.

But any deployment of naval ships will depend on NATO member Turkey, which controls access to the Black Sea through the Turkish Straits under a long-standing international treaty, the 1936 Montreux Convention.

Since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Ankara has blocked entry of Russian and Ukrainian warships or military vessels belonging to NATO members without a Black Sea coast, arguing for a diplomatic solution.

In recent weeks the Turkish government has sought to broker a ceasefire on commercial shipping, without success. Isik claims that failure, coupled with the latest escalation in attacks, is increasingly calling into question Ankara’s reliance on diplomacy alone.

“Either they’re going to have a breakthrough and the Kremlin is going to de-escalate, or Ankara is going to accept the reality that there needs to be a more credible force here – bigger vessels have to come,” the analyst said.

He pointed out that the navies of Romania and Bulgaria are not equipped to handle such an operation alone, with Cold War-era ships nearing the end of their lifespan.

“So Turkey's engagement is key to any successful NATO planning in the Black Sea.”

Russian leverage

Despite Turkish-owned cargo ships coming under attack in recent weeks, and Turkey’s deep reliance on Black Sea trade, Ankara has so far kept its powerful navy on the sidelines.

International relations expert Huseyin Bagci, of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University, says Turkey fears an escalation in the conflict and will be wary of allowing NATO ships into the Black Sea.

“I do not think the government would dare,” said Bagci. “Probably the government considers this a provocation to drag Turkey into the war... Turkey is afraid of getting involved in the Black Sea against Russia, this is somehow a trauma in the Turkish mind.”

Moscow also retains powerful leverage over Ankara, he suggested.

Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom is about to complete a multi-billion-dollar nuclear power station in Akkuyu, southern Turkey. Ankara sees it as vital to the drive to reduce its heavy dependence on imported energy. “It is illogical to oppose Russia now while you let the Russians complete the nuclear plant,” said Bagci.

Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies

Ankara also knows that letting NATO vessels in while barring Russian warships could provoke Moscow into contesting Turkey’s prized status as the gatekeeper to the Black Sea.

However, retired Turkish diplomat Selim Kuneralp, an expert on the Montreux Convention, warns Turkey’s control over Black Sea access is likely already in Russian President Vladimir Putin’s sights.

“This has probably had an impact on Russia’s ability to conduct the war, and I doubt that Putin is very happy with the situation,” said Kuneralp. “So if he were to win the war, there is a very strong risk that he will take the initiative of saying: ‘this is unacceptable and we want to have free passage of warships from now on, regardless of whether there is a war’.”

As a signatory, Moscow has the right to call for a revision of the Montreux Convention every five years.

For centuries, Russia fought repeated wars with the then Ottoman Empire for control of the Turkish Straits. In the early years of the Cold War, even Joseph Stalin tried his hand, but the United States intervened and thwarted him.

Now Ankara walks a tightrope between Moscow and its NATO partners to avoid a resurrection of those historical rivalries.

World.title: 'We don't have to wait for others to support us': Myanmar refugees find hope in Thailand's work program
World.content:
A year ago, Thailand granted long-staying refugees from Myanmar the right to work legally. Refugees and rights groups welcome the move but say the program's first year has exposed significant shortcomings.

At a glance, Ray Boe doesn't stand out from the tens of thousands of other foreign workers toiling at countless construction sites that push Bangkok's soaring skyline ever higher.

Unlike most of them, though, the 31-year-old came to Thailand's capital from one of the country's nine camps for refugees who have fled Myanmar's decades of civil strife.

The camps, which hug the Thai-Myanmar border, are home to more than 100,000 people — in some cases since the 1980s when the refugees first started arriving.

Until a year ago this month, the Thai government had refused to let them leave the camps to find work, forcing most to live hand-to-mouth on foreign donor aid.

That changed in October 2025, after foreign aid cutbacks — mostly by the United States — forced the camps to slash the food support and healthcare they could provide.

Around the same time, fighting between Thailand and Cambodia over territorial claims had sent hundreds of thousands of migrant workers from Cambodia back home, leaving behind a yawning labor gap.

New Thai labor scheme offers hope for Myanmar refugees To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Myanmar refugees allowed to work outside of camps

To cope with the aid cuts and labor deficit, the Thai government reversed decades of policy and began issuing the refugees permits to work outside the camps, to help them meet their own needs.

Ray Boe is one of the 6,800 camp refugees the government says have entered the Thai labor force in the first year of the program.

"After the cuts by USAID and other organizations, there is no more regular support for our daily needs, like rice and other rations. And there is not enough healthcare in the camps anymore," he said.

The cuts forced him and his parents to borrow from neighbors and to pare down their already modest meals.

Since last month, he has earned 400 baht (about $12) a day pouring concrete and erecting scaffolding around what's to be a 12-story apartment building in central Bangkok. He hopes to start sending money home soon.

"It will help us pay for food and other basic needs, and for health care for my parents," Ray Boe said.

"Compared to how we were living in the camp before, it will be a big difference, having my own income and supporting my family on my own, not having to wait for other people to support us day to day," he told DW.

Underpaid and overworked: Myanmar migrants in Thailand To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Refugee work program offers hope but faces a rocky start

The program allows the refugees to work in 43 of Thailand's 76 provinces and in any sector not reserved by law for Thai citizens only.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs says the government has improved the vocational training on offer inside the camps to better prepare refugees for work outside.

"We are hopeful that this policy would enhance opportunities and empower the [refugees] to realize their potential, as well as contribute to Thai socio-economic development," said Praporn Waenluang, a spokesman for the ministry's information department.

Labor and refugee rights groups have welcomed the program.

"I have met a lot of camp [refugees] who have come outside and worked. They are so happy to work and earn money, a lot of money compared to what they [can] get in the camp," said Siwawong Sooktawee, Thailand project coordinator for the International Detention Coalition.

"This is good because they feel they can help themselves, they can support themselves, not depend on aid anymore," he added.

Yet he and others say the program has gotten off to a slow start, with many flaws to work out.

They say many of the refugees who have taken part have not been given contracts by their employers, only to find the conditions rougher, the work harder, or the pay lower than what they were promised before leaving the camps. The program also lacks a clear system for lodging and settling complaints, they say.

"Many refugees go, come back, go, come back so many times. Some refugees, their families have to raise funds or borrow money in the refugee camps so that their father or their family member will be able to return," said K'nyaw Paw, general secretary of the Karen Women's Organization, an NGO serving the camp's ethnic Karen.

Myanmar workers in Thailand struggle to work legally To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Financial burdens placed on Myanmar refugees

Siwawong and K'nyaw Paw say refugees are sometimes made to repay employers through wage deductions for hiring them, including medical exams, government permits and transportation to job sites. As a result, they often start work already in debt, sometimes without prior warning.

Akwah, a father of two who goes by one name, left his camp with 20 other refugees in November 2025 for what was supposed to be a job harvesting sugarcane on a farm on the other side of the country for 250 baht per day.

When he arrived, however, he was told to cut eucalyptus trees — a much more difficult and dangerous job, he says — for 200 baht per day. They had to sleep outdoors, with no electricity and only a nearby pond for water.

"We spoke to the boss, but the boss did not care. He said, 'Just do the work because you are already here.' But we said we could not do it," said Akwah, and they left after three months.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not reply to DW's request for comment on the program's alleged problems. The Labor and Interior Ministries, which mainly oversee the program, did not reply to requests for an interview either.

Rights groups say program still needs to improve

Siwawong and K'nyaw Paw say refugees who take part should be guaranteed clear and detailed contracts — translated if needed into Burmese, Karen or Karenni, the main languages spoken in the camps — and an easy-to-access system for filing and settling complaints.

They also suggest that the government open more provinces up to the program and screen the job brokers coming to the camps as middlemen, to weed out the unscrupulous ones.

They say their NGOs and others are working with the government on making some of the upgrades, and that they're hopeful the program will improve with time, so that more of the refugees are able and willing to take part.

For all the program's flaws, though, they say most of the refugees are still eager to apply, even those who have run into problems.

"I had a bad experience, but I still want to go again, because food in the camp is a problem," said Mu Dah Hsit, who fell ill at her job and had to quit after her boss refused to cover the health insurance the program is supposed to guarantee.

"I have no mother, and a father who is sick, and siblings I have to take care of," she said. "So, I have to go; otherwise, we cannot live."

The Thailand-Myanmar border clinic for people fleeing war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: Rubio visits India with a trip to the world's largest oil refinery topping the agenda
World.content:
A visit to India this week by Washington's top diplomat will skip New Delhi and instead include the world's largest oil refinery, which processes massive amounts of Russian crude. Is Trump looking for a new deal?

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio kicks off a three-day visit to India on Monday in the finance hub of Mumbai, before heading to Jamnagar, home to a major oil refinery owned by industrial titan Reliance Industries.

Rubio's business-oriented visit comes as trade talks remain stalled amid continued ambiguity on punitive measures from the US over India's purchases of Russian oil.

Reliance is a top buyer of Venezuelan oil. The refinery can process 1.4 million barrels of crude oil a day, so it's a valuable exporter of diesel fuel for global markets. The refinery has also been a major buyer of Russian Urals crude, making it a significant part of India's energy relationship with Russia.

In March, Washington unveiled plans for a new oil refinery in Texas, backed by Reliance.

US President Donald Trump has put the value of the project at $300 billion (€258 billion) and presented it as a way to help reduce the US trade deficit with India. Whether the project moves forward, and on what terms, will be closely watched.

An elusive US-India trade deal

Since taking office for a second time in 2025, Trump has gone back and forth on tariff threats with India over what he considers to be unfair trade practices, along with India's continued purchases of Russian oil amid the war in Ukraine.

How India has become Russia's trade lifeline To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In February 2026, Trump announced a "trade deal" that slashed US tariffs on Indian goods, in exchange for India lowering trade barriers and halting purchases of Russian oil. Trump had claimed that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi promised to stop buying Russian oil. However, this has never been confirmed by New Delhi.

While maritime data from Kpler, a commodities and energy-market intelligence company, showed Indian refiners briefly diversified supply away from Russia to avoid tightening sanctions, India's deep reliance on discounted Russian crude continues to be a cornerstone of its energy strategy. Russia remains India's top supplier of crude oil.

In mid-September, Trump signed the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act," imposing 100% tariffs on top buyers of Russian oil and gas, which includes India.

However, last week, just days before the legislation was due to go into effect, Trump signed an executive order pausing the sanctions.

Rubio: Trade deal 'very close'

Before traveling to India, Rubio was in Uzbekistan for a meeting of the "C5+1" diplomatic platform comprising the US and five Central Asian countries. In remarks on the sidelines, Rubio said trade talks with India are taking place with the sanctions waivers in mind.

Jamnagar is the largest single-site oil refinery in the world Image: Reliance Industries Limited/AP Photo/picture alliance

"We have had to waive sanctions over the past few months, looking at the global supplies, looking at global prices, and the impact it was having on other countries," he said.

"We're trying to finalize a trade deal with India right now. We're very close to doing that," Rubio added.

In an interview with Indian broadcaster NDTV, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said that Jamnagar could be a valuable source of diesel for the US.

Foreign policy analyst C Raja Mohan of Jindal Global University in India told DW that Rubio skipping a visit to the Indian capital in favor of Mumbai and Jamnagar should not be considered a diplomatic snub, as the refinery has international importance amid the global energy crunch brought on by the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.

He said Jamnagar is an "important node in global trade" because it processes Russian oil and serves as a conduit for refined Russian petroleum products reaching Western markets.

Although Trump's sanctions reprieve offers New Delhi temporary relief, the underlying threat remains. Washington retains the option of imposing punitive tariffs, leaving Russian oil as a potential source of leverage in wider trade negotiations.

Former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, cautioned against reading too much into Rubio's decision to skip Delhi amid political criticism in India.

"The focus of his current trip is on energy, and he is visiting the Reliance refinery in Jamnagar," she told DW. "The high price of fuel, particularly diesel, has become a political liability for the Trump administration, which wants to be seen taking action on this issue."

Diesel prices have skyrocketed around the world following the Iran war and the ensuing disruption of supply from the Middle East. In waiving Russia sanctions, Trump has tried to blame Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities as being the cause of high prices.

Shankar pointed to Reliance's proposed Texas refinery, noting that the state is "one of the states in play" in the upcoming midterm elections in the US.

"Some forward movement on the investment would be welcome," she said.

Can Trump’s diesel deal bring down US fuel prices? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump eroding trust in Delhi?

The two governments continue to describe their ties as a comprehensive global strategic partnership spanning defence, trade, technology and energy.

Analyst Mohan argued that describing the US-India relationship as uniquely transactional was misleading.

"Every nation ultimately acts out of national self-interest, rather than pure altruism or shared values," he said.

The current friction, in his view, is part of a normal negotiation between two sovereign powers, not proof that the partnership was failing.

Besides Russian oil, another potential area of complication is the Trump administration suspending a scheme allowing US companies to sponsor skilled foreign workers.

On October 8, the Trump administration suspended new and pending applications under the US Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program at several technology companies amid investigations into alleged visa fraud and the displacement of US workers.

The process is a key step for employers seeking permanent residency for foreign staff, including Indian professionals.

Harsh Pant, vice president for studies and foreign policy at the Delhi-based Observer Research Foundation (ORF), said Trump's own words and actions had damaged ties despite regular high-level engagement.

"Even as he calls Prime Minister Modi a good friend, he has damaged the relationship by targeting India, and his supporters have been targeting Indians," Pant told DW.

Pant said inconsistent messaging from Washington was eroding trust and could have consequences well beyond Trump's presidency.

"The sense that America is unreliable, that America can't be trusted, is beginning to come back into policy discourse," he said.

The damage, he warned, could reach beyond government-to-government relations to Indian students, professionals and the middle class, whose goodwill has helped sustain ties through earlier disagreements.

"If public sentiment goes against a country, then it becomes very difficult for the policy-makers to craft an alternative policy,” Pant said, adding that US actions affecting Indian students and professionals "will have consequences."

India: From tariff fortress to free-trade powerhouse To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: UN food program cuts aid to 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza
World.content:
Amid funding shortages, the World Food Program has said it is being forced to reduce necessary aid. Over two-thirds of Palestinians in Gaza are facing acute hunger, according to the agency.

The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) has been forced to cut its monthly food aid to the war-ravaged Gaza Strip , where some two-thirds of the population are struggling to get food, the agency said on Monday.

The WFP said it was reducing the number of people receiving aid from 1.6 million to 1.1 million, leaving some 500,000 people without support.

The UN program is facing severe funding shortages. "WFP no longer has sufficient funding to sustain this level of support," the organization said.

What UN aid is being cut in Gaza?

Beyond the cutting of aid to some half a million recipients in the region, the WFP is also:

Reducing rations by half

Cash assistance has been cut for some 75,000 families

Hot meals for those unable to cook have been reduced from 250,000 to 150,000

Some 1.4 million people in Gaza are facing crisis levels of food insecurity according to the WFP, with 200,000 living in emergency conditions.

Despite a US-brokered ceasefire that came into effect last year, Israeli strikes have continued and aid has remained restricted, with little progress toward a final end to the conflict.

"It's a year into the agreement of this ceasefire. Well, life is still brutal here. There is no proper shelter. There is no ⁠basic ​services. There is no safety, no security," acting Executive ​Director of the World Food Program WFP Carl Skau told Reuters in Gaza.

"These cuts are happening ​just as we are facing the fourth winter. You know, I've been through the winters here, absolutely brutal," he added.

Gaza's children bear lasting scars three years into war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Why is aid being cut to Gaza?

The UN program urgently needs $450 million (€400 million) to keep funding its critical operations in Gaza and the West Bank over the next six months.

"We tell the world now ⁠is not ​the time to look away. This is the time to step up to sustain this support, to protect the progress that has been made, but also to push for early recovery," Skau said.

The WFP had already announced cuts to aid for the West Bank in early September, citing funding shortages and donor fatigue.

The Israeli authority responsible for the Palestinian territories, COGAT, says the supply of aid deliveries into the strip exceeds the demand for food and it claims there is no acute food insecurity in Gaza.

World.title: From delivery driver to global fame: A Korean writer's journey
World.content:
You Yeong-Gwang's The Rainfall Market tells the story of a mysterious, hidden shop that only opens when it rains. For a debut novel by an unknown author, it was a massive success.

For ten years, publishers rejected You Yeong-Gwang's book. Yet before it was even printed in South Korea, the once-abandoned manuscript had international publishers flocking to secure translation rights.

"I'm so grateful that the book has now been published in more than 20 countries. Even more astonishingly, it also appeared on the Der Spiegel bestseller list in Germany," he told DW while attending the 2026 Frankfurt Book Fair.

For a debut novel by an unknown author, it was a massive success, securing publication in 15 languages, including English, German, Spanish and traditional Chinese.

"The Rainfall Market" tells the story of a mysterious, hidden shop that only opens when it rains. In the shop, visitors can exchange their deepest unhappiness for a ticket to a brand-new destiny. The plot revolves around Serin, a disheartened young girl who stumbles into the marketplace run by whimsical spirits, finding a warm, comforting space.

"In fact, Serin's story is my story," author You said. "For a long time, I even wondered how wonderful it would be if I could sell my unhappiness and use the money to buy happiness."

While writing the book, he was going through a difficult time himself.

"I had to care for my mother, who had been ill for a long time, and I had also been responsible for supporting my family financially for many years. Life felt incredibly heavy," he reflected.

"But when I was writing, I could immerse myself in the world of the story and, even if only for a short while, forget about those circumstances. That's why writing made me so happy. I truly enjoyed it."

On the creation of 'The Rainfall Market'

The idea of rain is inspired by his own life.

"At that time, my circumstances felt as though it were raining constantly," You said.

You Yeong-gwang, author of 'The Rainfall Market' Image: ClayHouse

The story draws heavily on traditional Korean folklore, serving as a quintessential "healing fiction" tale in which its young protagonist must weigh the true cost of seemingly perfect lives.

"When I was writing, I wasn't consciously trying to write healing fiction. At the time, I didn't even really know that such a label existed."

He initially planned to publish a book independently and started crowdfunding. But as the funding failed, he used all his savings and printed 200 copies, which bookstores refused to take. In a month, he only sold five copies. "I thought that's it. I really have to give up now.”

"At the time, I had undergone eye surgery and due to complications, I couldn't see, so I started working at a call center, where I could work using my voice." You said. "During the week, I worked at a call center, and on weekends I went to a computer academy. I learned how to make books on my own for a few years."

He then taught himself how to use the software needed to create books on his own.

While running one of the crowdfunding campaigns, he started working as a food delivery driver. "The round trip between my home and the area where I delivered food took about four hours each day. So I wrote on my phone's memo app while traveling on the subway."

"Even when I was going through very difficult circumstances, I was able to keep writing because the moments when I was writing were so joyful. For a little while, I could forget about the difficult situation I was in," You explained.

Finally a breakthrough

"I gathered those pieces of writing together and launched what I intended to be my final crowdfunding campaign," he said.

The campaign was intended to fund the publication of "The Rainfall Market."

"To my amazement, the campaign succeeded, and I was able to publish the book commercially for the first time," he said.

How K-pop pushes appetite for Korean ramyun noodles To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Following the crowdfunding success, the novel was acquired by Clayhouse, a prominent South Korean publishing company.

Before it was even published, he had received offers from publishers in five countries and signed international publishing contracts.

And in the first month after publication, the original South Korean language edition sold 30,000 copies across all formats, ranking as the bestselling e-book and third-bestselling physical book.

"I still find it hard to believe that all of this has happened and that I'm here at the Frankfurt Book Fair. I'm incredibly grateful and happy," said You.

A new horizon for Hallyu, or the 'Korean Wave:' K-Comfort Fiction

Korea's newest soft power is K-literature, which sold about 1.2 million translated copies abroad in 2025 for the second consecutive year.

And You's book belongs to a trending genre called Korean comfort fiction.

"When readers closed the book, I wanted them to feel a little warmth in their hearts," he said.

Although Korean literature was first known for darker, more pragmatic books about societal realities, K-comfort fiction is the child of South Korea's pressure-cooker modern society. It offers an answer to the human need for escapism and a transient antidote to the reality of a hyper-competitive education system, brutal job market and intense corporate pressure.

"When I was writing, I was going through a very difficult time myself, and I wished someone would comfort me. So, I thought, why don't I try reading something like that myself? Why don't I write something that can comfort me?" You wondered.

With burnout on the rise globally, more readers are seeking soul-soothing literature with exhausted protagonists they can relate to. Usually without a need to defeat a villain, the stories follow protagonists with a deep desire for rest, community and emotional repair.

The whimsical fiction aspect is the missing element allowing them to step away from reality. The genre originally gained traction through indie productions, online crowdfunding and endorsements from high-profile K-pop artists.

How South Korea is cashing in on 'KPop Demon Hunters' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Despite the Korean context, this style of storytelling quickly went global, capturing different international audiences, including those already familiar with cozy K-dramas or those simply looking for a gentle refuge from the anxieties of the modern world.

Last year, the bestselling Korean novel abroad was "Welcome to the Hyunam-dong Bookshop," according to the Literature Translation Institute of Korea. The novel belongs to the same genre as "The Rainfall Market."

While readers embrace the genre, critics view it with literary skepticism. They point out that it relies heavily on a predictable, repetitive formula, often built around a single magical space, with simplistic prose and low-stakes conflicts that prioritize cozy vibes over deep character development.

Reviewing "The Rainfall Market" for the Korea Times, Peter Juhl, a literary critic, described healing fiction as light, feel-good stories and argued the boom reflects a deliberate effort to write global novels for international markets.

Future aspirations and message to readers

"Of course I'm happy that my book is receiving so much love and that I'm able to write. But more than anything, I hope my mother gets better and regains her health," You said after mentioning that his mother underwent surgery a week before his arrival at the book fair.

Beyond the book itself, people seem to relate to and appreciate the story of his own life.

"If I have the opportunity, I'd like to share more stories about hope and dreams with people who are going through circumstances similar to mine," said You. "If my story can help one person even a little, in any way, I don't think anything could make me happier."

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

World.title: The homeless man living in front of a London mega-mansion
World.content:
Anders Fernstedt lives in London without any money. The Swedish native has built a most unusual home under the porch of a house worth over €200 million. How did that happen?

There's a lot of stopping and staring in Knightsbridge. This part of central London is within a stone's throw of Buckingham Palace, Hyde Park and Harrods, bringing inquisitive tourists in droves.

While it may not divert quite as many eyeballs as the seat of the British monarchy, a curious collection of plants, garden umbrellas, shopping bags and children's toys filling a building's entrance causes many a curious glance.

The peculiar arrangement on a grand portico is what Anders Fernstedt, a man from Sweden who fell on hard times, has been calling home for more than three years already.

That building hosting his makeshift setup was, just a few years ago, London's most expensive house.

The mega-mansion at 2-8A Rutland Gate sold in 2020 for a then-record £210 million (€244 million, $278 million) to Hui Ka Yan, the founder of China's Evergrande group, who was sentenced to life in prison last month.

Hui never moved in and the house was registered under his wife's name. The freezing of her assets means it can't be seized by liquidators and the house is in a state of limbo.

Chinese court hands Evergrande property tycoon life sentence To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

So too was Fernstedt when he first stumbled across it. "I just thought, it would be a shelter for the night. I'm an avid camper, like an amateur botanist. I'm not afraid of nature," he told DW.

'Camping on the balcony'

Fernstedt has never been inside the property, which appears to be in a state of disrepair. Instead, he gradually built his home in the portico, where grand columns guard the 45 rooms, indoor swimming pool and 116 windows. Year round he sleeps under the portico roof and a large umbrella which provides a hidden nook in which he's placed mattresses and bedding.

"I haven't had a bad night's sleep for as long as I can remember. And that goes for four seasons. It's not cold in the winter, and because I don't have walls, I get the breeze in the heat," he said.

"My conceit when I started was that sort of fake dream. Oh, I'm just a boy, my parents are in the house, everything's normal, I just asked them for permission to camp on the balcony."

2-8A Rutland Gate sold for €244 million in 2020 but has been unoccupied since Image: Dan Redding/DW

Fernstedt was raised by his mother in Sweden before embarking on a range of careers at home and in the US, building a name for himself in the tech world.

In 2016, he moved to England where he worked as a journalist and fact checker at publications including The Economist, before work dried up around the time of the COVID pandemic.

A share in a tech company from his days in the US gave Anders a nest egg he relied on. But it couldn't last forever and he found himself living in a tent and then temporary accommodation, where he experienced violence and brushed up against people with severe addictions.

"Perhaps in this contemporary world, the biggest curiosity about my lifestyle is I'm completely off money," he said.

Community support powers unusual lifestyle

Fernstedt has built relationships with bakeries, cafes and florists in which he gets unused food, flowers for his home and use of power. He also makes use of a homeless charity in nearby Victoria for showers, clothing donations and socializing. But he's also made himself a broadly accepted part of one of London's most affluent neighborhoods.

Fernstedt's home evolved over several years, through donations and gifts Image: Dan Redding/DW

"This is a very sophisticated neighborhood. I'd stayed for a few weeks and I knew everybody knew that I was here. And I thought, how can I sort of convey my presence without being present? And I thought, my constituency has to be the neighbors' children and grandchildren. Because if they plead my case at the kitchen table, my prospects improve," he said, by way of explaining the toys that line his abode.

"It is, in a way, a squirrel's nut collection," he added, when asked if he's worried about leaving his possessions out in the open. "I have so many nuts that I won't notice when something disappears."

There are some neighbors who do object to his presence, but Anders does his best to keep his home neat and his life quiet. Indeed, many others feel his presence prevents the house being a target for thieves or vandals. Overall though, he's found the community welcoming.

"Sometimes they introduce themselves asking what might I want or need. And my stock answer being: 'well, what you just gave me, a little bit of normal time, right? And neighborly banter'," he said. "Sometimes I'll be given food and very elegant Italian dinner jackets and clothes have arrived on a few occasions."

Homelessness a growing concern in London

Not all homeless people in London have found such a stable lifestyle. Homeless charity Crisis estimates that there are over 200,000 people classified as homeless in England's capital, where "4,392 people were recorded sleeping rough in London between April and June, up from 4% on the same time last year. This is up 58% compared to 10 years ago."

According to government figures, there were 105,138 empty homes in London in 2025, or 1 in every 37 homes. Andy Burnham, who became British Prime Minister in July, has since vowed to offer "every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas."

Britain's new PM takes on fight against homelessness To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With such an enormous price tag, even after six years of being abandoned, Fernstedt knows that the house he lives at could potentially become untenable at virtually any moment.

But over the last few years, it's given him something he craved when pitching up his tent or being moved from one scary temporary residence to the next.

"I'm no longer really worried that I'll cycle around the corner and everything will be gone. Because I've been here so long, I'm free of worrying now, and if we worry too much, we won't be happy."

Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier

World.title: Greece: At least 12 die in migrant drownings overnight
World.content:
Authorities say 12 people, including an infant, have drowned in Greek waters in two separate incidents overnight. Another 22 people were rescued. A search-and-rescue operation is ongoing.

Greek Coast Guard officials say 12 migrants were killed in the Aegean Sea overnight in two separate boating accidents.

In the first incident, six people — four men, a woman and an infant — were killed in waters off the coast of Lesbos when "a speedboat carrying migrants collided with the port side of a police patrol vessel," according to the Coast Guard.

Eight people were reported rescued.

In the second incident, six people — five men and a woman — drowned after their boat capsized off the coast of Samos, while 14 were rescued.

A search-and-rescue mission is ongoing in the area.

Authorities say they arrested a 37-year-old Turkish national among the survivors in the first incident, identifying him ‌as ​a suspected smuggler and the operator of the speedboat.

Greece's Minister of Shipping and Island Policy Vassilis Kikilias blamed migrant traffickers for all of the deaths, posting on X, "Our position is non-negotiable: Zero tolerance for smugglers."

Turkey to Greece: Deadly migrant passage to Europe

Greece has long been a gateway ​to Europe for migrants and ⁠refugees from the Middle East, Africa and Asia who usually set off on the notoriously deadly sea voyage from Turkey.

According to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), refugee arrivals in Greece are declining this year.

As of October 11, 2026, some 25,000 arrivals had been recorded compared to 42,000 in 2025.

Almost one million migrants and refugees landed on Greece's shores during the 2015/2016 migration crisis, here, too, mainly from Turkey.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

World.title: Australian MP seriously hurt in suspected car attack
World.content:
Helen Haines, an independent federal lawmaker, has been struck by a car in what Australia's prime minister has called an apparent attack.

Australian police are investigating a suspected car attack that has left independent MP Helen Haines with critical injuries.

Counterterrorism investigators have joined the probe following the incident, which occurred outside Haines' constituency office in Wangaratta, northeast of the Victorian capital, Melbourne.

What do we know about the suspected attack on Haines?

Haines, 65, was hit by an SUV, said by police to be a white Toyota, outside her office, leaving her with serious injuries, particularly to her lower body.

Broadcaster ABC cited witnesses as saying they had heard a bang and then saw a woman pinned between two cars.

The driver, described as a 43-year-old man, has been arrested, according to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.

Investigators are reported to have found a knife in the car.

Prime Minister Albanese has said the incident seemed 'no accident' Image: Marek Ladzinski/ZUMA/picture alliance

Apparently deliberate attack: PM Albanese

"This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear," Albanese told ABC.

He said it was too early to speculate about the possible motive behind the suspected attack, but pointed to rising political violence.

"The temperature has increased in recent times," Albanese added, "I've expressed that concern to people in the media."

Ben Carroll, the state premier for Victoria where Wangaratta is located, said he was "appalled" by the attack, adding: "I know how devastating this will be for the Wangaratta community and all those who Helen represents."

At a separate press conference, Albanese said everyone was "praying for her full recovery."

Although it has not yet been established whether the incident was deliberate, there has been an increase in threats and harassment targeting lawmakers and other senior public officials in Australia and elsewhere in recent years.

Haines had worked as a nurse and a midwife before entering parliament in 2019. She is known for her stance on stronger climate action.

World.title: Ukraine got 'no warning' of Russian ballistic strikes, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
Massive strikes overnight hit the capital Kyiv, and damaged power stations, killing at least one person and cutting power to hundreds of thousands.

A barrage of Russian ballistic miles struck Kyiv and the surrounding region on Monday, killing at least one person and knocking out power to over half a million homes, Ukrainian authorities said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Telegram that Russia had launched 16 ballistic missiles, targeting Ukraine's energy facilities, 10 of which were hit, cutting power to some 550,000 households.

The president also lamented the lack of warning from Ukraine's international partners.

"Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners," he wrote.

Ukraine's Air Force reported strikes, which included cruise missiles and drones, hitting 25 locations. Of the 269 recorded Shahed drones deployed in the overnight attack, Ukrainian air defenses reportedly downed or suppressed 243, as well as four missiles.

Ukraine strikes Putin's hometown, as Trump eases pressure on Russia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Moscow says it hit drone, missile hubs in Ukraine

Russia's Defense Ministry also confirmed the "massive strikes" on Monday, saying it had targeted Ukraine with "ground-based high-precision weapons and strike drones."

The ministry said it had hit a Ukrainian data center, a logistics hub storing components for drones and cruise missiles, a train depot storing missiles and an industrial facility involved in the production of drones.

It also said it had struck a bulk carrier in the Black Sea, some 130 kilometers (80 miles) from the port of Odesa, which the ministry said had been carrying military and dual-use cargo.

Ukraine did not confirm those targets but said that a medical facility had been hit in the capital, as well as one of the city's metro stations, according to a post by the Kyiv City Military Administration on Telegram.

A police officer inspects the site of a fitness club that was hit by a missile Image: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS

Kyiv, Washington disagree over pause to intelligence sharing

The overnight strikes come amid contradictory claims by both Ukraine and the US about pauses to intelligence sharing.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that Washington had not paused some of its intelligence sharing, denying a statement Zelenskyy made on Sunday.

"I don't know where [Zelenskyy's] getting these things ​or why he's saying these things to the press. You should go back and ask him. There's been no pause," Rubio said during a visit to Uzbekistan.

"What he should ​focus on, and what we want to be focused on, is bringing an end to this war. That's what he should be focused on," he added.

Ukraine is dependent on the ability of US intelligence to spot fast-moving ballistic missiles fired by Russia. Some recent attacks have taken place without warning, Ukrainian officials have reported.
