World.title: Última hora del temporal en España, en directo | Asciende a cuatro la cifra de muertos en el temporal que ha dejado inundaciones en Valencia y Alicante
World.content:
Cataluña afronta 18 horas de “aguaceros intensos” con posibles crecidas de ríos y rieras

Cataluña afrontará 18 horas de “posibles aguaceros intensos” que afectarán sobre todo la zona del litoral y del prelitoral y que evolucionarán de sur a norte, lo que podría comportar la crecida importante y súbita de rieras y de cabeceras de ríos como el Llobregat, el Ter o el Muga. Así lo han anunciado este lunes en una rueda de prensa en la Conselleria de Interior el responsable del área de predicción del Servei Meteorològic de Cataluña (Meteocat), Santi Segalà, y el subdirector general de Programas en Protecció Civil, Sergio Delgado. Segalà ha señalado que se han activado 3 avisos de situación meteorológica de peligro: uno por intensidad de lluvia de más de 40 milímetros en 30 minutos, otro por más de 60 litros por metro cuadrado en 3 horas y, el tercero, por acumulación de lluvia de más de 100 litros por metro cuadrado en el litoral y prelitoral, pero también en zonas del interior y hasta el Pirineo y Prepirineo central y oriental.

Por su parte, Delgado ha alertado de que, localmente, en algunos puntos del litoral y prelitoral, especialmente entre Tarragona y Girona, se podría producir una crecida “importante y súbita” de alguna riera o río menor, lo que podría comportar situaciones de riesgo. El otro foco importante de alerta se sitúa en las cabeceras de los ríos de todo el el ámbito del Pirineo Central y Oriental, donde también puede registrarse una crecida de los caudales.

Delgado ha señalado que, por el momento, la situación es “de riesgo importante, pero no extrema”, por lo no se han adoptado medidas restrictivas, aunque no se descarta dependiendo de cómo evolucione este fenómeno de lluvias. En cualquier caso, ha dicho que el escenario no tiene “nada que ver” con lo sucedido en las últimas horas en la Comunitat Valenciana ni con el episodio de lluvias de hace 15 días en Cataluña, aunque ha subrayado que eso no quiere decir que no exista un riesgo. No obstante, ha pedido a la ciudadanía que, en momentos de lluvia intensa, evite la movilidad, sobre todo por vías secundarias, y que “nunca” se intente cruzar una riera o cualquier zona por la que el agua circule con fuerza. “Aunque tenga solo un palmo de profundidad, tiene fuerza suficiente para tumbarnos, para arrastrarnos y llevarnos hasta un río y, posteriormente, incluso llegar hasta el mar y perder la vida”, ha alertado. (EP)

World.title: Todos los ojos se vuelven al norte: lo que pasa cuando se empuja a los creadores
World.content:
Faro Santander, el nuevo espacio cultural y museístico del norte de España, lanza la II convocatoria de Ayudas a la Creación para artistas cántabros de cualquier disciplina, un programa que, además de ayuda económica, provee de asesorías especializadas y garantiza una muestra pública e[MR1.1]n el museo. Los ganadores de la primera convocatoria cuentan su experiencia

Suelen identificarse solo a toro pasado: aquel momento me cambió la vida. Hay oportunidades, sin embargo, cuyo brillo se deja ver desde el principio. Esta es una de esas. Faro Santander lanza su II Convocatoria de Ayudas a la Creación, un programa que ofrece a los proyectos seleccionados una dotación económica de 10.000 euros, seminarios y mentorías con profesionales, la ocasión de compartir proceso creativo con otros artistas y, como remate, una muestra pública en un espacio tan espectacular como el Edificio Pereda, convertido desde su reciente rehabilitación y apertura en Santander en uno de los grandes focos culturales de todo el norte de España.

Hasta el 15 de febrero de 2027 puede disfrutarse gratuitamente, comisariado por Ane Rodríguez, del resultado de los cuatro proyectos becados en la primera edición. Talento cántabro que, a partir de distintas manifestaciones culturales ligadas a esa verde tierra, ha generado un trabajo variado, muy contemporáneo y de vocación universal. En Flesh & Films / Pieles y pantallas, Itsaso Iribarren y Germán de la Riva recuperan materiales de un archivo de educación sexual de hace décadas; una obra, la que proponen, que cultiva la sensibilidad, que induce a la reflexión sobre gestos cotidianos como el abrazo. En Una forma minúscula, de Salón de belleza, nombre del colectivo formado por Manuela Gutiérrez y Cristina Somavilla, el cine de arte y ensayo sirve como pretexto para encontrarse y hablar, para crear comunidad y traer a la conversación la olvidada contracultura santanderina. La pintora Amaia Bregel, por primera vez en su carrera en piezas de gran escala, en Ludarquías muestra instalaciones y dispositivos impregnados de todo su saber pictórico (“Casi todo el arte contemporáneo es hijo de la pintura”, cuenta). El dúo Casapalma —Irene Atienza y Yoel Molina—, cuya música bucea en el folclore cántabro, ha logrado terminar el rodaje de un documental titulado La Suite de los Riconchos que se estrena el próximo 22 de octubre y nos trae ese ancestral conocimiento que se esconde en las danzas tradicionales y la etnografía.

Entre todos los aspirantes, el jurado escogió proyectos en los que, además de formatos convencionales, cupieran investigaciones artísticas y apuestas valientes: se valora documentación, proceso, método y pensamiento tanto como pieza final. Una característica de este programa de ayudas que los cuatro beneficiarios destacan, por inusual en el panorama nacional: “Ojalá mantengan este espíritu”, indica Germán de la Riva. La visibilidad que les ha otorgado este reconocimiento, sobre todo al verse expuestos en Marisma, en la primera planta de Faro, vecinos a una colección permanente que abarca obra desde El Greco a Frida Kahlo, es el otro gran privilegio que los artistas unánimemente señalan: “Para mí supuso un punto de inflexión”, confiesa Amaia Bregel; para ella, esta ha sido la puerta hacia otras becas o ferias de enorme prestigio, como la de Casa Velázquez o Estampa.

“Animaos a participar, sea cual sea vuestra idea”, ese es el mensaje común de los primeros beneficiarios para quienes les sigan.

Segunda convocatoria Becas Plazo de admisión 2026 15 octubre -

09 de noviembre Dotación económica 10.000 euros Beneficiarios Cuatro artistas (o colectivos de artistas) de cualquier disciplina, residentes o nacidos en Cantabria Así funciona el programa de acompañamiento: El proyecto debe desarrollarse en Cantabria, entre enero y junio de 2027

Se priorizarán aquellos que fomenten la generación de tejido artístico en el territorio

Se realizará un encuentro inicial entre comisarios, coordinadores y beneficiarios

Los beneficiarios dispondrán de cuatro seminarios y talleres con profesionales invitados, uno a la semana durante el primer mes de trabajo

Estos encuentros colectivos periódicos que estarán abiertos a otros artistas que deseen inscribirse

Los beneficiarios podrán solicitar tutorías personalizadas y seguimiento continuo

Al final del programa, se organizará una muestra pública en Faro Santander, a partir de septiembre de 2027

Amaia Bregel y

Ludarquías

Cuando Amaia Bregel volvió a Santander en marzo de 2020, con la pandemia, no tenía intención de quedarse. Se había graduado en Bellas Artes en Valencia, donde continuó con un máster de Producción de Arte y Pensamiento Contemporáneo y donde, sin aquel terremoto mundial, seguramente se habría imaginado residiendo todavía. Hoy, sin embargo, reivindica las posibilidades halladas en su ciudad: “Mucha gente de mi generación volvió y entre todos hemos creado una red. Soy la que más defiende Santander ahora mismo”, reclama entre risas.

05:15 Amaia Bregel | Fundación Santander

Al borde de la treintena, la ayuda de Faro ha supuesto para ella un cambio de escala, literal y profesional. Su proyecto, Ludarquías, le ha permitido abordar una producción que no habría podido llevar a cabo en las condiciones con las que venía trabajando. La artista lo resume sin rodeos: «Para mí a nivel profesional es un antes y un después». Ha podido tomar por primera vez decisiones plásticas sin ver constreñida su ambición por cuestiones estrictamente económicas y, además, ha contado, cuando la duda más quemaba, con el consejo de la consagrada artista limeña Andrea Canepa. “Fue un regalazo”, cuenta. Fruto de toda esa meticulosa labor es el objeto pictórico titulado Escalera de Jacob. Uno de los imperdibles de la muestra.

Amaia Bregel y

Ludarquías Las ayudas supusieron la oportunidad para Amaia Bregel de llevar sus objetos pictóricos a unas dimensiones nunca antes experimentadas. En la imagen, parte del trabajo de montaje final de la instalación móvil. (Crédito: Jabata Films) Antes de llegar al objeto pictórico grande, Bregel trabaja con maquetas. La propia escala presenta problemas que ha de ir afrontando en el proceso plástico y que necesitan de ingenio. En este proyecto, contó con la asesoría de la artista peruana Andrea Canepa. (Crédito: Jabata Films) Su obra parte de lo pictórico y lo deriva hacia objetos donde el color y sus vibraciones son habitables. Amaia Bregel sigue considerándose, ante todo, pintora, aunque se maneje en muchos lenguajes y métodos. Esta pieza expuesta en Marisma, en Faro Santander, lleva por título ‘Escalera de Jacob’ y puede contemplarse así, como un cubo completo, o abierta. (Crédito: Jabata Films).

Casapalma y

La Suite de los Riconchos

Su álbum debut, Montañesas (2023), mezclaba canción tradicional con sonidos electrónicos; con JOTAS (2025) profundizan en la importancia de la pandereta y de una música que, sobre todo, estaba hecha para bailar. Y ahí, en todo ese universo —de los ritmos de percusión y los pasos de danza a la alfayatería y los trajes tradicionales— encuentran el germen del documental La Suite de los Riconchos que ahora estrenan en la Filmoteca de Cantabria y que esperan que tenga un gran recorrido por festivales y salas. Música y patrimonio, arte y sociología.

08:08 Casapalma | Fundación Santander

Las ayudas, además del crucial aporte económico para completar el rodaje que finalizaron en agosto (“¡Hacer una película es muy caro!”, exclama Atienza), le han procurado otra experiencia de esas difícilmente olvidables. Tocaron en la inauguración de Faro Santander, pudieron, gracias a la celebración de ese concierto, “subir a un escenario enorme el folclore de Cantabria para que lo viera toda la ciudad”.

Casapalma y

La Suite de los Riconchos Fotograma de ‘La Suite de los Riconchos’, con Yoel Molina (izquierda) a la guitarra e Irene Atienza a la pandereta. Molina se formó en Musikene (País Vasco) y en el Conservatorio Superior de Ámsterdam. Atienza, que vivió varios años en Brasil, regresó a su ciudad, Santander, tras la pandemia. Para la grabación del documental han llevado a cabo una importante investigación musicológica y etnográfica. El baile estaba en el centro del propósito de estas músicas, y esa misma relevancia tiene en la película. Los trajes tradicionales de montañesa suelen componerse de camisa de manca ancha, saya larga de colores con detalles de terciopelo y detalles como pañoleta o faltriquera. La película documental musical, que contó con la asesoría de grandes profesionales coreográficos y estudiosos de la etnografía de la región, se estrenó en la Filmoteca de Cantabria el 22 de octubre y está pendiente de su distribución en festivales y salas.

Para una formación que trabaja con el patrimonio inmaterial, con buena reputación ya bien ganada y una trayectoria importante en el campo de la música, compartir el proceso de su película con otros artistas con métodos y objetivos más abstractos, inmersos en proyectos de lenguajes variopintos, ha sido otro de los aprendizajes más enriquecedores. Cuenta Irene que, tras esta experiencia en común, Aurelio Vélez, vinculado al colectivo etnográfico Brañaflor y asesor fundamental del filme, tomó la determinación de presentar una propuesta sobre costura y cuadros de la colección permanente a la convocatoria que ahora se abre. “Él no se imaginaba que pudiera ser candidato a unas ayudas de arte, pero programas como este son una forma de abrir la mente”.

Salón de Belleza y

Una forma minúscula

Una conversación entre dos amigas, Manuela Gutiérrez y Cristina Somavilla, que eclosiona al abrirla al resto: así podría definirse qué es Salón de Belleza, el colectivo artístico que ambas fundaron y para el que ver películas, discutirlas y cuestionar ideas anquilosadas sobre el gusto o la cultura es la razón última de ser. Una forma minúscula parte de un hallazgo accidental: se toparon con el largometraje de Jesús Garay Manderley (1981) sobre la figura del artista y activista LGTBIQ+ José Pérez Ocaña y se obsesionaron con la peli: “Le pregunté por ella a mi padre”, cuenta Somavilla, “y me contó que él había conocido aquí a Ocaña”. Ahí comienza su investigación, ¿qué relatos de aquella Cantabria habían quedado fuera de la historia oficial? “Hemos abierto fisuras en lo que se supone que es Santander: hay mucho más”, explican.

06:42 Salón de Belleza | Fundación Santander

La ayuda les ha permitido poner en marcha un grupo de investigación intergeneracional en el que la memoria oral y el intercambio de pareceres ha ido hilando una conversación inacabada e inacabable (“¡seguiremos con estos encuentros y clubes en el futuro!”), siempre dispuesta a fluir fuera de cauce y al vaivén de las sorpresas, una investigación recogida parcialmente en textos y materiales de archivo disponibles en la muestra. “Nos gustaría ahora que la gente se acercara al espacio museístico, que Faro Santander se convirtiera en ese lugar de participación y encuentro que ha sido para nosotras”.

Salón de Belleza y

Una forma minúscula Sesión de trabajo del proyecto ‘Una forma minúscula’, en la que, a partir del visionado de una película y de ciertos materiales de archivo, se abre una conversación. Fotograma del drama dirigido por Jesús Garay ‘Manderley’, estrenado en 1981. La trama acompaña a tres jóvenes homosexuales que, en un mal momento personal, deciden pasar un verano juntos en Cantabria. Entre los protagonistas, destaca el ‘performer’ José Pérez Ocaña. Además de la película, las sesiones del proyecto utilizan material que reconstruye el contexto cultural en que surgió el filme para indagar más allá del relato oficial. En la imagen, el informe de calificación por edades de ‘Manderley’ (Archivo General de la Administración). Otro de esos materiales empleados fue el libro del artista e historiador Adolfo Fernández-Punsola ‘Nuestras vidas’, editado en 1996, que recoge fotografías y documentos de las décadas que retrata la película.

Itsaso Iribarren y Germán de la Riva y

Flesh & Films / Pieles y pantallas

Nunca sabe uno adónde le va a llevar abrir unas cajas viejas. Germán de la Riva recordaba vagamente el contenido de las que sus padres habían acumulado en la consulta. Psicólogos, fueron pioneros en materia de educación sexual en Santander en los años 80 y 90, con métodos traídos de su experiencia en Latinoamérica y EE UU. Dentro de las solapas de cartón, películas con imágenes artísticas pero explícitamente sexuales convivían con artículos y tesis científicas, un archivo que resultó idóneo para la labor investigadora que De la Riva lleva tiempo desarrollando junto a la también doctora en Bellas Artes y bailarina de danza contemporánea Itsaso Iribarren. Para ellos, toda su obra empieza en el cuerpo.

06:28 Itsaso Iribarren y Germán de la Riva | Fundación Santander

Memoria, sexualidad o cómo nos relacionamos físicamente son cuestiones que se pueden abordar apelando a los sentidos y la intuición. El arte tiene su propio camino hacia el conocimiento y, para Iribarren y De la Riva, mostrar ese proceso junto a la obra puede ser la mejor manera de hacer pedagogía: “El público entiende más o menos lo que ocurrió en las artes hasta las Vanguardias, pero existe un vacío, una desconexión, con las artes vivas y el presente de la creación”. Justo por ello, valoran y agradecen el compromiso de Faro Santander al generar un espacio que puede proveer al espectador de las piezas de puzle que le faltan.

Itsaso Iribarren y Germán de la Riva y

Flesh & Films / Pieles y pantallas Itsaso Iribarren y Germán de la Riva, doctores en Bellas Artes y practicantes de danza contemporánea y artes vivas, inician todas sus investigaciones plásticas a partir del cuerpo: el movimiento, el tacto, los sentidos. Es otro de los caminos de conocimiento que permite el arte y que merece exploración. Para documentar el proceso del proyecto ‘Flesh & Films / Pieles y pantallas’ y generar un resultado expositivo, han empleado, entre otros métodos y lenguaje, la filmación analógica en 16 milímetros. Las artes vivas son una disciplina contemporánea en la que las fronteras genéricas se borran, donde conviven ‘performance’, danza, teatro físico, música, texto y artes visuales. De la Riva y Iribarren aplauden la apuesta de Faro Santander por proyectos así, donde mostrar el proceso creativo es casi más importante que alcanzar un resultado final.

Son cuatro historias, cuatro pulsos creativos distintos que, sin embargo, pintan un mapa justo de los derroteros del arte español de hoy, siempre vivo y siempre a punto del naufragio, sin tablas de salvación como la que ofrece esta convocatoria de Faro Santander. Hay oportunidades que de verdad cambian vidas, instituciones que verdaderamente tienen la capacidad de generar un tejido cultural que cosa todo el norte de España y enseñe el tapiz con lo mejor de nuestra creación fuera.

Para presentarse a la nueva convocatoria no hace falta tener respuestas, tan solo ganas de pelearse con el runrún que provocan esas preguntas que merece la pena hacerse.

World.title: Viaje a la remota isla escocesa de Islay y a la aún más inaccesible Jura, donde Orwell terminó ‘1984′
World.content:
Una escapada entre destilerías, turba y ciervos donde el paisaje se mete en el cuerpo, las canciones guardan la memoria de quienes se fueron y aún parece posible perderse entre acantilados e historias

Cuando George Orwell llegó a la isla escocesa de Jura para aislarse del mundo en 1946, escribió en su diario: “Este es un lugar extremadamente inaccesible”. Basta con intentar llegar hasta su casa en Barnhill para comprender que no exageraba: Jura está al otro lado de Islay y, una vez en esa isla, todavía hay que seguir avanzando hacia el norte por carreteras y caminos que parecen empeñados en devolver al viajero al punto de partida. Tengamos en cuenta este dato: en Jura viven 250 personas y 5.000 ciervos. Jura es la hermana pequeña de Islay, una de las islas más narcóticas de las West Highlands escocesas (las tierras altas del oeste) y donde viven 3.000 personas que gozan del lujo medioambiental yendo a donde el viento quiera, un viento con propiedades altamente saludables, que despeja y ventila como una verdad incómoda y con el que uno acaba empatizando porque, al fin y al cabo, él también parece tener prisa por detenerse a contemplar.

Para llegar hasta estas dos islas de las Hébridas Interiores, lo primero es aterrizar en Glasgow (bendito problema), la ciudad más divertida del Reino Unido, y si hay que pasar la noche, mucho mejor, porque los bares Nice ‘N’ Sleazy y Stereo no cierran nunca.

Más información En la isla de Rügen, un patrimonio entre lo mitológico y lo real

Observando la silueta de Islay por la ventanilla de la avioneta antes del aterrizaje, uno ya intuye que lo mejor será ser presa de la isla, un grano de arena entregado al aislamiento. Islay tiene algo de territorio que se ha quedado al margen por vocación. El mar, el viento y la turba han definido el carácter de las cosas, y hasta el silencio tiene una textura particular. Es una isla de horizontes bajos, carreteras estrechas en las que más de una vez hay que echarse atrás para dejar pasar al que viene, playas que cambian de humor con la marea y pequeños pueblos donde la vida transcurre como debería transcurrir la vida en todas partes. El whisky parece estar flotando en el aire, en las bodegas y en una forma de entender el paisaje. Islay no se visita, se entra en ella para dejarse llevar.

Vista de Portnahaven, un pequeño pueblo situado en el extremo sur de la isla de Islay. Paul Carroll Y Mhairi Carroll (GETTY IMAGES)

Veamos cinco puntos fuertes para hacernos una composición de lugar y extraerle el mayor partido más allá del tópico de las destilerías y apostar por el paisaje, la fauna, el bienestar, la gastronomía y la hospitalidad local.

1. La costa de Islay desde el mar

Una manera de acercarnos a esa hospitalidad de sus gentes y de su territorio es dejar las cosas en el hotel y acudir a la localidad de Port Ellen para sumarse al recorrido en bote de tres horas con comida (inolvidable) incluida de Islay Sea Adventures. El capitán Harold nos recibe empuñando una gaita cuyos fogonazos conmovedores consiguen caldear el viento.

La destilería de whisky Lagavulin, y los restos del castillo Dunyvaig, en la isla de Islay. Patsy Davies (Alamy / CORDON PRESS)

Desde el mar se contemplan las tres grandes destilerías del sur —Laphroaig, Lagavulin y Ardbeg— y, delante de cada una, la tripulación sirve un trago de whisky para que cada marca se fije en la memoria con el pegamento de haberla probado allí donde nace. Así continuamos hacia el Área Especial de Conservación de Islay, un espacio protegido al que solo se puede acceder para contemplarlo desde el agua. Mientras los simpáticos patrones van contando historias de la isla, su pasado y su patrimonio, recorremos la costa sudeste, entendiendo uno de sus paisajes más hermosos y también uno de los más ricos en fauna. Aquí vive una importante colonia de focas, además de delicados ciervos rojos que te miran con una pureza con la que mira un niño a su rey mago. Con un poco de suerte, durante la travesía pueden aparecer incluso águilas de cola blanca y delfines.

Parte de la actividad organizada por Islay Sea Adventures consiste en un pícnic de marisco tras un paseo en barco. Ben Shakespeare (Islay Sea Adventures)

El momento más extraordinario llega al alcanzar las aguas tranquilas de los islotes del sudeste de Islay (South-East Islay Skerries), porque es entonces cuando empieza el festival del marisco fresco capturado prácticamente a la puerta de la mesa: del mar al plato apenas hay unos pocos kilómetros. Langosta, bocas de buey de mar, salmón ahumado y, aparte, las vieiras, que son las protagonistas. Porque es un placer ver cómo Harold las cocina a bordo, sobre una barbacoa, con mantequilla, ajo y chile. Se agradecen el pan fresco, la ensalada y las salsas caseras, pero como decoración. Comer así es la experiencia que mejor explica la isla. Ningún folleto, ningún libro, ninguna foto puede superarlo. El único problema de esta actividad puede ser el precio: 115 libras (unos 135 euros, al cambio actual)

2. Vida de isla: tartán, ‘fish and chips’, folclore, Hollywood y Port Charlotte

Con un clima tan contradictorio, en el que un amanecer soleado puede transformarse en cinco minutos en un chubasco pasajero, conviene vestirse correctamente. Se explica así que la lana y el tartán sean tan importantes y se hayan convertido en una de las señas de identidad de las Highlands. Para hacerse una idea de hasta qué punto forman parte de su cultura, merece la pena visitar Islay Woollen Mill, una fábrica con una historia estupenda: allí se diseñó y produjo el tartán utilizado en la película Braveheart. La propia fábrica conserva y comercializa la colección Braveheart y ha trabajado también para otras producciones cinematográficas. El tartán es ese tejido de líneas de distintos colores que se cruzan en ángulo recto formando una trama de cuadros y que acabó convirtiéndose en uno de los signos visuales de Escocia. El que aquí se fabrica lo hemos visto también en Rob Roy, Highlander, Harry Potter (forma parte del uniforme de Hogwarts) e incluso en Forrest Gump, aunque en esta película el tartán juega ya como estampado universal y no tanto como emblema escocés.

El taller de Islay Woollen Mill, que trabaja con los tejidos de forma artesanal. Kenny Lam (VISIT SCOTLAND)

Al hilo de la tradición y para ver esas vestimentas, nada como una noche en el pub del Port Charlotte Hotel, en el pueblo de Port Charlotte, uno de esos rincones dulcemente extendidos frente al mar, reconocibles por sus casas blancas de dos alturas, tan bien conservadas. El local es un punto de reunión donde convergen la nostalgia y la identidad. Su fish and chips es tan interminable como irresistible. La sala tiene el encanto de los negocios eternos que abren fuera de temporada. La cerveza acompaña la llegada de los músicos, que se van sumando como si bajaran a la calle para encontrarse con sus amigos. El fiddle (violín tradicional), el acordeón, las guitarras, las mandolinas y la gaita van llenando el pub de canciones y viejas melodías de las islas, como si cada una trajera consigo un pedazo de memoria o una lágrima que se disuelve en el vaso. Cuando suena Westering Home, no hay nada ni nadie que pueda deshacer el nudo del estómago.

Esas canciones, esa música tradicional gaélica o folk, parecen creadas por la naturaleza, el viento, la lluvia, en ese mar que se lleva a la gente de aquí a probar suerte en otros mundos que difícilmente serán mejores. Y es que cuando uno se va, lo único que de verdad se lleva encima, incrustado, es la música: la canción de cuna que le cantaba su madre, las canciones que moldearon su infancia. Es la prenda mayor.

3. Excursión a Jura

Si Jura no es una isla inventada para perderse, no lo es ninguna. Lo que decíamos antes —250 vecinos rodeados por unos 5.000 ciervos— se comprueba nada más cruzar en ferri el kilómetro —apenas cinco minutos— que separa ambas islas. Bienvenidos a las montañas, las turberas, las costas solitarias y los Paps de Jura, esas tres cumbres que dominan el horizonte como una presencia casi mitológica.

Tres ciervos junto a la costa de la isla escocesa de Jura. Chris Morson (Alamy / CORDON PRESS)

Hacia el norte está Barnhill, la remota casa donde George Orwell se refugió para terminar 1984. Pero la historia del escritor británico y Jura había empezado antes. Él y su mujer, Eileen, llevaban tiempo pensando en abandonar Londres y marcharse a las Hébridas. Tanto era así que Orwell ya había iniciado las gestiones para encontrar allí una casa cuando, en marzo de 1945, Eileen murió inesperadamente durante una operación. Tenía 39 años. Orwell se quedó viudo y con Richard, el hijo que ambos habían adoptado pocos meses antes.

Un año después, David Astor, su amigo y editor del periódico The Observer, le sugirió que se marchara a Jura. La familia de Astor tenía propiedades en la isla y conocía Barnhill, una granja aislada en su extremo norte. Orwell llegó en mayo de 1946 y acabó alquilando la casa. Lo que había sido un proyecto compartido con Eileen se convirtió así en su refugio: un lugar donde alejarse de Londres, del periodismo y del ruido del mundo. En Barnhill, sin electricidad, teléfono ni vecinos a mano, encontró el aislamiento que buscaba y terminó escribiendo 1984.

Más amable es la parada en Lussa Gin, donde la ginebra se elabora con botánicos recolectados en la isla. Georgina y Claire nos enseñan su huerto, donde crecen algunos de sus ingredientes: enebro, rosas y tomillo limonero. Allí nos presentan su licor, extraordinariamente botánico, antes de mostrar su nueva creación, una ginebra homenaje a George Orwell llamada Nineteen Eighty Four, con notas de té Assam, cardamomo y rosas. El licor sirve también para hablar del escritor, que nació en la India en junio de 1903, hijo de un funcionario del Imperio británico. Con apenas un año, su madre se lo llevó a Inglaterra. Luego participó en dos guerras, experiencias que acabarían alimentando buena parte de su obra.

Parte del equipo de la destilería Lussa Gin. Lussa Gin

Cuando nos vamos, le digo a Georgina que pensamos comer en The Antlers. Su respuesta llega inmediata:

-Oohh, The Antlers... Desde que abrió, la gente de Jura está más gorda y es más pobre.

Le sobra razón. Esta bakehouse (panadería) roba el corazón hasta a la persona más evitativa con su pastrami y sus sausage rolls (rollos de salchichas). En The Antlers, la gastronomía vuelve a poner los pies en la tierra después de tantas millas de paisaje. En Jura todo parece estar desproporcionado: hay más ciervos que personas, más naturaleza que habitantes y una sensación de espacio que hace que incluso el silencio parezca perdido.

4. El imprescindible paseo al American Monument

Hay que dejar el coche en el aparcamiento de la reserva natural de The Oa, al final de la carretera que atraviesa esta península del sur de Islay. Desde allí comienza el camino hacia el American Monument, un paseo de unos treinta minutos, aunque lo razonable es hacer la ruta circular completa, de unos tres kilómetros y medio, sin ninguna prisa. Y, sobre todo, reservar otra hora para quedarse allí.

El camino es un abrazo constante de la naturaleza: la hierba, el viento del Atlántico, el salitre y esa sensación de ir dejando atrás el mundo... Hasta que aparecen los acantilados, el mar y el monumento, levantado en memoria de los soldados estadounidenses que murieron en los naufragios del Tuscania y el Otranto en 1918, que desde lejos parece suspendido sobre el océano.

El faro de Carraig Fhada, situado en la isla de Islay, es un faro emblemático en forma de torre cuadrada. Catherine Gilbrook (Alamy / CORDON PRESS)

Hay algo de templo en este lugar: un santuario sin techo ante el que uno acaba pidiendo deseos al mar, como quien deja una ofrenda y confía en que alguien, o algo, se encargará de ella. Y luego está el viento, que aquí parece tener permiso para hacer lo que quiera. Empuja, despeina, zarandea, te da la vuelta y te hace gritar al vacío. Un grito que mezcla la alegría y el dolor, la satisfacción de estar allí y la emoción que uno carga.

Después de este paseo solo quedan dos opciones: volver al whisky o entregarse al hotel. La primera pasa por Bowmore, una de las destilerías históricas de Islay, fundada en 1779 y una de las más antiguas de Escocia. Está a orillas del Loch Indaal y conserva uno de los elementos que mejor explican su carácter: sus almacenes de maduración, algunos de ellos situados prácticamente al nivel del mar. Aquí el whisky sigue teniendo algo de paisaje: turba, agua, sal y años de espera convertidos en una bebida.

La segunda opción es bastante más peligrosa para el presupuesto: irse al hotel, pero, en fin, tampoco todos los días se despierta uno en Islay.

5. The Machrie, un hotel convertido en galería

El hotel The Machrie está frente al Atlántico, entre dunas y junto a una playa de siete millas, pero quizás lo más sorprendente está dentro. La colección de arte, reunida y comisariada por su fundadora, Sue Nye, convierte el alojamiento en una especie de galería habitada: las obras aparecen en los pasillos, las habitaciones, el restaurante, la recepción o el gimnasio. Hay artistas escoceses como John Bellany, Pat Douthwaite, Peter Howson o Elizabeth Blackadder, junto a nombres como Tracey Emin, Antony Gormley, Peter Blake, Picasso, Miró, Dalí o Banksy. El arte forma parte de la vida cotidiana.

El hotel y campo de golf The Machrie. KEVIN MURRAY (THE MACHRIE)

Y luego está el paisaje, la ubicación. The Machrie recibe también a muchos jugadores de golf, que encuentran aquí un tapete verde frente al Atlántico. Para quien disfrute dándole a una pelota con un palo y persiguiéndola después por la hierba, probablemente no se pueda pedir más. Para los demás siempre queda sentarse frente al mar. Porque las vistas de la hierba y el océano son de esas que consiguen que uno se quede un rato sin hacer absolutamente nada. Uno mira cómo el viento mueve la hierba y cómo la isla continúa con su vida. Quizá ese sea el lujo verdadero de The Machrie. Y, puestos a confesarlo todo, quizá también el único que importa, junto a la poesía, porque ante este paisaje por fuerza vuelven a la cabeza aquellos versos de Wislawa Szymborska: “Comprendo que mi tristeza no frenará la hierba. Si los tallos vacilan será sólo por el viento”.

World.title: Body of missing woman from Amsterdam found in suitcase
World.content:
The body of a woman who went missing after taking a lift on a bike with an unknown man has been found in a suitcase in Amsterdam.

Police said the remains were discovered last Friday in the Amstel river and identified as a woman named as Hajar, who was last seen two weeks ago near the Rai conference centre.

She left in the direction of Buitenveldert on October 4 on a black ladies’ bike with a man whom police are now trying to trace.

Police would not confirm reports on AT5 that a passer-by found the suitcase containing the body on Saturday morning, or that messages were sent to local neighbourhood app groups later that day asking if people had noticed anybody acting suspiciously with a suitcase.

She is described as between 1.65m and 1.70m tall with dark curly hair and dark eyes. The day before she was last seen alive she was wearing a tiger print dress and white New Balance shoes.

Anyone who saw Hajar between October 4 and October 17 or has any information can contact police on 0900 8844, via www.politie.nl, or anonymously via 0800 7000 or at Meld Misdaad Anoniem.

World.title: How expats tackle Dutch language issues without giving away data
World.content:
A letter from the Belastingdienst has landed on the doormat, and it might as well be written in code. At work, the team meeting that began in English has drifted into Dutch, and you’re nodding along while hoping nobody asks for your opinion. Sound familiar? We spoke with OmniForge, a tech company helping expats tackle the language barrier online.

Why the usual AI tools fall short

AI assistants promise to help with both of these challenges, but they have their limits. Firstly, many recording and transcription tools only support a handful of major languages, which leaves plenty of expats working in English by default, says Daniel G. Ríos, co-founder and CEO of OmniForge. Secondly, most of them process everything in the cloud, which is less than ideal when it comes to an employment contract, payslip or document with your BSN on it.

The risk is not theoretical. When hackers posted Odido’s customer data online, millions of people were reminded how far personal data can travel. “In the best case scenario, your data might be used to profile you for ads,” Daniel says, “but in the case of data exfiltration from cloud providers, your data might also be used for nefarious purposes.”

A local alternative, built by expats

OmniForge is a privacy-first AI desktop app for macOS and Windows that transcribes meetings and answers questions about your documents, all on your own computer. It was built by a team of expats in the Netherlands who, as Daniel puts it, “experience the exact same bilingual friction our users do.”

https://omniforge.online/dutchnews

“People should not have to compromise on their personal information in order to benefit from a service,” he says. In practice, the AI engine lives on your machine rather than in a data centre. “You could disconnect your WiFi entirely, and it will still securely transcribe your meetings and analyse your documents.” Only account login and subscription management are online.

There’s an environmental upside too, Daniel argues: running AI on your own computer’s spare processing power, what he calls “Green AI at the Edge,” can avoid the electricity and cooling water that big cloud models require from data centres.

When the meeting switches language

Language is where OmniForge stands out. It transcribes audio in 25 languages, including Dutch, English, German, French, Spanish and Polish, and can write summaries and answers in around 200 languages. In other words, a meeting held in Dutch can be summarised in whichever language you read most comfortably.

Then there’s the meeting that starts in English and slides into Dutch. Other tools make you pick a language in advance, Daniel says, whereas OmniForge listens for mid-sentence switches. He admits the transcript does not always get the spoken language right, but because the summary can be generated in any supported language regardless of the input, the gist still comes through.

A typical user, he says, is an international professional in a technical project meeting where half the team defaults to Dutch. Instead of stopping the flow to ask for translations, they record locally, having the assurance that a full English summary will be waiting the moment the meeting ends.

Decoding the paperwork

The same tool works on documents, not just audio. You can drop a Dutch PDF into OmniForge, whether it’s a letter from your landlord or your VvE, a payslip or a notice from the Belastingdienst, then ask questions and get an explanation in English.

Phone calls are covered, too. If you’re talking to the gemeente, put the phone on speaker and record the conversation: even if you feel lost during the call, OmniForge transcribes it so you have a comprehensive summary to review the moment you hang up. “It takes the stress out of local administration,” is how Daniel puts it.

Built for international teams

For employers, the same features make onboarding and internal meetings more inclusive: colleagues who are not fully fluent can follow along through a summary in their preferred language. And because OmniForge records locally, there’s no bot joining your video calls. A project manager juggling several projects can also keep a workspace for each, store meetings and documents together, and ask the assistant for recaps or highlights.

Moreover, local processing represents a win for compliance: HR handles sensitive employee data, and client confidentiality is non-negotiable. Companies are increasingly wary of staff feeding sensitive information to AI chatbots, Daniel explains. “Keeping everything in-house means GDPR compliance by default.” Many cloud tools go to great lengths to get certified, he notes, “but that just means they took steps to secure their customers’ data. With OmniForge, each customer is the sole owner of their data.”

Limitations and next steps

Daniel is upfront about OmniForge’s limits. Because everything runs on your device, transcription speed depends on your hardware: a brand-new machine will get through an hour-long meeting much faster than an older laptop. The assistant is above-average at summaries, highlights and finding information in your documents, “but it cannot compete with the likes of ChatGPT or Claude in terms of raw intelligence,” Daniel concedes, since it has a fraction of the resources.

OmniForge’s next steps will focus on speeding up the models on older hardware and adding more regional dialects. A mobile version is also planned, depending on how many people adopt the app.

Try it on your next confusing letter

The best first step, Daniel says, is to try OmniForge on your next meeting or baffling Dutch letter. Paid tiers start at €9.99 per month for unlimited quotas for individual users. But there’s a generous free tier so you can try before you buy: 40 complimentary minutes per recording and 50 indexed files. All you need to do is download OmniForge for Mac or Windows for free and register.

Prime minister Rob Jetten is going to become a father next year, he announced on social media on Monday.

He and his partner, Argentinian professional hockey player Nicolás Keenan, wrote on Instagram: “Someone very special is on the way. See you in 2027, little one.”

The couple posted the message with a photo of themselves holding an ultrasound scan.

The pair also posted a picture with the baby’s surrogate mother, named as Lisa.

“There are no words big enough to thank our egg donor, our surrogate mum Lisa and both their families,” they wrote. “None of this would be possible without you.”

The message was written in Dutch, Spanish and English. A statement on the website of Jetten’s party, D66, says the surrogacy is not commercial and that Lisa and the donor, who are both Dutch, are acquaintances of Jetten and Keenan.

“I grew up in a warm and loving environment and now have a fantastic family of my own,” Lisa said in the statement. “With the unconditional support of our loved ones, surrogacy feels like a very special way to contribute to making our dear friends’ dream come true.”

World.title: England’s Dutch coach Sarina Wiegman extends contract until 2029
World.content:
Dutch football coach Sarina Wiegman has extended her contract with the England women’s team by two years, taking her up to the 2029 European Championships.

Wiegman, 56, led the team to two European titles in 2022 and 2025, as well as their first World Cup final in 2023, when they lost to Spain.

Prior to that she won the European Championships with the Dutch national team in 2017 and reached the World Cup final two years later, losing 2-0 to the United States.

“I am so happy to be able to carry on with this squad and cannot think of a better job in football,” she said in a statement released by the English Football Association (FA).

“Working for a world-class organisation like the FA, and alongside so many people dedicated to winning England teams and the growth of our game, excites me every day.”

FA chief executive Mark Bullingham described Wiegman as “an incredible coach with an unparalleled record in major tournaments”. He added: “There is no one better to lead the Lionesses into the next two tournaments.”

Commentators had widely expected the Dutchwoman to leave her post after next year’s World Cup, after England failed to qualify automatically for the tournament.

A 4-0 loss to Spain in June, the team’s heaviest defeat since Wiegman took charge, means they will have to come through a play-off tournament with Greece, Ukraine and Slovakia to reach the finals in Brazil.

Wiegman said: “Anyone who knows me will understand that my main concern right now is absolutely the World Cup, and helping this squad realise their potential in the years to come.

“We have an important job to do to confirm our place in Brazil, and hopefully we can do that and give the country another special summer to remember next year.”

World.title: Border police won’t publish Schiphol e-gate investigation
World.content:
Hundreds of people missed their flights and thousands more faced long delays at Schiphol on Sunday after all 78 of the airport’s automatic passport gates went down at around 6am.

The Royal Marechaussee, the military police force responsible for border checks, said the outage was caused by an IT malfunction and that there was “no indication whatsoever” of a cyberattack.

The exact cause is still being investigated, but the results will not be made public, Marechaussee head of press, Major Mike Hofman, told Dutch News.

“For operational reasons, we do not comment regarding the further configuration, operation and technical details of our systems,” he said.

With the e-gates down, everyone flying to or from a country outside the Schengen area had to be checked manually by hand, including passengers in transit. The Marechaussee opened every desk and carried out less thorough checks to keep the queues moving.

Passengers waited an hour on average, and some waited up to an hour and a half, Schiphol officials said. The gates were working again by around 3pm.

KLM held departures where possible, and Transavia said it would be flexible with rebookings. A claims specialist told the Telegraaf the number of people affected in some way could run into the tens of thousands.

Few are likely to receive compensation, experts told the paper, because the outage will probably count as force majeure since the e-gates are run by the Marechaussee, not the airlines. The Marechaussee said travellers who missed their flights should contact their airline.

The outage happened during one of the busiest weekends of the autumn, as the one-week October school holiday began in the middle and south of the country and ended in the north. The Amsterdam marathon on Sunday also attracted thousands of runners to the city from all over the world.

World.title: Police investigate Grolsch beer tasting contamination
World.content:
Eleven people fell ill on Saturday afternoon after tasting water during a tour of the Grolsch brewery in Enschede. The water may have been contaminated with caustic soda, according to local broadcaster RTV Oost.

The group of nine visitors and two guides had been given shot glasses of the spring water used to brew the beer, a tasting that has been part of the tour for years.

One of the victims told RTV Oost that several people noticed a strange, sour taste and a burning feeling in their stomach after drinking it. Members of the group became nauseous and vomited, and the broadcaster said they may have suffered internal burns to the throat, oesophagus and stomach.

Several ambulances went to the brewery, and a German trauma team was called out but turned out not to be needed. All 11 were out of hospital on Sunday, and one spent the night in hospital, Grolsch told public broadcaster NOS.

Police have started a forensic investigation, and the labour inspectorate is also investigating. A police spokesperson told NOS it could have been an accident, “or something else could be going on”.

Grolsch said the tap the group drank from is separate from the rest of the production process, and that the quality and safety of its beer “are not and have not been at risk”. The company said it would not comment on possible causes while the investigation is ongoing.

World.title: Feyenoord stretch lead ahead of Eredivisie top clash against PSV
World.content:
Feyenoord have opened up a three-point lead at the top of the Eredivisie ahead of next weekend’s clash with PSV, following the defending champions’ shock defeat at ADO Den Haag.

The Rotterdammers were made to work for their points in a seven-goal thriller at Telstar.

They took the lead after just 25 seconds when Gaoussou Diarra finished off a sweeping move and were 3-1 up after 32 minutes when Sem Steijn profited from good combination work by Gjivai Zechiël and Givairo Read.

Patrick Brouwer reduced the deficit five minutes later, but a second-half penalty by Steijn proved to be enough despite Noach Shenkman scoring a third for Telstar on 69 minutes.

Peter Bosz refused to blame the last-minute defeat at ADO on his injury crisis as he looks ahead to a testing week, with a trip to Porto in the Champions League on Tuesday followed by the visit of Feyenoord on Sunday.

PSV looked to be on course for a routine win when Sven Mijnans put them ahead in the 21st minute. But the midfielder’s dismissal just before half-time triggered a second-half collapse that culminated in Matej Sin’s headed winner for ADO in the 93rd minute.

Mijnans, who played as a makeshift striker, will be suspended for the game against Feyenoord, while Guus Til also went off after complaining of blurred vision after landing hard on his neck in the first half and is doubtful for the next week.

But Bosz said he did not fear his team was sliding into a “tricky situation” in the absence of other senior players such as Jerdy Schouten, Ricardo Pepi and new signing Sami Ouaissa.

“This is another chance to win a game,” he said. “Stick our chests out and not think in fear.”

AZ drop points

AZ Alkmaar also dropped points against a newly promoted club as they could only draw 2-2 with Cambuur Leeuwarden even after the Friesland club lost Devid Bouah to a second yellow card early in the second half.

Twente Enschede missed the chance to leap into second place as Spanish striker Ángel Alarcón scored two superb goals for Utrecht to lift Anthony Correia’s team to 11th place.

Julian Brandt and Jorthy Mokio both scored twice as Ajax won 5-2 in Groningen in a match that saw both goalkeepers save penalties.

A double by Anthony Descotte looked to have earned Fortuna Sittard the points at NEC until Willum Thór Willumsson popped up with an injury-time header to snatch a draw for the struggling Nijmegen club.

World.title: Major infrastructure projects shelved to clear €18bn for repairs
World.content:
The government is shelving dozens of new road, rail and waterway projects so it can spend €18 billion on overdue and essential maintenance over the next 15 years.

Plans to extend the RandstadRail metro link between Rotterdam and The Hague, upgrade the A28 between Amersfoort and Hoogeveen and make the island of Ameland more accessible are among the 29 projects being put on hold.

Infrastructure minister Vincent Karremans, announcing the list on Friday, said the government was having to make “painful choices” in order to catch up on the backlog of repairs built up under successive governments.

Many of the Netherlands’ roads, bridges and viaducts were built between the 1950s and 1970s, but the two main maintenance programmes have been structurally underfunded for years.

Karremans told parliament he was “reprioritising” the list of planned new projects “that we have been dreaming of for years because we need to carry out essential maintenance and modernisation”.

Last year the Mobiliteitsfonds and the Deltafonds faced a shortfall of €80 billion for the period up to 2040, though this figure has been trimmed to €65 billion in the light of investments announced in the coalition agreement and next year’s budget.

Roads, railways and canals

The highways and waterways agency warned last year that an extra €34.5 billion was needed to repair tunnels, locks and bridges, while railtrack operator ProRail says it needs another €20 billion between now and 2038.

Last week the Court of Audit said another €9.5 billion needed to be spent to make motorways and railways strong enough to transport military supplies during a war.

Karremans’ redistribution will allow maintenance to be undertaken on critical infrastructure such as the pumping station at IJmuiden, which needs a €2.3 billion upgrade. The current pump, which drains an area where four million people live, was built in 1975, while the sluice dates from 1940.

Another €2.4 billion has been ringfenced for completing essential projects such as the Zuidasdok, a tunnel and motorway intersection in Amsterdam’s business district, and improving a 47km stretch of the A27 between Houten and Hooipolder.

High-speed line

On the railways, the government says €2 billion is needed for the high-speed line between Schiphol and Rotterdam, where speed limits have been imposed because 10 viaducts are in need of repair, while another €1.9 billion will be spent on introducing the European Rail Traffic Management System.

Another €635 million has been earmarked to improve connections in the so-called “Brainport” region around Eindhoven by building two platforms at Eindhoven Centraal station, a neighbouring bus station and widening roads around the city’s airport, where chip machine maker ASML is extending its campus.

Karremans has also set up a special task force known as ADIEU to bring regulations down to the “bare minimum”, which he believes can save €2 billion.

But the decision to suspend dozens of projects has come as a blow, particularly in rural areas that depend on road and rail connections.

Lelylijn funding

Ameland council said dredging the channel between the island and Holwert cost the government €3 million a year and a new route was essential to enable islanders to reach the mainland for services such as hospital care.

Nearly all projects in the northern provinces of Groningen, Friesland and Drenthe have been put on hold, although the Nedersaksenlijn, a rail route between Groningen and Enschede, is going ahead at the cost of €2 billion.

There are also fresh doubts about the viability of the Lelylijn, the long-cherished high-speed rail link between Groningen and Amsterdam.

Junior infrastructure minister Annet Bertram said on Friday that the line “forms an opportunity to connect the northern part of the country better with other areas and possibly with Germany”.

But she also admitted that the cabinet could not commit to the €15 billion annual investment for the project and other funding sources would have to be identified.

World.title: Poland breaks up international criminal group accused of laundering €77 million
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland says it has broken up an international criminal group responsible for laundering an estimated 337 million zloty (€77 million) by using currency exchange offices to illegally process money obtained from internet scams. Nine suspects – eight Ukrainians and one Belarusian – have been detained in a series of raids, which also resulted in the seizure of gold and cash worth over 1 million zloty. Służby rozbiły międzynarodową grupę zajmującą się praniem pieniędzy z oszustw inwestycyjnych i kryptowalut. Zatrzymano 9 osób, a skala transakcji przekroczyła 337 mln zł. Zabezpieczono złoto i gotówkę wartą ponad 1 mln zł. @Straz_Graniczna @PolicjaCBZC @ABW_GOV_PL pic.twitter.com/g2NQoqaPvP — Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) October 19, 2026 The accused – four women and five men aged between 26 and 53 – were arrested in Łódź, Warsaw and Małopolska province, announced Krzysztof Kopania, spokesman for the Łódź regional prosecutor’s office, which is leading the investigation. The detainees are four female cashiers, three men running the exchange offices, and two couriers used to transport money. All have been charged with participating in an organised criminal group and money laundering. They could face up to 15 years in prison if convicted. Prosecutors say that the gang, which operated in the cities of Warsaw, Lublin, Wrocław, Katowice and Gdańsk, collected money that had been obtained through internet fraud and transported it to cryptocurrency exchanges. It was then processed without complying with anti-money laundering procedures. Proceeds were then transferred to bank accounts, sent abroad by car, or concealed in fictitious purchases of gold. Most money was ultimately invested in cryptocurrencies. “The scale of the operation was enormous,” said Kopania. “It is estimated that between February 2025 and July 2026, members of the group took steps to conceal the origins of approximately 337 million zloty.” The ringleader was a 34-year-old Ukrainian national who made the key decisions and oversaw the domestic and international channelling of funds obtained from illegal sources, according to the Internal Security Agency (ABW) and border guard, which were also involved in the operation. Seven of the accused have been placed in pre-trial detention for three (or in one case two) months, while two have been bailed and ordered not to leave Poland. World.title: Lithuania says Ukrainian drone that struck car entered its airspace from Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. This article has been updated to include a statement from Poland’s defence ministry issued on Monday afternoon. Lithuania says there is “no doubt” that a Ukrainian drone which exploded on its territory on Sunday, hitting a moving car, entered its airspace from Poland. However, Poland has so far said that there is no confirmation of an object crossing the border. Meanwhile, Ukraine has apologised for the incident, saying that Russian electronic warfare had diverted the drone’s path during an operation against military targets in Russia. Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and EU. This morning, NATO fighter jets stationed at Šiauliai Air Base scrambled once again after an unidentified object entered Lithuanian airspace. What appears to be a drone exploded… — Gitanas Nausėda (@GitanasNauseda) October 18, 2026 On Sunday morning, Lithuania confirmed that a drone had entered its airspace and exploded, causing damage to a moving vehicle. NATO jets were scrambled in response to the incursion but were not able to visually identify the object. President Gitanas Nausėda said that the incident was further evidence that “Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and [the] EU”. Meanwhile, Lithuanian defence minister Robertas Kaunas revealed that preliminary information indicated the drone had entered from Polish airspace. “I have already contacted the Polish defence minister and asked Poland to join the investigation so that we can look into this incident together,” said Kaunas, quoted by broadcaster LRT. However, a spokesman for Poland’s defence ministry, Janusz Sejmej, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) on Sunday that “there is no confirmation [from our radar systems] of [an object] crossing the border from Poland to Lithuania”. Polsat, a leading Polish broadcaster, cited unnamed sources at Poland’s defence ministry saying that they believed the drone in fact took off from within Lithuanian territory, around 30 kilometres from the Polish border, and then flew deep into the country. In response, Deividas Matulionis, an advisor to the Lithuanian president, told the Baltic News Service (BNS) on Monday that “I can say very unequivocally we have credible evidence that the drone crossed the Polish border”. Later, the country’s prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, said that “there is no doubt that it entered…from the Polish side”. He also confirmed that the evidence indicates the drone “is of Ukrainian origin”. We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia. We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have… — Heorhii Tykhyi (@SpoxUkraineMFA) October 18, 2026 Those remarks followed a statement on Sunday afternoon from Heorhii Tykhyi, the spokesman for Ukraine’s foreign ministry, who appeared to confirm that the drone was Ukrainian. “We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia,” wrote Tykhyi. “We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have caused.” The spokesman said that Ukraine would “share all relevant information with our Lithuanian partners to establish the full circumstances of the incident”. However, he gave no further information on what type of drone was involved, where it was launched from, and what its target was. Lithuania borders Belarus, an ally of Russia, and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, as well as Poland and Latvia. In March and May this year, a number of Ukrainian drones aimed at targets in Russia entered the airspaces of NATO members Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia and Finland, likely due to Russian electronic jamming. On Monday afternoon, Poland’s defence ministry issued a statement “strongly refuting” media reports suggesting that sources within the ministry had identified the drone as having taken off within Lithuania itself. It added that the ministry, in cooperation with its Lithuanian partners, was still “conducting a detailed analysis” of what had taken place. Masked Israeli settlers attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, prompting European condemnation. The violence comes amid unprecedented settler pogroms during the olive harvest. pic.twitter.com/wsP6edL62y — Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) October 18, 2026 On Saturday, the delegation – which included members from France, Belgium and Poland as well as representatives of the Catholic church – visited the mostly Christian Palestinian village of Taybeh near Ramallah in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. Attacks on representatives of the diplomatic corps are absolutely unacceptable.” The spokesman said that Poland now “expects urgent and detailed explanations from the Israeli authorities” and for the perpetrators of the attack to be identified and held accountable. “We also expect effective measures to prevent similar incidents in the future.” ❗Potwierdzamy, że na Zachodnim Brzegu Jordanu doszło do ataku na konwój, w którym znajdowali się przedstawiciele korpusu dyplomatycznego, w tym polscy dyplomaci. Many more municipalities in Poland will be allowed to charge a daily fee for tourists and other overnight visitors after a change to the law dropping environmental requirements for levying such charges. Kraków, which received 8.7 million overnight tourists last year, had in particular been pushing for the change. However, Poland as a whole has seen a recent boom in visitor numbers, recording the EU’s second-fastest growth in the number of nights in tourist accommodation last year. #Krakow #opłataturystyczna #ustawa 🚨🔥Z OSTATNIEJ CHWILI! 🔥🚨 📢 Prezydent RP podpisał nowelizację przepisów dotyczących podatków i opłat lokalnych, PIT oraz PCC. 🏨 Najważniejsze zmiany dla branży turystycznej dotyczą opłaty miejscowej i uzdrowiskowej. 🗓️ Od 2027 r. za jej… pic.twitter.com/9ATvENvNol — Kraków (@krakow_pl) October 15, 2026 Until now, a “visitor’s fee” could be levied by municipalities with beneficial climatic features, “scenic qualities” and the capacity to accommodate people visiting to benefit from these attributes, as well as localities in areas with the status of a “spa protection area”. In practice, this largely applied to seaside and mountain resorts. Kraków did charge a visitor’s fee between 2004 and 2015, but was subsequently unable to do so due to a toughening of environmental requirements. The city has long suffered from bad air pollution, though it has taken significant steps to tackle the issue. Now, under new legislation proposed by the government earlier this year and signed into law by President Karol Nawrocki this week, the requirement for beneficial climatic features has been scrapped, meaning many more places will be able to charge the visitor’s fee. From 1 January, municipalities with scenic qualities will be able to charge visitors up to 5 zloty (€1.14) for each night they stay in hotels, guesthouses and short-term rental accommodation for up to one month, a rise on the current maximum of 3.46 zloty. Additionally, whereas previously only people visiting for the purposes of tourism had to pay, the fee now applies to all visits, including for work or health purposes, reports broadcaster TVN. People with significant disabilities, children with certified disabilities and their carers will be exempt from the fee. In another change, fees will be collected directly by accommodation providers, who will be required to maintain detailed records, reports the Infor news service. Passing fees on in a timely manner will entitle providers to receive at least 10% of the money they collect. Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026 In 2024, Kraków appealed to the government to be allowed to charge tourists a fee, noting that “overtourism leads to tensions and social discontent”, as the “local community suffers” and “residents increasingly feel like tourists in their own city”. With its UNESCO-listed Old Town, Wawel royal castle, and former Jewish district of Kazimierz, Kraków is regularly named as one of Europe’s best tourist destinations. Last year, a record 16.25 million people visited the city, of whom 8.7 million stayed overnight. While that is a boon to the local economy, it also often causes tensions with residents, who complain about noise and disruption. In 2024, the city created the new position of “night mayor”, whose role is to reconcile the needs of tourists, businesses and residents. Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals of the type offered through services such as Airbnb. Such accommodation has boomed in recent years, often prompting a backlash from local residents https://t.co/8MRfRWTDxd — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 3, 2026 Following this week’s change to the law, Kraków city hall confirmed that it would now again be able to collect a visitor’s fee “if the statutory conditions are satisfied and the municipal council adopts an appropriate resolution”. The city’s recently elected new mayor, Łukasz Gibała, who will be sworn in next week, said before Sunday’s election that he was in favour of a tourist tax of at least 20 zloty per night, four times the new maximum. “In western European cities there are rates of that size and higher,” Gibała said, quoted by financial news service Money.pl. “Maintaining the city in the face of the influx of tourists is costly. In Kraków, private business owners profit from tourism, whilst the city and its residents foot the bill.” Poland as a whole has also experienced a boom in tourism. Last year, the country recorded the European Union’s second-largest growth in the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation. Its increase of 7% was behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta (9.9%). World.title: Poland drops proposal to criminalise providing help to illegal migrants following outcry
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland’s interior ministry has withdrawn a proposal to make it a criminal offence, punishable by up to three years in prison, to provide support to migrants who are in the country illegally. The idea had prompted criticism from human rights groups and even opposition from within the government. The interior ministry said the amendment had been intended to clamp down on migrant smuggling. But activists feared it would criminalise humanitarian aid, such as that provided to migrants who have irregularly crossed the border from Belarus. Za udzielenie bezinteresownej pomocy migrantom nie będzie groziła kara do trzech lat więzienia. Po burzy, którą wywołała publikacja „Rzeczpospolitej” i po sprzeciwie resortu rodziny, MSWiA wycofuje się z pomysłu „karania za podanie posiłku”.https://t.co/Q0N52IMRVn — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) October 15, 2026 Under current Polish law, anyone who facilitates the illegal stay of a person in Poland in exchange for financial or personal benefit can be jailed for up to five years. However, this week, the interior ministry proposed an amendment that would also have penalised anyone who knowingly “enabled or facilitated” the illegal stay of someone in Poland, even if not for financial or personal benefit. The offence would have been punishable by up to three years in prison. “Currently, this behaviour is not criminalised, creating a loophole for those who exploit such situations and, under the pretext of helping migrants, aid them in their illegal stay, thus serving as a springboard for further illegal migration,” wrote deputy interior minister Czesław Mroczek, quoted by the Rzeczpospolita daily. That immediately prompted concern that the law could be used against volunteers and residents of border areas who provide aid – such as food, water, medical treatment, clothing or shelter – to migrants who have crossed illegally from Belarus. Since 2021, tens of thousands of people, mainly from Asia and Africa, have tried to cross that border with the encouragement and support of the Belarusian authorities. They have sometimes used violence against Polish border officers. Poland and the EU accuse Belarus of “weaponising” migration as part of the “hybrid warfare” being waged by Russia and its allies against European countries. They have implemented tough border protection measures to prevent crossings and facilitate “pushbacks” of those who cross. However, many human rights and aid organisations argue that the migrants – over 100 of whom have died around the border since 2021 – are often victims of this process and need humanitarian support. Two dead bodies found in the river on Poland's border with Belarus likely belong to migrants from a group seen being pushed into the water by Belarusian officers as part of efforts to encourage irregular crossings into the EU, says a Polish minister https://t.co/xsnPd6FeO3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 16, 2025 In response to the interior ministry’s proposal, 61 organisations, including Amnesty International, the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights and the Auschwitz-Birkenau Foundation, signed a joint statement condemning the plans, which they said “violate international standards binding Poland”. The organisations warned that the proposed wording could expose medical staff treating migrants, lawyers providing legal assistance, facilities working with children, and organisations supporting victims of human trafficking to criminal liability. “This measure is not aimed at smugglers, but rather at activists or residents of border areas who provide humanitarian aid to foreign nationals who have crossed the border illegally and are present in Poland,” attorney Radosław Baszuk told the Rzeczpospolita daily. Baszuk previously represented five Polish activists who were prosecuted for providing food, clothing and shelter to a group of Middle Eastern migrants who had entered Poland from Belarus in 2022. A group of five activists have been found not guilty of enabling the illegal presence in Poland of Middle Eastern migrants whom they provided aid to after they had irregularly crossed the border from Belarus. Prosecutors had been seeking prison sentences https://t.co/RpfhVWL4hY — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 8, 2025 They were acquitted last year, with the ruling made final in March this year after an appeal. But Baszuk told Rzeczpospolita that, under the interior ministry’s proposed amendment to the relevant law, his clients could been convicted. On Wednesday, Poland’s commissioner for human rights, Sylwia Gregorczyk-Abram, also wrote to the justice ministry to “express concern” that the proposed changes “could lead to criminal liability for charitable or humanitarian activities undertaken towards individuals whose residence status has not yet been regulated”. Even a member of the government, the minister for family, labour and social policy, Agnieszka Dziemianowicz-Bąk, expressed her “firm opposition” to the plans on social media. She is from The Left (Lewica), one of the junior partners in Poland’s ruling coalition. ‼️ Ciepły posiłek, nocleg, potrzebne leki – za to wolontariusz ma trafić do więzienia nawet na 3 lata? 😡 Nie ma zgody Lewicy na kryminalizowanie pomocy humanitarnej! Ministra Agnieszka Dziemianowicz-Bąk zwróciła się do ministra Waldemara Żurka ze stanowczym sprzeciwem wobec… pic.twitter.com/QskUfJmgsu — Lewica (@__Lewica) October 14, 2026 In response to the growing criticism, the interior ministry announced on Friday that it was withdrawing the proposal, saying it decided to do so “to eliminate any doubts and prevent the misinterpretation of regulations”. “From the beginning, the ministry’s sole objective has been to tighten the system and target the organisers of this practice [of migrant smuggling],” said the ministry, quoted by Rzeczpospolita. “Legal provisions must effectively protect the state’s borders against organised crime, while simultaneously fully safeguarding humanitarian values ​and life-saving activities.” The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 Both the former Polish government and the current one, which took power in December 2023, have regularly faced criticism from human rights groups over their response to the migration crisis on the Belarus border. Earlier this year, the previous human rights commissioner, Marcin Wiącek, expressed concern over a ban on asylum claims introduced by the government in March 2025. He noted that the measures had been described as a temporary solution, but have remained in place ever since. The government, however, argues that its measures have been effective in preventing the illegal trafficking of migrants. Its data show that attempted border crossings from Belarus fell from around 15,500 in the first half of last year to less than 250 in the same period this year – a drop of over 98%. It also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally. World.title: Heads of Polish and Ukrainian national remembrance institutes hold first meeting since 2018
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Senior delegations from Poland and Ukraine’s state institutes of national remembrance have held talks in the Ukrainian city of Lviv, marking the first time the heads of the two organisations have met in eight years. The meeting, at which the two sides discussed issues including exhumations of World War Two victims and possible joint research projects, comes as Poland and Ukraine seek reconciliation over historical issues that have regularly caused tensions between two otherwise close allies. 📢 14 października 2026 r. we Lwowie delegacja Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej spotkała się z przedstawicielami ukraińskiego Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej. Było to pierwsze bezpośrednie, robocze spotkanie szefów tych instytucji od 2018 r. ➡️ Stronie polskiej przewodniczył kierujący… pic.twitter.com/qHpZwLeCEa — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) October 14, 2026 News of the meeting was announced on social media by Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), which noted that it was “the first direct, working meeting between the heads of these institutions since 2018”. The IPN is currently headed by its deputy president, Karol Polejowski, because Poland’s parliament has been unable to agree on a permanent new president. The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINR) is led by Oleksandr Alfyorov. “The first topic of discussion,” according to the IPN, was the planned reburial of 115 Polish soldiers recently exhumed in Lviv, where they died in 1939 defending the city (then part of Poland and known as Lwów) during the Nazi-German and Soviet invasions. Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of 115 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending Lviv – now in Ukraine but then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of WWII https://t.co/yQNeq2D54E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026 Their exhumation resulted from a diplomatic breakthrough last year between Warsaw and Kyiv that saw Ukraine lift a moratorium on exhumations that had been in place since 2017 in protest at the dismantling in Poland of a monument to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). Ukraine has also allowed the exhumation on its territory of Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres, which were led by the UPA. Poland likewise recently granted permission for Ukraine to search for Ukrainian victims of a massacre led by the Polish Home Army in the village of Łasków (Laskiv in Ukrainian). At this week’s meeting, the UINR gave an update on its work in Łasków, where it has uncovered the remains of 30 people. The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance has found 30 human remains in a village in Poland where Polish partisans killed Ukrainian civilians in WW2 It thanked Poland for permission to search the site, calling it a step towards "true reconciliation" https://t.co/BeeEtl6gCa — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026 The IPN and UINR also discussed planned exhumation work in the now-depopulated village of Huta Pieniacka (Huta Peniatska in Ukrainian), where the local Polish population was massacred in 1944 by a Nazi SS regiment mainly made up of Ukrainians. There was also “willingness on both sides to restore cooperation in the field of historical scientific research”, said the IPN. “The possibility of undertaking joint educational initiatives was also discussed.” The two sides also agreed to hold another meeting in Warsaw, though no date has been set. This week’s meeting comes after a period of tension over historical issues between not only Poland and Ukraine more broadly, but also the two countries’ remembrance institutes. In February this year, the IPN criticised Alfyorov over an interview in which he initially called the Volhynia massacres “one of Poland’s state myths”, before later appearing to correct himself and saying it was “not a myth, but one of the key elements of the Polish grand narrative”. By contrast, “for most Ukrainians, this is just a local episode of history”, added Alfyorov. Referring to Poland’s recognition of the massacres as a genocide – a term Ukraine rejects – he asked if Polish massacres of around 28,000 Ukrainians during the war should also be called a genocide. In response, the IPN called Alfyorov’s remarks “outrageous” and declared that the Volhynia massacres were “not an ‘episode’, but rather one of the largest genocides against civilians in 20th-century Europe”. It also condemned Ukraine for honouring figures associated with the massacres. The UINR, for its part, criticised a law proposed by Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki (a former head of the IPN), that would criminalise the promotion of ideologies associated with World War Two Ukrainian nationalist groups. Ukraine has criticised a law proposed by Poland's president that would criminalise promotion of historical Ukrainian nationalist ideologies, equating them with Nazism and communism It warns of "retaliatory measures" if the bill is passed https://t.co/TaX2Vj5z8v — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2025 In another sign of reconciliation, in May the UINR and Poland’s Mieroszewski Centre held a historical congress in Warsaw, bringing together more than 100 historians “to discuss complex issues of the shared past and explore common approaches to their interpretation”, in the words of the Ukrainian foreign ministry. However, that same month, President Volodymyr Zelensky prompted a diplomatic crisis by approving the naming of a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. Since then, both sides have made efforts to reach a diplomatic solution, including a pledge by Zelensky to “grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. World.title: Ukraine finds remains of 30 people in search for victims of massacre by Polish WWII partisans
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
