World.title: Why Your Ancestor’s “Austrian” or “Italian” Passport Doesn’t Mean You Aren’t Legally Croatian
World.content:
October the 19th, 2026 – Croatia hasn’t always been the Croatia we know. You may have ancestors that are listed as being Austrian, Italian or Hungarian, but you might still be legally Croatian.

If you’ve curiously started digging into your family’s emigration history, you have likely unearthed a treasure trove of century-old documents: ship passenger manifests, American or Canadian naturalisation petitions, and faded, yellowed draft cards. However, for a massive segment of the Croatian diaspora, specifically those whose families left Europe during the peak migration waves between the late 1800s and the 1920s, these documents often bring a frustrating surprise.

Under the column labelled “Country of Origin” or “Nationality,” your ancestor’s record might not say “Croatia” at all. Instead, it might explicitly state “Austria,” “Hungary,” “Yugoslavia,” or even “Italy”. For many diaspora members, this feels like an immediate dead end. The common assumption by the mere mortal is as follows: If my great-grandfather left Europe as a citizen of the Austro-Hungarian Empire or the Kingdom of Italy, I must not qualify for Croatian citizenship by descent. Despite this being a common assumption, it’s fortunately totally incorrect. In the eyes of modern citizenship law, an imperial passport from 1910 doesn’t erase your legal right to a modern Croatian passport today. However, proving your lineage across a century of shifting borders requires navigating a complex historical and bureaucratic maze.

roots don’t recognise changing borders, but the ministry of the interior does

To understand why your ancestor’s old paperwork says “Austria” or “Italy,” you have to look at the tumultuous geopolitical history of not only Croatia but the wider region. Before the modern Republic of Croatia declared independence on October the 8th, 1991, the territory was repeatedly carved up, absorbed, and governed by various empires and federations, with a lot of bloodshed in between.

First we need to go all the way back to pre-1918 when Croatia was part of the once mighty Austro-Hungarian Empire. Emigrants from Zagreb, Slavonia, Dalmatia and even the furthest-flung islands all travelled on Austrian or Hungarian documentation. Then came the interwar period & WWII. Following the Treaty of Rapallo in 1920, sections of Istria, Rijeka, Zadar, and several Dalmatian islands (including Cres and Lošinj) were annexed by what was then the Kingdom of Italy. People from these regions suddenly became legal Italian citizens, changed their names to Italian variants, and emigrated under the documentation bearing the Italian flag. Then, from 1945 to 1991, Croatia and the countries of the region became part of the various iterations of Yugoslavia.

You can see how Croatian citizenship applications can often become very confusing territory, but the authorities are fully aware of Croatia’s blurry past and as such even blurrier documentation. When the Croatian Ministry of the Interior evaluates an application for citizenship by descent, they don’t care what a clerk at Ellis Island wrote down way back in 1912. They care about geographic reality that corresponds to modern-day Croatia and historical municipal tracking.

Under the current Croatian Citizenship Act, the key question is whether the specific town or village your ancestor emigrated from sits within the modern, legally recognised borders of Croatia as it is today. If your great-grandfather was born somewhere near Split back in 1905, he was technically born under Austro-Hungarian rule, but because Split is indisputably Croatian territory today, the bloodline connection remains legally valid, long after Austria-Hungary’s demise.

here’s where diy croatian citizenship applications often come to grief…

While the law very much allows for these problematic and complex geographical and historical shifts, the burden of proof rests entirely on the applicant. This is where DIY applications frequently fall apart, stall, and end up shoved to gather dust on a shelf somewhere. If you submit an application to a Croatian consulate with an American death certificate stating your grandfather was born in “Austria,” alongside a modern birth record request, the reviewing officers require a meticulous paper trail that bridges the historical gap. You must prove two things simultaneously in such cases.

The first is what’s known as the registry match. Initially, you need to locate the original historical birth or baptismal record in the local municipal registry or church archive within Croatia, confirming they were registered on that specific territory once upon a time. After you’ve cleared that hurdle, you need to deal witu name and identity reconciliation. What this means is that you need to prove that the “Giovanni” or “Giuseppe” listed on an Italian emigration record from Istria is legally the exact same person as the “Ivan” or “Josip” recorded in the local village archives. You can imagine how difficult this is without administrative help.

If your family came from an area like Istria or Zadar that switched between Italian and Slavic administration, records may be split between different archives, written in different languages (Latin, Italian, or old Croatian scripts), or filed under completely altered surnames.

solving the runaway border problem

Navigating various international treaties, century-old municipal border adjustments, and dual-language archives is a daunting task for anyone working from North America, South America, or Australia. It requires a level of historical expertise and local administrative access that standard translation services or internet databases simply cannot provide. This is where the specialised, ground-level infrastructure put in place by services like Croatian By Descent becomes an invaluable asset for the busy American diaspora.

Instead of letting your application get derailed and shoved to the back of a massive pile by a confusing historical paper trail, their team functions as both legal researchers and archival detectives. They know exactly how to trace your mysterious, multi-national ancestors through the shifting territorial registries, cross-referencing old land records and municipal books to establish an airtight geographic proof for the Ministry of the Interior. They dismantle Croatia’s age-old runaway border problem by making sure your ancestral files are organised, properly reconciled, and professionally translated, transforming deeply confusing geopolitical hurdle into a successful, legally sound submission package.

Skip the administrative confusion and verify your historical eligibility with the expert team at Croatian By Descent, who can make sure changing borders and complicated political histories don’t come between you and your EU passport. This service uses knowledgeable lawyer partners who can readily assist clients with obtaining their family’s records from Croatia, as well as dealing with them after the fact throughout the process.

World.title: Croatia Has Been Unable to Connect Istrian Railway for 150 Years
World.content:
October the 19th, 2026 – The Austro-Hungarians constructed the Istrian railway in just 3 years, but Croatia has been totally unable to connect it for 150!

Istria is the only Croatian region from which trains don’t actually run into the rest of Croatia. Although trains have been running across the peninsula for 150 years, a direct connection of the Istrian railways with the Croatian railway system is only now being planned. Dubravko Grakalic reports for Index that the Istrian railways are connected, primarily because of geography, to the neighbouring Slovenian ones – a project from the 19th century and the era of Austro-Hungarian rule. Back in 1867, when the line was opened to traffic, Emperor and King Franz Joseph I arrived in Pula by train via Slovenia. To this day, Istrian railway destinations are still reached in the same way.

From Zagreb to Pula by train, via Ljubljana, one travels only at weekends. The train departs on Friday and after a seven-hour journey arrives at Pula station. From Pula back to Zagreb it returns only on Sunday. Passengers are also offered transport by train to Lupoglav, then by bus to the Rijeka–Zagreb line. The paradox of the Istrian railways, which today mainly serve freight traffic and local travel to Buzet, has an interesting historical and political context.

austria-hungary’s railway construction

“The railway in Istria was built back in 1876, with the line from the direction of Divača in Slovenia to Pula 122 kilometres long and a branch line 21 kilometres long from Kanfanar to Rovinj, which until that time had been the strongest economic centre of Istria. Although the Istrian population had wanted a railway earlier, because of other interests in the centre of the state in Vienna, whose primary goal was the construction of the line to the main maritime port of the monarchy in Trieste, completed in 1857, the construction of the railway in Istria was of secondary importance,” Dr. Sc. Josip Kajinić, curator of the Croatian Railway Museum of HŽ Infrastruktura and one of the authors of the recent exhibition on the railway in Istria, told Index.

“Circumstances changed as a result of foreign-policy circumstances that led to the construction of the monarchy’s main naval base in Pula in 1853, alongside which a shipyard was also launched. In those new circumstances the monarchy needed a safe and good transport link for the delivery of raw materials and military equipment, and given the poor and sparse road network and the danger from the sea for maritime traffic that threatened from the Kingdom of Italy after its unification, the decision was finally taken to build a railway line in Istria.

The line to Pula was built because of the naval base and the shipyard, and its branch to Rovinj for economic reasons. Because of the already mentioned danger that threatened from the sea, the Istrian railway was built through the interior,” Dr. Kajinić notes. The Istrianer Staatsbahn, as the railway through Istria was called in Austria-Hungary, was built at state expense. The law on it was passed on 22 April 1873, while the 122-kilometre line was built in less than three years by the company Frolich from Graz. Work began in Pazin in December 1873, and some twenty thousand workers worked on it. The cost was lower than planned – 12,760,469 florins. The line was solemnly opened in August 1876, and regular traffic started the same year in September.

By way of comparison, HŽ Infrastruktura began in 2025 the reconstruction of fifty kilometres of the line from the state border to Sv. Petar u Šumi. The plan is for the reconstruction to be completed by the end of 2028. Austria-Hungary built thirteen railway stations, five bridges and the Hum tunnel on the Istrian line.

the development of the line

In 1878 a track was built on the Pula waterfront, from the station to the shipyard. A more interesting line was built in 1887, a twenty-kilometre stretch from the Slovenian Hrpelje via Kozina to Trieste, which shortened the journey between Pula and Trieste. It operated until 1959 and is now an arranged cycling route. A similar fate befell the route of the narrow-gauge railway Poreč–Trieste, known as the Parenzana, Porečanka or Istranka.

“The former 123-kilometre-long narrow-gauge Parenzana line connected Trieste and Poreč, and for a length of 78 kilometres it passed through Croatian areas of Istria. It was built in 1902 and was in use until 1935. Its route is very well preserved and is today used for tourist purposes,” Josip Kajinić adds. The cycling and walking path is called the “Path of Health and Friendship” because it connects three countries.

from the former yugoslavia to the modern day

After the collapse of the once mighty Austria-Hungary, the first extension of the Istrian railways was launched by the then Yugoslavia with the construction of the Lupoglav–Štalije line in 1951. With it the railway was brought to the port in Raša Bay. The Kanfanar–Rovinj line was suspended in 1966 because of the developed road traffic.

“Throughout history the railway in Istria was managed by several administrations – from the Austrian, the Italian, briefly the German during the occupation in the Second World War, and after it the Yugoslav Railways, and since 1991 it has been under the management of the Croatian Railways, today HŽ Infrastruktura d.o.o.,” curator Josip Kajinić says and adds: “Today on the railway line between the Croatian-Slovenian border and the terminal station in Pula there are eight stations and 16 stops. This line is special in that it is probably the most authentic on the entire railway network in the territory of Croatia, with the largest number of originally preserved station buildings and other track facilities.”

michael portillo spotlights a vodnjan station

The cult British travel writer Michael Portillo presented in 2025 in the BBC series “Great Continental Railway Journeys” the station in Vodnjan with its old-fashioned technology that is still in use today.

The story of the railways in Istria is also shown by the recent exhibition “Gremo na makinu!” at the Historical and Maritime Museum of Istria in Pula, as well as the steam locomotive of the FS 835 series located next to the station building in Pula, which is a protected cultural asset and part of the holdings of the Croatian Railway Museum. “With the exhibition we wanted to show how important the railway was for the development of Istria, not only in a transport and economic sense, but also in the everyday life of people. We sought, along with a historical overview of the construction and development of the lines, to present objects that tell us about the functioning of the railway and the people who worked on it. It is particularly interesting that part of the exhibited material is available to the public for the first time, and the former lines that, although they no longer exist today, played an important role in connecting Istria are also covered,” they say for Index at the Historical and Maritime Museum of Istria in Pula.

The government and Croatian Railways have also revived the plan to connect with the Istrian lines by a tunnel through Učka. Although the foundation stone for the construction of the tunnel under Ćićarija was laid as early as 1993 by the then Croatian president Dr. Franjo Tuđman, the state company HŽ Infrastruktura only in May 2026 signed a contract for the documentation and conceptual design of that tunnel. The project should be completed in two years and will cost around two million euros. When the Istrian railways will be directly connected with the rest of Croatia is still not remotely known.

World.title: New Interactive Earthquake Map Reveals Where Danger in Croatia is Greatest
World.content:
October the 19th, 2026 – A new interactive earthquake map reveals here the danger in Croatia is the greatest, with southern Croatia in particular in quite the precarious spot.

Croatian scientists have produced a new seismic hazard assessment for Croatia that incorporates the experiences of the Petrinja earthquake and data on the soil beneath our cities. Index/Nenad Jaric Dauenhauer reports that the danger is greatest along the Adriatic coast, especially down south in the wider Dubrovnik area. The results also reveal something a little less obvious: for low and rigid buildings, including family houses, the new assessment along the coast and far inland in the area of Petrinja gives higher seismic loads than those prescribed, while for high buildings, it mostly gives lower ones.

This new map could serve as a scientific basis for a new Croatian national annex to Eurocode 8, the European standard for earthquake-resistant construction. It describes how strongly the ground could shake, with a certain probability, but it does not announce the date of the next earthquake nor does it itself reveal which building will survive.

why does croatia need a new earthquake map?

The Zagreb earthquake of magnitude 5.5 that struck back in March 2020 and the Petrinja earthquake of magnitude 6.2 later that same year in December showed just how devastating the combination of strong shaking and vulnerable buildings can be. Dubrovnik was almost destroyed in 1667 by an earthquake of estimated magnitude around 7, and Zagreb was struck in 1880 by an earthquake of magnitude around 5.9.

“Destructive earthquakes here are not a footnote in history. That is precisely why probabilistic seismic hazard assessment is the right framework for design and spatial planning across Croatia,” explained Professor Snježana Markušić from the Geophysical Department of the Faculty of Science (PMF) in Zagreb, the first author of the paper. The current Croatian seismic hazard map, an integral part of the national annex to Eurocode 8 from back in 2011, is based on earlier research. In the meantime, scientists have collected new earthquake records and data on local soil conditions, and in 2024 the second generation of Eurocode 8 was also published.

The new assessment was prepared by Snježana Markušić, Iva Žilić, Tomislav Fiket and Anja Majurec from the Geophysical Department of PMF in Zagreb, Davor Stanko from the Faculty of Geotechnical Engineering in Varaždin, and Tvrtko Korbar from the Croatian Geological Survey. The paper was published on the 17th of September 2026 in the journal Bulletin of Earthquake Engineering (BEE).

earthquakes don’t care about borders

Seismic hazards in Croatian cities are also influenced by earthquakes outside of Croatia. For Dubrovnik, for example, the seismic areas located on the territories of both Montenegro and Albania are very important. That is why the processed area is considerably wider than Croatia. Foreshocks and aftershocks were removed from the earthquake catalogue, because the model describes the long-term frequency of mainshocks. “90,003 mainshocks remained, only 14.9 percent of all recorded events. Almost three quarters were aftershocks,” says Tomislav Fiket from PMF.

The authors divided the wider area of Croatia and neighbouring countries into 32 zones according to geological structure, seismic activity and faults, and performed the calculations in the open-source program OpenQuake. “Three large tectonic units – the Adriatic Foreland, the Dinarides and the Pannonian Basin – create very different conditions in the Earth’s crust, so faults across the country move in different ways. We incorporated that diversity into the model, for each zone separately,” explains Tvrtko Korbar from the Croatian Geological Survey.

Two similar houses, one on solid rock and the other on thick deposits of softer soil, will not shake equally during the same earthquake, because softer deposits can amplify the shaking. An important novelty of the paper is therefore the inclusion of soil data, instead of calculating only for solid rock. “A model that includes the actual surface of the terrain directly encompasses the amplification of shaking due to local soil, instead of it being subsequently estimated with a simplified factor,” says Davor Stanko from the Faculty of Geotechnical Engineering. How important local differences are is also shown by a study of Zagreb published in 2025, in which Markušić and Stanko participated. It turned out that in the central and south-eastern parts of the city thick, unconsolidated deposits can amplify seismic waves.

dubrovnik and central dalmatia are areas of concern

The overall seismic hazard is by far the greatest along the coastline, especially down in the Dubrovnik-Neretva area and a little further north in central Dalmatia. Scientists express this danger by the maximum ground acceleration during shaking, in units of g. One g is equal to the acceleration of gravity (9.81 m/s²), so a value of 0.40 g means that the maximum horizontal ground acceleration during shaking reaches 40 percent of that amount. The greater the acceleration, the greater the loads buildings are generally exposed to, but their response also depends on the properties of the structure.

With actual soil conditions taken into consideration, the new assessment gives around 0.40 g across Dubrovnik, 0.32 g in Split, 0.27 g in Rijeka, 0.24 g in Zagreb, 0.22 g in Petrinja and 0.08 g in Osijek. This means that in each of those cities there is about a 10 percent probability that the peak ground acceleration in the next 50 years will exceed the stated value. This is not the strongest possible shaking, nor is it the magnitude of the earthquake: magnitude describes the energy released at the earthquake focus, while ground acceleration describes how strongly the ground shakes at a particular place. “The areas of Sisak, Moslavina and Petrinja, despite the strong earthquake sequence of 2020, according to our results belongs to the group of moderate hazard,” says Markušić. Nevertheless, even weaker shaking can cause great damage if buildings are poorly constructed.

earthquakes have no schedule

The information that a certain level of shaking has a return period of 475 years is easily misleading. It does not mean that such shaking comes once every 475 years and that after it follows centuries of calm. It’s a statistical description: the annual probability of exceedance is about 0.2 percent, which over 50 years, the usual lifespan of a building, accumulates to about 10 percent. The model assumes that earthquakes have no “memory”, as with rolling a die: the previous result does not determine the next one. For critical infrastructure a rarer, stronger shaking is also important, with a return period of 2,475 years and about a 2 percent probability of exceedance in 50 years.

what a single house does and what a building does during an earthquake are very different…

Every building has a natural period of oscillation, the time of one full swing, and it amounts to about a tenth of a second per storey: a family house oscillates with a period of about 0.1 to 0.2 seconds, and a building of about ten storeys with a period of about one second. A building sways most strongly when oscillations of a period similar to its own predominate in the ground motion, similar to a swing that we push at the right moment. According to the new assessment, that shaking is strongest in all the observed cities for a period of 0.2 seconds, i.e. precisely for low buildings.

That’s why low and rigid buildings on the coast and in Petrinja could be exposed to higher seismic loads than those provided for by the current design spectrum. For high and flexible buildings, which sway more slowly, the new assessment almost everywhere gives lower loads than those prescribed. The comparison is nevertheless not entirely equal because the current spectrum refers to solid rock, while the new assessment also includes local soil.

“The results indicate that a map prepared for a uniform reference rock, when local soil is taken into account, can in some places underestimate and in others overestimate the hazard. There is no single correction factor applicable throughout the country,” Markušić explains.

“For the faults responsible for the strongest earthquakes in Croatia, such as the Petrinja and Pokupsko faults, there are still not enough complete data for them to be reliably modelled separately. Their inclusion is a priority for the next generation of models,” explained Korbar. “Croatia’s database of strong earthquake records is still relatively small. Its expansion, together with the preparation of a more detailed national soil database, is one of the key next steps,” adds Žilić.

will the new map force construction rule changes?

The new research represents a scientific study of probabilistic seismic hazard assessment, not a national annex to the standard, and does not prescribe legally binding design values. “We offer a scientific basis on which the competent authorities can rely when they start preparing the new annex that Croatia must adopt for the second generation of Eurocode 8,” Markušić emphasises. The new Croatian earthquake danger map will therefore not change the regulations overnight. It gives the competent authorities a new basis for decisions, and citizens a clearer picture of the hazard. The safety of an individual building still needs to be assessed according to its structure, condition and the soil on which it stands. The greatest value of the new map will be that better knowledge about earthquakes is turned into safer construction.

World.title: 40% of Croatian Retirees are in Poverty, Soup Kitchen Use Increases
World.content:
October the 19th, 2026 – An appalling 40% of Croatian retirees are now living in poverty according to the latest data, with soup kitchen use increasing in a country that keeps pushing the inflationary limits.

According to the latest data from the Croatian Bureau of Statistics, almost every fifth citizen of Croatia lives on the absolute brink of poverty. Index reports that for Croatian retirees, the figures are even more disgraceful, as almost 40% of them actually do live in poverty. What a staggering paradox it is when a country so full of highly expensive resorts and throngs of tourists is also dealing with growing queues in front of soup kitchens.

After decades of work, many people still do not have enough to live a dignified life. “In general, I think that the majority of pensioners don’t live with dignity. I consider a dignified life to be when a person who has worked for 40 years can in retirement live normally, afford to go to the theatre or cinema, and afford the majority of ordinary things,” stated Višnja Stanišić, president of the Croatian Pensioners’ Trade Union.

When a large part of the pension goes on utility bills, many have no choice but to seek help. In the soup kitchens they are greeted every day by volunteers. “Some come who don’t even have boxes to pack the food into, they come literally with ordinary plastic bags and pack the food into them. Quite a lot of poor people come,” volunteer Lovro Maričić revealed.

The situation is also worsened by Croatia’s constantly rising prices. Inflation in September amounted to a deeply concerning 4.7%, which is the second consecutive month of growth. The biggest cause is energy prices, which have risen by approximately 20%. Such growth hits those with the lowest incomes the hardest.

“Every single pensioner has their own personal inflation to try to deal with because they spend on five to six products whose prices have risen considerably more than the official rate, for some by as much as 10%,” Stanišić explained.

“We’ve proposed an amendment with which we’ll cover more than 30,000 pensioners living within the City of Zagreb. We intend to raise the threshold for financial assistance from a pension of 350 to 500 euros,” said Matej Mišić, president of the SDP of the City of Zagreb. While politicians announce more measures, in the soup kitchens the situation is getting harder and harder. “It could be said that the number of users is even higher than last year. Today was quite busy and a lot of people came,” volunteer Lovro Maričić concluded.

World.title: Former Mayor Claims Split Has Been “Disgraced” Worldwide
World.content:
October the 19th, 2026 – Former Split mayor Ivica Puljak has claimed that Split has been “disgraced” worldwide after the violent clash between Torcida and Ajax.

Former Split mayor Ivica Puljak commented on Torcida’s procession ahead of the Hajduk–Ajax match, when antisemitic, Nazi and Ustaše slogans were chanted through the city streets. Index reports that he said that the footage has spread around Europe and the world and that Split has been disgraced. “We owe an apology to the Jews and to all decent people because that is not us, that is not our city,” Puljak stated, Dalmacija Danas reports.

Puljak stressed that condemnations of the incident are not enough if one wants to prevent the repetition of such events. He believes it is necessary to speak openly about the causes and sees responsibility in politics and in the authorities’ attitude towards the return of extremist symbols into public space. “This didn’t start last Thursday and it didn’t start on the street. For years, we’ve been watching a politics for which the most important thing is to stay in power and which for that reason has allied itself with anyone, regardless of where they come from. That same politics has for years silently watched as the dark past returns to public space,” Puljak said.

an (expected) swipe at hdz…

He added that tolerating such phenomena can be understood as permission and opened the question of possible deals between members of the ruling party and fan groups. He also expressed suspicion that this is a staging by HDZ.

“Have certain people from the ruling party made a deal with fan groups that they will have their support at elections, and then these will tolerate everything they do? And who knows what else is hidden behind those deals,” Puljak asked. As a second important problem Puljak singled out clientelism and employment in the public sector. According to his estimate, in Croatia there are at least 10,000 managerial jobs that were not created because of the needs of society, but because of HDZ’s needs for employment.

“croatian society needs to be reset”

He called for the abolition of such positions and said that a change of government must not mean the replacement of party cadres. “The rule must be simple and without exception: always and only the best,” he said. Puljak stated that Croatian society needs to be “reset” and placed on the foundations of science, reason and humanism.

“Those who shouted through Split last Thursday were not defending Croatia, nor Christianity, nor humanism, but were disgracing all three,” he declared. He explained that the symbol of his political option is a broom, with which he wants to convey that long-standing problems need to be removed. “We need to sweep away what has been accumulating in the corners for years, and that is clientelism, corruption and tolerance of hatred,” he said. He concluded his message with a call to citizens for joint action. “Croatia deserves it. Split deserves it. Let’s do it together,” he urged.

World.title: The Krk Cave With Stories of Smugglers, Treasures & Bears
World.content:
October the 18th, 2026 – There’s a mysterious Krk cave that carries strange stories of smugglers, treasure and even cave bears…

The underground world deep beneath Croatia is home to an incredibly rich and fascinating world, and the Cerovačke and Baraćeve caves, the Blue Cave on Biševo and Manita peć in Paklenica National Park are just some of the caves you should visit at least once in a lifetime. Putni kofer writes that the island of Krk also has its own magical cave. It’s called Biserujka and is located not far from Slivanjska Bay and near the small village of Rudine in the north-eastern part of the island. This underground beauty is rich in impressive stalactites, stalagmites and speleothem columns, and an interesting story of pirate treasure is also associated with it.

THE CAVE TAKES ON BROWN, GREY AND REDDISH COLOURS BECAUSE OF MINERALS

It is also known as Vitezić Cave or Slivanjska Jama, and the name Biserujka, at least according to legend, is owed to the treasure that was once hidden in it. It supposedly belonged to local pirates, and after it was found it was moved to an unknown place. Where did it end up? According to tradition, only “Ive Gospodin” knows that, whose house stands at the entrance to the village of Rudine. Biserujka is not a huge cave. It is only 110 metres long, and from the entrance to the bottom its depth is 13 metres. It stretches relatively shallowly beneath the surface, yet it abounds in diverse cave decorations. They can be brown, grey and reddish, and their colour is given by various minerals, especially iron and manganese oxides.

The overburden of Biserujka is thin and nowhere exceeds six to eight metres. During rainy periods water penetrates into its interior: it passes through the limestone and dissolves calcium compounds that gradually deposit in the cave and form speleothems. How slow the entire process is is sufficiently illustrated by the fact that for a layer only one millimetre thick it takes from 10 to 30 years. Visiting the cave is very simple and requires no speleological experience or special equipment. From a stone cottage you descend by stairs into a small hall called the Balcony, from which you pass through the Window, the narrowest part of the arranged path. The path then leads into the Great Hall richly covered with speleothems, the Hall with Bridges and the Cypress Hall, in which the speleothem columns resemble a petrified cypress forest. The final part is so close to the surface that it contains soil and plant roots.

graffiti through the ages can still be seen within the cave

In the deeper part of Biserujka the temperature of the ground and air is around 15 degrees, while the relative humidity is around 95 percent. The lowest point of the cave is 30 metres above sea level. The first record of Biserujka dates from 1834 and is connected with the arrest of a smuggler from Senj who was allegedly hiding in it.

In around 1850, its entrance was closed with a door, which was the first time in Croatia that such a method of protecting a cave was applied. It was arranged for tourist visits in 1913, when the stone cottage and stairs were built. The long history of visiting is also witnessed by numerous graffiti. Many have been removed in the meantime, but some have been preserved as a trace of the past, among them the oldest from 1859.

Biserujka also has interesting inhabitants: 28 species of organisms have so far been discovered in it, among them six stenoendemics, i.e. narrow endemics of the Kvarner area. Bones of a cave bear about 16,000 years old have also been found in the cave. That animal lived there at the end of the Ice Age, when due to the lower sea level Krk was connected to the neighbouring mainland. The cave is connected by an educational walking path to the bay of Slivanjska. The walk takes about 30 minutes, and the path passes through a typical karst landscape, past dry-stone walls and rocky pastures lashed by the bora, all the way to the bay with a small harbour and a sandy beach. The ticket for Biserujka costs €7 for adults, €5 for children from three to 12 years old, while children under three pay nothing. During the winter months a visit is possible by prior arrangement.

World.title: New Catamaran Line to Pučišća and Postira Begins on 1st of November
World.content:
October the 18th, 2026 – A new catamaran line will begin sailing to Pučišća and Postira starts as of the 1st of November, claiming it will reach Split in 70 minutes.

After a months-long procedure and administrative wrangling, the new state high-speed line Pučišća – Postira – Omiš – Split is expected to begin regular service on Sunday, November the 1st 2026. Morski reports that this significantly changes the everyday life of numerous islanders for whom a trip to Split on the mainland previously meant travelling by road via Supetar and then by ferry to the mainland.

The new line number 9605 will be operated by the catamaran Tropic, owned by Krilo Fast Ferries. The vessel was built in 2022 and can carry 332 passengers. This is a year-round state line, so it is not just a “summer line”, but a concrete benefit for the residents of the island of Brač.

The sailing schedule is still being finalised; it is known that the catamaran would depart daily from Pučišća at 06:15, stop in Postira and then continue across the channel to the mainland to reach the Port of Split. The journey would take about one hour and ten minutes. The return departure from Split is planned for 16:15, while Omiš, a little further south along the coastline, would be included in the sailing on Saturdays and Sundays.

Despite the great satisfaction felt as a result of this in the island communities of Pučišća and Postira, the question of including Povlja in the new catamaran connection remains unresolved. Several models were considered and were on the table, specifically seasonal stops and a smaller number of weekly departures during winter, just enough for the islanders. Support was given by the mayor of Selca Ivan Marjanović, and even by people in the County and at state level, but Povlja were left “empty-handed”, i.e. they were not included in the new state line, which after numerous announcements is quite disappointmenting.

World.title: Varaždinske Toplice Thermal Water Was Healing People 2,000 Years Ago
World.content:
October the 18th, 2026 – Varaždinske Toplice is known for its thermal water, but not everyone realises just how far back its popularity stretches, having healed people 2,000 years ago.

Spring thermal water has a beneficial effect on rheumatic ailments, the skin, relaxation… We know that today, but it was also known by the innovative Roman conquerors 2,000 years ago. Less than an hour’s drive from Zagreb lies a place whose healing warm water, with a temperature reaching 58 degrees, was used by the Romans, who built temples, pools and baths right there. Putni kofer writes that an entire complex dedicated to that healing water. Varaždinske Toplice, which is still popular today, is home to some fascinating archaeological heritage that has just received new confirmation of its value.

The Archaeological Zone of Varaždinske Toplice recently received the temporary status of a cultural asset, which, according to the explanation of the Ministry of Culture, it will hold until a decision is made establishing the status of a permanent cultural asset or for a maximum of six years.

“Thermal water began attracting the first human groups back during the Palaeolithic era, as evidenced by finds from the large tufa cave 5 Gradišće on the western side of Toplička gora, while finds from the Neolithic and Bronze Age tell us about the continuity of settlement in the wider area of today’s settlement. In the 3rd century BC, the Pannonian Iasi lived here, after whom the Romans named this place Aquae Iasae. The Roman settlement of Aquae Iasae was inhabited from the 1st to the 4th century, and at that time Toplice was a significant health, ritual, cultural and even economic centre of Upper Pannonia,” it is stated, among other things, in the explanation of the protection decision.

THE ROMANS BUILT TEMPLES, POOLS AND A LUXURIOUS BATH COMPLEX AROUND THE SPRING

The warm springs therefore attracted the population way back during prehistory. Over time, one of the important ancient spa centres on the territory of present-day Croatia arose around them. The thermal sulphurous water, which emerges to the surface at a temperature of as much as 58 degrees Celsius, was so highly valued that the Romans built an entire complex of public buildings around it. The spring is still active today: the water emerges at the same place and supplies the Special Hospital for Medical Rehabilitation Varaždinske Toplice. The phenomenon that attracted people several thousand years ago lives on today.

Today’s archaeological park is home to the impressive remains of an expansive Roman complex that developed from the 1st to the 4th century. Systematic research, which began back in 1953, has uncovered the remains of ancient buildings on an area of approximately 6,000 square metres. There were baths with pools, a forum surrounded by porticoes, temples dedicated to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, and a monumental pool that encompassed the spring itself. Parts of walls two to three metres high, floors, stone thresholds, frescoes and systems for the supply and drainage of water have also been preserved.

THE ORIGINAL ROMAN POOL IN WHICH THE WATER WAS COOLED BEFORE USE

Particularly fascinating is the original Roman pool measuring approximately 8 by 13.5 metres. It was built of large stone blocks, and water flowed from it through special channels towards the baths. The Romans also had to solve a very practical problem: the water that emerges at 58 degrees is too hot for direct bathing. The large pool helped cool it, while an elaborate system of channels enabled the controlled use of the precious spring.

17,000 COINS THAT THE ROMANS THREW FOR LUCK WERE FOUND AT THE SITE

For the Romans thermal water was not only a natural resource. They believed that the springs also had supernatural power, so the area around them was a place of worship of various deities, especially nymphs whom they associated with water and healing. During research at the site around 17,000 Roman coins were found that people from the 1st to the 4th century threw into the sacred spring as votive offerings. Numerous altars, reliefs, inscriptions and sculptures of deities were also found.

THE REMAINS OF THE ROMAN SETTLEMENT CAN TODAY BE VIEWED IN THE PARK AND IN THE MUSEUM

During its long history, Aquae Iasae was not spared wars and destruction. At the beginning of the 4th century the complex suffered during Gothic invasions, but its importance was so great that the Roman emperor Constantine the Great ordered its reconstruction. After the collapse of the ancient world many buildings disappeared under layers of earth, but the spring continued to be used. It is precisely the thermal water, or rather the deposition of tufa, that is responsible for the exceptional preservation of parts of the Roman complex.

Today, the remains of the former settlement can be viewed in the Archaeological Park Aquae Iasae, located in the town’s spa park. The park itself was landscaped as early as 1820, and its history is another reminder of the centuries-long connection of the town with thermal water. In addition to the archaeological site it is worth visiting the Local History Museum in the Old Town, where valuable finds from the Roman period are exhibited. In this way time for relaxation in Varaždinske Toplice can be combined with exploration and incredible historical stories.

World.title: Attorney: Police should not be given right to confiscate scooters without court order
World.content:
Police should not be allowed to confiscate noncompliant personal light electric vehicles without court approval, as doing so would seriously infringe on property rights, Sorainen attorney Marcus Niin told ERR.

ERR reported Monday that amendments to the Traffic Act awaiting their second reading in the Riigikogu would give police the authority to confiscate electric scooters that do not meet legal requirements without a court order. Currently, such personal light electric vehicles can only be confiscated with court approval, but so far, courts have not granted a single request.

Attorney at law Marcus Niin criticized the proposal, noting that one important principle that must be taken into account is the inviolability of private property.

"This is an important principle for us and it can only be restricted in circumstances expressly provided for by law and generally in exchange for compensation. In other words, our legal system does not allow property to simply be taken away without compensation," Niin said.

Another consideration is that confiscation constitutes a very serious infringement of property rights, he added.

"Confiscation means property is permanently taken away without any compensation. Under the current legal framework, the Penal Code provides that confiscation can be ordered by a court and that authority should remain with the courts. Otherwise, if we start giving the executive branch the power to decide at its own discretion whether to seize someone's property, it could lead to serious infringements of rights and considerable public resentment," Niin said.

"In the longer term, this could also set a dangerous precedent. If we make a concession here, where will the next situation arise in which someone decides that, for one reason or another, the authorities should be given the power to confiscate property?" he added.

Even if compensation were paid for confiscated property, the police should not be the ones making that decision. Instead, Niin argued, the decision about what to do with the property should remain with its owner, in keeping with property rights and legal principles.

According to Niin, this is a fundamental question of whether the executive branch should be given the authority to interfere significantly with an individual's property rights when that power currently rests solely with the courts.

The attorney added that if courts have so far refused to allow police to confiscate personal light electric vehicles that do not meet legal requirements, the solution cannot be to create a legal shortcut allowing police to confiscate property directly.

According to Niin, the proposal is not made any more acceptable by the fact that the bill would require police to assess the circumstances of each case and determine whether confiscation is necessary.

"It's understandable that they want to create a system that gives officers discretion, but this question should not be left to police officers in the first place. It is such a fundamental and important matter that the decision on whether to take away someone's property should remain with the courts," he said.

World.title: Külli Taro: When the parliament seems to just get in the way
World.content:
For every election promise, it is worth asking what problem it solves, who it helps and at what cost, Külli Taro finds.

With political parties leading the charge, we are preparing for elections to the Riigikogu, the country's most important democratically elected representative body. The first campaign ads are already airing, parties are testing the popularity of their election promises and news about who will run alongside whom will soon become a daily occurrence.

Although the Riigikogu is Estonia's most important institution, tasked with debating and deciding all major issues, particularly those involving questions of values, discussions sometimes leave the impression that parliament is an obstacle to making necessary decisions quickly. This seems especially true when following discussions within government agencies where the prevailing attitude appears to be that things would work so much better if only the Riigikogu were not in the way.

A problem needs solving, an idea is on the table, but then come the questions, disputes, negotiations, consultations and proposed amendments. Why can't we just get something done without a time-consuming and exhausting parliamentary debate?

The Riigikogu seems to be getting in the way. If implementing an idea requires changing the law, the preference is to look for ways around that requirement.

Consider the police experiment with "cooling-off stops" several years ago. Speeding drivers were offered the option of waiting by the roadside instead of paying a fine. The experiment effectively introduced a new enforcement measure, with the police taking it upon themselves to shape penalties policy in place of parliament. Only later was the law amended to give police the authority to test cooling-off stops as an enforcement measure.

Or take the infrastructure fees imposed by local governments, which the chancellor of justice has challenged before the Supreme Court because such fees are, in essence, local taxes. We have agreed in the Constitution that local governments may impose and collect taxes and impose obligations only on the basis of law.

Existing laws do not authorize the introduction of infrastructure fees. There is no dispute that building the social infrastructure needed to accommodate new residential developments requires funding. But it is parliament that must make the value judgment about how much of the cost of new schools, kindergartens and other facilities necessitated by new residents should be borne by developers and, ultimately, homebuyers and how much should be funded from municipal budgets as a general public service. Municipal councils cannot take the place of the Riigikogu by invoking their right to manage local affairs independently.

Examples of government agencies taking it upon themselves, rather than leaving it to elected representatives, to decide how medical records, banking information or other data may be used have caused considerable public outrage. And rightly so.

The Riigikogu must decide whose medical records may be accessed, when, under what conditions and to what extent. Information entrusted to doctors must be protected by clear legal safeguards.

It is parliament's responsibility to set limits on government agencies' access to bank account statements through the enforcement register. Bank statements reveal details of people's private lives and even when an agency is pursuing what it considers a noble objective, that does not entitle it to disregard other values.

The purpose of the police's automatic license plate recognition cameras is also understandable. But what caused the greatest outrage was the realization that mass data collection had been organized without broader public debate or even widespread public knowledge.

Technological advances increasingly confront us with the question of whether we, as a society, actually want everything that technology makes possible. Technological solutions must be accompanied by value judgments that distinguish between what we can do and what we want to do. Smart use of data and regulation must not be treated as opposing goals.

These questions require answers enshrined in law. Resolving them means deciding how much power we give the state and how that power may be exercised. The Riigikogu is supposed to debate these issues. That is precisely why we elect a parliament.

Advisory councils and decision-making committees established on any other basis cannot replace a democratically elected representative body. Elected representatives must, of course, listen to outside advice, but parliament cannot be relieved of its responsibility for decisions, its obligation to conduct transparent and wide-ranging debate or its duty to seek additional expertise when necessary.

If the quality of debate in the Riigikogu is unsatisfactory, the solution is not to sideline parliament but to demand more of it. We should insist on more precise questions and clearer answers.

An avalanche of election promises will soon be upon us. That will give us another opportunity to practice holding politicians to higher standards. With every promise, we should ask what problem it solves, whom it helps and at what cost. A catchy idea about "doing something new or exciting" is not enough on its own. We need solutions that genuinely help and whose objectives, costs and limits we can agree on. Reaching that agreement is precisely the job of parliament.

World.title: EU to fund permanent magnet production line in Estonia
World.content:
A new permanent magnet production line will be built in Estonia after the European Commission agreed to fund a project from Neo Performance Materials, which owns the Silmet plant and a magnet plant in Ida-Viru County.

On Monday, the European Commission selected 77 European net-zero technology projects to receive a total of €3.4 billion in funding from the Innovation Fund call for applications launched in December 2025.

Among the funding recipients is Canadian-registered Neo Performance Materials, which owns the Silmet plant in Sillamäe and the permanent magnet factory in Narva, both located in eastern Estonia.

The Silmet plant, owned by Neo Materials, is dependent on raw materials from Russia but has pledged to phase them out. The plant has come under scrutiny after Estonia requested that its supplier be exempted from European sanctions.

"The project will establish a rare-earth permanent magnet production line in Estonia, covering separation, metallization and magnet manufacturing. The line will be capable of producing up to 3,000 tons of permanent magnets annually, one-third of which will be supplied to EU offshore wind farms," the project description states.

According to plans, the project will prevent the emission of more than 3.4 million tons of CO2 equivalent during its first 10 years of operation.

The funding will come from the Innovation Fund, using revenues from the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS).

The final terms of the grant agreements will be made public in the first quarter of 2027.

The Innovation Fund aims to channel an estimated €40 billion in revenue from the EU Emissions Trading System between 2020 and 2030 into investments in cutting-edge low-carbon and net-zero technologies to support Europe's transition to climate neutrality.

A methanol plant planned for Pärnu has previously received funding from the same program in Estonia.

World.title: Supermarkets seeing organic egg shortage as producers replace flocks
World.content:
Customers hoping to buy organic eggs in Estonia's supermarkets may have been left empty-handed in recent weeks due to supply chain issues, as producers are currently replacing their flocks.

The shortages have affected both major retail chains and smaller stores. Retailers recommend visiting first thing in the morning, as organic eggs can sell out by lunchtime.

Selver communications manager Mariann Järvela told ERR that Estonian producers of organic and free-range eggs are currently in the process of replacing their flocks, resulting in temporary supply difficulties.

"According to suppliers, the new hens have already started laying eggs, and normal availability should be restored in December," Järvela said.

Lauri Bobrovski, a member of the management board of Äntu Mõis OÜ, which produces Kikerikii eggs, said flock replacement has resulted in an 80 percent shortfall in production.

Chickens (picture is illustrative). Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

"The reason is something that happens every year. We are too small. We do not have enough eggs, especially when flocks are being replaced. We have five flocks, and this year the interval between the replacement of four of them was a little too short. The schedule for the arrival of chicks was tighter than we had planned, meaning the new flocks haven't started laying eggs by the time the other flocks have to be sold off," Bobrovski said.

Production always declines during flock replacement, but this has usually happened in the summer, whereas this year it fell at the beginning of fall.

Bobrovski suspects this also makes the shortage more noticeable. Customers are used to finding eggs on store shelves when they return to the city from the countryside in the fall, school starts and life returns to its usual rhythm.

He added that because Äntu Mõis accounts for approximately 50 percent of the domestic organic egg market, any shortfall in its production is immediately felt across the market.

"We are not happy about this situation ourselves either. In about another month, things will start to improve," Bobrovski said.

Eggs. Source: Aili Vahtla/ERR

Äntu Mõis plans to build a new chicken barn in the near future, which is expected to significantly increase the company's production capacity. Bobrovski said this will hopefully stop the supply problems.

But even when organic eggs return to the shelves, consumers' problems may not be over. Prices are expected to rise in November.

Bobrovski explained this is not related to the temporary egg shortage but rather to developments in the broader economy, as input costs are rising.

"Obviously, egg production is not a business where you get rich or make enormous profits. To survive, there is no alternative but to raise prices," the Äntu Mõis management board member noted.

Rimi Estonia purchasing manager Marta Palm said the company's inventory and sales of free-range eggs are well balanced, although a promotional campaign for free-range eggs has just ended.

"Due to demand during the promotion, shelves in some stores may indeed have been emptier at times, depending on how quickly the stores managed to restock them," Palm said.

World.title: Toto to perform in Tallinn in July 2027
World.content:
American pop rock band Toto will perform at Unibet Arena in Tallinn on July 29 next year.

American rock band Toto was formed in Los Angeles in 1977, and their debut album was released in 1978. Their breakthrough came with the 1982 album "Toto IV," which won several awards at the 1983 Grammy Awards, including Album of the Year, and featured the hits "Africa" and "Rosanna."

The band will celebrate its 50th anniversary with its 2027 tour. Toto will arrive in Tallinn with a lineup led by longtime guitarist and singer Steve Lukather and vocalist Joseph Williams. They will be joined on stage by Warren Ham, John Pierce, Keith Carlock, Dennis Atlas and Rai Thistlethwayte.

The band has sold more than 50 million albums. The song "Africa" has also achieved diamond certification in the U.S., meaning it has sold more than 10 million copies.

The band's latest and 14th album was released in 2018 and also features Skrillex.

World.title: Young audiences theater festival Naks kicks off in Tallinn and Narva
World.content:
The Naks theater festival for young audiences takes place in Tallinn and Narva from October 19 to 24, offering a varied program for children, young people, families, teachers and theater professionals.

This year's Naks will take place mainly in the border city of Narva from October 20 to 24. On the festival's opening day, October 19, audiences can see productions by two internationally acclaimed companies specializing in theater for young audiences at Tallinn's Salme Cultural Center: Kompani Giraff from Sweden and Le Moana from New Zealand.

For the youngest audiences — babies and their parents — the festival program includes Draakonipesa's "Talvevõlu," ("Winter Magic") a wordless visual journey into an enchanted winter world inhabited by rabbits, goats and Arctic foxes. After the performance, children can get to know the puppets used in the production.

For preschoolers and children in grades one through three, Sweden's Kompani Giraff offers the magical circus production "ABC," in which performers help audiences learn letters and the alphabet through play.

Finnish-Czech company Krepsko brings a miniature world all its own to Narva. "Fabsurdia" is a small, richly detailed world that audiences can do more than simply watch: They can also explore it up close and touch it.

Estonia's VAT Teater brings "Luukere Juhani juhtumised," ("Juhan the Skeleton's Adventures") an adventure production for children based on Triinu Laan's book, to the festival.

For audiences in grades four through nine, New Zealand dance company Le Moana presents "Shel We," a playful tribute to writer and poet Shel Silverstein and his beloved children's book "The Giving Tree." The production brings together trees, ghosts, goats and mischief.

Contemporary circus company Kompani Giraff also brings its second production, "A Study of Losses," to Narva. Combining aerial acrobatics, object manipulation and music, this visual journey reflects on lost worlds, memories and objects. Its musical world was created by Zach Condon, who performs as Beirut.

For students in grades seven through nine and upper secondary school, the program includes Miksteater's "Oskar ja Roosamamma. Kirjad Jumalale." ("Oscar and Pink Momma. Letters to God") This heartfelt, thought-provoking production tells the story of Oskar, a boy with cancer who spends the final days of his life in a hospital with his caregiver, Roosamamma.

Kuressaare Theatre's "Koleda tüdruku päevaraamat" ("An Ugly Girl's Diary") is also suitable for audiences ages 12 and older. It is a moving, honest story about young people that speaks to anyone who has felt left out.

The festival also includes several workshops, educational programs and a play reading.

World.title: Women's épée team takes home World Cup bronze
World.content:
Estonia's women's épée team recorded several impressive victories at the World Cup event in Casablanca, Morocco, but fell to Russia in the semifinals.

Estonia's women's épée team faced Turkey in its opening match and, after a shaky start, eventually secured a convincing 45-26 victory. Katrina Lehis and Irina Embrich lost their opening bouts, leaving Julia Beljajeva trailing 9-6 at the start of the third, but Estonia won the remaining seven bouts.

Estonia took the lead after the fourth bout, in which Embrich defeated Nilahsen Erten 8-5. The gap widened significantly in the seventh bout, when the experienced Embrich beat Nisan Dincel, 28 years her junior, 9-2. Victories by Beljajeva and Lehis eventually extended Estonia's winning margin to 19 touches.

In the round of 16, Estonia faced Germany, but the Estonians dominated their opponents to claim a 38-24 victory. Estonia led 15-11 heading into the fourth bout and never allowed Germany to close the gap.

In the quarterfinals, Estonia faced a strong French team but continued its excellent form, building a six-touch lead after the third bout. The advantage continued to grow, with Estonia leading by 10 touches after the sixth bout before sealing a convincing 45-34 victory.

In the semifinals against Russia, Estonia trailed 14-10 after three bouts, but Beljajeva then produced an excellent performance to level the score. However, the tie was short-lived and Russia opened up a 30-21 lead after the sixth bout. Estonia was unable to recover from the deficit and suffered a 45-34 semifinal defeat.

In the bronze medal match, Estonia faced the United States, which had lost its semifinal to Italy 38-31. The Americans posed little resistance and the Estonian quartet secured the World Cup bronze medal with a commanding 45-22 victory. Russia went on to win the event, defeating Italy 32-31 in a closely contested final.

Estonia's men's épée team defeated Greece 45-31 in the opening round but lost 45-38 to fourth-seeded Italy in the next round. Kazakhstan won the men's competition, beating Russia 45-40 in the final.

World.title: AI recordings of doctor-patient conversations the new norm for Estonian hospitals
World.content:
Artificial intelligence systems that record conversations between patients and doctors, produce written summaries and help physicians make diagnoses and recommend next steps are already a reality in a number of hospitals.

Confido CEO Edvard Garder told ERR that the company began testing AI solutions last year, making it one of the first in Estonia to do so.

"The solution is now in use in several departments and we plan to roll it out across the entire organization. Patients have responded positively to the solution because doctors have more time to spend with them," Garder said.

Narva Hospital is currently seeking Estonian-language speech recognition and transcription software through a public procurement process. The software would convert conversations between doctors or nurses and patients into electronic text that can be processed, automatically translated, played back and stored.

Narva Hospital also wants the AI assistant to suggest medical codes and support doctors in making decisions. However, the procurement requirements emphasize that doctors must remain the decision-makers in all processes. AI-generated content that has not been reviewed and approved by a healthcare professional must not be entered into patients' medical records.

Tartu University Hospital began testing AI in its emergency department in mid-October and plans to continue the trial for three months. If the technology proves useful, the hospital will extend the trial period to obtain definitive confirmation of the application's benefits.

"The aim of using the EMO24 application is to reduce the time doctors and nurses spend on documentation. It also helps eliminate duplication where patients have to describe their condition to different staff members multiple times," said Aime Keis, head of the hospital's emergency department.

Heba Clinic also uses AI to compile patients' medical histories before appointments, document conversations during visits and subsequently prepare summaries and explanations for patients.

Heba Clinic CEO Ain Aaviksoo noted in an opinion article (in Estonian — ed.) published by ERR last week that AI cannot make decisions on behalf of doctors but should support solutions that help people manage their own health and enable doctors to assist them in doing so.

Every hospital looking for its own AI assistant

The Ministry of Social Affairs has not conducted a comprehensive assessment of the current use of artificial intelligence solutions across all hospitals, said Nele Labi, the ministry's deputy secretary general for innovation. However, the ministry is aware of several initiatives.

"We see that private hospitals have generally made the fastest progress in testing new solutions," Labi added.

According to Labi, there is no unified nationwide system to help hospitals streamline their work using AI and hospitals are largely seeking solutions independently based on their own needs.

"At the national level, however, two major AI-based solutions are currently under development: a transcription tool for family medicine and a transcription tool for the electronic ambulance system. The state has several other AI projects, but these two are expected to have the greatest impact on healthcare professionals' administrative workload in the near future," the deputy secretary general said.

Confido's CEO noted that healthcare professionals welcome the opportunities offered by AI and that skepticism is relatively rare. According to Garder, there is no significant difference between medical specialties in terms of the potential benefits as automated transcription tools and clinical decision support systems can reduce the documentation burden in virtually every field.

"This gives doctors more time for direct interaction with patients and also means that discharge summaries and other medical reports reach the national health portal more quickly," he said.

However, adopting AI does not mean immediate cost savings for hospitals, as initial investments are required. Garder nevertheless believes the technology will help reduce workloads and burnout among doctors and nurses, although the financial benefits of improved employee well-being cannot always be measured precisely.

The Ministry of Social Affairs also confirmed that projects in other European countries have clearly demonstrated the positive impact of such solutions in reducing administrative workloads.

"Estonia's approach is to seamlessly integrate general-purpose tools such as speech recognition and transcription into our hospitals' workflows so that medical professionals can spend their time on patients rather than paperwork," the deputy secretary general said.

Patients must be notified of AI involvement

A separate question is how to ensure that information exchanged between patients and doctors remains confidential and does not fall into the wrong hands.

According to Garder, Confido considers the solutions it currently uses to be secure and continues to do everything possible to mitigate potential risks. Nevertheless, Confido patients have the option to decline the use of AI during their appointments.

Tartu University Hospital also said participation in its AI pilot project is voluntary. If an emergency department patient does not wish to use the application, information gathering, diagnosis and treatment will proceed as before.

The Ministry of Social Affairs' deputy secretary general confirmed that strict data protection rules apply to the processing of such information and that patients must be informed about recordings and their purpose.

"However, because the technology is developing very rapidly, we need greater legal clarity and must ensure that patients understand how it is used and that the process is transparent. Working groups have already been established at the ministry to address this issue," Labi said.

Confido's CEO believes the state should develop a standard for security criteria. However, Garder does not consider it necessary for the state to develop a single AI solution for all healthcare institutions.

"Especially since tying all healthcare providers to a single system would create a monopoly and stifle innovation. Moreover, I'm not sure that would be the most efficient use of public funds," Garder said.

Instead, he believes the state should focus on ensuring that all data in the national health portal can be processed by AI, which would in turn speed up preparations for medical appointments.

"At present, the state is clearly moving far too slowly in adopting AI," the Confido CEO said.
