Meanwhile, several members of the yoga group died, including Wu’s husband, or moved away to live with their children. Many of those remaining in the village are either too old to achieve difficult positions or have debilitating health issues.

Jin stepped down as the village’s director of women’s affairs in 2021. Residents say her successor promised to pay for yoga participation, but the money never materialized, so they stopped attending.

Liu Runtao, 58, took the role this year and has been struggling to put the team back together. She’d never practiced yoga before returning to the village in recent years. Now, when she posts notices about training sessions, usually only her relatives show up.

In villages like Yugouliang, organizing events and upgrading infrastructure often depend on approval and funding from town or county authorities. However, as officials change, so do their offices’ priorities.

Lu told Sixth Tone that he would sometimes win a higher official’s backing for a project only to see them transferred out before anything was finalized, taking things back to square one. Even when the village was at its most popular, funding to update its tourism facilities was slow to come.

Lu stepped down as resident first secretary in 2023 and returned to the vocational college in Shijiazhuang. Now 60, he still returns for major events and helps promote Yugouliang, but he feels it’s now someone else’s responsibility to keep the “yoga village” narrative alive.

Winding down

On one sunny July afternoon, a group of villagers sat chatting at a bus stop. Services pass through here just twice a day. Apart from the occasional truck carrying agricultural supplies, the main road is largely silent.

Liu had arranged a yoga training session, but just nine elderly women showed up. Most residents can no longer achieve the poses that made them famous. Only the septuagenarian Zhang can still balance with both feet off the ground.

The new resident first secretary, Li Jidong, who worked for the same Shijiazhuang college as Lu, watched from the sidelines. He has little interest in yoga, apparently seeing it more as a liability. “What if someone has a brain hemorrhage while doing it?” he said, after interrupting the session to suggest the elderly women attempt a safer activity.

Li believes that Yugouliang’s remote location and climate make Lu’s vision of building a tourism industry here difficult to realize.

“I don’t have that kind of ability. No single institution or person can solve a problem this big on their own,” he said. Li has only been in the job for two years but admits that he already wants to leave.

During a recent yoga event, Li asked people to help with livestream sales of local farm products, but the results were disappointing.

The village Party secretary, Zhang Pengcheng, who took over from his father in 2021, said he has also tried encouraging residents to make short videos and livestream, but many struggle even to use smartphones, let alone speak standard Mandarin with viewers online.

Yet he sees the remaining yoga team as the “embers” to spark a tourism boom. In 2025, he organized a gala in which the team performed on ice beside a bonfire. A livestream of the event drew about 100,000 viewers.

But for now, the priority is improving infrastructure. In July last year, the township government and local businesses funded the opening of a guesthouse with room for up to 86 guests. It has yet to turn a profit. When Sixth Tone visited, its doors and windows were shuttered.

The village has also built a canteen for pensioners, with dishes starting at just 2 yuan. It was also temporarily closed in July because of a staff shortage.

Before stepping down, Jin earned a yoga instructor qualification in Nanjing, capital of the eastern Jiangsu province, and has since relocated to Zhangbei Town, about 60 kilometers from Yugouliang. She offers free classes to locals and teaches online six days a week.

Of the few residents still practicing yoga in Yugouliang, Zhang Xiying, despite her age, remains the most able and enthusiastic — though not for the village’s benefit, but for her own family’s.

“Exercise keeps me healthy,” she said, after wrapping up a practice session. “And I need to take good care of my old man.”

Additional reporting: Wu Huiyuan; editor: Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Villagers practice yoga together on a summer afternoon in Yugouliang, Hebei province, July 2026. All photos by Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019121/Divorcés Starring in TV Romances? China’s Internet Isn’t So Sure
World.title: Divorcés Starring in TV Romances? China’s Internet Isn’t So Sure
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019121/Divorcés Starring in TV Romances? China’s Internet Isn’t So Sure
World.content:
Popular Chinese TV drama “Against the Current” has sparked debate about power dynamics between divorced male characters and their female counterparts after featuring a romantic plot between a low-ranking young woman and a high-status divorced man.

The discussion began after the 48-episode drama premiered Sept. 11 on Tencent Video, its international platform WeTV, and Disney+, and was bolstered by this month’s release of a similar drama also featuring a divorcé, “Irreplaceable.”

Set in the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), “Against the Current” follows Shen Jialan, whose privileged life is upended when her grandfather, a renowned academician, is falsely accused of treason, endangering the lives of her entire family.

In exchange for a previous act of kindness, a couple allows Shen to take on the name of their late daughter, Xu Lanxiang, to escape execution. Under her new identity, Shen goes to work as a maid for her former fiancé, Lin Jinqi, who has since married another woman. Lin eventually divorces his wife to marry Shen.

After its release, the series became the most popular series on Disney+ in markets including North America and Spain, and topped WeTV charts in the U.S. and at least seven Asian countries outside China. Domestically, it currently tops analytics platform Yunhe Data’s long drama most-viewed list, with over a third of market viewership on Oct. 12.

Though the drama has been applauded for its storytelling and nuanced character development, some viewers have criticized Lin’s characterization, arguing that the show romanticizes unequal relationship dynamics, fueled by his status as a male divorcee. Lin, who divorces his wife after she cheats on him, curries favor with the King, asking him to force Shen to marry him against her will.

The debate has spread to other Chinese romance dramas that increasingly feature divorced and remarried male leads, from past hits such as “The Story of Minglan” (2018) and “The Glory” (2025), to dramas like “A Splendid Match” and “Irreplaceable” released this year.

Viewers have critiqued the imbalanced power dynamics in these series, which feature powerful, wealthy divorcés who offer protection, stability, and emotional guidance, often to younger, naive heroines from lower social statuses.

The recent popularity of remarried male leads marks a departure from the decadeslong shuangjie, or “purity on both sides,” trope in Chinese romance dramas, which favors depicting couples with no prior romantic or sexual experience before they fall in love.

In these stories, male leads are usually portrayed as successful, devoted figures whose affection belongs exclusively to the heroine, while female leads are frequently portrayed as innocent and kind.

Social media users have linked the shift to changing social realities, including rising divorce rates and the growing visibility of divorce and second marriages. Others have criticized it as a cheap way to create attention-grabbing plot twists, adding that the trend risks turning divorced males into a symbol of maturity and status while reinforcing unequal relationship dynamics.

Viewers point to the gender gap commonly found in romance narratives between divorcés and their female counterparts. When dramas instead feature divorced female protagonists, the corresponding male leads are often single or younger, and the story follows them as they “catch up” to their female counterparts professionally.

In the modern drama “Sniper Butterfly,” for instance, divorced protagonist Cen Jin reunites with a younger man who later becomes a successful professional in his own right as well as her business partner.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A still from “Against The Current.” From Douban)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019117/Zheng Qinwen’s China Open Win Swamps Her Sponsor’s Tea Shops
World.title: Zheng Qinwen’s China Open Win Swamps Her Sponsor’s Tea Shops
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019117/Zheng Qinwen’s China Open Win Swamps Her Sponsor’s Tea Shops
World.content:
A daylong, nationwide buy-one-get-one-free promotion by Chinese milk tea brand Chagee, launched in honor of Zheng Qinwen becoming the first Chinese woman to win the China Open title on Sunday, saw its online ordering systems crash amid inundated orders.

The company made the announcement via its official account on microblogging platform Weibo the night of Zheng’s win, saying the sales promotion would run throughout Monday, calling it a “new (moment) in history worth raising a glass to together.” The tennis player has been a Chagee brand ambassador since 2024.

The sudden traffic surge beginning around 8 a.m. Monday crashed the brand’s mini program on super app WeChat, leaving many users unable to place orders. The crash sparked heated discussion online, with a related hashtag on Weibo attracting over 180 million views as of Tuesday and rising to the platform’s trending topics list. A check by Sixth Tone later on Monday found the problem had been resolved.

At the China Open, Zheng defeated Russia’s Mirra Andreeva, the French Open champion, in two straight sets, catapulting her to the 23rd-best women’s tennis player in the world. Last June, Zheng ranked world No. 4, a career high, but injuries over the past year forced her to stop competing and caused her ranking to drop to No. 160. She entered this year’s China Open as a wildcard, invited directly by the organizing committee.

After the win, several photos of Zheng lifting the China Open trophy were posted on her official Weibo account. A caption alongside the photos reads: “The weight of this trophy is the weight of a dream, dedicated to the younger me who always worked hard for that dream.”

According to domestic media outlet ChinaStarMarket.cn, Zheng currently holds 14 brand endorsements spanning cosmetics, sportswear, luxury accessories, cars, and technology, among others. Her endorsements include international brands such as Nike, Dior, Rolex, and Wilson, as well as Chinese brands such as Chagee, Alibaba-owned digital payment system Alipay, and large language model Qwen, also owned by Alibaba.

During Zheng’s break from competition, none of her brand endorsements were terminated, according to domestic media outlet Jiemian News. Instead, many companies increased their support, with Chagee upgrading her title from Global Health Ambassador to Global Brand Ambassador, and Wilson launching a Zheng-inspired signature tennis racket.

According to Forbes’ world tennis player earnings list, released in August and covering the 12 months prior, Zheng was the only Chinese player in the top 10, ranking seventh globally with $22.6 million — with over 97% reportedly coming from brand endorsements.

Zheng also earned roughly 474 million yuan ($71 million) in prize money and endorsements between 2024 and 2026, matching in three years what Chinese tennis legend Li Na made over her entire 15-year career.

Zheng’s commercial breakthrough came in 2024, when she finished runner-up at the Australian Open, her best Grand Slam result and the second-best by a Chinese player after Li Na. She went on to win the Paris Olympics women’s singles title that year, becoming China’s first Olympic tennis singles champion.

At the Guangzhou Auto Show in November 2024, Audi’s Chinese sub-brand AUDI named Zheng a brand ambassador. In January 2025, Dior selected her as its global brand ambassador, making her the first Chinese athlete to hold the role.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: China’s Zheng Qinwen poses with the trophy after defeating Mirra Andreeva in the women’s singles final of the China Open at the National Tennis Center in Beijing, Oct. 11, 2026. Fred Lee/Getty Images/VCG)

World.title: Alex Eala kicks off Ningbo Open campaign with win over Diane Parry
World.content:
VICTORY. Filipina tennis star Alex Eala advances to the round of 16 at the Ningbo Open after defeating France's Diane Parry.

Filipina tennis star Alex Eala advances to the round of 16 at the Ningbo Open after defeating France's Diane Parry in straight sets

MANILA, Philippines – Alex Eala got off to a strong start at the Ningbo Open in China as she defeated France’s Diane Parry, 6-3, 6-1, in the round-of-32 match on Monday, October 19.

The match, which lasted one hour and 17 minutes, had seen the two players tie at 3-3 before Eala found her momentum to eventually defeat Parry in straight sets.

The 21-year-old Filipina will advance to the round of 16 and will face either sixth-seeded Diana Shnaider of Russia or qualifier Yulia Putintseva of Kazakhstan.

“I’m very happy with my performance. I think it was a really good first round, a tough first round. Diane is a great player and I think she’s had a really good year so congrats to her for the year she’s done. I’m really happy to be in the second round,” Eala, who’s currently ranked world No. 20, said in a post-game interview.

The Filipina tennis ace’s Ningbo Open victory came just after her early exit at the Wuhan Open, where she conceded to World No. 177 Shi Han of China, 6-4, 3-6, 3-6, in the round of 64.

Previously, Eala had also settled for bronze at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, after absorbing a 3-6, 6-3, 6-2 loss at the hand of China’s Wang Xiyu in the semifinals of the women’s singles. – Rappler.com

World.title: Gawilan bags Philippines’ first gold at 2026 Asian Para Games
World.content:
GOLDEN. Ernie Gawilan celebrates after winning a para swimming gold at the 2026 Asian Para Games in Nagoya, Japan.

Veteran para swimmer Ernie Gawilan delivers for the Philippines anew, winning the country’s first gold at the 2026 Asian Para Games in Japan

NAGOYA, Japan – Filipino para swimmer Ernie Gawilan captured the Philippines’ first gold medal after ruling the men’s 400-meter freestyle S7 of the 5th Asian Para Games on Monday, October 19, at the at the Rainbow Pool of the Nagoya City General Gymnasium.

The 35-year-old Davao City native, who has underdeveloped extremities, topped the event in 4 minutes and 56.72 seconds.

Gawilan overcame a fierce challenge from China’s youthful Zhang Yilong (silver, 5:01.36 minutes) and a familiar foe in Singapore’s Toh Wei Soong (bronze, 5:24.23 minutes).

It was Gawilan’s third straight gold in the event and fifth overall, following his three-gold haul at the 2018 edition in Jakarta, and his gold conquest in Hangzhou, China in 2023.

His clocking also secured him a spot at the 2028 Los Angeles Paralympics, according to national para swimming coach Tony Ong.

“He’s already qualified in the 2028 LA Olympics because of his time,” Ong said.

In the morning preliminaries, Edwin Villanueva finished 10th and last in the men’s 400-meter freestyle S8 in 6:22.33, while Muhaimin Ulag placed 12th and last in the men’s 200-meter individual medley SM9 in 3:04.30.

Over at the Izu Velodrome, Patrick Lee and Arthus Bucay finished 12th and 14th in track cycling’s 1,000-meter time trial, clocking 1:14.888 and 1:19.496, respectively.

National cycling coach Norberto October had earlier said they did not expect a medal on the track but vowed to bounce back in the road race, where they stood a better chance of a podium finish, possibly a gold.

In judo at the Aichi Prefectural Martial Arts Hall, Edmond Montecillo fell to Uzbekistan’s Ibrokhimjon Akbarov by ippon in the men’s J1 -70kg round of 16.

The defeat left Al Jaed Pacheco as the last Filipino judoka standing. He will battle Iran’s Mahdi Borchlou in the men’s J1 -81kg division on Tuesday, October 20.

The country’s table tennis bets also fell like dominoes, with Lhey Manginsay and Billy Cartera bowing out of singles contention at Sky Hall Toyota.

Manginsay lost to the more experienced Kim Kun-Hea of South Korea, 3-11, 3-11, 2-11, in women’s singles Class 9, while Cartera absorbed a 4-11, 3-11, 3-11 defeat against Thailand’s Norakan Chanphaka in men’s singles Class 4-5.

Johna Pena suffered a 9-11, 6-11, 3-11 loss to South Korea’s Kim Seongok in women’s singles Class 7, while Noriko Batuhan succumbed to China’s Huang Zhirui, 5-11, 11-6, 3-11, 1-11, in women’s singles Class 3. – Rappler.com

World.title: League-leading NU wants to prove doubters wrong this time
World.content:
NU looks driven to turn its early dominance into a championship after last year’s heartbreak, but UP remains close behind at the end of the UAAP men’s basketball first round

MANILA, Philippines – NU boasts the best record again after the first round of eliminations in the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball tournament. This time, however, the Bulldogs want to finish the job.

After topping last season’s eliminations, the Bulldogs suffered a Final Four exit, losing to eventual champion La Salle.

But the Bulldogs are determined to prove doubters wrong. NU head coach Jeff Napa knows consistency will be key, as well as the mindset that securing the No. 1 seed means little without a championship.

“We need to set standards. That’s what I told them, we needed to achieve in the first round,” Napa said in Filipino after the Bulldogs wrapped up the first round with a 69-65 win over the FEU Tamaraws for a 5-2 record.

“Heading into the second round, we need to remain consistent,” he added. “The players are proving to the doubters that they can compete in the UAAP.”

NU’s only losses came against the Ateneo Blue Eagles and La Salle Green Archers, both teams finishing tied for sixth place at 3-4.

The UP Fighting Maroons, another perennial title contender, also wound up with a 5-2 record, but NU gained the upper hand by winning their first-round meeting, 72-64.

Since falling to Ateneo, the Bulldogs have won three straight games, including an overtime thriller against the UST Growling Tigers and Adamson Soaring Falcons, who are both tied at 4-3.

Last season, NU ruled the elimination round with a league-best 11-3 record, but lost twice to La Salle in the semifinals.

Napa hopes that establishing a consistent standard of play will prevent a similar late-season collapse.

“Our mindset is that winners need to live up to the standards of winners,” Napa said. “We need to be consistent in everything we do. We shouldn’t relax just because we’re number one. We still have a long season ahead of us, and we have a lot of work to do.”

Unlike last season when NU could turn to Jake Figueroa in crucial moments, the Bulldogs have spread the scoring load more evenly this year.

MVP frontrunner Reinhard Jumamoy and PJ Palacielo have emerged as key contributors in a balanced offensive attack.

Jumamoy averaged 13.29 points per game and 5.14 assists per contest, the second-highest mark in the league during the first round.

Palacielo, meanwhile, posted averages of 12.0 points, 6.29 rebounds, and 4.43 assists per game.

NU also had three other double-digit scorers in Paul Francisco (10.86 points per game), Tebol Garcia (10.43), and foreign student-athlete Mo Diassana (10.29).

With the Bulldogs now carrying the league’s best record, Palacielo stressed that the team cannot afford to become complacent.

“It will be the same in the second round. We’ll stick to what our coaches, Coach Jeff (Napa) and the rest of the staff, prepare for us and focus on the roles they assign,” Palacielo said.

“We’re happy that we managed to get the win [against FEU], but we can’t afford to relax. We have to move forward and focus on the next game. This one is already behind us.”

Palacielo also emphasized the importance of having the entire roster ready to contribute, especially as the competition intensifies.

“All 16 players need to be ready whenever their number is called. Our primary players and those in Coach Jeff’s rotation won’t always have good games,” he said.

“We keep reminding them that if we want to reach the finals and become contenders, we need all 16 players to step up, not just the 10 players who usually see action on the court.”

UP takes lessons to Round 2

After finishing the first round strong, UP also aims to stay consistent.

The loss to NU, followed by a defeat to FEU, served as a wake-up call for the Fighting Maroons, as they bounced back with wins over La Salle and UE to close out the round.

But their narrow escape against the winless Red Warriors showed there is still plenty of room for improvement.

UP allowed UE to dictate the pace for much of the game, with the Red Warriors building a lead of as many as 10 points before the Fighting Maroons rallied to avert a major upset.

For UP head coach Goldwin Monteverde, the comeback offered a valuable lesson ahead of the second round.

“Actually, UE got ahead of us in a way. That was a test for the team, having to come from behind and play tough defense to get back into the game,” Monteverde said.

“Along the way, of course, we need to learn how to start strong. I guess that’s something we’ll learn as we go through the season.”

Veejay Pre led UP in scoring during the first round, averaging 12.86 points, 6.43 rebounds, and 2.57 assists per game. Rey Remogat followed with 12.0 points per contest.

With another round ahead, Monteverde expects his players to learn from both their wins and losses as they pursue a return to the UAAP Finals for the sixth consecutive year.

“Good or bad experience, it’s still a good experience that will lead us toward our same goal,” Monteverde said.

UP will open the second round against UST on Wednesday, October 21, at the Mall of Asia Arena, while NU will face Adamson on Saturday, October 24, at the Blue Eagle Gym. – Rappler.com

World.title: Senate resolution seeks to declare Chinese envoy ‘persona non grata’
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – Senator Erwin Tulfo on Monday, October 19, filed a resolution seeking to declare Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan a “persona non grata” over his recent remarks, which the Philippine government described as a “thinly veiled threat of the use of force.”

In filing Senate Resolution No. 739, Tulfo expressed the Senate’s “serious concern” over the controversial statement of the Chinese envoy, who said China could easily defeat the Philippines if it resorted to using force.

“We should feel fortunate enough that you have a neighbor like China in this region. If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we’ll not use force. We love peace,” Jing said.

The Department of Foreign Affairs admonished Jing over his remarks. It also summoned the diplomat to express the government’s serious concern and strong objection to his public statement.

“It is hereby resolved by the Senate of the Philippines to express its serious concern over the remarks made by the Ambassador of China to the Philippines Jing Quan, suggesting the potential use of force against the Philippines,” the resolution read.

“Resolved further to urge the [Department of Foreign Affairs] to recommend to the appropriate authorities the declaration of Ambassador Jing Quan as persona non grata in view of the severity of his remarks and their implications for Philippine sovereignty, national dignity, and bilateral relations,” it said.

Senator JV Ejercito, over the weekend, first raised the possibility of senators filing a resolution to declare Jing persona non grata after the Chinese Embassy in Manila dared Philippine officials to do so.

“Some anti-China politicians talked about declaring the Chinese ambassador persona non grata (PNG). Over the past 30 years, anti-China forces have been repeatedly doing the same thing to threaten our embassy. We are fed up with these old and low tricks. If they really want to do something, do it quickly and immediately, please,” the embassy said.

“While diplomacy is based on reciprocity, we will not welcome them to China. Simple and fair enough,” it added.

Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea, including areas part of the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone. China refuses to acknowledge the landmark 2016 Arbitral Award, which affirmed the Philippines’ EEZ and found China’s supposed historical claim invalid.

Under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., Manila has been both assertive and transparent in protecting both its sovereignty claims and rights in the West Philippine Sea. China’s claims have meant that, for Filipino frontliners — the Navy, Coast Guard, and even fisherfolk — harassment at the hands of Chinese maritime agencies is a risk in flashpoints in those waters.

After Monday’s filing, the Senate will discuss and vote on Tulfo’s resolution during the resumption of its plenary session on November 9. If approved, the upper chamber will adopt the resolution. – with reports from Bea Cupin/Rappler.com

World.title: Champi now a super typhoon again ahead of entry into PAR
World.content:
CHAMPI. Satellite image of Super Typhoon Champi outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility as of October 19, 2026, 4 pm.

The trough or extension of Super Typhoon Champi may already trigger scattered rain and thunderstorms in Catanduanes, Northern Samar, and Eastern Samar, says PAGASA on Monday afternoon, October 19

MANILA, Philippines – Champi re-intensified into a super typhoon on Monday afternoon, October 19, ahead of its expected entry into the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).

Champi’s maximum sustained winds increased from 175 kilometers per hour to 185 km/h, said the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) in an advisory issued at 5 pm on Monday. Its gustiness is now up to 230 km/h from the previous 215 km/h.

The super typhoon was located 1,515 kilometers east of southeastern Luzon as of 4 pm, moving west northwest at a slightly slower 15 km/h from 20 km/h.

It is still projected to enter PAR by Tuesday morning or early afternoon, October 20. Upon entry, it will be given the local name Rosal.

PAGASA said Champi will continue to move west northwest until Wednesday, October 21, before moving generally northwest starting Thursday, October 22. It is likely to stay over the Philippine Sea, where it could strengthen further before gradually weakening Thursday onwards.

Even before Champi enters PAR, its trough or extension may already trigger scattered rain and thunderstorms in Catanduanes, Northern Samar, and Eastern Samar in the coming hours. Flash floods and landslides are possible.

The super typhoon could be closest to the Philippines’ northernmost province of Batanes on Friday, October 23. It is expected to bring heavy rain to extreme Northern Luzon, or the Batanes-Babuyan Islands area, even though it is unlikely to make landfall.

Tropical cyclone wind signals might also be raised for the northern and eastern portions of Northern Luzon and even parts of Bicol as early as Monday evening or Tuesday morning. The weather bureau’s latest forecast shows Signal No. 2 or 3 could be the highest, while Signal No. 4 is no longer seen as a possibility.

PAGASA added that most parts of Luzon and the Visayas, as well as portions of Mindanao, are likely to experience gusty conditions beginning Wednesday.

As for coastal conditions, moderate to rough waters are expected in the northern and eastern seaboards of Luzon and the eastern seaboards of the Visayas and Mindanao on Tuesday.

Starting Wednesday, very rough, high, or very high waters may affect the northern and eastern seaboards of Luzon.

Champi may exit PAR by Saturday, October 24.

ALSO ON RAPPLER

Aside from the trough of the super typhoon, other sources of rain in the coming hours include the intertropical convergence zone (ITCZ) and the easterlies.

The ITCZ is a belt near the equator where the trade winds of the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere meet, while the easterlies are warm winds from the Pacific Ocean.

Scattered rain and thunderstorms will persist in the Zamboanga Peninsula and Palawan due to the ITCZ, while isolated rain showers or thunderstorms may hit Cagayan Valley, the Cordillera Administrative Region, and the Ilocos Region because of the easterlies.

The Philippines is currently in a transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan, following the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat, which was announced last October 5.

The northeast monsoon typically brings surges of cold temperatures, but the upcoming amihan period could be warmer as the existing strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean is predicted to become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Rappler’s Best] And our jaws dropped
World.content:
The impeachment court is on recess until November 9, when it’s the defense’s turn to present its case. What would the defense’s counter move be?

My apologies for missing last Monday’s newsletter as I took a short break.

This week is the start of the public interviews of five aspirants to the post of chief justice, which will be vacated by Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo on November 6. He is retiring after over five years since he was appointed by then-president Rodrigo Duterte.

It’s President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s first and only chance of choosing the head of the High Tribunal, which is packed with Duterte appointees, before he steps down in 2028. Two of the aspirants, Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen and Associate Justice Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa, were appointed to the Court by the late president Noynoy Aquino. The Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) will hold public interviews with both on Thursday, October 22.

The three other aspirants — Duterte appointees associate justices Rodil Zalameda, Japar Dimaampao, and Jose Midas Marquez — will be interviewed by the JBC on October 26.

With a Supreme Court in transition, we can’t expect it to rule on anything that could potentially shuffle the appointing power’s deck of cards.

Which is why, from a purely tactical point of view, it does make sense for the prosecution in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte to have made a bombshell bet last week — “all in,” in the words of lead prosecutor Jinky Luistro — by dropping all but one of the four articles of impeachment it lodged against her before the Senate impeachment court.

Unlike last year, when the Court saved the day for the Vice President by barring the first attempt to put her on trial, the defense could feel the winds shifting. “As for certiorari (before the Supreme Court), we are not considering it at this point,” said defense spokesperson Michael Poa in this story.

It’s the handwriting on the wall. In August, the SC dismissed two petitions, including one filed by Duterte herself, that questioned the impeachment proceedings against her, saying they were already moot since the trial had already proceeded.

A month later, Duterte lost the second time around, when the justices unanimously dismissed a petition against the Senate court’s decision to adjust the voting threshold to convict the Vice President.

On Day 39 of the trial last week, House prosecutors dropped three complaints against her — misuse of confidential funds, grave threats, and bribery — in a legal maneuver that upset the defense and made lead counsel Sheila Sison bristle with a staccato of qualms and unease. This should not tie our hands, she told the impeachment court.

The prosecution’s move partly stemmed from its reading of the defense’s strategy, which, they say, is to delay the proceedings and bore the public to death. Prosecutors believe they have gained momentum from their latest witness, accountant-lawyer Alex Cabrera, and wanted to go for the kill, so to speak.

Presiding officer Senator Chiz Escudero issued a quick decision that sided with the prosecution, thus retaining just one charge to be judged by the senator-judges: Duterte’s estimated P1.5-billion unexplained wealth, per Cabrera’s numbers.

Who benefits from this situation? In this story, political reporter Dwight de Leon tells us who, plus the fact that timing is already pretty tight, given the 2027 budget that needs to be passed and Manila’s hosting of the ASEAN Summit in mid-November.

For now, the impeachment court is on recess until November 9, when it’s the defense’s turn to present its case. What would the defense’s counter move be? Possibly two things, according to lawyer Lulu Reyes, Rappler’s resident panelist in our coverage of the trial. Watch it here.

The defense could seek an outright dismissal of all the articles of impeachment and no longer present its arguments, citing a mistrial.

It could file a demurrer to evidence with the impeachment court, a plea to dismiss the case because the prosecution failed to present sufficient evidence, i.e., Cabrera’s “false assumptions.”

Either way could force an early vote from the senator-judges, according to Reyes.

Truly a sui generis. Spin a win!

Here are some of Rappler’s bests that you shouldn’t miss:

Bea Cupin features the Philippine Navy’s ambitions as it shores up its capabilities to defend our waters. Part 1 tackles the Navy’s drones, dreams, and endless possibilities. Part 2 looks into the opportunities and challenges in the military’s path to modernization.

Shay Du tells us how the military’s structure has adapted to its plans to modernize.

Lourence Angelo Marcellana walks us through the armed forces’ modernization program. The latest proof of how the military is changing is the appointment of the first female officer to be the commandant of cadets at the Philippine Military Academy, as Mia Fokno writes in this story.

Eirene Manatlao looks into why Filipino women are opting out of motherhood. But can an aging Philippines avoid the fate of its neighbors? Read this report by Jake Gomez.

Shay Du shows us the peril of postponing, yet again, the barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections.

Taj Basman and Kat Tolosa explain why subsea cables are not the Philippines’ weakest link in its commitment to keep internet infrastructure resilient to attacks and accidents.

Gelo Gonzales introduces us to Maria Ressa’s latest book, The Fight Back: A Citizen’s Guide to Standing Up to Dictators, which talks about practical steps for citizens to reclaim control over the technologies shaping societies and the future.
