World.title: For Pru Life UK’s Cecille Marano, Filipinos deserve ‘peace of mind’
World.content:
Just like Pru Life UK, the vice president for corporate performance management marks her 30th year of providing Filipinos with protection

Editor’s note: This content is sponsored by Pru Life UK and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

September 16, 1996. There isn’t a single lull in Cecille Marano’s train of thought when remembering her first day at Pru Life UK.

“Pru Life UK was a new industry player back then,” she recalled their old office in Makati where office chairs and tables filled every available space as employees and agents alike were crammed together in a single floor. They had to make do with an open setup type of office until things could be sorted out in a more orderly fashion.

A glimpse of Marano’s life with Pru Life UK

“Zero to One” is how Marano would describe the company’s evolution story. She said that Pru Life UK started from scratch. It did not acquire nor sought partnerships with local insurance companies and relied solely on organic growth.

“5 in 5” was the slogan of the strategic campaign to leapfrog Pru Life UK among the top 5 insurance companies in terms of new business within its first 5 years of operations. Remarkably, it successfully breached into the top 5 group on the 4th year.

Competition continues to be tough in an industry long dominated by traditional players. Still, through persistence and unrelenting effort, Pru Life UK ultimately garnered the coveted Top 1 position in 2020 and retained market leadership as of 2025.

Over the last 30 years, Cecille witnessed how the company’s transformed from a budding new player to an industry leader. She also recalls how the company deftly navigated the Asian financial crises in 1997, the 2008 global financial meltdown, and the global recession in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Despite these headwinds, the company rapidly expanded market share just as the agency force grew by leaps and bounds. Today, Pru Life UK boasts of the largest sales force with more than 33,000 agents.

Her first day at Pru Life UK soon turned into 30 years – which is also celebrating its 30th year of business operations in the Philippines this 2026.

Photography by Lem Atienza; makeup by Dorothy Mamalio; hair by Marjorie Caballos

A persisting commitment

Marano, who currently serves as Pru Life UK’s vice president for corporate performance management, spends most of her week reviewing and analyzing vital financial data. She regularly coordinates with business owners for performance updates on key initiatives along with finalizing reports.

Wednesdays are often reserved for her team’s weekly engagement: discussing status and progress of deliverables, addressing new issues, time-sensitive work requirements considered as top priority, and projects for endorsement to the chief strategy officer, among others.

She attributes her long tenure with the company to the shared sense of purpose, passion, conviction and collective commitment of all employees in achieving the company’s goals and vision along with adherence to its core values.

An active and intentional service

If summed up to three words, Marano describes Pru Life UK’s employee culture with verbs, not adjectives: “listening, understanding, and delivering.”

Interestingly, these words also align with the company’s core values, showing how Marano has their vision and mission down pat. It also helps that she personally carries values that don’t stray away from what the company stands for.

“Integrity, trustworthiness, and empathy are the key principles that I embrace. I do believe in being truthful and transparent in dealing with everybody. It allows me to build a genuine and solid relationship with my colleagues,” she said, adding that these traits also help her to listen to people’s concerns effectively, which enables her to provide proper inputs to help them make sound decisions.

Photography by Lem Atienza; makeup by Dorothy Mamalio; hair by Marjorie Caballos

Empowering customers

After all, it’s always been about enabling Filipinos to think and act to achieve lifetime financial security.

But while there is a growing awareness and even desire among Filipinos to learn more about insurance, it can’t be denied that many still view it as an afterthought expense rather than a necessity. For Marano, Pru Life UK has actively worked on this by fostering financial literacy among ordinary Filipinos.

“Pru Life UK was the first to introduce the Variable Unit-Linked in the Philippines. It offered added flexibility for clients to buy insurance products with an investment element,” she explains.

Their financial literacy efforts also involve education at the grassroots level, engaging with government agencies and educators, and teaching school children the basic concepts of money and finance.

A two- (or even three-) way street

Now that Marano has served her 30th year with Pru Life UK, what does she wish for the company for its next 30 years?

“I wish to see the company continue to provide accessible and relevant insurance products to Filipino families and further intensify financial literacy efforts at the grassroots level.” She adds, “I also wish that Pru Life UK would continue to earn the trust of Filipino families and help them ultimately achieve financial freedom and the peace of mind that comes along with it.

A glimpse of Marano’s life with Pru Life UK

As a matter of fact, she considers “peace of mind” as closely associated with “protection” – the core of what Pru Life UK’s services are about, from health and critical illness coverage to investment-linked protection plans.

“For me, protection engenders peace of mind,” she says. “Filipino families have peace of mind knowing that they are financially prepared for uncertainties; agents have peace of mind and a sense of fulfillment in helping Filipino families secure their future; and employees have peace of mind and a sense of satisfaction safeguarding the future of Filipino families.”

And there’s no better testament to this than Marano’s story – which has always been filled with full-circle moments.

Cecille Marano caps off the interview by saying, “It is a great honor and privilege to serve and be part of Pru Life UK’s stellar journey over the last three decades and counting. I am truly blessed and grateful to Pru Life UK that helps me protect and provide for my family.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Why did 3 SET senator-members favor Erwin Tulfo’s ouster?
World.content:
ERWIN TULFO. Senator Erwin Tulfo pushes for stronger protections for persons with disability (PWDs) during the hearing of the Committee on Social Justice, Welfare and Rural Development on Monday, October 19, 2026.

'Justice and fairness went out of the window when three minority senator-members voted in favor of an out-of-time motion for reconsideration filed by a petitioner without legal standing,' says Senator Ping Lacson

The Senate Electoral Tribunal’s (SET) decision to affirm the dismissal of a petition to unseat Senator Erwin Tulfo over alleged citizenship issues was largely anticipated — the March ruling was anchored on insufficiency in form — but the votes of three senator-members favoring Tulfo’s ouster was not.

In a statement signed by SET Secretary Luis Jose Geronimo, the tribunal said it denied the motion for reconsideration (MR) filed by petitioner Berteni Causing, seeking to reverse its March 2 ruling summarily dismissing his quo warranto petition for being “insufficient in form.”

The SET said the MR was filed beyond the prescribed period and “failed to comply with the filing and service requirements of the 2020 SET Rules.”

The nine-member tribunal convened at the Senate on Friday, October 16, with the Supreme Court (SC) justices and senator-members in attendance. Six SET members voted to deny the MR, while three opposed the dismissal, reportedly minority senators Robin Padilla, Pia Cayetano, and Camille Villar.

SC Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen chairs the SET, with SC justices Henri Jean Paul Inting and Ramon Paul Hernando serving as members. Senators Kiko Pangilinan, Bam Aquino, and Lito Lapid represent the majority bloc in the tribunal while Padilla, Cayetano, and Villar represent the Senate minority.

“Let’s give credit to the three SC justice-members and the other three senator-members who undoubtedly knew the obvious procedural flaw which resulted in a 6-3 vote, thus dismissing the MR,” Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson said over the weekend.

Lacson, without naming the three minority senators, questioned their decision to favor what he described as an “out-of-time MR filed by a petitioner without legal standing.”

“Justice and fairness went out of the window when three minority senator-members voted in favor of an out-of-time motion for reconsideration filed by a petitioner without legal standing,” Lacson said in a social media post.

“Their motive may be deeper than personal issues against Sen Tulfo,” he added.

Tulfo has repeatedly clashed with minority senators in the months spanning Alan Peter Cayetano’s tumultuous Senate presidency, the subsequent leadership change, and the ongoing impeachment trial.

In June, Tulfo called out then-Senate president Alan, calling him “thick-skinned” for skipping Senate session for a second consecutive day, along with minority senators, preventing the upper chamber from holding sessions due to a lack of quorum. At the time, Cayetano said they would not attend the session to keep control of the Senate blue ribbon committee and other panels.

During the impeachment trial, Tulfo questioned whether the proceedings were the proper venue for senator-judges to discuss their personal legal issues. This came after Padilla denied allegations that he had ignored an Ombudsman order related to complaints accusing him of obstruction of justice.

Tulfo also figured in a heated exchange with Villar during a debate on whether to revisit the threshold for convicting an impeachable official.

Villar took offense and became emotional when she defended colleagues from Tulfo’s remarks that the framers of the 1987 Constitution did not anticipate that future senator-judges could face corruption-related cases, such as plunder and theft.

Asked to comment on the 6-3 vote at the SET, Tulfo did not confirm the names of those who voted against him but said he was “hurt.”

“We were hurt. As you can see, we were all interacting with each other and then suddenly, they will do that. We’re a bit sad but that is their right. I mean, what can we do?… Kung ‘yun ang pananaw nila, then so be it. Ipagpasa-Diyos na lamang natin (If that is their view, then so be it. I leave it up to God),” he said in an interview on Monday, October 19.

Tulfo was more candid on Facebook, where he shared an editorial illustration depicting himself being stabbed in the back by knife-wielding arms labeled “Sens. Padilla, Villar, Pia.”

“Nakita ko lang (I just saw this)…. tsk, tsk, tsk,” he said in his post on Saturday, October 17.

What other “deeper motive” could there be, as suggested by Lacson? Where could a senator’s removal from office have any significant impact?

If one were to consider the impeachment trial, had the SET removed Tulfo from office, the number of active senator-judges participating in the trial would have fallen to 19. Based on the denominator, 15 votes would have been needed to convict Duterte, while five votes would have resulted in her acquittal. – Rappler.com

World.title: Myanmar Regime’s Sittwe Counteroffensive Hits the Rocks on Nga Pyi Island
World.content:
The Myanmar military’s push to land troops on Nga Pyi Island in Rakhine State’s Pauktaw Township has suffered fresh setbacks as the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) strikes regime vessels and tightens its siege on the state capital Sittwe.

Frontline sources said AA artillery hit another navy vessel off the island on Sunday, the third to be damaged in recent days. “The boat was struck and caught fire,” a local source close to the AA confirmed. Intense clashes are raging both on and around Nga Pyi Island as regime forces continue efforts to secure a beachhead despite mounting casualties.

Sources said commanders are driving conscripts forward in near‑suicidal assaults, but few have managed to reach land.

Since Oct. 7, the military has deployed more than a dozen gunboats and landing craft backed by airstrikes and artillery from encircled Sittwe, in an effort to seize the island. The move aims to break the AA’s blockade of the Kaladan River corridor and shield the navy’s Shwe Mingan base in Sittwe, which sits on a peninsula surrounded by water on three sides.

Nga Pyi Island is a key AA stronghold, blocking regime access upriver to AA-controlled Pauktaw and Ponnagyun townships.

“Junta soldiers keep coming despite heavy casualties, but few have made it to shore,” said a source close to the AA.

Meanwhile, AA columns have seized several regime outposts elsewhere in Sittwe and are pressing toward Shwe Mingan naval base and the Sittwe Regional Operations Command.

The assault on Nga Pyi was launched as advancing AA troops threatened to encircle the military’s Sittwe stronghold. Fighting has also intensified just down the coast in Kyaukphyu Township, where AA forces are attacking outposts near Taung Maw Oo naval base.

The AA controls 14 of Rakhine State’s 17 townships along with Paletwa Township in neighboring Chin State, with the regime maintaining a foothold in Sittwe, Kyaukphyu, and the sparsely populated Manaung island.

A regime counteroffensive launched from neighboring Magwe, Bago, and Ayeyarwady regions is bogged down amid fierce resistance and heavy losses.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Defense Minister Claims Airstrikes Are Aimed at Achieving Peace
World.content:
Despite widespread domestic and international condemnation of the military junta’s airstrikes on civilian targets, newly appointed regime Defense Minister Lieutenant General Yar Pyae said the bombing operations were intended to achieve peace.

“Mainly, they [questions raised in the media] are based on human rights and humanitarian concerns regarding the bombings. From our perspective, the current military operations are actually steps taken to obtain peace,” Lt-Gen Yar Pyae, who also serves as chairman of the National Solidarity and Peacemaking Negotiation Committee (NSPNC), said during his closing address to a workshop marking the 11th Anniversary of the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement (NCA) on October 16.

The military regime routinely bombs civilian targets in resistance-held territories in an effort to undermine anti-regime groups’ administration and to coerce them into joining its purported peace talks. The tactic worked well in northern Shan State and Mandalay Region, where it managed to force the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and its ally, the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA), to stop fighting, agree to China-brokered ceasefires and hand over some seized towns.

The regime continues to use the tactic in other regions and states including Rakhine State, which is almost entirely controlled by the Arakan Army (AA), an ally of MNDAA and TNLA.

On September 28, the regime conducted an airstrike targeting the busy Indian Market in the AA-controlled town of Kyauktaw, killing at least 50 people. The attack drew fierce condemnation from the UN, the UK, ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights and various human rights organizations.

Since the 2021 military coup, the Myanmar military has consistently launched airstrikes across revolutionary strongholds, including the Anyar region (also known as the Dry Zone) and ethnic minority regions—targeting not only military sites, but also schools, hospitals, religious buildings and civilian homes.

Even as it makes peace overtures, the regime continues to engage in heavy fighting with the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) in Bhamo, and clashes are ongoing with the AA in Rakhine State. Airstrikes also continue to target civilians in the Anyar region, where People’s Defense Forces (PDFs) maintain a strong presence.

Amid the ongoing air raids on resistance-held areas, junta leader Min Aung Hlaing made what he called an unconditional peace invitation during the 11th NCA anniversary event in Naypyitaw on October 15. The regime nonetheless continues to pressure the PDFs—the main armed resistance groups across the country—to lay down their arms and surrender.

According to statements made during a press conference at the close of the NCA anniversary workshop, invitations to peace talks were extended to the KIA, but not to the AA.

Furthermore, Min Aung Hlaing stated on October 15 that if ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) wish to engage in politics, they must disarm and form political parties; if they wish to conduct business, they must do so legally; and if they wish to serve in defense, they must join the Border Guard Forces (BGF).

In 2009, the military heavily pressured EAOs to transform into Border Guard Forces. With few exceptions, however, the initiative largely failed.

The KIA, which is currently engaged in intense fighting with the military, was one of the major ethnic armed groups that refused to transform into a BGF at that time. During the Spring Revolution that erupted in response to the coup, the KIA earned the Myanmar military’s ire by providing military training, weapons and combat support to anti-junta PDF forces.

Similarly, following Operation 1027, the AA seized control of most towns in Rakhine State, including a regional military command center. Since then, the regime has launched several offensives to retake lost territory in the state.

While urging PDFs to surrender and asking EAOs to join the BGF, Min Aung Hlaing also told ethnic representatives attending the NCA ceremony that he would cooperate with those willing to work together on peace, while actively finding methods to handle those who refuse to cooperate.

World.title: Solar Mandate Crushes Myanmar Builders as Regime Chief’s Son Profits
World.content:
Contractors warn that a new regime mandate requiring installation of solar power systems in all high-rises and commercial buildings will send construction costs soaring in Myanmar. The directive further squeezes construction companies already pinched by a shortage of materials, import restrictions, and severe currency volatility.

The Yangon City Development Committee’s Engineering Department issued the order on October 1 as part of a nationwide push for solar amid deepening power blackouts.

From November 1, all commercial projects and high-rise buildings must install solar panels sufficient to power elevators and emergency lighting. For commercial buildings, solar systems must be integrated with power supplied by the Yangon Electricity Supply Corporation (YESC).

The order applies to existing projects, buildings under construction, and those awaiting Building Completion Certificates required for habitation.

“We have been handed the order at a time when prices of solar panels and related equipment are rising daily,” complained a Mandalay‑based builder. “Steel and cement prices are already soaring, so this adds yet another burden.”

Meanwhile, industry insiders warn of a scarcity of skilled technicians capable of installing large solar systems, creating technical and financial hurdles. “Household systems won’t power elevators, which require commercial‑grade solar systems,” the manager of a solar dealership explained. “Installation takes at least two months and costs around 100 million kyat.”

Solar imports to feed surging demand created by the new mandate are controlled by Aung Pyae Sone, son of regime chief Min Aung Hlaing.

Aung Pyae Sone swiftly cornered the lucrative market after his father’s regime waived tax on solar imports in April 2023 under the pretext of boosting the energy grid. His Venus Essential company also holds licenses to supply solar equipment for projects in Naypyitaw and planned 40-megawatt solar power plants in Taungdwingyi, Salin, Pakokku, Pauk, Chauk and Kyunchaung.

The solar mandate comes as regime energy rationing intensifies with more frequent rolling blackouts this year.

“They cut electricity during extreme heat, then order solar systems to be installed,” said a former political prisoner from Mandalay. “But only one company — belonging to the coup leader son — is allowed to import and sell the equipment nationwide. This is not aimed at solving the power crisis, but exploiting authority for personal profit.”

On October 5, the Electricity and Energy Ministry introduced rolling four-hour blackouts under the pretext of surging demand during the El Niño heatwave. Since then, households in Yangon, Mandalay and Naypyitaw have faced daily outages.

The power crisis has driven prices of solar panels and related equipment to record highs. In early August, a 500‑watt panel cost around 650,000 kyat. By mid‑October, the price had surged past one million kyat, putting solar systems beyond the reach of ordinary families.

World.title: An ‘All-for-Arakan’ Approach Is Needed to Address the Rohingya Refugee Crisis
World.content:
As resistance against long-term Rohingya presence in host countries grows, the refugees’ fate is back in the headlines. Malaysia is a recent example. Its government has yielded to growing hate speech against Myanmar refugees, and Rohingya in particular. In September, Malaysia and Myanmar negotiated a controversial repatriation agreement for 5,000 refugees that is not supported by the UN or its refugee agency. Resentment in India and Indonesia has also grown.

Following large-scale Rohingya returns from Bangladesh to Myanmar in the 1970s and 1990s, repatriation efforts started again in 2017, after the enforced flight of 750,000 Rohingya from Myanmar to Bangladesh. Initially, they were based on a Chinese offer to mediate between the two countries. Even though these and later efforts failed, Bangladesh’s pursuit of repatriation continues, and Malaysia has now joined in.

There are many reasons why the repatriation initiatives of the past 10 years have not been successful. A largely unmentioned one is that many initiators wrongly assume that traditional diplomatic relations between states can lead to meaningful dialogue and conflict resolution. This state-centric approach overlooks the key question at the heart of Myanmar’s decades-old volatility: how power and political authority are shared between Myanmar’s center and its highly diverse regions and ethnic nationalities. Moreover, since the country’s 2021 military coup, the regime in Naypyitaw has lost control over much of the country. In Arakan (Rakhine State), the birthplace of most Rohingya refugees—and where some 500,000 of them still live—the current regime has control over only three of the state’s 17 townships.

Today’s Myanmar is in transition. It is a country with multiple centers of authority. In some, local territorial control has been in place for decades; in others, it has been established since the military coup of 2021. These ethnic and regional authorities are not against a federal state as such. They are against the current federal union that is based on a constitution that concentrates significant power at the center, and particularly with the armed forces.

Right now, the key question is whether a new form of federalism can emerge, one that leaves a highly centralized system behind and, instead, focuses on existing and newly emerging centers of political authority. A long road lies ahead but in many parts of the country progress is clearly visible.

Arakan is a prime example. As the territorial dominance of the United League of Arakan/Arakan Army (ULA/AA) grows, particularly since 2023, it has been transforming into a central administrative authority with local administrative, security and judicial mechanisms. The Institute for Strategy and Policy in Chiang Mai recently reviewed the progress that has been made and concluded that “despite persistent challenges, a solid institutional framework is emerging”. But it also cautions that following rapid territorial expansion, a performance gap has emerged between public expectations and the administration’s delivery capacity.

A key reason for the delivery gap is that right now Arakan is a war zone with almost daily ground clashes between the AA and Myanmar’s armed forces, as well as attacks by Bangladesh-based Rohingya militias. Moreover, Arakan is now a prime target for attacks by Myanmar’s air force, which deliberately targets civilian structures with bombs of up to 500 pounds. The devastation on the ground is massive, with hundreds of civilians killed and maimed, while schools, markets, clinics and prayer houses have been destroyed. Physical infrastructure is also heavily affected, including by recent massive floods, leading to large-scale disruption of livelihoods and food security.

According to a recent report by the UN Development Programme, 68.4 percent of Arakan’s population (all ethnicities) experience multi-dimensional poverty, while a further 20 percent is at risk of falling into that category. Arakan’s current population is thought to stand at just over 2.4 million, while a Doctors Without Borders report in 2024 estimated that only 636,000 Rohingya remained in Arakan. Today that number will have fallen significantly, as approximately 150,000 more Rohingya have fled to Bangladesh since then.

To be clear, Rohingya repatriation from Bangladesh and other countries will take time. Refugees cannot return if armed conflict continues and before the underlying reasons for their flight have been addressed. To achieve this, a central role for both ULA/AA and the people of Arakan, including the Rohingya, is critical. But at the same time, various factions on the Rohingya side stand in the way of a united approach, particularly those supporting armed militias. Moreover, some of them have been used as a divide-and-rule tool by Myanmar’s military-backed regime.

Arakan’s problems are manifold and a broader vision of identity is critically important, one that acknowledges inclusion and equality as basic building blocks for a stable, secure and prosperous Arakan.

This understanding led the Rakhine Advisory Commission of 2016-17, chaired by former UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan, to focus on solutions to address the legitimate grievances and suffering of all Arakan’s diverse people. Its report and recommendations to Myanmar’s leaders remain highly relevant, based as they are on the central objective of developing conditions in Arakan that will lead to a peaceful, fair, harmonious and prosperous future for all communities. In 2018, the commission published a lessons-learned report focusing on how it operated in Myanmar’s highly politicized and complex context.

Obviously, much has changed since the report was released but it remains relevant, even after the National League for Democracy’s violent removal in 2021. It analyzes Arakan’s situation around three major crises: a security crisis, an economic and development crisis, and a human rights crisis. These crises persist and could form the basis for an all-of-Arakan approach.

Since 2017, the Annan report has been re-acknowledged annually by an overwhelming majority of the UN General Assembly and the UN Human Rights Council. Yet, no efforts have been made to establish how it might serve Arakan’s people under their current circumstances, and particularly since 2024, when most of Arakan came under the control of the ULA/AA.

Any process leading to a comprehensive plan for Arakan will be complex, not least because of the wide range of actors, functioning at diverse levels. In “The Dilemma of Hard Choices”, published in August, the Center for Arakan studies identifies the heterogeneity of agents as a key issue and adds that it is compounded by the problem of ownership, where most states, armed groups, civil society and international bodies each deflect overall responsibility while pursuing their own narrow strategic interests.

Precisely these diverging interests would make the Annan report a helpful starting point for dialogue. For good reasons, the commission’s recommendations are not highly prescriptive. Its general understanding was that, while basic principles of governance and human rights should guide the implementation process, details could be developed as part of dialogue processes. The report contains 88 recommendations on a comprehensive set of issues, ranging from economic and social development to freedom of movement, citizenship, health, access to justice, intercommunal cohesion, humanitarian access and internally displaced persons.

Obviously, dialogue cannot be based on the Annan report alone, but it could be a starting point. Additional questions must be raised to take account of developments since 2017. The first is the clarification of victimhood. Who are the victims of decades of oppression, persecution and violent conflict? A second is the “fog of war” that distorts a clear view of what is happening on the ground.

Obviously, it is not necessary to argue that the Rohingya are victims; that is accepted around the world. But what about the other communities in Arakan—the Rakhine, the Maramagyi, the Mro, the Chin, the Hindus and others?

They too are victims, yet their plight has been getting far less attention. They too have had their villages bombed and burned, their clinics, schools and livelihoods destroyed, while thousands are displaced in areas where relief goods cannot reach them. But their plight is not as widely documented. Acknowledgment that all Arakan’s people are victims could be a first step in reconciliation. And clearly, there are different degrees of victimhood and these too must be acknowledged.

The second point concerns the current “fog of war” and the urgent need to establish independent investigations. As in other places around the world, violent conflict, displacement and hunger obscure a clear view of developments on the ground. In such situations, deliberate disinformation thrives. We should not pretend that we have a clear view of what is happening in Arakan and in the refugee camps in Bangladesh. Lack of independent access and blocked internet facilities compound the problems.

Independent investigations will be needed to establish what has happened in Arakan and Bangladesh since 2017. While a significant body of research about the Rohingya exists, research on Arakan’s other communities remains scant. Moreover, research should also focus on disturbing allegations about what has been happening in Bangladesh. How did Rohingya militias manage to get a firm grip on the population in the refugee camps? Where did funding for their arms and operations come from? And how can large numbers of refugees and militia fighters continue to cross the Bangladesh-Myanmar border seemingly unnoticed?

Since 2018, the Independent Investigating Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM) has been collecting and preserving evidence to facilitate criminal prosecutions of those most responsible for atrocity crimes. But it only shares its findings with investigative, prosecutorial and judicial authorities in national and international courts. As a result, a vast body of information remains inaccessible to the public. Moreover, IIMM’s mandate does not cover other truth-seeking needs, such as documenting and public acknowledgment of crimes through truth and reconciliation bodies and publicly accessible archives. These limitations underline the importance of establishing additional mechanisms to ensure that accountability is pursued as an integral part of transitional justice and reconciliation. This should be part of a comprehensive approach: an all-for-Arakan approach.

Using the Annan report as a credible starting point for dialogue could be a first step towards creating a better understanding of the needs of all Arakan’s people. Moreover, its repeated recognition by the UN General Assembly might help to rally much needed support for such an exercise at a time when resources are scarce.

Laetitia van den Assum is a former Dutch diplomat. She was also a member of the Rakhine Advisory Commission (2016-2017), chaired by Kofi Annan, former UN Secretary-General.

World.title: US Holds Second Round of Talks With Myanmar Regime as Concerns Grow Over Policy Shift
World.content:
U.S. officials held a meeting with Myanmar miliary regime officials in Tokyo last week, Reuters reported on Friday, citing sources familiar with the meeting.

It was the second round of talks between the two countries within a month. A U.S. delegation led by Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance visited the regime’s capital Naypyitaw in mid-September.

Vance also led the delegation in Tokyo, which included over a dozen U.S. officials, while the identities of regime representatives and the issues discussed remained undisclosed, according to Reuters.

At the September talks, the U.S. delegation met with coup leader Min Aung Hlaing and secured the release of American businessman Adam Castillo, who had been detained upon returning to Yangon in June 2026 over a lawsuit filed against him.

The U.S. outreach led by Vance has focused on shutting down scam centers that target Americans, but could lead to broader engagement, including on Myanmar’s rare-earth mineral deposits, Reuters reported, citing current and former officials as well as others familiar with the U.S. policy shift.

The Irrawaddy has learned that during the Naypyitaw meeting, the U.S. side urged the regime to reduce attacks on civilians, crack down on money-laundering gangs, engage with ethnic armed groups, release political prisoners and allow unfettered distribution of humanitarian assistance.

Observers noted that the Trump administration has shifted its policy from isolating the Myanmar military-installed government to engaging with it.

The National Unity Government (NUG), a leading anti-regime revolutionary organization, said it was not overly concerned by the increasing engagement between the U.S. and the military junta.

Speaking to The Irrawaddy, NUG Foreign Affairs Minister Zin Mar Aung said the U.S. is engaging with both sides—the military regime and the revolutionary groups—purely based on promoting its own interests, without granting legitimacy to anyone.

“Its [U.S.] policy is already clear. They are taking a transactional, practical approach to tackle issue like TOC [transnational organized crime]. They will discuss matters that are crucial to U.S. interests,” she said.

“So, this is nothing unusual. Nor is it a shift in policy. Since the Trump administration took office, this is how the U.S. has been dealing with [all] countries, not just Myanmar.”

Banya Khung Aung, Secretary 2 of the Interim Executive Council of Karenni (Kayah) State, which largely controls the eastern Myanmar state, told The Irrawaddy he is concerned that increased U.S. engagement with the regime will harm the country’s federal democracy and human rights movements, whether financially, technically or operationally. As evidence, he pointed to the Trump administration’s recent cuts to USAID funding for Myanmar.

“If you look carefully at Donald Trump’s policies, everyone knows that he engages with all [sides] and highly considers his national interests. So, I am not surprised with [the administration’s ongoing] engagement with the regime,” he said.

He noted that foreign governments are no longer prioritizing democracy and human rights, and are instead focusing on their national and common interests.

“Because of that, whether it is a government or a dictatorship, if there are benefits for America, it is almost certain they will engage.”

Bertil Lintner, a Swedish journalist, author and strategic consultant who has been writing about Asia for more than four decades, echoed Banya’s comments.

“I am not surprised. Democracy has never been a top priority for the Trump administration. And more countries are starting to acquiesce to a fait accompli. The military-dominated government is there to stay for the foreseeable future.”

Following the 2021 coup, the U.S. under Joe Biden imposed sweeping sanctions against top regime generals—including Min Aung Hlaing and his family—as well as military-owned conglomerates.

But Trump has shifted U.S. policy from isolating the regime to engaging with it, including delisting junta cronies accused of aiding and abetting regime war crimes and crime against humanity committed against their own people.

Meanwhile, the country, whose economy has collapsed under the regime, has become a hotspot of transnational organized crime. Chinese-run scam syndicates under the protection of several armed organizations, including regime-controlled or aligned militia groups, defraud huge sums from victims globally, including Americans, who have lost billions of dollars annually in recent years.

Regarding U.S. engagement with the regime, Debbie Stothard, founder and coordinator of the Alternative Asean Network on Burma, said, “It looks like President Trump has been scammed by sham President Min Aung Hlaing. Trump is rewarding a criminal for committing more crimes.”

She warned that U.S. engagement with the regime not only poses risks to the country’s pro-democracy movement, but also endangers civilians in Myanmar and across the region. She noted that Min Aung Hlaing has escalated the country’s conflicts, causing mass displacement, while also driving a boom in transnational crime that targets victims regionally and globally.

“Embracing Min Aung Hlaing is embracing a nest of vipers. He has been intensifying threats to regional human security and economic stability,” Stothard said.

The U.S. State Department said it engages will all groups in Myanmar on issues affecting U.S. interests and has raised the need to cease violence and release political prisoners, according to the Reuters report.

World.title: Chinese Jet-Fuel Refinery to Bypass Sanctions, Myanmar’s Blood Timber Flows to China, and More
World.content:
China‑backed refinery lets regime bypass jet fuel sanctions

Myanmar’s military regime has restarted the Thanlyin No.1 Oil Refinery near Yangon, allowing it to bypass jet fuel sanctions and sustain its deadly air raids on the civilian population. According to Nikkei Asia, Phase 1 is designed to produce 150,000 metric tons of jet fuel annually, roughly equal to Myanmar’s import volume last year.

The refinery, operated by Myanma Petrochemical Enterprise (MPE), was taken offline in 2017 but rebuilt after the 2021 coup. The engineering, procurement and construction contract was awarded to Peiyang Chemical Engineering Service Corporation (PCCS), a Singapore-registered subsidiary of Peiyang Chemical Equipment in Tianjin.

Anhui Tiankang Group supplied nearly 400 measuring devices for the various chemical processes, coordinated by Tianjin Sainuo Oil & Gas Technology. Some modules were fabricated in China and shipped via Singapore to Thilawa Port.

The regime says the project will reduce foreign currency outflow and stabilize supply. It has heavily relied on air power since 2022, killing thousands of civilians, and this dependency has only increased as the territory it controls continues to shrink. In the most recent atrocity, 50 civilians died and nearly 60 were injured when the regime bombed a busy market in Rakhine’s Kyauktaw.

China becomes biggest buyer of Myanmar’s blood timber

China has become the dominant buyer of Myanmar’s timber since the 2021 coup, according to UN Comtrade data cited by Australia’s Wood Central.

Last year, China’s purchases climbed to US$147.3 million, nearly double the pre-coup total of $78 million, while Western imports collapsed from roughly the same amount to just $1.2 million worth, according to Forest Trends, a Washington‑based non‑profit that monitors global forest trade and conservation finance.

The group’s analysis shows China’s share of Myanmar’s reported wood exports rose from 25.5 percent in 2019 to a peak of $228.7 million in 2024, nearly 80 percent of the total, before settling at 74.1% in 2025. Nearly three‑quarters of China’s imports since the coup were bound for companies registered in Yunnan Province.

Myanmar’s total reported wood exports rose from $304.3 million in 2019 to $370.6 million in 2022 but then fell to $198.9 million last year after the regime lost control over most of the border with Yunnan in Shan and Kachin states. But China continues to import timber through border crossings now controlled by ethnic armed groups.

Western buyers’ share now accounts for just 0.6 of Myanmar’s blood timber, but Forest Trends warns that the decline does not necessarily mean sanctions are working. Instead, the group believes much is “re-exported” to the West after “transiting through China,” though the flow is harder to trace.

Kokang scam warlord sentenced to death

A Chinese court on Tuesday sentenced three leaders of Myanmar’s notorious Wei clan to death as Beijing continues its public reckoning with the Kokang scam syndicates. The Quanzhou Intermediate People’s Court convicted Wei Huairen and two others of running violent fraud compounds that trafficked Chinese nationals, forced them into online scams, and murdered at least two victims.

According to Chinese state media, the Wei family’s network generated 12.2 billion yuan (US$1.8 billion) through online scams, drug trafficking, illegal casinos, and prostitution. Courts also handed life sentences to three associates and prison terms to 55 others, describing the gang as the “most violent criminal force in northern Myanmar.”

The Wei clan was one of four family crime syndicates in Kokang, which is now controlled by the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA). Wei Huairen was the chief of the regime-aligned Kokang Border Guard Force (BGF), in which capacity he created a much-emulated model of quasi-official armed protection of online fraud parks. The ruling follows earlier executions of Ming and Bai clan members.

Beijing renews outreach to Myanmar’s party leaders

The director‑general of the Chines Communist Party’s International Liaison Department, Peng Xiubin, met leaders of nine Myanmar political parties in Yangon on Tuesday, though none associated with the bona-fide opposition.

Present at the meeting were the usual suspects from the ruling Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) as well as a few co-opted ethnic political parties like the Arakan Front Party (AFP) and Shan and Nationalities Democratic Party (SNDP). Discussions focused on “bilateral ties” and Myanmar’s “peace and reconciliation,” according to participants.

SNDP chair Sai Aik Pao told the Popular News propaganda outlet that he urged Peng to help the central regime regain control over the Muse–Mandalay trade corridor, pushing out the MNDAA and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA).

“China has influence” over those armed groups, he was quoted as saying.

While the USDP remains at the center of party-to-party ties, China also often flies other party leaders to Kunming and Beijing for “study tours” and “cooperation forums.” Shortly after the regime announced its planned elections last year, the department hosted a delegation of several Myanmar political parties in Beijing.

Shan groups warn against MNDAA’s ‘Sinicization’

Eight Shan civil society and youth groups published an open letter to the MNDAA on Oct. 9, warning that its boorish cultural and administrative practices in northern Shan State threaten ethnic coexistence and China–Myanmar border stability.

The letter warns that the MNDAA’s military control is only temporary and urges it to respect local ethnic traditions, languages, and rights. The groups accuse the Chinese-speaking group of erasing Shan, Ta’ang and Burmese scripts from public signboards and replacing them with Chinese characters. They argue that imposing Chinese-style governance and financial systems without consultation undermines trust and risks fueling resistance.

Such actions could even jeopardize the future of the China–Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC), the letter warns, referring to the pet project of the MNDAA’s paymasters in Beijing.

Ta’ang civil society groups have similarly condemned the MNDAA’s actions. In April, six Ta’ang organizations said replacing Ta’ang signs with Chinese amounted to erasing an ethnic identity—a violation of international human rights law.

The MNDAA is busy consolidating its control of all major trade corridors linking to Yunnan Province.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Myanmar Regime Turns to Belarus for High Interest Loans as Fiscal Crisis Deepens
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime, squeezed by a worsening fiscal crisis, has turned to its ally Belarus for high‑interest loans, with its rubber-stamp parliament granting approval to borrow at rates nearing 10 percent.

On Wednesday, lawmakers endorsed coup leader Min Aung Hlaing’s proposal to secure loans from Belarus just eight days after he submitted the request to the Union Parliament. The loans will be used to purchase goods from Belarus.

The loans will come from the state-controlled Development Bank of the Republic of Belarus (DBRB) and Belinvestbank JSC, with maturities ranging from one to five years. The regime has not disclosed the total amount, but the high interest rates have already drawn criticism.

Deputy Finance Minister Than Than Lin told parliament on October 6 that rates would range from 2.25 to 9.33 percent. Her colleague Kyaw Htin argued on October 14 that the short‑term nature of the loans — capped at five years — would limit exposure to market volatility.

The loans can be denominated in Russian rubles, Belarusian rubles, yuan, US dollars, or euros, with interest rates varying by currency type and commodity group. The regime says it will pre‑screen payment channels to avoid currencies subject to sanctions.

Authorities plan to use the loans to import capital goods (machinery), intermediate goods (raw/semi-finished products), consumer products, and other commodities. Purchases of Belarusian‑made goods, machinery, technology, and services will be financed through Belarusian banks, with Myanmar ministries, agencies, or private firms acting as buyers. In effect, Belarusian exporters will supply the goods while Myanmar entities serve as importers.

Three state‑owned banks, Myanmar Economic Bank, Myanmar Foreign Trade Bank, and Myanmar Investment and Commercial Bank, have already signed banking arrangements with Belarus, and talks are underway to open accounts.

During Min Aung Hlaing’s August trip to Minsk, the regime signed nine agreements, including a loan framework deal between Myanmar’s Ministry of Finance and JSC Development Bank of Belarus.

While the junta chief has repeatedly insisted Myanmar must rely on domestic resources rather than foreign loans, his regime’s rush to secure Belarussian credit underscores the depth of its fiscal crisis. The loan approval came the same day that lawmakers nodded through the regime’s proposal to “borrow” up to 2.1 trillion kyats from the Central Bank of Myanmar to fill its 2026-27 budget deficit.

“Myanmar’s public will suffer from the high-interest loans, which will be repaid at the expense of education and health budgets,” said a Myanmar analyst.

Myanmar’s ties with Belarus were once limited to arms sales, but since the 2021 coup cooperation has expanded into politics, economics, and now finance. Belarus has emerged as a key ally alongside Russia, with Min Aung Hlaing visiting Minsk frequently while also hosting Belarusian strongman Alexander Lukashenko in Naypyitaw.

Lukashenko was the first foreign leader to visit Myanmar after Min Aung Hlaing installed himself as head of state in April.

Reports suggest the regime may next lean on Russia for credit, with President Vladimir Putin pledging financial sector cooperation in August while hosting Min Aung Hlaing in Moscow.

Meanwhile, the junta has cut imports of basic goods including fuel, cooking oil, and steel to save foreign currency, while squeezing revenue through tax hikes, natural resource sales, and tighter remittance rules for migrant workers.

After the World Bank, Asian Development Bank, and Western governments suspended aid and imposed sanctions following the coup, Min Aung Hlaing’s regime has been increasingly dependent on loans and support from his authoritarian allies, analysts say.

World.title: China’s Shrinking Politburo Has a Diversity Problem
World.content:
China’s Communist Party chose 24 men for its Politburo in October 2022, all of them Han Chinese. It was the first Politburo without a woman in 25 years, and it included nobody from any of China’s 55 officially recognized ethnic minority groups. After four years, the group is even more exclusive.

In October 2025, the party expelled Central Military Commission Vice Chairman He Weidong. Former Xinjiang Party Secretary Ma Xingrui followed in July 2026, and top general Zhang Youxia last month. Official notices accused all three of serious violations; the notice on Zhang also alleged disloyalty, “faction-building” and a remarkably large number of bribes. Their removal leaves an active Politburo of 21—a concentration that tells us something important about power under Xi Jinping. Diversity exists farther down the political system, often through quotas and administrative rules. It disappears where the most consequential decisions are made.

A narrowing funnel

The contrast starts with the membership. At the end of 2025, women accounted for 31.5 percent of the Communist Party of China’s 101.3 million members, while ethnic minority members made up 7.8 percent. Among people admitted in 2025, women made up 46.5 percent and ethnic minorities 10.2 percent, according to the Central Organization Department.

Representation was also visible at the 20th Party Congress. Its 2,296 delegates included 619 women or 27 percent, and 264 ethnic minority members or 11.5 percent, drawn from 40 minority groups. Then the funnel thins. Only 11 of the 205 full members elected to the 20th Central Committee were women, while nine came from ethnic minority groups. At the Politburo level, both figures fell to zero.

This isn’t a simple story of too few qualified candidates. Shen Yiqin, an ethnic Bai woman, had served as Guizhou governor and provincial party secretary before the 2022 congress. She became a state councilor in 2023 and later president of the All-China Women’s Federation, yet never entered the Politburo. Her current brief covers civil affairs, human resources, social security, veterans, sports and liaison with the ethnic affairs bureaucracy. Those duties matter, but a state councilor ranks below the Politburo members.

Rules stop below the top

China has spent decades building representation requirements. A 2001 party directive called for at least one woman in provincial and prefectural party, government, legislature and political advisory leadership teams, as well as in county party and government teams. It gave early priority to women in education, culture, health, family planning, civil affairs and similar departments. The 2021-2030 national program for women calls for more women in local government leadership, more female principal officials and better access to training, rotation and key posts.

Yet many targets use the phrase “gradually increase” without a numerical floor for the Central Committee, Politburo or its Standing Committee. The result is presence without a reliable route to the top.

A peer-reviewed study of every prefectural mayor and party secretary serving between 2003 and 2020 found that women followed faster but more restricted careers. Female officials were younger and better educated, but more often came through the Women’s Federation, Communist Youth League and other less powerful portfolios. Men had greater access to finance, development and core party offices. Women held only 135 of 1,987 mayoral posts and 88 of 1,694 party secretary posts.

The study also found a revealing pattern: about 20 percent of women mayors were ethnic minority members, compared with 13 percent of male mayors. One appointment could therefore satisfy expectations for both gender and ethnic representation, while leaving more positions open for Han Chinese men. The evidence supports this “tandem quota” effect at the prefectural mayor level, but it doesn’t establish that top leaders consciously use the same calculation when selecting the Politburo.

Ethnic glass ceiling

Ethnic minority cadres face a parallel divide. China’s ethnic autonomy law reserves the head-of-government in autonomous areas for a member of the relevant minority, but the more powerful party secretary post has generally gone to a Han Chinese official. For decades, minorities held roughly 10 percent to 11 percent of full and alternate Central Committee seats, yet most sat in the alternate tier.

No ethnic minority official has ever joined the Politburo Standing Committee. A handful reached the wider Politburo: Zhuang general Wei Guoqing and Mongolian leader Ulanhu served there during the Mao and early reform years; Hui Liangyu later served in the body and became a vice premier. Those cases show the barrier isn’t formal, but they also highlight how rarely it has been crossed.

Under Xi, official ethnic policy increasingly centers on “forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation.” At the 2021 Central Ethnic Work Conference, Xi linked good cadre standards to firm support for centralized party leadership and commitment to his national community project. The policy stresses political unity, shared identity and security more than representation by distinct groups.

Perhaps this policy did not directly cause the all-Han Politburo. Public records don’t reveal the bargaining, vetting or rejected candidates behind elite appointments. Still, the roster fits a system where minority identity can warrant representation in congresses and autonomous governments but offers little access to the center.

Diversity and decision quality

An all-male, all-Han Chinese Politburo doesn’t mean every member thinks alike. Nor does adding women or minority officials guarantee different policies. Officials who rise through the same selection system may share its priorities. But there is evidence that representation can affect what institutions do. Women held about one-fifth of the seats in China’s 12th National People’s Congress but sponsored 44 percent of legislative bill proposals and more than half of proposals concerning women’s rights and interests. That finding comes from the first systematic study of female legislators’ behaviour in the national legislature.

The useful question isn’t whether one woman or minority official would transform policy but whether the leadership is drawing on the country’s full pool of political experience. The body, after all, makes decisions on birthrates, employment, Xinjiang, Tibet and social welfare.

The practical tests are clear. Party authorities could publish measurable targets for women and ethnic minority officials at each rung of the promotion ladder, report compliance and place more candidates in finance, security, organization and provincial party secretary jobs that feed Politburo selection. They could also stop treating one minority woman as sufficient evidence that two representation goals have been met.

Watch the 21st Party Congress, expected in 2027. Count who enters the full Central Committee, who receives powerful provincial and central portfolios, and who reaches the Politburo. Speeches about equality are easy to issue. Twenty-one occupied seats provide the harder evidence.

Chandu Doddi is an Assistant Professor at the Centre for Chinese Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi.

World.title: Kazakhstan Resolves Long-Running Dunga Oil Dispute, Paving Way for New Development Plan
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan has reached an agreement to resolve a yearslong dispute over costs at the Dunga oil field in the Mangystau Region, clearing the way for a development plan targeting 67.4 million barrels of oil production through 2039, the Energy Ministry said in a written response to The Astana Times.

The agreement was signed on Oct. 5 by Kazakhstan’s Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov and KazMunayGas Deputy Chairman Ruslan Balykbayev, in the presence of representatives of PSA LLP, the country’s authorized body overseeing production-sharing agreements, and Dunga Operating GmbH, the field’s operator.

The ministry said the settlement would allow the parties to proceed with a new development plan for 2026-2039, which envisages substantial capital and operating investments in the field.

The document is expected to be submitted for signing to the consortium’s foreign partners, Oman Oil Company Limited and Thailand’s PTTEP Corporation.

The Dunga field was discovered in 1966 in the Tupkaragan district of the Mangystau Region in western Kazakhstan, entered trial production in 2000 and has been under full-scale development since 2007. The field operates under a production-sharing agreement originally signed between Kazakhstan and Oman Oil Company Limited in May 1994. In 2019, Kazakhstan and the consortium agreed to extend the Dunga production-sharing agreement by 15 years, from 2024 to 2039.

In November 2023, Kazakhstan’s national oil and gas company KazMunayGas acquired a 60% interest in the project from TotalEnergies for $358.5 million, according to the company’s financial statements.

The acquisition gave KazMunayGas control of Dunga Operating GmbH, which serves as the field’s operator. Oman Oil Company Limited and PTTEP Corporation each hold a 20% stake.

According to KazMunayGas, Dunga produced 677,300 tons of oil in 2025, compared with 630,000 tons in 2024 and 546,900 tons in 2023. Gas production exceeded 51 million cubic meters in 2025.

The dispute centered on whether certain historical expenses incurred by the project’s contractors were eligible for reimbursement under the production-sharing agreement. Such expenses from oil production are usually recovered before the remaining profit oil is divided between the state and investors.

Nurlan Zhumagulov, an energy analyst and founder of the Energy Monitor Telegram channel, said the project’s previous operator, France’s TotalEnergies, and other consortium partners, had recoverable costs amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars. He linked the resolution of the dispute with the field’s future production potential, saying it could help the operator to increase annual oil output to 850,000 tons.

According to Zhumagulov’s estimates, tax payments to Kazakhstan from the project totaled approximately 40 billion tenge (US$88.2 million) in 2025, including 32 billion tenge (US$70.6 million) representing the state’s share of profit oil.

The latest settlement also entails financial compensation to Kazakhstan. The Energy Ministry, however, did not specify the amount in its response to The Astana Times or provide a breakdown of the disputed historical expenses.

“The Dunga oil field has significant potential and is of strategic importance to the country’s energy sector,” said Kazakhstan’s Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov.

“The project’s development has long been hampered by unresolved disputes over non-recoverable costs. The agreements reached allow us to protect the state’s economic interests without lengthy legal proceedings and pave the way for a new investment cycle,” said Akkenzhenov.

The settlement is expected to facilitate implementation of the field’s development plan through 2039, with projected oil production of 67.4 million barrels over the period.

According to PSA, Kazakhstan’s authorized body overseeing production-sharing agreements, the third phase of Dunga’s development includes connecting previously drilled wells, expanding oil and gas processing capacity, upgrading export infrastructure and improving operational efficiency.

The settlement therefore removes a longstanding contractual disagreement from the project’s development agenda, allowing the consortium to move ahead with production and investment plans for the remaining life of the agreement.

World.title: Kazakhstan, US Reaffirm Strategic Partnership at C5+1 Meeting in Samarkand
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and the United States reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening their strategic partnership, expanding trade and investment, and advancing cooperation in energy, critical minerals, digitalization, and transport during meetings between Kazakhstan’s Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Samarkand on Oct. 19.

Kazakhstan-US talks focus on trade and investment

Tileuberdi and Rubio discussed prospects for developing the enhanced strategic partnership, emphasizing stronger trade, economic and investment cooperation, the ministry’s press service reported.

The officials noted the positive momentum in bilateral relations and reaffirmed their mutual interest in expanding practical cooperation, increasing trade turnover and implementing joint investment projects.

They focused on implementing agreements reached at the highest level, including those resulting from the meeting between President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and US President Donald Trump in November 2025.

Tileuberdi emphasized the importance of strengthening business ties, attracting U.S. investment and advanced technologies and developing cooperation in energy, critical minerals, digitalization and transport and logistics.

Tileuberdi and Rubio also exchanged views on preparations for the upcoming G20 Summit in Miami. Rubio confirmed his interest in visiting Kazakhstan soon after the summit.

C5+1 meeting advances regional cooperation

Tileuberdi also joined the C5+1 Ministerial Meeting with Rubio and the heads of foreign ministries of the Central Asian states.

Participants discussed expanding trade, economic, and investment cooperation; strengthening regional connectivity; and implementing joint initiatives to ensure sustainable economic growth.

Tileuberdi noted Kazakhstan’s and the United States’ historic role in establishing the C5+1 format, which has proven an effective platform for developing regional cooperation. He highlighted the importance of expanding trade, developing transport and logistics infrastructure, and diversifying supply chains.

Participants also considered prospects for implementing joint projects in critical minerals, energy, digitalization and innovation.

Following the meeting, the parties adopted a joint statement reflecting their readiness to strengthen long-term, mutually beneficial partnership and implement the agreements reached.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Exports Grow More Than Four Times Faster Than Imports in January-August
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s exports rose 19.5% year on year to $60.4 billion in January-August, outpacing import growth by more than four times and expanding the country’s trade surplus to $17.8 billion.

The country’s foreign trade turnover reached $103 billion, up 12.8% from the same period in 2025. Imports rose 4.5% to $42.6 billion, while the trade surplus widened from $9.8 billion a year earlier, QazTrade, the trade policy development center, reported on Oct. 16.

China remained Kazakhstan’s largest trading partner, with bilateral trade reaching $23.3 billion, or 22.7% of the country’s total foreign trade turnover. Russia ranked second at $18.3 billion (17.8%), followed by Italy at $11.8 billion (11.4%). Together, the three countries accounted for 51.9% of Kazakhstan’s foreign trade.

Türkiye ranked fourth, with trade turnover of $5.7 billion, followed by France at $4.5 billion. The Netherlands and Uzbekistan each recorded $3.8 billion, while trade with Germany reached $2.9 billion, the United States $2.7 billion and Spain $2 billion.

Trade flows varied by direction. Italy was Kazakhstan’s largest export destination, with shipments valued at $10.9 billion, narrowly ahead of China at $10.7 billion. Russia remained the country’s largest import supplier, accounting for $13.2 billion in imports.

Agricultural products and processed goods were among the fastest-growing export categories, reflecting stronger overseas demand for Kazakh products.

Sunflower oil exports rose 48.5% to $672.8 million, with shipments up 35.9% to 611,400 tons. Wheat exports rose 26.5% to $1.25 billion, with volumes up 13.8% to more than 5.5 million tons.

Wheat and wheat-rye flour exports rose 36% to $400 million, while shipment volumes increased 22.8% to 1.38 million tons.

Flaxseed exports more than doubled in value, rising 2.3 times to $387.8 million. Volumes increased 2.5 times to 780,800 tons. Exports of prepared animal feed products climbed 60.8% to $577.6 million, with physical volumes up 44.2%.

Combined exports of sunflower oil, flour and prepared animal feed products reached $1.65 billion, up around 48% year on year.

Metals and mining products also grew substantially. Copper and copper cathode exports rose 55.7% to $3.9 billion, while uranium exports increased 26.9% to $3.1 billion.

On the import side, industrial and energy equipment purchases expanded. Imports of electric generating sets rose 86.5% to $916.5 million, while imports of turbojet and turboprop engines, including gas turbines, increased 3.3 times to $611 million.

The January-August results highlight the expanding trade surplus, the growing contribution of agricultural processing to export earnings, and strong performance in metals and mining.

World.title: From Transit to Trade: Economic Opportunity After Avaza
World.content:
The eighth Consultative Meeting in Avaza, Turkmenistan, on Oct. 8 was the first regular summit since Azerbaijan became a full participant in the format in November 2025. It came in a year when the five Central Asian states and Azerbaijan mark the 35th anniversary of their independence. The six countries now have an opportunity to use this wider forum to build economic relationships that connect their producers and markets as closely as their transport routes.

Azerbaijan’s inclusion in the consultative format reflects the deep historical and cultural ties that have long connected the country with Central Asia. While the geographical boundaries of Central Asia remain unchanged, the expanded format creates new opportunities for political and economic cooperation across the Caspian. Its flexible nature allows governments to pursue projects that serve shared interests while preserving their sovereignty and independence.

At Avaza, Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proposed raising intraregional trade from about $13 billion in 2025 to at least $20 billion. Reaching that target will require greater attention to production and supply chains. More cargo moving through Central Asia does not automatically mean more goods being produced, processed or traded within the region. The challenge is to ensure that growing transit flows translate into stronger economic ties among the participating countries. Transport investment can support this growth when it helps local firms buy inputs from neighboring countries, reach new customers and invest across borders.

Together, Central Asia and Azerbaijan have more than 95.5 million people and an estimated combined GDP exceeding $645 billion. This is a substantial economic base for investments serving several national markets. Yet the potential of this market depends on how easily businesses can operate across borders. Simplifying customs procedures, reducing administrative barriers and making transport costs and delivery times more predictable would encourage companies to plan production and investment beyond their domestic markets.

None of the six countries has direct access to the open ocean, making reliable connections to international markets especially important. The Middle Corridor already links Chinese and European markets through Central Asia and the South Caucasus. Azerbaijan’s participation gives governments on both shores of the Caspian a regular opportunity to coordinate rail, port and shipping investment. Closer coordination could help address the gaps between national transport systems that affect the reliability of the entire route.

The World Bank estimates that, with infrastructure investment and reforms to improve transport efficiency, Middle Corridor volumes could quadruple by 2040 compared with 2023, while travel times could fall by two-thirds. The real measure of infrastructure investment, however, is not simply the capacity of individual railways or ports, but the reliability of the journey from producer to customer. A railway upgrade delivers greater economic value when cargo can move through the next port and border crossing without an avoidable wait. Improving connections between existing facilities is therefore as important as building new ones.

Tokayev also proposed that experts examine how the Middle Corridor could connect with TRIPP, the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity. An additional connection through the South Caucasus could widen Central Asian exporters’ options for reaching European markets. Its commercial value would depend on freight rates, transit arrangements and reliable onward connections. Assessing these factors at the expert level would help determine how the proposed link could complement existing transport networks and expand opportunities for regional trade.

Cooperation across the Caspian is also expanding beyond physical transport infrastructure. Kazakhtelecom and AzerTelecom have laid a 380-kilometer fiber-optic cable between Aktau and Sumgayit, with the new connection expected to become operational in 2026. This additional data route between Europe and Asia could support digital services and businesses that depend on reliable international communications. It also demonstrates how cooperation between Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan can create shared economic infrastructure in sectors other than freight transportation.

Another promising area is passenger connectivity. Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan are working to restore passenger ferry services between Kuryk and Baku, which could support joint Caspian tourism routes and allow visitors to combine destinations on both shores in one trip. Regular crossings would give hotels, tour operators and coastal communities access to a wider market, extending the benefits of regional connectivity beyond cargo transportation.

Stronger economic coordination could also improve the participating countries’ position in discussions with China, the European Union and other investment partners. Projects serving several national markets are more attractive when they form part of a coherent regional plan. By agreeing on common priorities and identifying missing infrastructure links, governments could give investors a clearer understanding of how individual projects contribute to wider trade networks. This would also help ensure that external investment supports local value-added production and mutually beneficial economic cooperation rather than transit capacity alone.

At the same time, closer cooperation with the South Caucasus should complement the priorities of the five Central Asian states. Water and energy remain particularly important because decisions about irrigation and hydropower affect agricultural production, electricity supply and investment across national borders. Regular information exchange and agreements that account for upstream and downstream needs would make economic planning more dependable. Progress in these areas would strengthen the economic foundations of Central Asian cooperation while creating more favorable conditions for wider partnerships.

Turning these opportunities into results will require consistent follow-up between summits. The consultative format does not need extensive supranational institutions to deliver practical benefits. It needs clear responsibilities, realistic timetables and regular coordination among the ministries, transport operators and businesses involved in joint projects. Identifying obstacles early and resolving them through existing channels would help ensure that political agreements translate into improvements that businesses can actually use.

Shared investments and regular commerce can give the countries that met in Avaza a lasting interest in one another’s economic success. For a producer in Central Asia, progress would mean being able to accept an order from abroad with confidence in the cost, the route and the rules for getting it to the customer. The success of the expanded consultative format will ultimately depend on whether stronger transport connections can generate more trade, investment and production among the participating economies. Moving from connecting routes to connecting economies would give this partnership a durable foundation for the years ahead.

Bauyrzhan Auken is a lead expert in the Department of Asian Studies at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies under the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan.

World.title: Kazakhstan Wins Two Gold Medals at Asian Para Games in Japan
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan won two gold medals at the fifth Asian Para Games in Japan, with Yerkin Gabbasov and David Degtyarev taking gold in para shooting and para powerlifting.

Gabbasov secured Kazakhstan’s first gold in the men’s 10-meter air rifle standing event (R1), scoring 249.1 points in the final, reported the National Olympic Committee’s press service on Oct. 19.

Degtyarev claimed the second gold in para powerlifting in the up to 54-kilogram category, lifting 191 kilograms to set a new Asian Para Games record.

Kazakhstan also earned silver in para powerlifting, with Tursynai Kabyl finishing second in the up to 41-kilogram category after completing all three attempts and lifting 104 kilograms in her final attempt.

The games opened in Nagoya on Oct. 18 and will run through Oct. 24 across venues in Aichi Prefecture and Nagoya, bringing together around 4,000 athletes from 45 Asian countries. Kazakhstan has sent 150 athletes to compete in 12 sports, including wheelchair tennis, where the country is making its debut.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Representative Elected OIC Assistant Secretary-General
World.content:
ASTANA – Deputy Foreign Minister Arman Issagaliyev called for resolving conflicts through political and diplomatic means during the 52nd Session of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) Council of Foreign Ministers in Baghdad on Oct. 18. Baghdad Amreyev was elected OIC assistant secretary-general for administration and finance.

Kazakhstan reaffirmed its commitment to resolving international conflicts through diplomacy and strengthening multilateral cooperation at the meeting, which brought together representatives of OIC member states to discuss regional and global challenges, the ministry’s press service reported on Oct. 18.

Delegations addressed the Palestinian-Israeli conflict, humanitarian crises and other security challenges affecting the Islamic world. Participants emphasized the need to intensify diplomatic efforts to de-escalate tensions in the Middle East and promote regional peace and stability.

In his statement, Issagaliyev stressed that conflicts should be resolved exclusively through political and diplomatic means, in accordance with international law and the United Nations Charter. He called for stronger multilateral dialogue and coordinated efforts among OIC member states to advance peace, security and sustainable development.

Kazakhstan also highlighted priorities including nuclear non-proliferation, food security, transport and logistics connectivity, artificial intelligence, digitalization and advanced technologies. The Kazakh delegation also raised environmental cooperation, notably the rehabilitation of the former Semipalatinsk Nuclear Test Site.

Kazakhstan’s representative elected OIC assistant secretary-general

A key outcome for Kazakhstan was the election of Baghdad Amreyev as assistant secretary-general of the OIC for administration and finance. The appointment reflects member states’ support for Kazakhstan’s active participation in the organization.

Following the session, OIC member states adopted a package of resolutions covering political, economic, legal, cultural and humanitarian topics. All initiatives proposed by Kazakhstan have been incorporated into the relevant outcome documents.

World.title: EFSD Raises Kazakhstan’s 2027 Growth Forecast to 5%, Expects Inflation to Ease
World.content:
ASTANA – The Eurasian Fund for Stabilization and Development (EFSD) has raised its forecast for Kazakhstan’s economic growth in 2027 to 5%, up from 4.6% in its previous outlook, while projecting a gradual decline in inflation through 2029.

The fund expects Kazakhstan’s gross domestic product (GDP) to grow by 5% in 2026, following 6.5% growth in 2025. Growth is projected to remain at 5% in 2027 before slowing to 4.2% in 2028 and 4.1% in 2029, according to the EFSD’s autumn regional economic outlook.

The revised forecast reflects expectations of sustained oil production, major investment and infrastructure projects, and a more expansionary fiscal policy. However, the fund warns that strong domestic demand and continued budget stimulus could complicate efforts to bring inflation under control.

“The main challenge for economic policy will be to strike a balance between supporting economic growth and maintaining price, fiscal and external stability,” said Sergei Ulatov, the EFSD’s chief economist.

Oil production and investment to support growth

The EFSD expects Kazakhstan’s economy to maintain relatively strong growth despite less favorable global conditions, including geopolitical tensions, higher transportation costs and volatility in commodity markets.

The fund forecasts 5% GDP growth in 2026, unchanged from its summer outlook. The estimate reflects the recovery of oil production at the Tengiz field to full capacity in the second quarter, steady performance in non-oil sectors and high investment activity by the quasi-public sector.

Additional support is expected from fiscal policy in the second half of the year, including a planned targeted transfer of 1.5 trillion tenge (US$3 billion) through the Infrastructure Development Fund.

Elevated commodity prices amid global uncertainty are also expected to support export revenues and activity in resource-producing companies. The outlook for 2027 has improved, with the EFSD raising its growth forecast from 4.6% to 5%. The revision is based on expectations that oil production will remain stable, large-scale investment and infrastructure projects will proceed, and fiscal policy will provide stronger support.

However, the fund expects consumer demand to remain relatively subdued because of moderately tight monetary conditions, slower retail lending and weak growth in real household incomes. In 2028-2029, growth is expected to moderate as the effects of increased oil production fade and domestic demand returns to more sustainable levels.

Inflation to decline gradually through 2029

The EFSD expects inflation to reach 9.5% by the end of 2026, down from its previous forecast of 9.8%. The revision reflects slower price growth amid weaker increases in regulated services and fuel and lubricants prices, as well as a stronger tenge.

Inflation is projected to decline further to 8.8% in 2027, 7.8% in 2028 and 6.8% in 2029. However, the fund expects inflation to remain above the National Bank of Kazakhstan’s 5% target throughout the forecast period.
