Ethnographer Svetlana Poghosyan argues that it is wrong to describe Armenians as unthrifty:

“The fact is that we do not have much trust in banks or investment funds. We know from various historical sources that Armenians preferred to buy valuable items. Women, in particular, regularly wore silver belts and headdresses, as well as gold jewellery. During disasters and wars, they could take these possessions with them. The same applies to household utensils. Families used their savings to buy items they could carry with them, such as copper vessels, jugs and tools.”

According to her, most Armenians remain thrifty today, using their savings to buy homes, cars and gold jewellery:

“But even now, many people keep their money under the mattress, just as their ancestors did. The banking collapse of the 1990s contributed significantly to this. People had saved money for years and trusted a banking system that collapsed overnight, leaving them with nothing. Both they and the next generation regard the banking system with caution and scepticism.”

As for young people, the ethnographer says they choose different ways to save and invest in their future:

“They consider education, travel and gaining experience to be investments in their future. These are indeed important investments nowadays. Young people may not accumulate savings in bank accounts or buy gold, but they are investing in their future. So rather than viewing our compatriots as a society that does not save, let us see them as a society that prefers different ways of saving, in response to the demands of the times.”

Svetlana Poghosyan notes that, according to various international surveys, people in many countries prefer to keep their savings in banks or investments. The picture in Armenia is different: one in three people keeps their savings at home, in the form of cash or gold jewellery.

“At the same time, some Armenian families believe that saving money does not mean financial security, but rather giving up life’s pleasures. Some people are against saving and want to spend whatever money they have immediately, getting the maximum enjoyment out of it. But this behaviour is not typical of the population as a whole.”

World.title: “We owe a debt to nature”: Leaders’ summit at COP17 in Armenia
World.content:
Leaders’ summit at COP17 in Armenia

A summit under the slogan “Leaders for Nature” is taking place in Armenia as part of the COP17 conference. Up to 15,000 participants from 196 countries are expected to attend the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity.

According to the organisers, representatives of governments, international organisations and civil society will gather from 19 to 30 October to “assess humanity’s progress in conserving biodiversity and discuss further joint steps”.

The leaders’ summit was opened by Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, who stressed that hosting the conference was a great honour for Armenia. He expressed hope that it would “be productive and contribute to protecting our planet’s biodiversity”.

“We – the citizens of Armenia, the government, state authorities and local governments – owe a debt to our nature,” the prime minister said.

He noted that the international community had already developed the concept of “living in harmony with nature” and adopted the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework in 2022, setting out goals and specific targets to be achieved by 2030.

“We are halfway towards achieving these goals, and we must honestly acknowledge that we are not yet moving in the right direction. Our task now is not to make new promises, but to fulfil the commitments we have already made,” Nikol Pashinyan said.

The COP17 conference is expected to adopt a declaration at leaders’ level. More than 30 documents are scheduled for discussion. If approved, the commitments set out in them will become legally binding on countries that are parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity.

Pashinyan: “Nature saved us in difficult times”

According to the prime minister, Armenia has a special responsibility towards nature because, during difficult times for the country, “it saved us, and we had the misfortune of abusing it”.

In particular, he referred to:

Widespread deforestation (“In the early 1990s, the country faced an energy and socio-economic crisis. Amid electricity and gas outages and shortages of petroleum products and coal, people heated their homes using wood-burning stoves”);

Poaching, including illegal fishing in Lake Sevan;

Cases of illegal exploitation of natural resources.

Pashinyan said that after becoming prime minister in 2018, he decided to put an end to illegal logging. The government also took steps to protect fish stocks in Lake Sevan, including introducing fishing regulations and establishing a water police force.

“And the results are clear. Over the past 10 years, the total stock (biomass) of whitefish in Lake Sevan has increased more than tenfold. From just a few hundred tonnes during the crisis of the mid-2010s, when the species was effectively on the brink of extinction, we have reached more than 4,500 tonnes as of July 2026,” he stressed.

At the same time, the prime minister acknowledged that violations continued despite the progress made. To address the problem, an environmental patrol service was established two years ago. It is already operating in four of the country’s 10 regions.

“The task of this service is to ensure round-the-clock environmental protection. We intend to continue developing it, both in terms of technical equipment and the scale of its operations, as well as the professionalism and integrity of its staff,”Pashinyan said.

UN Secretary-General: “We will inevitably face serious challenges”

António Guterres stressed that tackling three crises – climate change, biodiversity loss and environmental pollution – had become one of his main priorities as UN Secretary-General.

Guterres believes that humanity must unite and work together to protect nature:

“Water, air and soil are gifts of biodiversity that we all benefit from every day. However, climate change, the uncontrolled use of pesticides, heavy metal pollution, biodiversity loss and climate chaos are now putting these resources at risk.”

In his view, humanity will inevitably face serious challenges unless action is taken.

He also believes that previously adopted agreements alone are not enough to address these challenges. According to the UN Secretary-General, both state institutions and civil society must be involved in implementing them:

“The participation of young people and the involvement of women are extremely important. By placing knowledge at the heart of biodiversity efforts, we will be able to effectively manage the most powerful artificial intelligence systems.”

Speeches by leaders of neighbouring countries

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian:

“Wars do not only cause human casualties and destroy infrastructure. They also lead to the destruction of forests, fertile soils, wetlands and water resources. Moreover, the use of weapons releases hazardous chemicals and heavy metals into the environment.

The destruction of the natural environment is a direct consequence of war. This problem poses a serious threat to the well-being of future generations in our region, including in Iran.

The environmental consequences of military aggression require urgent action by the international community.

The war launched by the United States and Israel against Iran is causing severe damage to the country’s ecosystems.

We expect the international community to establish effective and transparent mechanisms to protect our natural heritage and biodiversity. No state should ever be allowed to turn nature into a silent and defenceless victim of war.”

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze:

“Georgia’s natural heritage continues to play an important role in the country’s economic and social development. Healthy ecosystems and sustainable agriculture help preserve water resources, attract tourists and create opportunities for small businesses to grow and develop.

Protecting them is therefore not merely an environmental responsibility, but an investment in improving economic competitiveness, creating jobs and ensuring long-term prosperity.

The shared ecosystems of the South Caucasus provide a foundation for closer regional cooperation and sustainable development.

Georgia is committed to working with its neighbours to protect this shared natural heritage.”

Turkey‘s Minister of Agriculture and Forestry, Ibrahim Yumaklı, also attended the leaders’ summit, although he was not among the speakers. There have been no reports of representatives from Azerbaijan arriving in Yerevan.

World.title: Why Abkhazia’s harvest festival became Russian tourists’ feast of gluttony
World.content:
Social media users in Abkhazia are sounding the alarm: the traditional harvest festival of Lykhnashta has turned into a food show. Video footage showing Russian tourists sweeping free food off the tables has sparked widespread outrage, verging on panic.

Lykhnashta is a traditional autumn harvest festival held in mid-October in a meadow of the same name in Abkhazia’s Gudauta district. Farmers showcase their produce and serve visitors traditional Abkhaz dishes. The festivities also feature folk celebrations, horse-riding competitions, archery and other traditional spectacles and activities.

The festival has a centuries-old history and holds great significance for Abkhaz people. However, in recent years, locals have increasingly complained that it has “mutated” into an all-you-can-eat buffet for greedy and ill-mannered tourists.

The authors of a popular blog about tourism say some travel agencies and unlicensed guides organise food tours on the day, advertising the food laid out on the tables as “free grub” without explaining the festival’s significance or the rules of behaviour to visitors.

As a result, tourists — mostly Russians, who make up the bulk of visitors to Abkhazia — sometimes do more than simply eat the food in unlimited quantities. They try to take as much as they can away with them, stuffing bags with anything they can reach and even stripping edible decorations from the displays.

Many locals now prefer to avoid the festival altogether rather than witness this disgraceful behaviour. Meanwhile, social media users are collectively trying to work out how to prevent the festival from being ruined for good. One proposal is to ban tourists from attending altogether.

ПProfessional event organiser Khibla Vozba believes such radical measures are unnecessary and that the problem lies not with the guests, but with the hosts. He says the festival has largely turned into a food event and that organisers need to restore its former, more culturally focused format.

“Why does the current format fail? Because if free food is the festival’s main attraction, it will draw people who come for the food. No amount of urging them to behave differently will change that. The structure needs to change.”

In his view, the emphasis should shift from food and hospitality to history. After all, the meadow where the festival takes place is a fascinating and sacred site where the Abkhaz people have gathered for centuries to discuss important issues collectively.

“I propose refocusing Lykhnashta on ethnography and history and turning it into Abkhazia’s biggest event, where visitors can discover our traditions, culture and rituals and learn about the people’s ancient history. Food will remain part of the festival, but it will no longer take centre stage,” Khibla Vozba writes.

In his view, the festival could centre on a theatrical performance featuring a historical re-enactment staged by professionals. Organisers could also offer something like an introduction to ethnography, explaining ancient customs and traditions.

Vozba acknowledges that this transformation will take more than a year and will not be easy, but believes it will be worth the effort.

“The first few years will bring resistance: both visitors and organisers will have to give up familiar habits. But the result will be an event that attracts a different audience, encourages different behaviour on site and projects a different image in the media. Lykhnashta will become a festival that people travel to Abkhazia for, including outside the summer season.”

He adds that each era has given the festival its own meaning, and that the task today is to restore Lykhnashta’s dignity and purpose.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Abkhazia’s harvest festival

World.title: 10,000 lari instead of flat: What Georgia’s government is offering displaced people
World.content:
Georgia’s housing programme for displaced people

The government is offering displaced families the option of receiving cash instead of housing. The compensation amounts to 10,000 lari (around $3,860) for each eligible family member. These are the terms of a new programme announced by the government formed by the Georgian Dream party.

The authorities hope this mechanism will speed up the process of resettling displaced people. However, experts warn that the sum is unlikely to cover the cost of buying a home. Families who accept the payment will also lose access to further government support.

What is changing?

The new programme gives displaced people an additional option: instead of waiting for the state to buy them a flat or house, they can apply for cash compensation.

Participation is voluntary. The government says it will continue building apartment blocks and running its housing purchase programme in rural areas for those who do not opt for compensation.

The housing programme for displaced people was launched under the Saakashvili administration. According to Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, it will continue for at least another ten years.

On 12 October 2026, Kobakhidze announced a new programme for those unwilling to wait for apartment blocks to be built. It offers compensation of 10,000 lari for each family member.

As Irakli Kobakhidze announced, the government has allocated 58 million lari (around $22.4 million) to the programme this year. He estimates that existing resettlement schemes will need at least another ten years to meet the needs of all the families still waiting for housing.

Who is eligible for the payment?

Under the ministerial order, people qualify for compensation if they hold internally displaced person (IDP) status, qualify for long-term housing assistance and have not previously benefited from the relevant government programme.

The agency will verify each family’s composition and check who lives at the address listed in the application. It will pay the compensation no later than 45 calendar days after the application period closes.

A family of four whose members all qualify would therefore receive a total of 40,000 lari. However, simply belonging to the same family does not guarantee eligibility: the authorities must confirm each person’s entitlement separately.

Does eligibility extend to children and descendants?

Internally displaced person (IDP) status does not apply only to people who personally left an occupied territory. A child whose parent holds IDP status can also qualify.

However, obtaining IDP status and applying for state-provided housing are two different things. A child’s IDP status does not automatically mean that the state must provide them with housing.

When allocating housing, the state considers people born before 1 January 2023. Those who were minors on that date count as members of their family when the authorities allocate housing to their parents or other adult relatives. In other words, the state takes children into account when determining the size and other parameters of the family’s accommodation, but they cannot claim a separate flat once they reach adulthood.

As a rule, the state’s obligation to provide housing does not extend to children born on or after 1 January 2023. There is one exception: if an IDP parent or parents die before receiving housing, the child becomes entitled to the accommodation that the state would have provided to their parent or parents.

Why is the programme facing criticism?

One of the main criticisms concerns property prices. Critics question whether families forced to leave their homes can afford to buy another property with the proposed payment, particularly if they have no savings.

The Social Justice Center has issued a statement on the financial compensation scheme for displaced people. The organisation warns that the initiative could leave families without housing or savings facing homelessness and social exclusion.

The Social Justice Center points out that the government has not explained how it calculated the 10,000-lari payment. It also remains unclear whether the authorities based the figure on any property market research. The organisation further stresses that even several tens of thousands of lari — the amount a large family might receive — may not be enough.

The organisation is also seeking clarification on whether families must use the money specifically to buy a home, and what support, if any, they can expect if they cannot afford one.

This question is particularly important because the official order defines the compensation as a form of “long-term resettlement”, implying that the payment comes in exchange for housing. The organisation is urging the authorities to explain the programme’s legal consequences in advance and guarantee continued support for families.

How many families are still waiting for housing?

According to the Public Defender’s report, Georgia had 300,492 internally displaced people and 97,280 displaced families at the end of 2025. Of these, 45,160 families had yet to receive long-term housing. Georgia

In 2025, various programmes resettled 4,636 families. The report continues to highlight delays in construction, insufficient funding for temporary rental accommodation and safety concerns over some residential buildings.

“You can buy a sofa for 10,000 lari, but not a flat”

“You can buy a sofa for 10,000 lari, but not a flat,” Koka Markelia, 26, tells JAMnews. His parents were displaced from Abkhazia.

Koka works as a programmer. He finished school in Zugdidi but could not find a job there, so he stayed in Tbilisi. He has been renting a flat with his parents for more than ten years.

He wants to get married and move out on his own. He says he has a stable job, but under the current rules, the bank will not approve a mortgage.

Everyone in the family works, although his parents are self-employed: his mother works as a nanny, and his father is a mechanic. Only Koka has an official income, so the bank will not grant the family a loan. He says 10,000 lari would not even cover the deposit required for a mortgage. As a result, he will not receive the compensation.

“How much do we pay in rent? If they had offered us a flat with a mortgage, we would already have our own home. What am I supposed to do with these 10,000 lari? What can I buy with that money? I would take it and spend it on little things because I could not do anything meaningful with it. So it is better not to accept the money; otherwise, I would lose the prospect of getting a flat one day,” Koka says.

We checked two popular property websites but could not find a house for 10,000 lari, either in Tbilisi or in the regions.

In Koka Markelia’s home town of Zugdidi, for example, we found just one house listed for 10,000 lari — and it is due for demolition. Even if the Markelia family pooled all its money, it could not buy a house in Zugdidi for 30,000 lari.

“We cannot even buy a house in Zugdidi for that amount. And even if we could, how would we move there? Would we find work? If I worked as a nanny there, I would earn less than a third of what I make now,” says Koka’s mother, Irma.

The government’s initiative has sparked sarcastic jokes online.

“I’m sitting here wondering whether to buy two flats with these 10,000 lari or compete with Coca-Cola,” Gela Khasaia, an activist displaced from Abkhazia who also rents a flat in Tbilisi, wrote on Facebook.

Why is resettlement taking decades?

The government laid the foundations for its long-term housing policy in a national strategy approved in 2007. In 2009, it also adopted an action plan to implement the strategy.

The process got off to a painful start, marked by serious disputes and human rights violations. A 2011 study by Amnesty International documented cases of forced evictions from temporary accommodation in Tbilisi, a lack of proper consultation with residents and difficulties finding sources of income after relocation.

At the time, the authorities offered people displaced from Abkhazia who lived in Tbilisi housing in other regions, prompting widespread protests. The main challenge of relocating to the regions was the loss of income and familiar social networks. Although families received renovated flats, they often found themselves in areas with few job opportunities and limited access to basic services.

Under the Georgian Dream government, the resettlement process has continued through several schemes: providing flats in newly built or renovated buildings, purchasing private houses and formally transferring ownership of homes that displaced people already occupy. According to the Public Defender’s report, 4,636 families received long-term housing in 2025, compared with 2,022 in 2024. Nevertheless, 45,160 families were still waiting for housing at the end of 2025.

The process continues to face construction delays and inadequate housing conditions. The Public Defender’s 2025 report notes that the 300-lari allowance for temporary rent does not cover displaced people’s needs. Concerns also remain over the safety of some buildings that the authorities have already transferred to families.

The parties also discussed opportunities to further strengthen mutual interest and cultural ties between the two nations through sports such as judo and sumo. The significance of prestigious competitions held in Azerbaijan in these sports was emphasized.

At the conclusion of the meeting, Jeyhun Bayramov expressed his gratitude to Ambassador Katsuya Watanabe for his efforts during his diplomatic tenure in Azerbaijan and wished him success in his future endeavors. The parties also exchanged views on other issues of mutual interest.

World.title: INPEX, Sumitomo Osaka Cement test reusable CO₂ capture technology
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 19. Japanese companies INPEX Corporation and Sumitomo Osaka Cement have launched demonstration testing of a technology designed to capture carbon dioxide (CO₂) using reusable calcium compounds, the companies said.

INPEX said on October 19 that the technology, known as calcium looping (Ca-Looping), converts captured CO₂ into calcium carbonate, which can be transported under normal temperature and pressure conditions.

“A demonstration facility has been installed at the National Maritime Research Institute in Mitaka City, Tokyo, where testing is currently underway,” said the company.

In the process, CO₂ from large vessels and other sources is captured using an alkaline solution and converted into calcium carbonate through a reaction with calcium hydroxide. The material is then transported to a CO₂ storage site, where it is processed to release CO₂ for permanent underground storage. The resulting calcium oxide is subsequently regenerated into calcium hydroxide for reuse.

The companies are initially developing the technology for installation on large vessels, as international regulations on shipping emissions become increasingly stringent. They also aim to expand its application across other sectors and contribute to the effective use of CO₂ storage sites operated or owned by INPEX in Japan and overseas.

INPEX said the initiative aligns with its Vision 2035, which identifies research and development as a key driver of competitive advantage and future growth.

Sumitomo Osaka Cement, meanwhile, aims to advance carbon-related businesses in line with its SOCN2050 carbon neutrality vision, which includes the production and use of artificial limestone and the exploration of carbon capture and storage (CCS) in cooperation with partners.

By combining INPEX’s expertise in CO₂ separation, capture, and geological storage with Sumitomo Osaka Cement’s carbon mineralization technologies, the companies aim to accelerate the development of solutions supporting decarbonization.

World.title: After MP 'attacked' in the street, our democracy is facing its biggest test
World.content:
"This wasn't an accident."

With those words, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese laid bare the horrifying nature of an attack that has sent shock waves through Australia.

Independent MP Helen Haines was going about her day in the regional Victorian town of Wangaratta when a four-wheel drive struck her outside her electorate office.

The 65-year-old, who has represented the people of Indi since 2019, suffered critical injuries in an attack now under police investigation.

A man is in custody, and while it is too early to conclude whether his alleged actions were politically motivated, the possibility alone is deeply disturbing.

Australians are accustomed to seeing their local politicians in the supermarket, at the footy or simply walking down the street.

They knock on doors, hold mobile offices, attend community events and make themselves available to constituents who want to raise concerns or have a chat.

It's easy to be cynical about politicians, but their accessibility is one of the great strengths of Australia's democracy.

That will now be seriously tested.

Loading...

Shock across political spectrum

Albanese was understandably emotional as he spoke about the attack on Haines just hours later.

He was joined by voices from every corner of Australian politics in expressing his horror at the incident and wishing the MP a full recovery.

While careful not to pre-empt the police investigation, Albanese also took the opportunity to repeat his calls to turn down the temperature of political debate.

He has often said parliamentarians should be able to carry out their work without fear of threats or intimidation, and warned about the consequences of personal vilification and increasingly aggressive political commentary.

Those concerns are not confined to the prime minister.

For years, the Australian Federal Police has been highlighting an alarming rise in threats directed at politicians, their families and staff.

The latest figures show the AFP received 1,067 reports of threatening, harassing, nuisance or offensive behaviour involving federal parliamentarians, high office holders and protected locations in the past financial year.

That was a 12 per cent increase on the previous year and almost double the 555 reports recorded in 2021-22.

Not every report involves a credible threat of violence, and the figures cover more than MPs and senators alone.

But they demonstrate the scale of the hostility increasingly confronting people in public office.

Loading...

AFP's warning

In March last year, then AFP commissioner Reece Kershaw delivered a sober warning to a parliamentary committee about the threats facing politicians ahead of the federal election.

He revealed some male politicians had been sent bullets in the mail, while female parliamentarians were subjected to particularly disturbing abuse, including threats of sexual violence.

In some cases, the threats extended to their children.

Just this month, AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett told the ABC she expected "high office holders and politicians will continue to be targeted by those who hold grievances".

She said while terror investigators were increasingly seeing cases with "ideological" motivations, another factor was emerging: "grievance".

Barrett said people who were feeling distanced and alone were "looking for something to attach to, to give them meaning and purpose".

"We are seeing a bit of a shift there that the grievance is what's actually driving them and then they're looking for some sort of ideological motivation to attach to," she said.

Examples mount across parties

There has been no shortage of examples demonstrating why police are concerned.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has spoken publicly about the threats directed at her and her family, and the security arrangements she believes are necessary to protect her.

Liberal MP Andrew Hastie has faced threats serious enough to prompt additional security arrangements at his home and electorate office.

Just last week, Labor minister Anne Aly revealed she had received 19 death threats in a week.

Others have faced criminal threats serious enough to result in charges.

Earlier this year, a Sydney man was charged after allegedly threatening to kill a federal parliamentarian over the phone.

Last year, Victorian men were charged in separate cases involving alleged death threats against federal MPs, including antisemitic abuse.

These are not isolated concerns confined to one political party, one side of an ideological divide or one contentious policy debate.

Nor are they limited to the anonymous abuse politicians have long endured online.

The rise in incidents has raised the question of whether elected representatives can safely do their jobs.

Loading

Warnings come to pass

The AFP has established specialist investigative teams to respond to the growing threat, while security arrangements for individual politicians have come under greater scrutiny.

But there are limits to what even the most extensive protective measures can achieve without changing the way politicians interact with the public.

Police officers stationed outside every electorate office or security checks at every community event would represent a very different Australian democracy.

Voters are entitled to be angry with their elected representatives, but there is an important distinction between robust debate and intimidation or threats.

Police must now be allowed to establish the facts of the attack on Haines.

But the incident has brought into sharp focus the safety concerns that security agencies and parliamentarians have been warning about for years.

World.title: What we know about the 'attack' on Helen Haines
World.content:
The road outside the electorate office of independent MP Helen Haines has become an active police scene after the 65-year-old was allegedly struck by a vehicle this afternoon.

Ms Haines was critically injured in the incident, which has been described by the prime minister as an "attack".

Here's what we know.

What happened?

According to police, initial investigations have determined Ms Haines was struck by a Toyota LandCruiser about 3:30pm on Murphy Street, outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, Victoria.

One witness told the ABC she heard a bang and saw a woman pinned between two cars.

Loading...

A 43-year-old Tarrawingee man was stopped by a member of the public and has since been taken into custody, police said in a statement.

Police said a knife was found in the vehicle and they were investigating whether the incident was "intentional".

But Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has described the incident as a deliberate attack.

The prime minister told 7.30: "We know that this was a serious incident."

"The first I was told was that there'd been a car accident, so I did not think of anything other than an accident," he said.

"This wasn't an accident and the suspect is in custody."

Helen Haines hit by car Independent MP Helen Haines has been critically injured in what the prime minister says was a deliberate attack, sparking shock and anger across the political spectrum.

It is understood the driver is known to police and will undergo a mental health assessment.

Acting Superintendent Ashley Mason said the scene was "quite dynamic" and that detectives from the Major Collision Investigation Unit would be investigating.

Mr Albanese has said a joint counter terrorism unit had been activated but it was too early to say what was behind the incident.

MP suffers critical injuries

Victoria Police said Ms Haines had suffered critical injuries as a result of the alleged attack.

She was rushed to hospital and flown to Melbourne to undergo emergency surgery for severe injuries to her lower body.

Ms Haines's family has released a statement on the incident, thanking first responders for their swift response and asking for privacy amid the ongoing investigation.

"This afternoon, our beloved Helen was involved in an incident outside her Wangaratta Electorate Office, and is receiving medical care," the statement reads.

"Our family, and Helen's staff, will be making no further comment at this time, and ask that their privacy be respected by the public and media.

"Please keep Helen in your thoughts."

How have politicians responded?

Ms Haines has been described as a respected political figure across party divides.

Mr Albanese has called Ms Haines a "beacon of light" for the regional community in Northern Victoria.

Anthony Albanese speaks to 7.30's Sarah Ferguson about the Helen Haines incident. (ABC News)

He said Ms Haines was someone "loved and admired because she's someone of integrity".

The prime minister also called for the "political temperature" to be lowered amid increasing rhetoric of violence against representatives.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said he was deeply shocked by the incident.

"Our nation cannot become a place where violent attacks are normalised," he said.

Victorian Premier Ben Carroll said he was "appalled" by the "violent attack" on Helen Haines.

Live: Indi MP Helen Haines critically injured after 'attack' at electorate office Anthony Albanese says counter-terrorism police are investigating and a man has been arrested after Indi MP Helen Haines was "attacked" near her electorate office in Victoria's north-east. Follow the latest in our live blog.

"My thoughts, and the thoughts of all Victorians, are with Helen, her family, her friends, her colleagues and her community," he said.

"I know how devastating this will be for the Wangaratta community and all those who Helen represents.

"Thank you to police, paramedics, firefighters and witnesses for their immediate response.

"An individual has been apprehended, and I thank police for their swift action."

Who is Helen Haines?

Helen Haines has long served regional communities in Victoria both as a nurse and midwife, most recently as a member for parliament, representing Indi as an independent leader since 2019.

She became the first independent elected to succeed another independent in the federal parliament.

On her website, Ms Haines introduces herself as a health care professional from a small farming community.

She says she grew up alongside her four brothers on a dairy farm in the south-west of the state, where she learned "the value of pitching in and looking out for others".

As a 26-year-old, Ms Haines took on the role of matron at Chiltern Bush Nursing Hospital.

She also worked at Wangaratta Hospital, leading midwifery services and helping build one of Australia's longest-running rural midwifery programs.

"Over three decades, I've worked across rural health as a nurse, midwife, researcher and academic," she wrote.

Years later, Ms Haines, says her formative career in nursing remains a guiding force in her political work.

"As a nurse and a midwife, you're with people in their most joyous and difficult moments," Ms Haines wrote.

"It's taught me that life is precious, that everyone deserves dignity and respect, that good policy starts with listening, and — as a health researcher — that facts matter," she wrote.

World.title: Israel police arrest suspects over settler attacks
World.content:
Israeli police say they have arrested 10 people in the West Bank after settler attacks on an American photographer and a French mayor.

The arrests were made after calls from the United States to crack down on settler violence and for the perpetrators of the attack on the Washington Post photojournalist to be jailed.

France, Belgium and Poland, whose diplomats were attacked, have also called on Israel to take action.

The police said that they raided several locations across the West Bank and also seized potential evidence related to the attacks, which have stepped up as settlers disrupt Palestinians' annual olive harvest.

"Following the severe incidents of violence over the past weekend, including the assault of a media worker and the suspected attacks on foreign civilians, an arrest operation was conducted before dawn," said Major General Moshe Finchi, the Israeli police's West Bank commander.

"Suspects were arrested on suspicion of involvement in the violent incidents, violating a military commander's order concerning a closed military zone, and illegal construction."

Loading...

The attacks come after global outrage over mounting settler violence in the West Bank.

Masked settlers

Masked Israeli settlers were filmed on Friday assaulting Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, a US citizen, who was covering a Palestinian olive harvest in the West Bank.

Levine was hospitalised after sustaining a number of injuries in the attack and underwent surgery on a finger.

On Saturday, French, Belgian and Polish diplomats as well as a French mayor were attacked by masked settlers in another part of the West Bank.

Loading...

The settlers beat up Bernard Baudoux, 78, the mayor of the northern French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries, an advocate of the Palestinian cause who had come on a goodwill visit and was helping harvest olives.

A Belgian diplomatic vehicle was also damaged.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and the military have blamed "Israeli rioters" for the attack on the diplomats.

However, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority at the October 27 election, has been more circumspect.

Olive harvest sees surge in settler violence in West Bank Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinians and journalists in the occupied West Bank, using slingshots to hurl rocks from hilltops.

He has said the diplomats entered a "sensitive area with a history of confrontations" and without coordinating with the military.

He has also said that the facts ​of the attack on Levine were "unclear".

Levine has said she was attacked by settlers and Israel President Isaac Herzog has apologised.

Settler attacks ​on the Palestinians ⁠are surging, with at least 170 since September 27, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group.

Journalists, Israeli activists and foreign observers have also been targeted.

'Stain on Israel's image'

Benjamin Netanyahu is projected to lose its governing majority at the October 27 election. (Reuters: Ronen Zvulun)

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is facing a tight race for a new mandate in October 27 elections, has tried to shore up his right-wing base and had cast doubt on the circumstances behind the recent settler attacks.

The opposition described the attacks on Westerners as a stain on Israel's image and accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of allowing the violence to happen.

Rights groups note that Israel rarely prosecutes settlers when the victims are Palestinian.

Settler attacks against Palestinians, including killings, beatings, vandalism and arson, averaged six a day in the first half of the year, according to the United Nations.

ABC/Wires

World.title: Tropics attract city dwellers in regional migration trend
World.content:
City dwellers are moving to regional Australia at rates not seen since the COVID pandemic, according to new data.

The movement of people out of Sydney and Melbourne is captured in data from Commonwealth Bank, which the Regional Australia Institute (RAI) has analysed to track migration trends.

Sydney accounted for 52 per cent of the net population outflow to Australian regions in the June 2026 quarter. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

The not-for-profit organisation said migration from capital cities to regional Australia during the June 2026 quarter matched the record set in June 2021.

Those moving to the regions outnumbered those moving to the cities by 30 per cent, and Sydney and Melbourne recorded the largest losses of residents.

Sunshine Coast is the region that city movers are favouring most. (Supplied)

The Sunshine Coast remained the most favoured region for those leaving capital cities, followed by Greater Geelong in Victoria.

In the 12 months to the June 2026 quarter, the Sunshine Coast received 8.7 per cent of total net migration share.

Victoria's Central Goldfields and the New South Wales Snowy Mountains were the most popular for movers already living in regional Australia.

Beyond the stand-out markets, the RAI highlighted significant growth in north Queensland in the 12 months to the June 2026 quarter.

Geelong trailed the Sunshine Coast with the second-largest share of total net internal migration. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

Tropical takeover

The sugarcane and horticultural mecca of the Burdekin, south of Townsville, saw a 238 per cent annual increase in the number of city movers choosing the region.

Retail operator Candace Young moved from Dalby to the Burdekin in 2023.

She said since the move, she had noticed a stream of southerners moving to the shire of 17,000 people.

"We are getting a lot of city people coming up here, customers coming to the shop who have moved from Victoria or Tasmania," she said.

"Here, you can drive five minutes in any direction and take the kids fishing or camping, and those things are free activities.

" Regional towns are worth it and the people make you feel at home. "

The Atherton Tablelands region, south of Cairns, received a 131 per cent annual increase in residents from capital cities.

'A good-news story'

RAI chief executive Liz Ritchie said the latest quarterly data showed people still wanted to move to regional Australia in droves, years after the pandemic-inspired tree and sea changes.

"It is those southern states that are really feeling the pinch in terms of how people are measuring their lifestyle and what they're hoping for," she said.

"It is a good-news story for Queensland."

Liz Ritchie says one in three city dwellers were planning a regional move within five years. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

Ms Ritchie said the RAI was lobbying to establish a national population plan to assist regional planning.

"We continue to under-project population in regional Australia, and our regional communities suffer because of that," she said.

"People on the ground know when their town is growing, and they know when they're feeling the pinch."

World.title: Funeral held for Corporal Brendan Hannam killed in military exercise
World.content:
An Australian Army soldier killed during a military training exercise in the Northern Territory earlier this month has been remembered as "a man of character, a loving partner and most of all, a devoted father".

The Australian Defence Force (ADF) confirmed Corporal Brendan Hannam died after a troop carrier rolled at the Mount Bundey Training Area, south of Darwin, two weeks ago.

Five other men were also injured in the crash.

Brendan Hannam died aged 28 during training exercises near Mount Bundey earlier this month. (Supplied: ADF)

The 28-year-old father-of-two was farewelled today in a funeral service held at the Lone Pine Chapel at Robertson Barracks in Darwin.

Speaking at the service, Lieutenant Colonel Ash Zimmerlie paid tribute to his colleague's more than nine years in the ADF, saying Corporal Hannam "served Australia with distinction".

He told mourners the late soldier's service included international deployments to Afghanistan in 2019 and Ukraine in 2023.

"Corporal Hannam's career was characterised by loyalty to his battalion, dedication to his profession and commitment to his mates," Lieutenant Colonel Zimmerlie said.

Corporal Brendan Hannam was carried into the Lone Pine Chapel during a funeral service at Robertson Barracks in Darwin. (Supplied: Sera Mar/ADF)

"He served this country honourably and he's earned the respect of those alongside whom he served."

Lieutenant Cooper Bridgeman remembered the 28-year-old as someone who was trustworthy "because he was steady, capable and never made it about himself".

"He didn't accept excuses because he held himself and those around him to a high standard," Lieutenant Bridgeman said.

Loading...

"Brendan didn't need to be the loudest in the room. He never talked to fill the silence.

"When he spoke it was because he had something worth saying, a sharp observation, a practical solution, or a joke that could break the tension exactly when the team needed it."

Lieutenant Bridgeman said while his fellow soldier was respected as a "dedicated", "selfless teammate and valued leader", he was a family man above all.

"You had the privilege of having him for everything he was, a man of character, a loving partner and most of all a devoted father," he said.

Brendan Hannam leaves behind his partner and two young children. (Supplied: ADF)

"I know that he was extremely proud of you and everything that he did was for you, the people that he loved deeply and without reservation."

In the wake of the junior non-commissioned officer's death, Chief of Army Susan Coyle said a thorough investigation of the crash was underway.

The defence force also paused the use of the Supacat HMT (High Mobility Transporter), the troop carrier involved in the fatal crash.

World.title: Massive whale carcass leaves council with $180k bill, budget headache
World.content:
The cost of removing a massive humpback whale that washed up on a Perth beach cost ratepayers almost $180,000, with the local council footing the bill pleading for the state government to chip in.

The Town of Cambridge was tasked with removing the 31-tonne humpback whale from City Beach on September 27.

Initial estimates on its removal ranged from $40,000 to $100,000.

The 13-metre long carcass was transported from the popular beach using a 72-tonne crane to Red Hill landfill in the city's north-east on October 1.

The whale carcass was placed on a truck and moved away from the beach. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

While a full breakdown of the $180,000 bill is not yet available, Cambridge Mayor Gary Mack said coordinating the carcass's 44-kilometre journey to the waste management facility involved several costly moving parts.

"Hiring specialist cranes and their operators was an additional expense that we didn't fully anticipate," he said.

"We had to engage a large truck that was sealed, so whale exudate didn't go on the freeway as it was driving.

The whale carcass washed ashore late last month. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

"All these things had costs and individually they may not seem a lot, but when you put them all together, it adds to the expense."

Costly carcasses a statewide expense

Historically, the cost of carcass removal in Western Australia has varied widely.

The City of Karratha spent as little as $10,000 to remove a 14-metre humpback in 2009, while $188,000 was spent by the City of Stirling to remove a larger 17-metre whale from Scarborough Beach in 2014.

Mayor Mack said he suspected the City Beach clean-up effort presented more logistical challenges than a carcass disposal in regional WA.

"We had thousands of people turn up to view it because there was a huge curiosity factor," he said.

The carcass attracted large crowds to City Beach. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

"But we had to make sure that those people were kept safe from the actual heavy earth moving equipment operations.

"I would expect that the cost of carcass removal in country areas would be less than the in the city areas."

A motion for the town to call on the state government to establish a state-funded whale carcass response mechanism, which would see local governments reimbursed for the cost of removal, has been slated for October 27.

Wiildlife officers examine the carcass. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Mayor Mack said if the state didn't foot some of the bill, the town would likely pull funding from infrastructure projects already approved in this year's budget.

"We can't increase the rates because the rates have already been sent out and people have paid their rates," he said.

"It really is a matter of looking to recover that cost from other programs and other services."

A WA government spokesperson said the cost of removing whale carcasses falls to the land owner, in this case the local government.

They said the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions supplied technical support and access to specialist equipment.

World.title: NT public housing tenants told 'three strikes' and you're out
World.content:
Northern Territory public housing tenants will be evicted if they receive three strikes for anti-social behaviour under a new policy beginning today.

The three strikes system replaces a red card scheme in which tenants could be evicted if they accumulated six demerit points.

Under the new three strikes rule, "minor" anti-social behaviour breaches attract one strike, "moderate" breaches two and three strikes can be handed down for "significant" breaches.

Existing demerit points will be converted to strikes, with one demerit point equivalent to one strike.

Under the new policy, public housing tenants will get up to three chances before being evicted. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

NT Housing Minister Steve Edgington said if a tenant received three strikes, including via a single breach, they would now be evicted.

"Three strikes could be the result of serious anti-social behaviour where people may be threatened, the property may be damaged," he said.

" Ongoing repeated anti-social behaviour could lead to three strikes and immediate action taken towards removing that tenant from their home. "

Mr Edgington said the NT government had acted on concerns raised by neighbours of public housing tenants, particularly in the Darwin region.

Steve Edgington says procedural fairness is "a big part" of the new regime. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"All we're expecting is pay your rent, look after your home and be a good neighbour," he told 105.7 ABC Darwin.

"What we're doing is clamping down on those that are causing distraction, sometimes violent behaviour, noise complaints, graffiti, ongoing anti-social behaviour."

Medically vulnerable shelter residents moved 100km As Darwin's largest short-stay accommodation centre closes its doors today, some medically at-risk residents say they are being moved to the replacement site an hour away despite government promises to the contrary.

He also said tenants could respond to allegations before being reprimanded.

"There'll be an opportunity for the tenant to not only respond to the complaint, but to provide any information which may or may not differ from the allegations being made," he said.

"Procedural fairness is a big part of this policy.

"It needs to be investigated and from there, we'll issue a strike if that's the outcome of the investigation."

Termination proceedings are progressed by the Housing Department in the NT Civil and Administrative Tribunal.

CLP 'racially controlling' Aboriginal people

Responding to the policy announcement today, Labor opposition MLA Chansey Paech accused the Country Liberal Party (CLP) government of attempting to "racially control" Aboriginal people for its "own benefit".

"That's to win votes," he said.

"They're not targeting any problem, they're just moving the problem on."

Mr Paech said the government's new three strikes policy was one of several that would overwhelmingly impact Indigenous people, including the recent closure of Darwin's YiSSA homelessness shelter.

Chansey Paech says evicting public housing residents only makes the NT's "homelessness problem" worse. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"Look at the decisions the CLP government [is] rolling out every day," he said.

"They closed down YiSSA — predominantly Aboriginal.

"They're evicting public housing tenants — predominantly Aboriginal.

"They're stalling on the remote housing program — predominantly Aboriginal people."

Mr Paech said tenants needed to be better supported, instead of evicted.

"We can do the work to help them have a home for their families, not kick them out onto the streets where guess what — kicking people out and making them homeless doesn't address the homelessness problem in the Territory.

"It makes it worse."

A spokesperson for Mr Edgington said public housing policy applied to every tenant equally.

Northern suburbs hotspot

Doreen Dyer built her home in the northern Darwin suburb of Karama in 1981, when the area was first developed.

Karama and nearby Malak have long had pockets of high-density social housing, but Ms Dyer said in the past 10 years, the anti-social behaviour problem had deteriorated.

"We had issues with fighting and arguing and coming up into the court to go through the walkway at the end of the court," she said.

Doreen Dyer says it is often visitors to public housing rather than the residents themselves who cause problems. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"Yards unkempt, houses that have been damaged and windows boarded up and generally, it's affecting the whole neighbourhood, particularly with anyone wanting to sell."

Ms Dyer said it was tough to see how the suburb had changed over the years.

"When you have pride in your own place and have the long-term knowledge of the suburb and how great it was, it used to be a young family suburb, and it ran sort of fairly normally, as you'd expect," she said.

" It hurts you to think that it's been allowed to deteriorate to that degree. "

Ms Dyer said often it was visitors, not tenants themselves, that were causing problems.

"Often those visitors get abusive and try and climb over the high gates and cause a lot of issues," she said.

Doreen Dyer says "everybody deserves to live a peaceful life in their own home". (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

A former Labor voter until the last NT election when she backed an independent candidate, Ms Dyer said she supported the CLP's three strikes policy.

"Hopefully it means that tenants that have caused issues don't necessarily get kicked out, that they actually take advantage of the first strike and do something about the behaviour that's affecting the neighbourhood," she said.

"I don't want to see people lose their home, but I don't think that we can keep on keeping on with behaviour in public housing that seems to have been accepted as it's just Karama, it's just Malak.

"Everybody deserves to live a peaceful life in their own home."

World.title: Wind makes conditions tricky for fire crews in Tasmania's north
World.content:
Crews have been kept busy by windy conditions and a "difficult to control" bushfire which threatened properties in Tasmania's north.

On Monday afternoon, Tasmania Fire Service (TFS) issued a Watch and Act for Patersonia Road at Nunamara, about 30 kilometres east of Launceston, urging the community to monitor changing conditions.

The fire was then downgraded to Advice level as of 7:45pm on Monday evening, with the TFS saying conditions were "expected to improve" and there was "no immediate threat".

The fire had been travelling in a south-easterly direction.

The TFS previously said nearby residents should check their bushfire plans, and anyone who planned to leave should decide early and make sure they had a clear path to a safer place.

It said embers, smoke, and ash could threaten people and homes before the main fire, and that it could become difficult to see and breathe.

Bushfire information: In a life-threatening emergency, call 000

For the latest advice, visit the TasAlert website or check ABC Emergency

For information on current road closures, visit the Tasmania Police website

People at higher risk from the effects of smoke, including those with medical conditions, are advised to have a personal plan for avoiding smoke and managing their health

Advice is available from the Department of Health website regarding air quality or at the Asthma Australia website

The TFS's Jeremy Ripper told ABC Northern Tasmania that three aircraft, 10 ground crews and a dozer were working on the blaze.

"It's pretty difficult to control; it's a lot of bush out there," he said.

"The wind is swinging around a lot, which is contributing to the difficulty [in] controlling it.

"We have had two properties under threat, which are sort of up in the bush there; we've got ground crews doing asset protection on them.

" But this is going to be difficult to control fire for quite a while, we think. "

Nunamara bushfire, seen in an image shared by Michael Ferguson, October 19, 2026. (Facebook: Michael Ferguson)

Mr Ripper said there were not many properties in the area, but accessibility was the biggest challenge for crews, and the dozer was trying to establish tracks to help firefighters get closer.

He said although the wind was changing, it was not overly strong.

As of Monday evening, the fire had burned across 35 hectares.

'We all look after each other out here'

Tim Lockrey, from the Nunamara Hub, said there was "a lot of smoke" and he had seen embers flying earlier.

"We're all on high alert, that's for sure," he said.

"[I've] got a farm and a lot of animals. Maybe if the wind comes to my place, we'll be moving a lot of animals down the Tasman Highway."

Mr Lockrey said he had sheltered a man who had left his home.

"He was here for a while just hanging out and we said to him, 'It's alright, you know, we all look after each other out here'. We said, 'Come and stay at our place'," he said.

The local roadhouse owner said he had prepared 20 meals for firefighters.

World.title: Weston, Dwyer talk new Diamonds dress, Super Netball fixture and that shot
World.content:
SportNetballSuper Netball Weston, Dwyer talk new Diamonds dress, Super Netball fixture and that shot Roy Ward October 20, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A lot has happened in the months since the last pass was thrown in the Super Netball grand final in July: a dramatic player movement period, a uniform controversy for the national team and a history-making semi-final loss at the Commonwealth Games. Now fans can begin the countdown to the new season, which begins on April 10 next year when the Vixens and the Mavericks meet in the opener, after Super Netball revealed the fixture for 2027. Sophie Garbin of Australia, left, and ’Otolose Fainga’anuku of Tonga in action during the the women’s netball. Steve Welsh/PA via AP Australian stars Jo Weston and Sophie Dwyer were right in the middle of the netball controversy over the off-season, part of the Diamonds team that failed to make the gold medal match at the Commonwealth Games for the first time. They were also part of what Weston describes as a “sticky situation” – and what became known in some circles as “Dressgate”.



One of the enduring memories of the Glasgow Commonwealth Games will be the social-media-fuelled outrage over the Diamonds’ dresses appearing to be ill-fitting and riding up during games. The players weren’t as perturbed about it as many fans, but when new apparel partner Asics came in, the company asked Weston and teammate Jamie-Lee Price to help design the dresses. Courtney Bruce of Australia, right, in her 100th match on Sunday as the Diamonds donned their new dress. Getty Images “It was such a fun collaboration, especially with Jamie who’s such a fashionista,” Weston said. “That was a sticky situation and everyone was talking about it, but as an athlete, you were there to represent your country, and Valour [the Games uniform supplier] had done such an amazing job with the uniform, so you are not wanting to be like ‘oh, it doesn’t quite fit as expected’.



“But, if people are talking about netball, then I’m not opposed to that.” Price took to Instagram recently to playfully “test” the dress in her room to avoid what she called “Dressgate 2.0”. While in Glasgow, Price had made a similar video showing “the dress that was getting more attention than the netball”. Weston is currently on holiday in a remote Mexican mountain village after choosing to have a proper off-season break. It means she wasn’t there for the Diamonds’ Constellation Cup campaign opener against New Zealand on Sunday, which Australia lost.



Dwyer, however, was. “We didn’t buy into the [dress] stuff too much, and I think the girls made all the TikToks and funny dances to get some more eyeballs on netball,” Dwyer, who is sponsored by Asics, said. “The Asics dress is amazing and I know Jamie has done a little tester and jumped around and all that.” A new season Weston has remained at the Vixens, but will be part of a very different team to the one which lost last year’s grand final to the Adelaide Thunderbirds.



The Vixens have turned over half their roster, and they have snared some boom recruits, led by New Zealand internationals Carys Stythe, Amelia Walmsley and Mila Reuelu-Buchanan. It’s a stark reminder of the controversy that dominated the Super Netball off-season when star Kiwi players moved to Australia en masse due to a financial crisis that left New Zealand’s ANZ Premiership facing an uncertain future following a $3.7 million loss and the lack of a broadcaster. Melbourne Vixens netballer Jo Weston competes in the Super Netball League. Rachel Bach A rescue plan for the league was later announced, but by then many of the Silver Ferns had been picked up by Super Netball clubs, sometimes at the expense of local players. Weston said it was good that the Vixens had refreshed, but acknowledged the scale would be a surprise to some.



“People probably didn’t predict how big the change-up would be, with 50 per cent of our team being new,” Weston said. “It’s an interesting position for me and Kate Moloney, our captain, who have been in the team for a long time, as there is a bit of the unknown until we start training together, but I think it will give us a dimension we might not have had over the previous years. Hopefully, it puts us back in the grand final in 2027.” New Vixens signing Mila Reuelu-Buchanan of New Zealand attacks against the Diamonds on Sunday night. Getty Images Weston admitted it was difficult to see much-loved teammates, including Emily Mannix (retired), Rudi Ellis (NSW Swifts) and Kate Eddy (Melbourne Mavericks), move on. “There is always going to be change, but some of it was disappointing for me as I’ve played with these girls for a long period of time, and we’ve formed great partnerships on court and amazing friendships off it,” Weston said.



“We will always hold on to those memories, and wish them the best, but it’s going to be weird seeing them in opposition colours next year. Big changes for us.” Weston noted that Super Netball has featured foreign stars from Jamaica, England, New Zealand, South Africa and even smaller nations, such as Malawi, for years. Vixens defender Jo Western reaches for the ball last season. Getty Images “I’m curious to see how it unfolds in the future and whether [NZ players] keep coming, or things will move on. I feel like the latter has always been the case,” Weston said. “I’m always going to advocate for Australian athletes who are ready to take the step up. I think international athletes make our competition so much more dynamic and offer us an international audience too – it’s about finding the right balance.”



Nine, owner of this masthead, returns as Super Netball’s broadcaster in 2027. It will show the season-opening game between the Vixens and Mavericks live on its main channel to celebrate the start of a five-year deal, under which all Super Netball games will be streamed live and free on 9Now. A new era Another big change this season is the rebranding of the Giants, who are now the Sydney Sirens. Dwyer, a Sydney-raised shooter, spent seven years with the Giants, and is bracing for not only the change of team colours and identity, but many other differences now the team has new owners in Craig Hutchison’s Sports Entertainment Group.



She is certain the rivalry between the Sirens and mainstay NSW Swifts will be fiery from the get-go. The two clubs meet for the first time in round six (May 16) at Ken Rosewall Arena. Dwyer was in the thick of the semi-final action in Glasgow and had the heartbreak of missing a shot after the siren that could have forced the game into overtime. Australian teammates Kate Moloney and Sophie Dwyer console each other after the Diamonds won the bronze medal at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games. SNS Group via Getty Images “You probably saw on the broadcast there was a lot of tears,” Dwyer said. “But for me, it did come down to remembering that the Commonwealth Games experience wasn’t just one shot – there was a lot of games and good moments throughout.



“I have high expectations of myself, and it was really disappointing that shot didn’t go in, but I had to remember there was more to my game and my experience than just that shot.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.
