World.title: Helen Haines attack as it happened: Indi MP critically injured outside Wangaratta office; alleged attacker arrested by police
World.content:
Thank you for following the latest developments as the nation reacts to a shocking attack outside the Wangaratta office of Indi MP Helen Haines. This is where we leave our coverage for this evening.

A 43-year-old man is in custody after he was arrested at the scene. Haines has been flown to Melbourne for further treatment.

Australia’s politicians have reacted with shock and distress throughout the evening after the attack on a highly respected member of parliament.

While the motivation for this attack is not yet known, the presence of Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke alongside a visibly shaken Prime Minister Anthony Albanese “spoke volumes about what the government seems to believe has occurred”, writes chief political commentator James Massola.

World.title: What we know so far about the attack on Helen Haines
World.content:
PoliticsFederalHaines attack What we know so far about the attack on Helen Haines Natassia Chrysanthos October 19, 2026 — 11:13pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Independent MP Helen Haines is in a critical condition after being struck by a four-wheel drive vehicle outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east Victoria, on Monday afternoon. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said it was an intentional attack that is being investigated by several agencies, including counter-terrorism teams. One man was arrested at the scene and is in police custody. Here’s what we know so far. Who is Helen Haines? Helen Haines, 65, is the independent federal representative for Indi, a north-east Victorian electorate that stretches up to Wodonga near the NSW border.



Before entering parliament, Haines had a decades-long career in healthcare. She worked as a nurse, midwife and health researcher, publishing dozens of academic articles. She grew up on a dairy farm in Eurack, in southwestern Victoria, and has been married to her husband, Phil Haines, since 1986. The couple have raised three children and live on a beef farm outside Wangaratta. Independent MP Helen Haines is being treated in hospital after the attack. Alex Ellinghausen Haines’ political career began when she was elected as an independent in the 2019 election. Her predecessor in the seat, Cathy McGowan, in many ways pioneered the community independent movement in 2013, when she won Indi from the Coalition with the backing of grassroots campaigners. It had been safely held by conservative parties for the previous 80 years. Haines seized on the same momentum and was endorsed by McGowan to run as the local MP. She was the first independent to succeed another independent in federal parliament, and has held Indi on an 8 per cent margin in the two elections since. “When people can see another way, it’s empowering,” Haines told Good Weekend in 2023. “The fact that the nation has chosen a parliament that has the biggest crossbench in history since federation demonstrates the need for a diversity of views and greater collaboration.”



Related Article Haines attack Independent MP Helen Haines in critical condition after ‘attack’ outside her office Haines’ recent election campaigns have been backed by the Climate 200 fundraising vehicle, although she keeps a distinct profile from the “teal independents” who have won city seats with a similar community campaigning model. Haines has advocated for climate change action and regional services, particularly healthcare. She has also been a strong advocate for integrity and transparency in politics, and was instrumental in campaigning for a national anti-corruption body. Haines is a widely respected member of parliament. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described her as an incredibly hardworking MP on Monday night. “She is fiercely intelligent, but most importantly, she’s just a thoroughly decent human being, full of integrity, respected right across the parliament, and from everyone who comes into contact with her,” he said.



What happened at her Wangaratta office? Haines was returning to her electorate office in Wangaratta after attending a sod-turning event in the nearby town of Mansfield on Monday afternoon, when she was struck by a white Toyota Landcruiser at about 3.35pm. Police at the scene. ABC Witnesses told Nine and the ABC they saw Haines pinned between two vehicles just outside her office as she was near her own car. Police said that witnesses arrested the driver of the Landcruiser at the scene. A knife was also seized from inside the car.



What is her condition? Haines was in a critical condition on Monday night. Victoria Police Acting Superintendent Ashley Mason confirmed Haines suffered critical injuries. Haines was taken to Northeast Health Wangaratta by ambulance and was airlifted to The Alfred hospital in Melbourne for further medical treatment on Monday night. Helen Haines arrives at The Alfred hospital in Melbourne on Monday night after being airlifted there. Nine News What have the authorities said?



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke held a press conference in Sydney on Monday night. Albanese said it appeared to be a deliberate attack, not an accident. He said the Australian Federal Police, Victorian Police and domestic spy agency ASIO were working on the case, and the joint counter-terrorism team had been activated. Related Article Analysis

Haines attack Helen Haines attack must be a turning point for Australia Mason, from Victoria Police, said investigators from the major collision investigation unit were on their way to Wangaratta on Monday night, and would thoroughly process the crime scene. Victoria’s crime and counter-terrorism command were also assisting investigators. Albanese and Burke said it was too soon to speculate about the motive behind the attack. “We’re still very early in the investigation, but importantly, someone is in custody,” Burke said.



Who is the suspected attacker? Police said they have arrested a 43-year-old local man from Tarrawingee, a town of about 400 people that lies 12 kilometres east of Wangaratta. Police seized a knife from his car. The man was being held in custody at the Wangaratta police station on Monday night as investigators began examining his history in search for a motive. He will be interviewed by police. Victoria Police said there was no indication at this stage that the man and Haines were known to each other, but that will be a subject of the investigation. Police said they were treating it as an isolated incident, and there was no ongoing threat to another person or the broader community. “We’ve got quite an extensive crime scene,” Mason said. “We have investigators present and they’ll continue to work through and try and collect all available evidence to ascertain exactly what has occurred and how it has occurred.”

World.title: Independent MP Helen Haines in critical condition after ‘attack’ outside her office
World.content:
NationalHaines attack Independent MP Helen Haines in critical condition after ‘attack’ outside her office Paul Sakkal, James Costa and Jack Gramenz Updated October 19, 2026 — 9:42pm ,first published 6:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Federal MP Helen Haines is in a critical condition after she was struck by a four-wheel drive near her office, in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said was an intentional attack being investigated by counterterrorism police. Haines, a mother of three and grandmother, as well as a widely respected independent MP, was badly injured just before 4pm, realising the nation’s fears about an attack on a high-profile public figure or politician. She was airlifted to The Alfred hospital in Melbourne for treatment on Monday night. Loading A 43-year-old man was arrested near her regional Victorian electorate office in Wangaratta, in the state’s north-east. Witnesses told both Nine and the ABC that they saw Haines pinned between two vehicles just outside her electorate office as she was near her own car, causing severe leg injuries. Witnesses also said a man was pulled out of a white Toyota Landcruiser.



Police said a knife was seized from inside the Toyota and that the suspect, from Tarrawingee, 12km east of Wangaratta, was detained at the crash scene by a passerby. “This wasn’t an accident. This was a deliberate act, it would appear,” Albanese told ABC TV on Monday evening, confirming ASIO was involved and that Haines had been airlifted to Melbourne for medical treatment. “We don’t know what the motivation is. That is the work being undertaken [by authorities].” Independent MP Helen Haines. Alex Ellinghausen The incident appears to be Australia’s first major attack on a federal politician resulting in serious injury, mirroring similar events in the US and UK. Details remain scant, but the shock attack prompted politicians across the spectrum to underscore what authorities have identified as a more dangerous society and a higher volume of politically motivated violent threats.



Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said: “This is a shocking day for our nation. Australians will be angry and appalled by the attack on Helen outside her electorate office in Wangaratta. Our nation cannot become a place where violent attacks are normalised.” In a message to Coalition MPs, Taylor said it would be wise to avoid undue speculation. “Now is a time for unity, not division. All parliamentarians have a responsibility to stand firmly against political violence and uphold democracy.” Victoria Police Acting Superintendent Ashley Mason would not say whether the man was known to police and described the incident as “horrific” for those who saw it. He said there was no ongoing or further threat to the community at this stage. Albanese thanked first responders.



“I can provide some assurance to the community that we certainly do not have any intelligence that there is any further or ongoing threat to any other person or the broader community,” he said. “We are treating this as an isolated incident at this point in time.” Haines’ family asked that the public keep the 65-year-old in their thoughts, after Albanese and Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke delivered a brief and sombre press conference in Sydney to inform the nation of the incident. “This afternoon, our beloved Helen was involved in an incident outside her Wangaratta electorate office, and is receiving medical care. We thank the swift assistance of bystanders and the dedicated health workers who assisted her, and police for their response,” the family statement read. “Our family, and Helen’s staff, will be making no further comment at this time, and ask that their privacy be respected by the public and media. Please keep Helen in your thoughts.” Helen Haines arrives at The Alfred hospital in Melbourne on Monday night after being airlifted there. Nine News



Haines, 65, was born in Colac, Victoria, near Geelong. She was a regional midwife who became an academic and published dozens of peer-reviewed articles on maternal health before entering politics in 2019. She replaced Cathy McGowan in the former Liberal seat of Indi, becoming an important figure in the regional “Voices” movement that displaced several regional Liberals and helped influence the city-based teal movement. Related Article Exclusive

National security Twenty violent threats to PM before courts as politicians across divide face record menace Labor senator for Victoria Michele Ananda-Rajah told this masthead she was with Haines until about 3pm in the nearby town of Mansfield at a sod-turning event. Haines left Ananda-Rajah to drive to her office to conduct a television interview. “We had a cuppa with locals. She was in high spirits. She is the loveliest, warm person,” Ananda-Rajah said. “I pray healthcare professionals … bring her back to her family.”



Independent MP Allegra Spender said Haines was a “true inspiration” who was respected across the aisle, did not engage in ugly forms of politics, and was a leading advocate for a federal corruption commission and stripping corruption out of federal grants. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said: “Violence against any elected representative, whoever they are and whatever they stand for, is never acceptable in Australia. Members of parliament and their staff must be able to serve their communities without fearing for their safety.” Authorities have become increasingly worried about the risk of a public official being killed or hurt. Security officials privately cite the long tail of the pandemic fuelling distrust and conspiracies, segments of the Muslim community being less willing to work with police after October 7, social media desensitising a generation of young people, and increased frustrations with the cost of living and global instability. The rise of the pseudo-legal “sovereign citizen” movement has also caused police to be worried after the deaths of two police officers at the hands of Dezi Freeman.



Speaking after the incident, Albanese used his often-repeated line on the need to “take the temperature down” in political debate. “It has changed,” he told ABC TV when asked if the nation’s character had altered over time. “There’s no question social media is a part of that, but so is the contest for clicks [by media outlets].” “I don’t want to see a political system in which you can’t have conversations with people at the supermarket, in the street, at street meetings, public forums - that’s an important part of our democracy. More debate and less shouting would be a good thing.” Loading



New National Security Investigations units were set up by the Australian Federal Police late last year to target politically motivated violence, maintain social cohesion and protect democratic institutions. Police data shows threats to MPs and electorate officers grew from 555 reports in 2021-22 to more than 1000 the next year. In the latest reporting period, between July 2024 and February 2025, there were more than 700. Related Article Good Weekend ‘I had a really good life’: So why did Helen Haines decide to run for parliament? Haines’ sprawling regional Victorian electorate spans from Marysville to Wodonga and Mount Hotham, and takes in towns including Lake Eildon, Beechworth, Corryong, Myrtleford and the alpine town of Porepunkah, where Freeman shot and killed officers Vadim De Waart-Hottart and Neal Thompson in August last year. Haines has advocated for better telecommunications infrastructure and for the establishment of the National Anti-Corruption Commission.



The regional city of Wangaratta, about two hours and 40 minutes’ drive northeast of Melbourne, is home to about 30,000 people. 

Helen Haines attack must be a turning point for Australia What we know: The attack on Helen Haines Be the first to know when major news happens.

NationalWAFremantle Dockers ‘Uncomfortable’: Fremantle captain Alex Pearce speaks out on Woodside sponsorship Indigo Lemay-Conway October 19, 2026 — 9:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Fremantle Dockers captain Alex Pearce admits addressing the club’s major sponsor Woodside at a clean energy summit makes him “uncomfortable”. But he believes that while boards and clubs make the ultimate decision, community members and fans can have a significant sway. Alex Pearce, Fremantle AFL footballer speaks during Global Citizen NOW: Perth at Perth Convention and Exhibition Centre on October 19. Graham Denholm/Getty Images for Global Citizen Pearce spoke to an audience of 200 people at the Global Citizen NOW: Perth event on Monday as part of a panel about Protecting the Places we Play. When asked by moderator and AFLW St Kilda player Nicola Barr how he was faring after the Dockers devastating grand final loss, Pearce said it had been a work in progress.



“If you asked me two weeks ago, I would have a very different answer. But no, I’m going well physically and emotionally,” he said. “The support of our community in Fremantle has been incredible, and I think like all Dockers fans, I went through a few stages of grief over the week post the game. “But I’ve got through it and been able to see the season for what it was, and was very proud of what we were able to achieve along with all of our fans.” Barr went on to ask Pearce a question which inevitably stirred up the audience: “How much of a say do you think players should have when a sponsor’s values don’t line up with your own?” Pearce’s response was honest, and he did not shy away from the controversial topic.



“I’m not sure why I’ve gotten this question,” he said with a laugh. “Look, I’m really glad that this is a hard question to answer, and I’m really glad that it’s a topic that’s discussed, and it’s controversial because I think it does show that within the community, we can have influence on who sponsors our teams and who sponsors different areas within our community.” Oil and gas titan Woodside has sponsored the Dockers since 2010 and fans have not been quiet about their distaste towards the partnership. A petition urging the Dockers to ditch Woodside was signed by 8000 people back in 2023, when the sponsorship deal was up for renewal. Recently Kevin Parker, Tame Impala frontman and the Fremantle Dockers’ number one ticket holder was spotted sporting his team’s jersey while performing on the band’s Deadbeat tour in America, but had blocked out the Woodside logo.



“Often these decisions are made at boardroom level and are out of our hands and are out of the fans and members’ hands,” Pearce said. “But we’ve seen plenty of instances where public opinion has been able to affect change, and ultimately the boardrooms and the presidents who run our sporting organisations and our community areas are serving the members and fans and players and those that are taking part. Nicola Barr, AFLW Player, St Kilda FC; Project and Engagement Director, FrontRunners, Alex Pearce, Fremantle AFL footballer, Amy Steel PhD Candidate, Climate Adaptation; Former Australian Netballer and Ashton Turner, Captain, Perth Scorchers; Non-Executive Director, WA Cricket Foundation speak during Global Citizen NOW: Perth. Graham Denholm/Getty Images for Global Citizen “So we do, as fans, players, leaders, have influence in some of these decisions. Sometimes it’s hard, and we have to use that influence in different ways. “But the fact that I’m up here getting asked that question, it’s a little bit uncomfortable, but I think is a great thing, and as I said, it shows that no matter how big that influence is, no matter who you are as a stakeholder, you can have influence in what goes into funding our sports and our community programs.”



Pearce grew up in Tasmania and said sport has been a central part of his life, but said he worries about what sport could look like for future generations as climate change continues to make temperatures hotter. Related Article Fremantle Dockers Tame Impala frontman reignites calls for end to Woodside’s Dockers sponsorship “To think about what sport could look like in years down the track in 2050 or 2080, when we hear from climate scientists about what the world could look like, the temperature that we could get to, the increase in natural disasters we’ve already seen over the last decade,” he said. “Looking and thinking about these next generations of young athletes growing up in Australia, for our national fabric to potentially shift and to not revolve around playing sport in the summer and being outside and having that opportunity that I did growing up is really frightening.” Pearce said the Dockers are familiar with playing and training in warm temperatures but unlike community sporting teams, have access to a plethora of health services.



“Thirteen years ago when I started playing football, training in the summer in Perth is really hot, and we had a bit of an old school mentality of the heat makes us better, and water is for the weak, and you just push through, and you be strong, and you find a way to get through,” he said. “Whereas now, over the last couple of years, we have had lots of conversations with our medical team and players about how we’re going to navigate the heat, how we’re going to stay safe. “But I have access to all of these resources. I have two doctors on hand for every training session, multiple strength and conditioning staff, and what seems like unlimited funds to help. “All of our community sports throughout Australia don’t have access to this.” Pearce said it sparks a necessary conversation around whether things need to change in terms of how sports are played in Australia.



“The problem here is: are we putting our children at risk and our community sports teams and players at risk by continuing to play as we always have done and do we need to rethink how we go about our sport?” he said. “As a leader of a professional sporting organisation, do we have a responsibility for these junior and community sporting groups to help keep them safe and have a duty of care to ensure that they can play and train safely, just as we do?”

“Can we abolish this imported ‘Trick or Treat’ American custom (C8)?” implores Dave Horsfall of North Gosford. “Hallowe’en itself is an ancient British custom going back many centuries, but ‘Trick or Treat’ is purely commercial in nature. And in this day of ‘stranger danger’, who in their right mind would send their kids out knocking on the doors of total strangers? Next we’ll be observing Thanksgiving!”

“It’s off to the place of my birth for the Second Test,” observes Don Bain of Port Macquarie. “Looking forward to hearing how our commentators handle the city’s new name – Gqeberha!”

Garry Thomas of Oatlands feels sorry “for Geoff Goodfellow trying to pronounce Marky Mark’s (C8) name. When he played for Eastwood, we gave up and just called him Alphabet! Didn’t have the problem for long as he moved on quickly.”

Completing the sports report is George Zivkovic of Northmead: “One of the headlines the day after Australia’s opening game at the Rugby League World Cup bleated ‘Moses injures calf in World Cup’. I wasn’t aware that representatives of the RSPCA were also present in the bunker that night.”

“Who says the economic gods don’t have a sense of irony?” questions David Scandol of Balmain. “On the day that 600 blast furnace employees from the Whyalla steelworks lost their jobs, it seems ironic that our tour of the site was abandoned mid-way through because our bus broke down. The bus was made in China.”

World.title: Crisafulli and Co try passing the buck on call to give probe more powers
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPublic service Crisafulli and Co try passing the buck on call to give probe more powers Matt Dennien October 19, 2026 — 8:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: how the government is trying to avoid answering growing questions about its inquiry, the construction probe gets its lunch eaten, the outgoing Governor’s farewell tour, and new LNP figures pull into port. It’s been more than a week now since the state’s peak union body called on the government to consider setting a special prosecutor to work alongside its major inquiry into the CFMEU and construction sector. Since then, even Geoffrey Watson – the man whose report provided the LNP its catalyst to launch the Stuart Wood-led probe – has backed the idea. But it’s been almost silence from Crisafulli and Co in response. The Crisafulli government has so far declined to be drawn publicly on growing calls to give its pet project some greater prosecutorial punch. Dan Peled After nudging the government on no less than four separate days since October 9, we thought maybe we’d had a breakthrough when one notification pinged the Circus phone on Monday.



Lo and behold, it was nothing more than a “background” message from a ministerial office telling us it was a matter for Wood’s inquiry. Of course, when we put questions to the $95 million inquiry 10 days ago, it said this was a decision for the government. Given Wood has no power to establish anything like a Victorian-style special prosecutor, we can see why Attorney-General Deb Frecklington’s office wouldn’t want such a line attributed to it. But in lieu of an actual response from the office of Premier David Crisafulli or his deputy and recently unleashed IR attack dog Jarrod Bleijie, that’s about the best we’ve got.



It’s perhaps more telling than a follow-up statement from a Frecklington spokesperson, which reiterated that the inquiry had heard evidence of various wrongdoing within the industry and allegations relating to the former Labor government. Related Article Exclusive

Building Bad His report helped spark Qld’s CFMEU probe. Now he wants a special prosecutor to act “The Crisafulli Government established the CoI [Commission of Inquiry] to ensure these serious matters are thoroughly examined and will continue to support the Commission in carrying out its important work,” they said. That will do little to reassure critics the government believes in the idea of a serious probe that delivers more for Queensland than a rubber-stamp for its policy agenda, social media tiles for Bleijie, and political ammunition for the 2028 election year. Or maybe the hush is because the inquiry is gearing up to recommend referrals for prosecution in an interim report to be handed to government this month.



Who knows? (The tent is always open, anonymously and confidentially, if you do.) Government’s IR review eats a chunk of CFMEU inquiry lunch When it was set up, the CFMEU inquiry was told not to duplicate the work of the Queensland Productivity Commission, which reported back in January. But the government appears to have forgotten to tell its workers’ compensation and industrial relations law review not to step on Wood’s toes. (This is Glenn Ferguson and Gary Black’s report, tabled in parliament last week, along with a response that drew immediate blowback from unions.) Circus noted with interest the government’s controversial new bill included the establishment of a “fit and proper person” test for union officials.



Considering this test was part of the parcel of work handed to Wood by the government, along with possible changes to “whistleblower laws”. This, of course, is another thing Bleijie’s bill will address, with protections for union figures wanting to speak out. Finance Minister Ros Bates has made some new party-linked appointments to the port bodies she jointly oversees. Matt Dennien Two new LNP-linked board directors pull into regional ports Just when you think the Crisafulli government may have run out of board appointments to make, there comes another Friday afternoon media release.



So it was last week, when Finance Minister Ros Bates and Transport Minister Brent Mickelberg announced eight new directors across four of the state’s port authorities. Among the appointments, two names jumped out: Candice Stower at the Gladstone Ports Corporation and John Hathaway at the Port of Townsville. Stower is a registered (and quite active) lobbyist with her pseudonymous shop, chief executive with Queensland United Egg Producers, former ministerial advisor to Nationals figures David Littleproud and Matt Canavan, and a chief of staff to Morrison government minister Keith Pitt. Hathaway, on the other hand, was an army officer of 30 years (rising to the rank of Lieutenant Colonel) before being elected as the LNP’s Newman-era member for the state seat of Townsville. Hathaway’s successor in the seat was Labor’s Scott Stewart – one of the few folks from the other side of the political aisle handed gigs by the government, who Hathaway will now funnily enough join on the board.



Young squeezes in a royal farewell tour with all the stops With little more than a week until the changing of the guard up on Fernberg Road, outgoing Governor Jeannette Young has embarked on a final official jaunt to the motherland. On the agenda? A “farewell call” with King Charles – the kind of royal facetime Jarrod Bleijie was unable to land on his trip this month. But that wasn’t all. View post on X The vice-regal Twitter/X feed, still the platform of choice for day-to-day updates, laid out the itinerary of Young and her husband, Professor Graeme Nimmo, in detail.



There was a church service and reception in St James’ Palace, visits to three museums and galleries, and the laying of a wreath at the Australian War Memorial at Hyde Park Corner. Not to mention a meeting with High Commissioner Jay Weatherill and his deputy Elisabeth Bowes, a morning tea with Trade and Investment Queensland staff, “working lunch” with other top TIQ folks, and a dinner for “inspiring Queenslanders living and working” in the UK. Inspiring stuff. The trip marks Young’s first overseas engagement in more than a year, with her office’s recent 2025-26 annual report noting an active period of domestic travel across the period instead. This included 62 visits to locations across 30 Queensland council areas, including 25 public hospitals and 13 state schools – with Townsville the single-most visited place at four trips. The travel bill for the financial year ran to $208,000, down from the $447,000 in 2024-25 – said to have been due to travel to the UK and Europe, Japan and India “at the request of the Queensland state government”.

World.title: Weston, Dwyer talk new Diamonds dress, Super Netball fixture and that shot
World.content:
SportNetballSuper Netball Weston, Dwyer talk new Diamonds dress, Super Netball fixture and that shot Roy Ward October 20, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A lot has happened in the months since the last pass was thrown in the Super Netball grand final in July: a dramatic player movement period, a uniform controversy for the national team and a history-making semi-final loss at the Commonwealth Games. Now fans can begin the countdown to the new season, which begins on April 10 next year when the Vixens and the Mavericks meet in the opener, after Super Netball revealed the fixture for 2027. Sophie Garbin of Australia, left, and ’Otolose Fainga’anuku of Tonga in action during the the women’s netball. Steve Welsh/PA via AP Australian stars Jo Weston and Sophie Dwyer were right in the middle of the netball controversy over the off-season, part of the Diamonds team that failed to make the gold medal match at the Commonwealth Games for the first time. They were also part of what Weston describes as a “sticky situation” – and what became known in some circles as “Dressgate”.



One of the enduring memories of the Glasgow Commonwealth Games will be the social-media-fuelled outrage over the Diamonds’ dresses appearing to be ill-fitting and riding up during games. The players weren’t as perturbed about it as many fans, but when new apparel partner Asics came in, the company asked Weston and teammate Jamie-Lee Price to help design the dresses. Courtney Bruce of Australia, right, in her 100th match on Sunday as the Diamonds donned their new dress. Getty Images “It was such a fun collaboration, especially with Jamie who’s such a fashionista,” Weston said. “That was a sticky situation and everyone was talking about it, but as an athlete, you were there to represent your country, and Valour [the Games uniform supplier] had done such an amazing job with the uniform, so you are not wanting to be like ‘oh, it doesn’t quite fit as expected’.



“But, if people are talking about netball, then I’m not opposed to that.” Price took to Instagram recently to playfully “test” the dress in her room to avoid what she called “Dressgate 2.0”. While in Glasgow, Price had made a similar video showing “the dress that was getting more attention than the netball”. Weston is currently on holiday in a remote Mexican mountain village after choosing to have a proper off-season break. It means she wasn’t there for the Diamonds’ Constellation Cup campaign opener against New Zealand on Sunday, which Australia lost.



Dwyer, however, was. “We didn’t buy into the [dress] stuff too much, and I think the girls made all the TikToks and funny dances to get some more eyeballs on netball,” Dwyer, who is sponsored by Asics, said. “The Asics dress is amazing and I know Jamie has done a little tester and jumped around and all that.” A new season Weston has remained at the Vixens, but will be part of a very different team to the one which lost last year’s grand final to the Adelaide Thunderbirds.



The Vixens have turned over half their roster, and they have snared some boom recruits, led by New Zealand internationals Carys Stythe, Amelia Walmsley and Mila Reuelu-Buchanan. It’s a stark reminder of the controversy that dominated the Super Netball off-season when star Kiwi players moved to Australia en masse due to a financial crisis that left New Zealand’s ANZ Premiership facing an uncertain future following a $3.7 million loss and the lack of a broadcaster. Melbourne Vixens netballer Jo Weston competes in the Super Netball League. Rachel Bach A rescue plan for the league was later announced, but by then many of the Silver Ferns had been picked up by Super Netball clubs, sometimes at the expense of local players. Weston said it was good that the Vixens had refreshed, but acknowledged the scale would be a surprise to some.



“People probably didn’t predict how big the change-up would be, with 50 per cent of our team being new,” Weston said. “It’s an interesting position for me and Kate Moloney, our captain, who have been in the team for a long time, as there is a bit of the unknown until we start training together, but I think it will give us a dimension we might not have had over the previous years. Hopefully, it puts us back in the grand final in 2027.” New Vixens signing Mila Reuelu-Buchanan of New Zealand attacks against the Diamonds on Sunday night. Getty Images Weston admitted it was difficult to see much-loved teammates, including Emily Mannix (retired), Rudi Ellis (NSW Swifts) and Kate Eddy (Melbourne Mavericks), move on. “There is always going to be change, but some of it was disappointing for me as I’ve played with these girls for a long period of time, and we’ve formed great partnerships on court and amazing friendships off it,” Weston said.



“We will always hold on to those memories, and wish them the best, but it’s going to be weird seeing them in opposition colours next year. Big changes for us.” Weston noted that Super Netball has featured foreign stars from Jamaica, England, New Zealand, South Africa and even smaller nations, such as Malawi, for years. Vixens defender Jo Western reaches for the ball last season. Getty Images “I’m curious to see how it unfolds in the future and whether [NZ players] keep coming, or things will move on. I feel like the latter has always been the case,” Weston said. “I’m always going to advocate for Australian athletes who are ready to take the step up. I think international athletes make our competition so much more dynamic and offer us an international audience too – it’s about finding the right balance.”



Nine, owner of this masthead, returns as Super Netball’s broadcaster in 2027. It will show the season-opening game between the Vixens and Mavericks live on its main channel to celebrate the start of a five-year deal, under which all Super Netball games will be streamed live and free on 9Now. A new era Another big change this season is the rebranding of the Giants, who are now the Sydney Sirens. Dwyer, a Sydney-raised shooter, spent seven years with the Giants, and is bracing for not only the change of team colours and identity, but many other differences now the team has new owners in Craig Hutchison’s Sports Entertainment Group.



She is certain the rivalry between the Sirens and mainstay NSW Swifts will be fiery from the get-go. The two clubs meet for the first time in round six (May 16) at Ken Rosewall Arena. Dwyer was in the thick of the semi-final action in Glasgow and had the heartbreak of missing a shot after the siren that could have forced the game into overtime. Australian teammates Kate Moloney and Sophie Dwyer console each other after the Diamonds won the bronze medal at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games. SNS Group via Getty Images “You probably saw on the broadcast there was a lot of tears,” Dwyer said. “But for me, it did come down to remembering that the Commonwealth Games experience wasn’t just one shot – there was a lot of games and good moments throughout.



“I have high expectations of myself, and it was really disappointing that shot didn’t go in, but I had to remember there was more to my game and my experience than just that shot.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Helen Haines attack as it happened: Indi MP critically injured outside Wangaratta office; alleged attacker arrested by police
World.content:
Thank you for following the latest developments as the nation reacts to a shocking attack outside the Wangaratta office of Indi MP Helen Haines. This is where we leave our coverage for this evening.

A 43-year-old man is in custody after he was arrested at the scene. Haines has been flown to Melbourne for further treatment.

Australia’s politicians have reacted with shock and distress throughout the evening after the attack on a highly respected member of parliament.

While the motivation for this attack is not yet known, the presence of Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke alongside a visibly shaken Prime Minister Anthony Albanese “spoke volumes about what the government seems to believe has occurred”, writes chief political commentator James Massola.

World.title: What we know so far about the attack on Helen Haines
World.content:
PoliticsFederalHaines attack What we know so far about the attack on Helen Haines Natassia Chrysanthos October 19, 2026 — 11:13pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Independent MP Helen Haines is in a critical condition after being struck by a four-wheel drive vehicle outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east Victoria, on Monday afternoon. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said it was an intentional attack that is being investigated by several agencies, including counter-terrorism teams. One man was arrested at the scene and is in police custody. Here’s what we know so far. Who is Helen Haines? Helen Haines, 65, is the independent federal representative for Indi, a north-east Victorian electorate that stretches up to Wodonga near the NSW border.



Before entering parliament, Haines had a decades-long career in healthcare. She worked as a nurse, midwife and health researcher, publishing dozens of academic articles. She grew up on a dairy farm in Eurack, in southwestern Victoria, and has been married to her husband, Phil Haines, since 1986. The couple have raised three children and live on a beef farm outside Wangaratta. Independent MP Helen Haines is being treated in hospital after the attack. Alex Ellinghausen Haines’ political career began when she was elected as an independent in the 2019 election. Her predecessor in the seat, Cathy McGowan, in many ways pioneered the community independent movement in 2013, when she won Indi from the Coalition with the backing of grassroots campaigners. It had been safely held by conservative parties for the previous 80 years. Haines seized on the same momentum and was endorsed by McGowan to run as the local MP. She was the first independent to succeed another independent in federal parliament, and has held Indi on an 8 per cent margin in the two elections since. “When people can see another way, it’s empowering,” Haines told Good Weekend in 2023. “The fact that the nation has chosen a parliament that has the biggest crossbench in history since federation demonstrates the need for a diversity of views and greater collaboration.”



Related Article Haines attack Independent MP Helen Haines in critical condition after ‘attack’ outside her office Haines’ recent election campaigns have been backed by the Climate 200 fundraising vehicle, although she keeps a distinct profile from the “teal independents” who have won city seats with a similar community campaigning model. Haines has advocated for climate change action and regional services, particularly healthcare. She has also been a strong advocate for integrity and transparency in politics, and was instrumental in campaigning for a national anti-corruption body. Haines is a widely respected member of parliament. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described her as an incredibly hardworking MP on Monday night. “She is fiercely intelligent, but most importantly, she’s just a thoroughly decent human being, full of integrity, respected right across the parliament, and from everyone who comes into contact with her,” he said.



What happened at her Wangaratta office? Haines was returning to her electorate office in Wangaratta after attending a sod-turning event in the nearby town of Mansfield on Monday afternoon, when she was struck by a white Toyota Landcruiser at about 3.35pm. Police at the scene. ABC Witnesses told Nine and the ABC they saw Haines pinned between two vehicles just outside her office as she was near her own car. Police said that witnesses arrested the driver of the Landcruiser at the scene. A knife was also seized from inside the car.



What is her condition? Haines was in a critical condition on Monday night. Victoria Police Acting Superintendent Ashley Mason confirmed Haines suffered critical injuries. Haines was taken to Northeast Health Wangaratta by ambulance and was airlifted to The Alfred hospital in Melbourne for further medical treatment on Monday night. Helen Haines arrives at The Alfred hospital in Melbourne on Monday night after being airlifted there. Nine News What have the authorities said?



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke held a press conference in Sydney on Monday night. Albanese said it appeared to be a deliberate attack, not an accident. He said the Australian Federal Police, Victorian Police and domestic spy agency ASIO were working on the case, and the joint counter-terrorism team had been activated. Related Article Analysis

Haines attack Helen Haines attack must be a turning point for Australia Mason, from Victoria Police, said investigators from the major collision investigation unit were on their way to Wangaratta on Monday night, and would thoroughly process the crime scene. Victoria’s crime and counter-terrorism command were also assisting investigators. Albanese and Burke said it was too soon to speculate about the motive behind the attack. “We’re still very early in the investigation, but importantly, someone is in custody,” Burke said.



Who is the suspected attacker? Police said they have arrested a 43-year-old local man from Tarrawingee, a town of about 400 people that lies 12 kilometres east of Wangaratta. Police seized a knife from his car. The man was being held in custody at the Wangaratta police station on Monday night as investigators began examining his history in search for a motive. He will be interviewed by police. Victoria Police said there was no indication at this stage that the man and Haines were known to each other, but that will be a subject of the investigation. Police said they were treating it as an isolated incident, and there was no ongoing threat to another person or the broader community. “We’ve got quite an extensive crime scene,” Mason said. “We have investigators present and they’ll continue to work through and try and collect all available evidence to ascertain exactly what has occurred and how it has occurred.”

World.title: Independent MP Helen Haines in critical condition after ‘attack’ outside her office
World.content:
NationalHaines attack Independent MP Helen Haines in critical condition after ‘attack’ outside her office Paul Sakkal, James Costa and Jack Gramenz Updated October 19, 2026 — 9:42pm ,first published 6:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Federal MP Helen Haines is in a critical condition after she was struck by a four-wheel drive near her office, in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said was an intentional attack being investigated by counterterrorism police. Haines, a mother of three and grandmother, as well as a widely respected independent MP, was badly injured just before 4pm, realising the nation’s fears about an attack on a high-profile public figure or politician. She was airlifted to The Alfred hospital in Melbourne for treatment on Monday night. Loading A 43-year-old man was arrested near her regional Victorian electorate office in Wangaratta, in the state’s north-east. Witnesses told both Nine and the ABC that they saw Haines pinned between two vehicles just outside her electorate office as she was near her own car, causing severe leg injuries. Witnesses also said a man was pulled out of a white Toyota Landcruiser.



Police said a knife was seized from inside the Toyota and that the suspect, from Tarrawingee, 12km east of Wangaratta, was detained at the crash scene by a passerby. “This wasn’t an accident. This was a deliberate act, it would appear,” Albanese told ABC TV on Monday evening, confirming ASIO was involved and that Haines had been airlifted to Melbourne for medical treatment. “We don’t know what the motivation is. That is the work being undertaken [by authorities].” Independent MP Helen Haines. Alex Ellinghausen The incident appears to be Australia’s first major attack on a federal politician resulting in serious injury, mirroring similar events in the US and UK. Details remain scant, but the shock attack prompted politicians across the spectrum to underscore what authorities have identified as a more dangerous society and a higher volume of politically motivated violent threats.



Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said: “This is a shocking day for our nation. Australians will be angry and appalled by the attack on Helen outside her electorate office in Wangaratta. Our nation cannot become a place where violent attacks are normalised.” In a message to Coalition MPs, Taylor said it would be wise to avoid undue speculation. “Now is a time for unity, not division. All parliamentarians have a responsibility to stand firmly against political violence and uphold democracy.” Victoria Police Acting Superintendent Ashley Mason would not say whether the man was known to police and described the incident as “horrific” for those who saw it. He said there was no ongoing or further threat to the community at this stage. Albanese thanked first responders.



“I can provide some assurance to the community that we certainly do not have any intelligence that there is any further or ongoing threat to any other person or the broader community,” he said. “We are treating this as an isolated incident at this point in time.” Haines’ family asked that the public keep the 65-year-old in their thoughts, after Albanese and Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke delivered a brief and sombre press conference in Sydney to inform the nation of the incident. “This afternoon, our beloved Helen was involved in an incident outside her Wangaratta electorate office, and is receiving medical care. We thank the swift assistance of bystanders and the dedicated health workers who assisted her, and police for their response,” the family statement read. “Our family, and Helen’s staff, will be making no further comment at this time, and ask that their privacy be respected by the public and media. Please keep Helen in your thoughts.” Helen Haines arrives at The Alfred hospital in Melbourne on Monday night after being airlifted there. Nine News



Haines, 65, was born in Colac, Victoria, near Geelong. She was a regional midwife who became an academic and published dozens of peer-reviewed articles on maternal health before entering politics in 2019. She replaced Cathy McGowan in the former Liberal seat of Indi, becoming an important figure in the regional “Voices” movement that displaced several regional Liberals and helped influence the city-based teal movement. Related Article Exclusive

National security Twenty violent threats to PM before courts as politicians across divide face record menace Labor senator for Victoria Michele Ananda-Rajah told this masthead she was with Haines until about 3pm in the nearby town of Mansfield at a sod-turning event. Haines left Ananda-Rajah to drive to her office to conduct a television interview. “We had a cuppa with locals. She was in high spirits. She is the loveliest, warm person,” Ananda-Rajah said. “I pray healthcare professionals … bring her back to her family.”



Independent MP Allegra Spender said Haines was a “true inspiration” who was respected across the aisle, did not engage in ugly forms of politics, and was a leading advocate for a federal corruption commission and stripping corruption out of federal grants. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said: “Violence against any elected representative, whoever they are and whatever they stand for, is never acceptable in Australia. Members of parliament and their staff must be able to serve their communities without fearing for their safety.” Authorities have become increasingly worried about the risk of a public official being killed or hurt. Security officials privately cite the long tail of the pandemic fuelling distrust and conspiracies, segments of the Muslim community being less willing to work with police after October 7, social media desensitising a generation of young people, and increased frustrations with the cost of living and global instability. The rise of the pseudo-legal “sovereign citizen” movement has also caused police to be worried after the deaths of two police officers at the hands of Dezi Freeman.



Speaking after the incident, Albanese used his often-repeated line on the need to “take the temperature down” in political debate. “It has changed,” he told ABC TV when asked if the nation’s character had altered over time. “There’s no question social media is a part of that, but so is the contest for clicks [by media outlets].” “I don’t want to see a political system in which you can’t have conversations with people at the supermarket, in the street, at street meetings, public forums - that’s an important part of our democracy. More debate and less shouting would be a good thing.” Loading



New National Security Investigations units were set up by the Australian Federal Police late last year to target politically motivated violence, maintain social cohesion and protect democratic institutions. Police data shows threats to MPs and electorate officers grew from 555 reports in 2021-22 to more than 1000 the next year. In the latest reporting period, between July 2024 and February 2025, there were more than 700. Related Article Good Weekend ‘I had a really good life’: So why did Helen Haines decide to run for parliament? Haines’ sprawling regional Victorian electorate spans from Marysville to Wodonga and Mount Hotham, and takes in towns including Lake Eildon, Beechworth, Corryong, Myrtleford and the alpine town of Porepunkah, where Freeman shot and killed officers Vadim De Waart-Hottart and Neal Thompson in August last year. Haines has advocated for better telecommunications infrastructure and for the establishment of the National Anti-Corruption Commission.



The regional city of Wangaratta, about two hours and 40 minutes’ drive northeast of Melbourne, is home to about 30,000 people. 

Helen Haines attack must be a turning point for Australia What we know: The attack on Helen Haines Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: ‘Uncomfortable’: Fremantle captain Alex Pearce speaks out on Woodside sponsorship
World.content:
NationalWAFremantle Dockers ‘Uncomfortable’: Fremantle captain Alex Pearce speaks out on Woodside sponsorship Indigo Lemay-Conway October 19, 2026 — 9:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Fremantle Dockers captain Alex Pearce admits addressing the club’s major sponsor Woodside at a clean energy summit makes him “uncomfortable”. But he believes that while boards and clubs make the ultimate decision, community members and fans can have a significant sway. Alex Pearce, Fremantle AFL footballer speaks during Global Citizen NOW: Perth at Perth Convention and Exhibition Centre on October 19. Graham Denholm/Getty Images for Global Citizen Pearce spoke to an audience of 200 people at the Global Citizen NOW: Perth event on Monday as part of a panel about Protecting the Places we Play. When asked by moderator and AFLW St Kilda player Nicola Barr how he was faring after the Dockers devastating grand final loss, Pearce said it had been a work in progress.



“If you asked me two weeks ago, I would have a very different answer. But no, I’m going well physically and emotionally,” he said. “The support of our community in Fremantle has been incredible, and I think like all Dockers fans, I went through a few stages of grief over the week post the game. “But I’ve got through it and been able to see the season for what it was, and was very proud of what we were able to achieve along with all of our fans.” Barr went on to ask Pearce a question which inevitably stirred up the audience: “How much of a say do you think players should have when a sponsor’s values don’t line up with your own?” Pearce’s response was honest, and he did not shy away from the controversial topic.



“I’m not sure why I’ve gotten this question,” he said with a laugh. “Look, I’m really glad that this is a hard question to answer, and I’m really glad that it’s a topic that’s discussed, and it’s controversial because I think it does show that within the community, we can have influence on who sponsors our teams and who sponsors different areas within our community.” Oil and gas titan Woodside has sponsored the Dockers since 2010 and fans have not been quiet about their distaste towards the partnership. A petition urging the Dockers to ditch Woodside was signed by 8000 people back in 2023, when the sponsorship deal was up for renewal. Recently Kevin Parker, Tame Impala frontman and the Fremantle Dockers’ number one ticket holder was spotted sporting his team’s jersey while performing on the band’s Deadbeat tour in America, but had blocked out the Woodside logo.



“Often these decisions are made at boardroom level and are out of our hands and are out of the fans and members’ hands,” Pearce said. “But we’ve seen plenty of instances where public opinion has been able to affect change, and ultimately the boardrooms and the presidents who run our sporting organisations and our community areas are serving the members and fans and players and those that are taking part. Nicola Barr, AFLW Player, St Kilda FC; Project and Engagement Director, FrontRunners, Alex Pearce, Fremantle AFL footballer, Amy Steel PhD Candidate, Climate Adaptation; Former Australian Netballer and Ashton Turner, Captain, Perth Scorchers; Non-Executive Director, WA Cricket Foundation speak during Global Citizen NOW: Perth. Graham Denholm/Getty Images for Global Citizen “So we do, as fans, players, leaders, have influence in some of these decisions. Sometimes it’s hard, and we have to use that influence in different ways. “But the fact that I’m up here getting asked that question, it’s a little bit uncomfortable, but I think is a great thing, and as I said, it shows that no matter how big that influence is, no matter who you are as a stakeholder, you can have influence in what goes into funding our sports and our community programs.”



Pearce grew up in Tasmania and said sport has been a central part of his life, but said he worries about what sport could look like for future generations as climate change continues to make temperatures hotter. Related Article Fremantle Dockers Tame Impala frontman reignites calls for end to Woodside’s Dockers sponsorship “To think about what sport could look like in years down the track in 2050 or 2080, when we hear from climate scientists about what the world could look like, the temperature that we could get to, the increase in natural disasters we’ve already seen over the last decade,” he said. “Looking and thinking about these next generations of young athletes growing up in Australia, for our national fabric to potentially shift and to not revolve around playing sport in the summer and being outside and having that opportunity that I did growing up is really frightening.” Pearce said the Dockers are familiar with playing and training in warm temperatures but unlike community sporting teams, have access to a plethora of health services.



“Thirteen years ago when I started playing football, training in the summer in Perth is really hot, and we had a bit of an old school mentality of the heat makes us better, and water is for the weak, and you just push through, and you be strong, and you find a way to get through,” he said. “Whereas now, over the last couple of years, we have had lots of conversations with our medical team and players about how we’re going to navigate the heat, how we’re going to stay safe. “But I have access to all of these resources. I have two doctors on hand for every training session, multiple strength and conditioning staff, and what seems like unlimited funds to help. “All of our community sports throughout Australia don’t have access to this.” Pearce said it sparks a necessary conversation around whether things need to change in terms of how sports are played in Australia.



“The problem here is: are we putting our children at risk and our community sports teams and players at risk by continuing to play as we always have done and do we need to rethink how we go about our sport?” he said. “As a leader of a professional sporting organisation, do we have a responsibility for these junior and community sporting groups to help keep them safe and have a duty of care to ensure that they can play and train safely, just as we do?”

World.title: Cashing in on cobwebs
World.content:

“Can we abolish this imported ‘Trick or Treat’ American custom (C8)?” implores Dave Horsfall of North Gosford. “Hallowe’en itself is an ancient British custom going back many centuries, but ‘Trick or Treat’ is purely commercial in nature. And in this day of ‘stranger danger’, who in their right mind would send their kids out knocking on the doors of total strangers? Next we’ll be observing Thanksgiving!”

“It’s off to the place of my birth for the Second Test,” observes Don Bain of Port Macquarie. “Looking forward to hearing how our commentators handle the city’s new name – Gqeberha!”

Garry Thomas of Oatlands feels sorry “for Geoff Goodfellow trying to pronounce Marky Mark’s (C8) name. When he played for Eastwood, we gave up and just called him Alphabet! Didn’t have the problem for long as he moved on quickly.”

Completing the sports report is George Zivkovic of Northmead: “One of the headlines the day after Australia’s opening game at the Rugby League World Cup bleated ‘Moses injures calf in World Cup’. I wasn’t aware that representatives of the RSPCA were also present in the bunker that night.”

“Who says the economic gods don’t have a sense of irony?” questions David Scandol of Balmain. “On the day that 600 blast furnace employees from the Whyalla steelworks lost their jobs, it seems ironic that our tour of the site was abandoned mid-way through because our bus broke down. The bus was made in China.”

World.title: Crisafulli and Co try passing the buck on call to give probe more powers
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPublic service Crisafulli and Co try passing the buck on call to give probe more powers Matt Dennien October 19, 2026 — 8:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: how the government is trying to avoid answering growing questions about its inquiry, the construction probe gets its lunch eaten, the outgoing Governor’s farewell tour, and new LNP figures pull into port. It’s been more than a week now since the state’s peak union body called on the government to consider setting a special prosecutor to work alongside its major inquiry into the CFMEU and construction sector. Since then, even Geoffrey Watson – the man whose report provided the LNP its catalyst to launch the Stuart Wood-led probe – has backed the idea. But it’s been almost silence from Crisafulli and Co in response. The Crisafulli government has so far declined to be drawn publicly on growing calls to give its pet project some greater prosecutorial punch. Dan Peled After nudging the government on no less than four separate days since October 9, we thought maybe we’d had a breakthrough when one notification pinged the Circus phone on Monday.



Lo and behold, it was nothing more than a “background” message from a ministerial office telling us it was a matter for Wood’s inquiry. Of course, when we put questions to the $95 million inquiry 10 days ago, it said this was a decision for the government. Given Wood has no power to establish anything like a Victorian-style special prosecutor, we can see why Attorney-General Deb Frecklington’s office wouldn’t want such a line attributed to it. But in lieu of an actual response from the office of Premier David Crisafulli or his deputy and recently unleashed IR attack dog Jarrod Bleijie, that’s about the best we’ve got.



It’s perhaps more telling than a follow-up statement from a Frecklington spokesperson, which reiterated that the inquiry had heard evidence of various wrongdoing within the industry and allegations relating to the former Labor government. Related Article Exclusive

Building Bad His report helped spark Qld’s CFMEU probe. Now he wants a special prosecutor to act “The Crisafulli Government established the CoI [Commission of Inquiry] to ensure these serious matters are thoroughly examined and will continue to support the Commission in carrying out its important work,” they said. That will do little to reassure critics the government believes in the idea of a serious probe that delivers more for Queensland than a rubber-stamp for its policy agenda, social media tiles for Bleijie, and political ammunition for the 2028 election year. Or maybe the hush is because the inquiry is gearing up to recommend referrals for prosecution in an interim report to be handed to government this month.



Who knows? (The tent is always open, anonymously and confidentially, if you do.) Government’s IR review eats a chunk of CFMEU inquiry lunch When it was set up, the CFMEU inquiry was told not to duplicate the work of the Queensland Productivity Commission, which reported back in January. But the government appears to have forgotten to tell its workers’ compensation and industrial relations law review not to step on Wood’s toes. (This is Glenn Ferguson and Gary Black’s report, tabled in parliament last week, along with a response that drew immediate blowback from unions.) Circus noted with interest the government’s controversial new bill included the establishment of a “fit and proper person” test for union officials.



Considering this test was part of the parcel of work handed to Wood by the government, along with possible changes to “whistleblower laws”. This, of course, is another thing Bleijie’s bill will address, with protections for union figures wanting to speak out. Finance Minister Ros Bates has made some new party-linked appointments to the port bodies she jointly oversees. Matt Dennien Two new LNP-linked board directors pull into regional ports Just when you think the Crisafulli government may have run out of board appointments to make, there comes another Friday afternoon media release.



So it was last week, when Finance Minister Ros Bates and Transport Minister Brent Mickelberg announced eight new directors across four of the state’s port authorities. Among the appointments, two names jumped out: Candice Stower at the Gladstone Ports Corporation and John Hathaway at the Port of Townsville. Stower is a registered (and quite active) lobbyist with her pseudonymous shop, chief executive with Queensland United Egg Producers, former ministerial advisor to Nationals figures David Littleproud and Matt Canavan, and a chief of staff to Morrison government minister Keith Pitt. Hathaway, on the other hand, was an army officer of 30 years (rising to the rank of Lieutenant Colonel) before being elected as the LNP’s Newman-era member for the state seat of Townsville. Hathaway’s successor in the seat was Labor’s Scott Stewart – one of the few folks from the other side of the political aisle handed gigs by the government, who Hathaway will now funnily enough join on the board.



Young squeezes in a royal farewell tour with all the stops With little more than a week until the changing of the guard up on Fernberg Road, outgoing Governor Jeannette Young has embarked on a final official jaunt to the motherland. On the agenda? A “farewell call” with King Charles – the kind of royal facetime Jarrod Bleijie was unable to land on his trip this month. But that wasn’t all. View post on X The vice-regal Twitter/X feed, still the platform of choice for day-to-day updates, laid out the itinerary of Young and her husband, Professor Graeme Nimmo, in detail.



There was a church service and reception in St James’ Palace, visits to three museums and galleries, and the laying of a wreath at the Australian War Memorial at Hyde Park Corner. Not to mention a meeting with High Commissioner Jay Weatherill and his deputy Elisabeth Bowes, a morning tea with Trade and Investment Queensland staff, “working lunch” with other top TIQ folks, and a dinner for “inspiring Queenslanders living and working” in the UK. Inspiring stuff. The trip marks Young’s first overseas engagement in more than a year, with her office’s recent 2025-26 annual report noting an active period of domestic travel across the period instead. This included 62 visits to locations across 30 Queensland council areas, including 25 public hospitals and 13 state schools – with Townsville the single-most visited place at four trips. The travel bill for the financial year ran to $208,000, down from the $447,000 in 2024-25 – said to have been due to travel to the UK and Europe, Japan and India “at the request of the Queensland state government”.

World.title: Residents stage sleep-out at empty Kāinga Ora block to be sold
World.content:
Residents have pitched tents to stay overnight at a block of shuttered Kāinga Ora homes, in a last resort to stop the sale of the Wellington site.

The sale deadline of 36 homes in Strathmore is on Wednesday. It has been desolate for years, with plans for development canned.

Protestor Lizzie Pringle told RNZ 10 tents were pitched on the grounds, and it was a chilly Wellington night.

She said the group had invited Kāinga Ora chief Tracey Taylor to join them for breakfast, though they were yet to heard back.

"We are doing a sleepout because we deeply care about Nuku Street remaining public housing.

"Nuku Street has been sitting empty ... it's a perfect site for public housing, there were great Kāinga Ora designs that haven't been followed through on."

Protestors pitch tents. Supplied / Strathmore Housing Action

She said about 80 people gathered at the site when the protest began at 5pm, bringing picnic rugs and food to share.

Pringle hoped the sleep-out sent a strong message to Kāinga Ora to not sell the land.

Ten organisations, including Wellington City Mission, Downtown Community Ministry, Pōneke Public Housing Futures, Renters United, and the Catholic Archdiocese, had previously written an open letter to Kāinga Ora chief executive Tracey Taylor urging a halt to the sale.

Kāinga Ora regional director Sarah Willson previously told RNZ the agency had no plans to review the sale of the properties.

"We decided to sell the properties after careful consideration and exploring several options for the site that showed it was not financially viable to deliver new social housing there."

Willson said the sale money would be reinvested in new social housing that better met tenants needs, and reinvesting the proceeds was an important part of its housing renewal programme.

"We understand the local community's desire for more social housing in Strathmore Park. While it is not financially viable for us to redevelop the Nuku Street site, we remain committed to delivering modern homes in the area."

World.title: Chris Hipkins challenges Christopher Luxon to debate on health
World.content:
Labour leader Chris Hipkins has challenged National leader Christopher Luxon to a debate on health.

It comes after Luxon denied the healthcare system was in crisis, even as a number of professionals sound the alarm about the state of the sector.

In a video on social media, Hipkins spoke directly to the camera, saying: "Christopher Luxon doesn't want to talk about it, but everyone else does."

"So today, I'm challenging Christopher Luxon: come and debate me on health."

Hipkins said the health system was "in crisis."

"That's one of the major issues we should be debating in this election campaign. Let's hear from the people who are being denied the healthcare they deserve. Let's hear from the medical professionals in our health system who are right at breaking point. Now let's answer their questions.

"I'm up for it. I challenge Christopher Luxon to join me."

He said New Zealanders deserved "straight answers about the state of their health system and what the future holds".

World.title: Gloriavale School board defends response to allegation of historic sexual assault
World.content:
Audio player for " Future of Gloriavale's school debated in court " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/education/2024693%2Fgloriavale-school-board-defends-response-to-allegation-of-historic-sexual-assault

Future of Gloriavale's school debated in court Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

The Gloriavale school board has defended its response to an allegation of an historic sexual assault involving a staff member.

Opening arguments have been made in the High Court at Wellington over the future of the West Coast Christian community's school.

The judicial review followed the decision by the Secretary of Education to cancel the private school's registration, over serious concerns that the school is not a physically and emotionally safe place for students.

On Monday, Gloriavale counsel Richard Raymond KC told a courtroom packed with supporters the decision was unlawful and flawed to such an extent it should be dismissed.

Gloriavale counsel Richard Raymond KC. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

He said closing a school was a last resort and the decision to cancel Gloriavale's registration was rushed and disproportionate.

Secretary for Education Ellen MacGregor-Reid told school leaders in December that she was cancelling its registration, but the 80-student school has remained open pending the High Court challenge by the board.

She again confirmed the move in September, after considering the findings of a special Education Review Office (ERO) report, with the ministry applying to lift interim court orders preventing the school's closure.

It was revealed in court on Monday, the Ministry of Education had been critical of the school board's response to an allegation of an historic sexual assault.

The Court suppressed any names and identifying details related to the matter.

Raymond argued the board acted appropriately when the complaint surfaced and took "all reasonable steps to obtain information" about the nature of the allegation.

Gloriavale. (File photo) RNZ / Jean Edwards

"Your honour will be well-aware, I'm sure... there are situations where someone wants information and you simply can't get it.

"There are charges before the court or there's a disciplinary inquiry pending, and it's not in the interests of the person under investigation to disclose it."

He told Justice Karen Grau there had been a factual error and false assumption by the ministry that something more could have been done.

"And with respect, your honour, it's quite telling that the ministry fails to articulate what could have been done. And I say the answer to that is simple. They can't identify it."

A Ministry of Education spokesperson confirmed to RNZ that, "how the board responded to a recent complaint was one of the aspects considered by the Secretary."

Raymond also took issue with earlier information provided to, and reported by, RNZ under the Official Information Act.

In June, RNZ reported a letter from ERO to Oranga Tamariki stating that Gloriavale's school "knowingly employed staff with prior convictions unsuitable for work with children" and "in at least one instance, the school failed to act when behaviours placing students at risk were identified".

Raymond said the information was false, and sought a correction from the Court arguing it had the jurisdiction and responsibility to correct matters in the public domain that had caused reputational damage.

"There are at least two government departments with this incorrect information.

"There has never been anyone employed by the Gloriavale school board who's had prior convictions that would make them unsuitable to teach children and it's incorrect, therefore, to say that when it was discovered that the board basically did nothing about it.

"It's a heinous, serious, highly damaging, very upsetting allegation that the school has had to deal with and we seek to remedy that."

Oranga Tamariki and ERO declined to comment as the matter was before the Court.

The judicial review continues on Tuesday.

World.title: Large vegetation fire which sent smoke billowing across Auckland's Upper Harbour Motorway under control
World.content:
A large vegetation fire which sent smoke billowing across Auckland's Upper Harbour Motorway is now out.

Fire and Emergency NZ said the smoke could be seen between Westgate and Brigham Creek on Monday afternoon.

The fire was in Whenuapai in the Trigg Rd area, it said.

Do you know more? Email iwitness@rnz.co.nz

A large number of firetrucks and firefighters responded to the scene, it said.

By 6.30pm the fire was out, Fire and Emergency NZ said, but three fire crews were still on site to dampen hot spots along with a water tanker.
