World.title: Kyle Whorrall trial: Supermarket run led to unprovoked murder, court told
World.content:
Kyle Whorrall had just made a routine night-time visit to the supermarket and was walking home when he sat down at a bus stop in the Auckland suburb of Meadowbank.

While he was at the bus stop, the Crown says the 33-year-old American PhD student was brutally murdered in an unprovoked attack in April 2025.

Four teens pleaded not guilty to his murder and aggravated robbery in the High Court at Auckland on Monday.

Jurors heard a fifth teenager had earlier pleaded guilty to both charges.

None of the young people can be named.

In his opening address, Crown prosecutor Taniela-Afu Veikune laid out the case and said Whorrall was making his way home from the shops, when the four teens drove past in a car.

"[The car] and its occupants drove past him again, and again, and again, five times, four U-turns going back and forth past Mr Whorall..."

Veikune said two people got out of the car, armed with a machete.

They robbed Whorrall and struck him in the head with the machete, splitting his skull.

"The defendants then left the scene with Mr. Whorrall's wallet, driving away in [the car], leaving him crumpled on the bench in the bus stop, dying from a catastrophic and ultimately fatal injury," Veikune said.

Audio player for " Teens on trial after pleading not guilty to murder of Kyle Whorral " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/crime-and-justice/2023162%2Fkyle-whorrall-trial-supermarket-run-led-to-unprovoked-murder-court-told

Teens on trial after pleading not guilty to murder of Kyle Whorral Checkpoint Download MP3 2m

The trial was less about the murder, and more about the extent of the actions of those involved, Veikune said.

He said the Crown did not have to prove who struck the fatal blow, only that those in the car knew what could have happened.

"The Crown says that the defendants agreed to target Mr Whorrall to rob him, and it would have been known to each of the four defendants, as it would be to any reasonable person, that the robbery could well result in the use of the machete."

Lawyers for the teenagers also gave opening remarks.

Paul Borich KC told the court with all the evidence, and with 18 months of detective work, the Crown still could not say who wielded the machete.

"You might think: 'Well, if the case is going to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt, and the Crown don't know, how can we as jurors know?'," he said.

Borich said it was the person who had already pleaded guilty who was the murderer.

"He used the machete, he is your murderer, the evidence will show that he is the person who did that."

Defence lawyer Harvena Cherrington said there were three questions the jury would need to answer for her client: Was he there, who got out of the car, and what knowledge did he have?

She said the jury should focus on the matters in front of them at trial and not other incidents the Crown referenced.

Veikune had earlier told jurors two of the defendants - Cherrington and Borich's clients - had previously been involved in robberies with a machete.

Another lawyer - Oscar Hintze - acknowledged the Whorrall family.

"We recognise the grief of the Whorrall family," he said.

"Their loss is real and permanent, nobody on this side of the courtroom disputes that Kyle died a terrible and senseless death, or whoever caused it did a grave wrong."

Hintze said feeling sympathy for Kyle and his family was natural, but reminded jurors those feelings had to be put to one side.

"When a young man is killed in a public place, there is an understandable urge for someone to pay, that urge is instinct for revenge," he said.

"You're not here to satisfy that, you're here to do justice, that is something much different and much harder."

Meanwhile, defence lawyer Marie Taylor-Ciphers said there was no evidence her client got out of the car that night.

She cautioned jurors that what they had heard earlier was just the Crown's version of events.

"That's what the prosecution say happened," she said.

"You must make your mind up once you've heard all of the evidence.

The four appeared before Justice Simon Mount, who reminded jurors it was up to the Crown to prove the charges against the group.

World.title: Police use of external AI systems raises 'high risks' of data breaches - expert
World.content:
Using external AI systems for criminal cases raises the risk that cases could be compromised and witnesses could be identified, says a privacy law expert.

Police investigators took evidence home and loaded it into unsecured artificial intelligence (AI) services on their own devices, in breach of police policy.

Documents released to RNZ have detailed some of the AI breaches and risks within the ranks.

Police have a detailed generative AI policy, and did successfully use the Whisper AI tool in the Gulf Harbour body-in-the-bag investigation in 2024.

But one investigator used Google Translate to decipher 350,000 lines of intercepted Chinese language audio. Documents also suggest that sensitive files have been uploaded to unsecured cloud services.

Audio player for " Police investigators uploaded evidence to AI against policy " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/crime-and-justice/2023450%2Fpolice-use-of-external-ai-systems-raises-high-risks-of-data-breaches-expert

Police investigators uploaded evidence to AI against policy Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

Barrister and privacy law expert Kathryn Dalziel told Checkpoint it was "absolutely unacceptable" that police were taking data home and loading it up into open source systems.

"There are high risks that a police officer is putting confidential information into their own environment, it opens themselves up to attack if that becomes known to cyber criminals, it opens up questions about integrations with police internal systems when that information is obtained and then put back into police systems.

"I can see a significant amount of high risk issues around taking things home to work on them."

Employment and privacy lawyer Kathryn Dalziel. Stephanie Defregger

Dalziel said using external AI systems could compromise evidence or an entire case.

"It might provide information or result in information getting out into the public that means it compromises the controls that a court might have over the evidence. If it's made public and jury members get to see it beforehand it could compromise a case; if there are ways to mitigate what's happened or to cover up what's happened, which prevents the police from doing their job."

There was also the possibility that witnesses could be identified.

"If, for example, we are looking at 350,000 lines of audio data, I'm anticipating that there might be a number of witnesses that could be involved in there and that could put them under threat.

Dalziel said there needed to be good policies, procedures and systems to ensure this kind of thing did not result in data breaches, including potentially personal details, legal case information and financial data.

She said police should have these systems available to them.

"We're in a data age, there is nothing new about that and it surprised me when I heard that police officers were going to Google Translate, rather than having a proper system internally to help them.

"I understand the problem for the police was that their internal systems were not assisting them. They had significant controls over Whisper AI that didn't allow them to use other languages and they had 350,000 lines of audio data in Chinese that needed to be quickly assessed in order to know where to direct their attention."

She said urgent resourcing was needed for tools that police could use and would be secure, internal and controlled.

The Privacy Act applies to agencies handling personal information, including when using AI tools. These agencies are expected to have an AI policy and to ensure staff are complying with it.

The office of the Privacy Commissioner says uploading personal information to platforms like Google Translate may be a disclosure under the Privacy Act.

Where sensitive personal information has been disclosed without authorisation, they expect the agency to consider whether it is likely to cause serious harm and requires notification to its office.

World.content:
(Getty Images)

Temba Bavuma knows he has a really tough task ahead of him tonight.

"It's probably going to be tough here in the morning," he said at the toss yesterday. "Overhead conditions, looks quite moist, the wicket, so we'll have to fight it out in the first session and set it up for the guys to come in later."

Given the conditions it looked like a bad toss to lose yesterday morning, although to be honest, Mitch Starc and Josh Hazlewood clearly struggled to get much of anything out of the spongy surface.

Perhaps it wasn't such a bad toss to lose?

In fact, if the pitch is soft enough for the ball to leave some indents on it in these opening two damp days, then perhaps it will become much harder to bat on later in the week?

It makes this partnership very important.

Bavuma resumes on 4 from 13 balls, with debutant opener Marques Ackerman sitting on 5 from 31.

(AP Photo)

I thought Ackerman played pretty well yesterday. He's not an opener by trade, this is the first time he's ever opened in any form of senior first class cricket, but he was circumspect and held onto his attacking instincts to play a very solid innings thus far.

He come in with good pedigree, the 30-year-old.

He averages 48.66 from 85 first class matches, having scored just shy of 6,000 runs and has a high score of 256.

He also captains Dolphins (KwaZulu-Natal) in the unimaginatively named CSA 4-Day Domestic Series.

He actually scored 107 runs at better than a run a ball for Dolphins against Western Province at Newlands in his last first class match in September, adding 60 in his second innings as the Dolphins fell 44 runs short in a thriller.

World.title: Aussie seamer Darcie Brown cut down by back injury
World.content:
Darcie Brown's bid to feature in the inaugural T20 Women's Champions Trophy in India has suffered a huge blow after she was ruled out of the upcoming WBBL season with a back injury.

The Adelaide Strikers' pace ace was diagnosed with a disc injury following her participation in the Australia A tour of India last month.

It was initially hoped a period of de-loading would allow Brown to recover in time for the WBBL season, which runs from October 29 to December 5.

But Cricket Australia confirmed on Monday the injury had not healed sufficiently to allow Brown to resume training.

The news is a big blow to Brown, who was dropped ahead of this year's T20 World Cup and was looking to win back her spot in time for the T20 Champions Trophy in India from February 14-28.

The back injury also ruled the 23-year-old out of Australia's recent 3-0 ODI clean sweep of Bangladesh.

Brown has played six Tests, 30 ODIs and 41 T20s for Australia, and will be a huge loss for the Strikers this WBBL season.

"Darcie is a quality player who will be missed on the field, but she remains a hugely important part of our squad," Strikers coach Luke Williams said.

"She brings outstanding experience, professionalism and leadership, and those qualities will continue to have a positive influence on our group throughout WBBL 12."

Australia are 1-0 up in their three-match T20 series against New Zealand after posting a tense two-wicket win at North Sydney Oval on Sunday.

Games two and three will be held at North Sydney Oval on Tuesday and Thursday.

World.title: St Kilda AFL player Charlie Banfield accidentally runs over friend with car
World.content:
St Kilda AFL player Charlie Banfield accidentally ran over his close friend with a car on a private property in Western Australia earlier this month.

The ABC was contacted by two separate sources who said the accident occurred at a party at a rural property in Yallingup, in the state's south-west.

The ABC has been told that the victim was hospitalised with broken bones.

But despite the severity of the injuries, the ABC understands emergency services were not called to the scene.

Do you know more? Contact Jessica Halloran at Halloran.Jessica@abc.net.au

If you require more secure communication, please choose an option on the confidential tips page.

St Kilda confirmed the accident occurred and said in a statement: "The St Kilda Football Club is aware of an incident involving Charlie Banfield on a rural private property in Western Australia.

"Our thoughts are with Charlie and the injured individual, who we understand will make a swift and full recovery.

"The club has already spoken to Charlie about this incident and will continue to support him through the matter."

It is understood the pair are close friends and no legal action would be taken against Banfield, as it was being treated as an accident.

Fiona Stanley Hospital has confirmed the young man was hospitalised but has since been discharged.

A WA Police spokesperson said it had not received any reports regarding the incident, while St John Ambulance said it did not have a record of attending the area that night.

Charlie Banfield with his mother Amber and his father Drew ahead of him making his AFL debut in May. (Instagram: @stkildafc)

The 19-year-old midfielder grew up in WA and made his AFL debut this year.

The ABC contacted Banfield's mother, Amber, who did not wish to comment.

Amber Banfield spent six years on the board of the West Australian Football Commission, while his father, Drew Banfield, was a two-time premiership player for the West Coast Eagles.

The teenager was picked up by the Saints after the Eagles decided not to match their bid in last year's national draft.

Banfield was recruited from the Claremont Colts in the WAFL, winning the Mel Whinnen Medal as best on ground in the 2025 WAFL Colts Grand Final.

He was also vice-captain at his prestigious Perth private school, Scotch College.

The AFL has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Chancellor announces Wallaroos retirement ahead of Scotland Test
World.content:
An emotional Emily Chancellor admits that if she were told she would feature in two Women's Rugby World Cups, earn 41 caps for the Wallaroos and spend eight years with the national team, she would have laughed.

Even after announcing her retirement from international rugby on Monday, the 35-year-old still cannot fathom what has really unfolded over her glittering career.

"Rugby wasn't an option for me growing up. I didn't know that it [the women's game] existed," Chancellor said as tears welled up in her eyes.

"Having found the game when I was at uni, playing sevens, dabbling in that, and then finding 15s in 2015. I knew from the start that this was a game that I wanted to be involved in.

"It [retirement is] a hard one because I'm still here, physically, and feel capable. But I also think I'm ready for the next chapter.

Chancellor a 'natural leader' for Wallaroos Emily Chancellor will captain the Wallaroos for the first time as Australia faces Wales in Brisbane.

"But if you told me then that I would have been playing internationally for eight years, I would have probably laughed at you."

Chancellor is set to play her final game for the Wallaroos when she runs out against Scotland on Friday at Canberra Stadium.

The back-rower's potential 42nd Test comes after she made her debut against New Zealand in 2018 aged 26, when she was awarded the player of the game.

"I was so terrified. I remember sitting in the change room, thinking, 'Oh my goodness, I'm playing against another country. I'm not good enough for this,'" she said.

"Then [I was] like, 'Well, of course I'm good enough. I've been picked to play for my country'.

"I'd been a rugby fan for a long time, gone to games with my dad and mum all the way through growing up. I just didn't realise that you could do it as a girl.

Chancellor only announced her retirement from international rugby. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

"As a curious person, someone who had always watched the game, [I wanted] to actually nail the detail, the intricacies of such a complex game."

The 35-year-old featured in her first World Cup in 2021 before suffering an ACL injury in 2024.

But the best was yet to come for the back-rower as she would become the Wallaroos' 19th captain last year before featuring in the World Cup campaign in England.

"If I can drive a standard and keep pushing a program to be better than we are, then I have done my job. And I think back to the years of being in this team, and I'm pretty proud of how I have tried to do that," Chancellor said.

"It's a really special team. I've played with 108 players across my [Wallaroos] career.

"We've seen the growth. We've been part of some crazy experiences … I wouldn't have pushed myself and my body and made the choices to choose this lifestyle for so many years if it wasn't worth it."

World.title: RLWC quick hits: Ponga's power, Tonga's triumph and Fiji's sunny day
World.content:
The first week of the Rugby League World Cup is in the books with stars new and old making statements across the tournament.

From the classic opener between Australia and New Zealand to Tonga's statement win over England and Papua New Guinea's handy victory over Lebanon there's plenty for the international football fan to sink their teeth into.

Here are the quick hits from the opening round.

1. Kalyn Ponga holds New Zealand's hopes in his hands

Ponga scored a double for New Zealand before departing late with a broken arm. (Getty Images: Matt King)

Over the past few months Kalyn Ponga has made a transformation from someone who can play great into a great player and if his World Cup is over due to a broken arm not only will the tournament be far poorer without him he might take New Zealand's title hopes home with him.

Ponga was magnificent in his Kiwi debut on Friday night, scoring two tries and running for 254 metres as he continued the form that helped drive Newcastle to the grand final earlier this month.

World Cup opener a reminder of Australia's glory days There was a time when Test matches were rugby league's biggest, best and bloodiest spectacles, and last night's World Cup opener between Australia and New Zealand was a reminder of those days.

His battles with Australia's Reece Walsh will take some beating as the defining memory from the entire World Cup even as New Zealand fell to a frustrating defeat where they dominated every major stat but the scoreboard.

Ponga has undergone surgery and will remain in camp but if his transcendent year is over, things might have peaked early for the Kiwis.

Keano Kini, a fine fullback in his own right, was terrific in New Zealand's Pacific Championship win last year and has the work rate and running game to break any match open.

But he is not Kalyn Ponga, who is not rare but unique. That means there's nobody else like him.

2. Speed can kill for lightning Samoan backline

Fa'alogo scored four tries off the bench for Samoa in their big win over France. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

It's a measure of the depth Samoa enjoy that Su'a Fa'alogo, Melbourne's player of the year and one of the most dynamic attacking weapons in the sport, could only crack a bench spot for their first match.

Even so, Samoa proved they could strike from anywhere at any time and through almost any player — Jermaine McEwan's 50 metre solo effort will be one of the best efforts of the entire World Cup.

But after Fa'alogo was pitched into the action early following an injury to Deine Mariner and finished with four tries, three try assists and seven linebreaks in this thumping victory it's clear he can act as the Toa's wildcard as they look to emulate 2022's brilliant run to the final.

Just where the Storm fullback fits into the side remains to be seen — Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow is a brilliant fullback in his own right and Fa'alogo's unfamiliarity with playing wing could be targeted by more dangerous opposition.

But speed can kill and when Fa'alogo is out there Samoa have enough to run and gun with anybody.

3. Future is now for Papua New Guinea

The looming presence of the PNG Chiefs is the subtext beneath every Papua New Guinea game in this World Cup and after this impressive win it seems they've landed a good one in Gairo Voro.

The 23-year old five-eighth is coming off a monster season with London Broncos in the English second division, where he scored 39 tries in 31 games to claim the competition's player of the year award.

He took that good form into this victory, scoring a long range try and creating another with his speed and footwork standing out against a Cedars side with plenty of NRL experience.

Tapping into as much local talent as possible will be crucial and if Voro's improvement continues very well could be one of their early success stories.

4. Powerful Tongan statement a long time coming

Tonga ran roughshod over a disappointing England side. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

Tonga's fourth win over a Tier 1 nation is by far their most dominant — the margin of victory is just one point more than the combined margin of all three previous wins.

Even though they've won just one of their past nine matches, have been building to a dominant performance like this for some time.

All nine of those games were against Australia, England, New Zealand or Samoa, and Tonga are now experience the gain from the pain of those defeats.

Tonga now have one foot in the semi-finals. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

The attacking cohesion between regulars like Isaiya Katoa, Haumole Olakau'atu and veteran Tui Lolohea was plain to see, as was the defensive combinations that held England to just two tries despite enjoying far better of the field position, and shows that the benefits of regular matches extends beyond than simply winning and losing.

Tonga have hit the ground running but will still have improvement in them. With a semi-final spot essentially at their mercy after this win, it's a good spot to be in.

England, by contrast, have paid the price for the same flaw that cost them in last year's Ashes series — a lack of spark inside the attacking 20. They've scored just 30 points across their past four matches and their inability to strike has them on the verge of their earliest ever World Cup exit.

5. Fiji makes hay while the sun shines

Solomone Saukuru of Fiji scores a try during the 2026 Men's Rugby League World Cup. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

With matches against Australia and New Zealand to come this might be as good as it gets for Fiji in this World Cup but you'd be hard-pressed to find a better day in the sun for the Bati than their opener against the Cook Islands.

After their women's side, the Bulikula, came within a whisker of pulling off a remarkable upset against New Zealand in just their ninth match ever they lined the tunnel to sing the men's team onto the field as they were led out by Fiji legend Akuila Uate carrying the national flag.

It was a potent mix of past and future combining in the present and didn't just Fiji duly responded, they looked good doing it.

Halves Kurt Donogohoe and Brandon Wakeham, who both played in last year's Pacific Bowl tournament together, showed the benefits of their combination with five try assists between them and Manly lock Caleb Navale was excellent in the middle of the field.

There will be harder matches to come but expect Fiji to hold the gloves up.

They haven't played a Tier 1 nation since the last World Cup but they have the talent, experience and cohesion to make Australia sweat for at least a little while.

World.title: Simmons says cruel injury ahead of NBA season 'not the end of my story'
World.content:
Ben Simmons's burgeoning NBA comeback has been halted after he suffered a torn Achilles during practice just days out from the season-opener.

The Australian had shown promising signs during the Sacramento Kings' pre-season contests after spending all of last season away from the NBA.

According to a Kings release, Simmons was injured during a live drill before an MRI scan revealed a torn right Achilles tendon. Simmons will undergo surgery.

The 30-year-old's career has been derailed by injuries over the past five years. Prior to his injury issues, Simmons made three NBA All-Star teams and was considered one of the best defensive players in the league.

Despite the setback, Simmons is adamant the injury does not spell an end to his NBA career.

"I've faced challenges before that tested me mentally, physically, and emotionally, and I've found a way through every single one of them," he wrote on Instagram.

"This injury is another chapter in my journey, not the end of my story.

"It's never easy being away from the game I love, especially after everything it took to get back here.

"But if there's one thing I've learned, it's that adversity doesn't define you. How you respond to it does.

"I've been knocked down before, and I've always found a way to get back up. This time will be no different."

Simmons signed a one-year deal with the Kings last month.

After playing 81 of 82 regular-season games in his rookie season, Simmons's durability has gradually waned.

He has not played in excess of 60 regular season games since the 2018-19 season, and he managed just 50 in his most recent NBA season with the Brooklyn Nets and LA Clippers in 2024-25.

Simmons recently detailed his career and his comeback attempt in an ESPN documentary where he hit back at critics who have questioned his love for basketball.

"Everyone has their thing that they love and they have passion for, and basketball is that passion for me," he said.

"All these people talk about I don't love the game. That's bullshit.

"I've played through the injuries. I've broken my foot, I've rehabbed, I've had multiple back surgeries. I've been through it all.

"If I didn't love the game, trust me, I would be at home, I'd be fishing … but I love this shit."

The NBA regular season kicks off on Wednesday morning AEDT when the Detroit Pistons host the Boston Celtics. Sacramento's season opener takes place in Los Angeles against the Clippers on Thursday afternoon.

World.title: Brighton winger's long-range goal conjures decades-old memories of Beckham
World.content:
A remarkable Diego Gomez goal from halfway has put an exclamation mark on Brighton's 5-0 English Premier League win over Crystal Palace.



The result marked another statement victory in a campaign that has already seen the south-coast team overwhelm Arsenal 3-0.



But it was Gomez, hitting it like Beckham, who stole the spotlight.

Collecting the ball near the halfway line, the Brighton midfielder advanced just inside Crystal Palace's half and launched a 50-metre shot over stranded goalkeeper Walter Benitez and into the net for a spectacular goal in the seventh minute of the EPL match at Amex Stadium overnight.

The Paraguay international's shot revived memories of a strike from a similar range from David Beckham when playing for Manchester United against Wimbledon on the opening day of the 1996-97 Premier League season.

It remains one of football's most famous goals and thrust Beckham into the global spotlight.

Gomez's goal put Brighton 2-0 ahead against its biggest rival — and the team went 3-0 up three minutes later before running out a 5-0 winner.

Brighton manager Fabian Hurzeler said Gomez tried a similar effort in the 2-0 win at Sunderland last weekend.

"There the wind wasn't perfect for this try," Hurzeler said. "Now the wind was better for him.

"I'm really happy that he gets this reward for all of the effort he's putting into the club, into his own development, and into the team."

Brighton's big win leaves it third on the EPL table behind Manchester City and Arsenal.

The side has scored a league-high 23 goals in seven games and has the best goal difference.

AP

World.title: 'Anxious' Smith's concussion admission after latest head knock
World.content:
Steve Smith has revealed his anxiety about another concussion after he was struck on the helmet in the first Test against South Africa.

Smith batted on after he was hit by Anrich Nortje in Durban, before staying off the field on day four once Australia declared.

The 37-year-old then passed checks for delayed concussions that evening and the next morning, before returning to the match on day five.

Quick hits: Boland's rain-soaked brilliance and a touching family moment Scott Boland makes a destructive return to the team and a South African debutant has a touching family moment as rain plays spoilsport in Gqeberha. Here are the quick hits from day one of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.

Smith has experienced concussions before, most notably when he was hit by Jofra Archer during the 2019 Ashes and missed the next Test.

"I was a little bit anxious to be honest after the hit," Smith said on Kayo Sports ahead of the start to the second Test.

"I've had a few in the past, and had a few concussions and I really don't like the way that makes me feel.

"The rest of that day I wasn't travelling too well. I think it was more to do with anxiety of hoping not to feel the way that I felt in the past, waking up the next morning and things like that.

"Fortunately I woke up well. I passed all the tests and things recovered pretty quickly."

Smith's catching remains as good as ever, despite his Test career slowly coming to an end. (Supplied: Fox Cricket)

Smith made scores of 25 and 27 in Australia's 214-run win in Durban, but his bigger contribution was his brilliant catching in the slips.

The right-hander's future has long been a talking point, with Smith often teasing that he could decide at any point he is ready to retire.

But Australia's captain Pat Cummins insisted in Gqeberha that may be a positive.

"A lot of people have a grand exit and plan it years ahead. But where he's at, and I totally get it, is 'I don't really want to think that far ahead'," Cummins said.

"That doesn't necessarily mean that something's imminent. I think it means he's in a really good place.

"You don't need to read into it any more than that … He's batting really well, catching really well. He seems to be enjoying himself around the group.

"Hopefully he's playing for a lot longer, but any conversation that I have isn't for a big grand exit that's very well planned ahead."

AAP

Tech.title: It’s hard to imagine wireless headphones ever getting lighter than these
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If you’re on the hunt for lightweight wireless headphones but wearing earbuds or clip-ons never feels comfortable or secure, a relatively obscure Japanese headphone maker could have the solution. Final’s new Porta headphones feature an on-ear design supported by a headband but with a structure made from a single piece of wire so they weigh just 40 grams. For comparison, Marshall’s recently-launched Milton A.N.C. are also designed to be smaller on-ear headphones but weigh 200 grams.

The Final Porta are available for preorder now through the company’s online store for 12,800 yen (around $80) with black or orange ear pads and shipping expected to start on October 23rd. The company also has an Amazon shop for US-based customers, but the Porta aren’t listed there yet.

The Porta come with either black or orange ear pads. Image: Final

Sporting a design that looks loosely inspired by the lightweight headphones Sony bundled with its Walkmans decades ago, the Porta’s functionality is unsurprisingly basic. A 57mAh battery charges over USB-C and provides up to eight hours of use while the Porta are wirelessly paired to a device using Bluetooth 5.4 and streaming audio over the SBC and AAC codecs. There’s no active noise cancelation which is not uncommon for on-ear headphones that don’t create a full seal, but with an IPX4 rating you should be able to use the Porta in the rain or while working up a sweat without worrying about them getting damaged by the moisture.

Tech.title: A hacker broke into John Deere and SharkNinja with an army of AI agents
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A hacker broke into more than 100 websites using an army of AI agents that mostly operated on their own, according to findings from the AI security firm Norforge. Though Norforge doesn’t name the targets, Reuters reports that the victims included companies like John Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins.

Concerns over AI-powered cybersecurity breaches have grown as the technology grows more advanced, with hackers using the tools to carry out large-scale attacks. At the same time, rogue AI agents are carrying out attacks of their own after escaping from testing environments.

Researchers at Norforge uncovered the attacks through exposed work on Cairn, an open-source AI platform that describes itself as a “general-purpose problem-solving engine.” With Cairn, users set a start and end point for the AI agents, which document their progress as they move forward with the task. However, as noted by Norforge, hackers can also use the tool to orchestrate cyberattacks using AI agents.

The hacker who broke into more than 100 sites was the “most active” among the exposed Cairn instances discovered by Norforge, waging attacks on companies based in the US, Canada, Australia, and Japan, as reported by Reuters. This attacker laid out “preferred intrusion tactics” using fewer than 100 Chinese characters, with successful breaches taking about 23 hours, according to Reuters. Overall, Nordforge found more than 20 exposed Cairn instances that are “likely malicious.”

In a statement to Reuters, a John Deere spokesperson said there is “no indication that ​sensitive information was accessed” as a result of the attack, while Cummins said it’s “investigating the report of a potential cyber-attack on a website operated by one of our third-party vendors.”

Meanwhile, SharkNinja says the breach impacted a standalone site with product support information, and that it has contained the threat. John Deere, Cumms, and SharkNinja didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

Nordforge says it’s working to get the malicious Cairn instances taken down. Cairn’s creator, who goes by @le1xia0, said earlier this month that the platform “was never a ‘hacking tool,’” adding that “misuse is a human decision, not a feature of the engine.”

Tech.title: Wyze moved the screen on its new smart scale to the handle so it’s easier to read at eye level
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Wyze announced a new version of its Ultra BodyScan smart scale that debuted nearly a year ago with additional electrodes on a retractable handle, allowing it to provide a breakdown of various health metrics across your arms, legs, and torso. With the new Ultra BodyScan Plus, Wyze is introducing a redesign that moves the scale’s 4.3-inch customizable color screen to the retractable handle so all the measurements are now displayed closer to eye level.

The Wyze Scale Ultra BodyScan Plus is available starting today for $149 through Wyze’s online store in black or white color options. That makes it about $30 more expensive than the $119.98 Ultra BodyScan, but the relocated screen isn’t the only upgrade. While last year’s model was able to measure 13 different body composition metrics, including weight, BMI, bone mass, body water percentage, and muscle weight, the new Plus model bumps that to over 50 metrics like visceral fat, protein, and basal metabolic rate, which is the minimum number of calories your body needs each day to sustain itself. And using bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA), it can provide a breakdown of those metrics across your body.

The handle and display dock to the scale, which can be used to make measurements without using the handle. Image: Wyze

Wyze’s competitor Withings revealed last week that new users will need to 

Image: Wyze

The scale can recognize and store health metrics and measurements for up to eight registered users while allowing an unlimited number of guests to take one-off measurements. There’s also a mode for measuring the weight of children, pets, and luggage while you’re holding them, but without the advanced health metrics breakdown.

Tech.title: Vibe coding is turning the music gear world upside down
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

If you spend any time on r/synthesizers or watch a lot of synth videos on YouTube, you’ve probably noticed the explosion of custom firmware for hardware synthesizers, samplers, and grooveboxes. What unites almost all of them is that they were made possible by increasingly sophisticated vibe coding tools.

These sorts of custom firmware were exceedingly rare in the pre-LLM days, and required both deep expertise and an incredible investment of time. It could take weeks or months to add a simple feature like velocity sensitivity to a Korg Volca. Now, hobbyist hackers are able to turn Temu synths into full-fledged grooveboxes in a matter of days.

Elektron’s budget-friendly Model:Cycles, Digitone, Octatrack, and Digitakt have all gained new capabilities with Claude’s help. Roland’s SP-404 MKII, Ableton’s Push 3 and Move, Akai’s MPC Live and MPC One, as well as the vintage MPC 2000, Novation’s Circuit, Arturia’s MicroFreak, and even Zoom’s 14-year-old Multistomp pedal line have all seen new custom firmware released in the last month or so.

Leading the charge is a tiny $70 Yamaha DX-7 clone: the M-Vave FM-1. It was already on its way to being the synth of the summer. The dirt-cheap price and faithful recreation of classic FM tones made it incredibly popular with first-time synth buyers, hobbyists, and synthfluencers alike. Inevitably, someone wondered how far they could push the hardware and, with the help of AI, kickstarted an arms race.

The FM-1 now has dozens of custom firmwares available. Many of the most popular — Felucca, Sloop, and x0x — list Claude as a contributor on their GitHub page or include explicit disclosures about their use of AI. Baudgirl is also suspected to have been created with the assistance of AI, but the developer did not reply to a request for comment.

What started as a surprisingly good, but basic DX-7 clone now supports a variety of synth engines, including virtual analog, sample playback, multi-track sequencing, and a variety of UI designs.

It’s not terribly shocking that someone was willing to risk bricking a $70 Temu synth. Generally, the gear that has benefited from this surge of vibe-coded custom firmware is older or more affordable.

Roman Rusinov, who posts on Reddit as themanro and releases music under Farlow, set his sights on the Zoom MS-70CDR. It’s a budget multi-effects pedal from 2012 that has a reputation for punching above its weight, making it a staple of affordable synth setups. He started by learning about ZDL, a project that reverse-engineered the Multistomp format, allowing for the creation of custom effects. He eventually coaxed the pedal into running NAM A2 Lite captures and custom impulse responses (IRs), turning it into a full-fledged modeler capable of emulating vintage amps.

“I was already using AI for some work stuff and figured this would be a great case to try learning some vibe-coding fundamentals and get a project going,” he told The Verge. “There was a lot of trial and error of finding the limitations of the hardware and software.” He says he’s thrilled to be part of a broader movement. “Somehow it all lined up with all these other projects pushing the boundaries of older hardware and breathing new life into it. I love that,” he said. “If you own the hardware, you should be able to do whatever you want with it.”

18nelli, the developer behind Modded Cycles, was similarly motivated by a desire to revitalize some forgotten gear. “I had an Elektron Model:Cycles that left me feeling frustrated,” he told The Verge. He said that it felt designed “just to push us to buy their more expensive gear.” But recent AI advances made him believe he could add features to the groovebox, which hasn’t had an official update since May 2021.

So he opened up his Cycles, documented all the parts, and started working with Claude Code to implement his first hack — six-track audio over USB. That has since exploded into a community project with multiple mods contributed by others, several standalone custom firmwares, and even the ability to turn your Model:Cycles into a Model:Samples. “I think not using LLMs would have been counterproductive,” he said. “I probably would have spent a massive amount of time and energy on just a single feature, whereas my real goal is to actually create and make music with amazing mods.”

Modded Cycles has certainly been one of the more frantic projects out there. I recently watched as five firmware updates hit the announcements channel on its Discord in one day. 18nelli has since said he plans to pause adding new features and slow development to polish the existing code and stomp out some bugs.

New mods and firmwares hit the web almost every day now. If there’s a favorite piece of gear in your arsenal that you wish had one killer feature, there’s a chance it might end up on a GitHub page sooner than later. Heck, if you just wish your pocket synth could play NES ROMs, that’s also a distinct possibility.

Of course, there is some risk here. These firmwares are often less thoroughly tested than the manufacturer’s official one. The response to the modding scene has varied from company to company, with many choosing to remain silent. Elektron banned links to custom firmware from their forums. In a statement posted on its official forums, the company said, “We would always warn against modifications to our firmware and/or machines that could brick them … Something that looks like a simple change in isolation can lead to major problems elsewhere, particularly when a later official OS arrives, and can confuse users about which features are officially available on our machines.”

Others, like M-Vave, seem to be embracing the movement. It recently announced FM1 Open, an open-source firmware with additional features, plus a development kit and a firmware-flashing tool for the community.

The response to music gear that uses AI and vibe coding has been mixed. Devices like the Polyend Endless have sparked some ire. And music-making subreddits are awash in people complaining about vibe-coded plugin slop. But so far the community has been less hostile to vibe-coded firmware. Maybe, in part, because breathing new life into old instruments helps keep their Gear Acquisition Syndrome (GAS) in check.

Tech.title: Democrats think cracking down on AI could give them an edge
Tech.content:
is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.

Democrats could win back control of Congress this November, and if they do, they’ll need to decide how to approach one of the country’s newest and thorniest political issues: AI.

Polls predict Democrats will flip at least one chamber of Congress in the midterm elections, which would put committee leadership back in their hands. That could usher in a wave of newfound scrutiny for AI companies. Top Democrats on key committees have already signaled their willingness to press the industry on tax credits tied to data centers and recent hacking incidents, and would be able to set committee agendas if they take over, allowing them to call CEOs to testify in Congress and demand documents that explain companies’ inner workings.

AI issues are already taking a leading role in campaign ads, particularly as data center development has driven residents across the political spectrum to packed local meetings. While President Donald Trump has opposed most regulation of the technology in favor of an accelerationist approach, public opinion polling has shown that Americans have widespread concerns about how AI will impact jobs, education, and other aspects of life. The direction and intensity of that oversight, though, is up for grabs.

The issue of AI is “a hundred percent ready for the taking,” says Jesse Lehrich, a Democratic strategist who previously ran a tech accountability advocacy group and worked for Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign. “The question remains open as to whether Democrats are willing and able to seize that opportunity.” AI issues currently include a lot of different things, from monitoring and restricting the development of frontier models to dealing with the effects of job displacement or data centers’ energy demands. Across both parties, lawmakers are still figuring out where to put their stakes in the ground, and early congressional proposals have yet to gain broad consensus.

“The question remains open as to whether Democrats are willing and able to seize that opportunity”

AI caught many lawmakers off guard, says Rob Flaherty, former deputy campaign manager for Kamala Harris’ presidential campaign and a Biden White House alum who cohosts a podcast with Lehrich. “For a long time, Democrats were afraid to talk about it, either for a mix of not understanding it, or being afraid of the money that was going to be poured in by the AI industry,” Flaherty says. But as AI becomes more salient for voters, “there will be immense profit to whoever can speak to the world that we’re moving into at a volume that voters can hear and can feel.”

Flaherty recently launched a super PAC called Tomorrow Together with Karthik Ganapathy, a former state communications director for Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaign. The group launched its first $4 million ad blitz last week in battleground House races, attacking Republican candidates as out of touch on AI and referencing issues like kids’ online safety and data centers. The group is looking beyond the midterms toward the 2028 presidential election, aiming to hone Democrats’ messaging to double down on what resonates most with voters.

While data centers have been the most visible AI issue in many communities, Flaherty says his group’s polling found sweeping bans on state AI regulation — repeatedly pushed by Trump and congressional Republicans — are even more broadly unpopular. Democratic donor and venture capitalist Ron Conway now regrets funding Marc Andreessen-backed pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future, Jay Carney, a former Obama press secretary who now runs communications for Conway’s VC fund, told Politico.

As of June, LTF spent nearly $45 million over almost a year, with $31 million left in the pot according to Federal Election Commission filings. “At a certain point, voters speak louder than money,” Flaherty says. Even governors who lean toward the center of the Democratic Party, like California’s Gavin Newsom or Pennsylvania’s Josh Shapiro, have taken bolder stances against AI in recent weeks. Newsom issued an executive order looking to create an AI “kill switch” after previously vetoing a bill that would have instituted some similar measures, and Shapiro reversed course against data centers.

Democrats are well positioned to capitalize on the negative sentiment toward AI

Democrats are well positioned to capitalize on the negative sentiment toward AI because Trump’s largely anti-regulation stance has boxed in his party. Though some Republicans, including Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO), have carved out a more skeptical approach to AI, Lehrich says, “I cannot think of a bigger political gift than Donald Trump just wholly bear-hugging the industry and declaring that we must let data reign and any community that rejects data centers is backwards and poor.”

A more sweeping AI regulatory agenda might include embedding independent researchers into frontier labs, requiring more safety checks up front, and imposing more liability on tech companies for anything from how their tools affect kids to whether they’re used to discriminate against workers or housing applicants. Lawmakers could also consider ways to meet demands from constituents that AI companies help pay for job displacement and other impacts they’ll have on people’s lives.

“I cannot think of a bigger political gift than Donald Trump just wholly bear-hugging the industry”

AI is still not the top issue driving voters to the polls, but Flaherty says that’s not necessarily the right way to think about it. “AI is not an issue as much as it is a story,” he says. “It’s a story of politicians getting bought off by industry. It’s a story of a bunch of guys making you foot the bill for them getting rich while they’re coming to make your life worse. It is a story that fits the national vibe.”

Where exactly different policy lines should be drawn on AI is still somewhat unsettled. But Flaherty warns that Democrats risk giving up ground if they fail to take big enough swings. Voters are “giving politicians a lot of leeway to take big swings and to really reimagine stuff,” he says. If politicians only stick to basics like plans to retrain workers at community colleges, “I think we’re going to miss the bigness and the ingenuity that the moment calls for.”

Tech.title: The Maeving RM2 is high-style electric riding with a few compromises
Tech.content:
There’s a fast-growing category of two-wheeled electric vehicles splitting the difference between high-end scooters and entry-level motorcycles, fresh bikes with avant-garde style but approachable performance.

I’m talking about offerings like the Infinite Machine P1 and BMW CE 02, similar concepts but with wildly different attitudes. Among this class, the Maeving RM2 stands out. It has a distinctly retrofuturistic flair, bringing together the vibe of classic British motorcycles like the Triumph Bonneville or Royal Enfield Continental GT, just without the literal vibes caused by internal combustion.

Quite the contrary, in fact. The RM2 is one of the quietest, smoothest motorcycles I’ve ever ridden. It also has an innovative solution to a common electric motoring problem. Unfortunately, its rough edges make the $10,995 asking price feel a bit extravagant.

Previous Next







1 / 5

Power for one

UK-based Maeving was founded in 2018 and currently has three motorcycles in its stable: the RM1S, the moody Blackout edition, and the RM2. All are based on the same basic drivetrain and battery technology, with similar power output and range.

The difference is the layout. The RM1S and Blackout offer a solo seat, while the RM2 has a longer saddle and beefier frame that lets you invite a friend along for a ride.

A lightweight friend, anyhow. The RM2 features a 15-horsepower, 193-pound-foot electric hub motor integrated into the rear wheel. That’s more torque than the beefiest of muscle motorcycles, so it gets off the line reasonably well. However, that anemic power figure means it struggles to pick up speed.

It’s officially rated for up to 70mph, but in its most powerful mode it barely clipped over 63mph with me holding the throttle wide open for as long as I dared.

If I put my chest on the tank and tucked in my elbows it crept up a few points to 67mph, but to hit 70 I had to wait for the road to pitch down into a valley. On the climb back out I struggled to maintain 60. (For reference, I weigh 172 pounds.)

That’s not the kind of performance that would make me feel comfortable riding with a passenger on the back. Power, then, is not the RM2’s forte, but that isn’t to say it’s lacking charm.

Previous Next











1 / 7

Smooth operator

While I do love the sound of many motorcycles, I’ve lately come to adore the serenity of riding electric. I’ve thrown a leg over plenty of electric bikes over the years, but none offered the peace and quiet of the RM2.

The hub motor design means there’s absolutely no drivetrain noise at all. Most electric motorcycles rely on chains or belts to send power to the rear wheel, and even the quietest add some sort of commotion to your commute. On the RM2, all I can hear is the wind.

Well, the wind and a persistent buzz from the front fender whenever I hit a bump. As many vehicle manufacturers have learned, the outright silence of an EV means that noises formerly drowned out by the white noise of internal combustion can suddenly become quite annoying.

That sadly wasn’t the only thing rattling on the RM2 I tested. The left bar-end mirror was so loose I was worried it might fall off, and the front wheel seemed to chatter over every asphalt imperfection, creating an unsettled feeling from the nonadjustable front fork.

Overall, the bike’s suspension just didn’t seem up to the task. Bigger bumps launched me out of the saddle so harshly that I got in the habit of standing up when approaching obstacles. And that’s despite my test machine having the $995 upgraded shocks at the back.

Previous Next







1 / 5

Practicalities

That rear suspension has more to do thanks to the weight of the hub motor. But mounting it there frees up room within the RM2’s frame, creating a delightfully simple look and keeping weight low: just 320 pounds. Combine that with a seat height of 30.5 inches and you have a wonderfully easy machine to ride.

The traditional engine spot in the frame is filled by a forward-leaning battery unit. Press a button on the left grip and the battery door swings open, exposing a pair of removable packs. Each has its own button to release it from the bike, then just swivel out the integrated handle and carry it inside to charge under your desk.

That’s the theory, anyway. In practice, you’ll have to hit that button a few times, as it never worked for me on the first try. Likewise, the bike often didn’t recognize when I’d closed the door again, showing an error code on the digital dash until I’d opened and slammed the door a few times.

Each of the 2.73-kilowatt-hour packs weighs 36 pounds and features an uncomfortably thin plastic handle. Want to feel what it’s like to carry one? Fill a 5-gallon bucket three-quarters of the way to the top with water, then lug it up to your office or apartment. While great in concept, it’s not something I’d want to do regularly.

Sadly, you might have to if you don’t have access to outside charging. The RM2 is officially rated for 80 miles on a charge, but I think the only way you’d hit that is by keeping to the bike’s default ride mode, limited to 45mph. In Sport mode, I averaged roughly 50 miles per charge.

If you don’t want to carry those packs around, you can charge the bike directly via a connector on the side. Sadly, it’s proprietary and only works with the included charger. Maeving does offer an adapter for charging on a standard SAE J1772 connector, but that costs a whopping $440 and doesn’t increase charging speed.

The good news is there’s room to store that charger right on the bike. What looks like a fuel tank is actually a locking storage compartment. It’s the perfect size for a quick run to pick up some milk or takeout from your local Thai place.

Charmingly flawed

The RM2 certainly has a lot of room for improvement, but at the end of my time with the thing, I was still quite charmed. It’s such a good-looking, easy-riding machine that I wanted to hop on it for every errand I had to run.

Well, every errand that didn’t take me on the highway or more than 25 miles away from home, anyway. I wouldn’t trust the RM2 to go any farther, and with an 80 percent charge taking four hours on the standard charger, road-tripping is out of the question.

And then there’s the cost. The Maeving RM2 starts at $10,995, but when you add the matte paint, upgraded suspension, and carbon fiber fenders of my test bike, you’re looking at $13,275. For that money, you could buy two Royal Enfield Continental GT motorcycles, and as much as I love electric motoring, that’s a tough financial pill to swallow.

Photography by Tim Stevens / The Verge

Tech.title: A Savannah police officer gave her Flock login to her ICE agent husband
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Now, former Savannah police officer Amber Harpe was fired in August following a department investigation that found she had shared her Flock login information with her husband, Tyler Harpe, an ICE agent. SPD does not share its Flock data with ICE and said sharing access to the system violated the department’s security protocols.

While he had unauthorized access to the system, Tyler Harpe conducted 983 searches related to 97 license plates, which were overwhelmingly registered to Hispanic drivers, according to Savannah’s local ABC affiliate, WJCL. The Harpes defended their actions, saying they didn’t use access for personal reasons and that the searches were strictly for “law-enforcement purposes.”

Interim Major Max Nowinsky originally recommended a light eight-hour suspension for Harpe. However, Major Michelle Halford and Assistant Police Chief Robert Gavin disagreed, and they removed her from the force. Harpe was fired, along with five other SPD employees, after an internal investigation uncovered Flock misuse. Four of them were later arrested; however, Harpe was not one of them.

Tech.title: Apple updates guidelines to ban nudify apps masquerading as regular apps to pass review
Tech.content:
Apple tightened its developer guidelines over the weekend to ban apps that use AI to create offensive content, as well as those that masquerade as regular apps to pass the App Store review process and then turn into nudify apps, or surface those features prominently.

The company updated its guidelines with strong language around AI and user-generated content, and how app developers should include enough preventative measures to moderate objectionable or offensive content.

“Apps that host user-generated content are required to filter objectionable material, give users a way to report offensive content, and let users block abusive accounts. Apps containing hidden or undocumented features are also prohibited on the App Store, including apps that misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as “nudification” — after approval, a tactic commonly known as bait-and-switch,” the company said in a blog post.

Apple said that it will remove apps that add features not present in the version submitted for App Store review.

The iPhone maker has also updated the language in its legal section to reinforce that it will bar apps promoting human trafficking and exploitation of children.

Apple said last year its review process blocked over 150,000 apps from reaching users, and removed 193,000 developer accounts on account of fraud and abuse.

In July, San Francisco ordered both Apple and Google to clean up and delete nudification apps from their app stores. City Attorney David Chiu accused the companies of profiting from these apps through store fees. And in April, a Tech Transparency Project report indicated that both tech giants’ stores hosted multiple nudify apps, some of which were rated as suitable for minors.

Tech.title: Musk pledges to give ‘every kid in America’ one of his SpaceX shares
Tech.content:
Elon Musk claims he will give one of his SpaceX shares to “every kid in America” in 2027, which would result in a gift worth more than $10 billion based on the current $146 share price of his combination spaceflight and AI company. That’s roughly 1% of his $1 trillion net worth.

It’s not clear how Musk plans to do this, though he said in a separate post that he wants to give the shares “directly to the public,” and that this will be the “first of many” shares he’ll donate.

President Donald Trump, who Musk spent around $300 million to help elect, has set up bank accounts for children through the Treasury, called Trump Accounts, that can accept stock donations from wealthy donors.

Musk did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Musk’s post came just a few hours after Anthropic promised to put 5% of its shares into a new “public benefit fund,” which it intends to use to make “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations” after its upcoming IPO.

On Sunday afternoon, Musk replied directly to Anthropic’s post on X about its new fund, suggesting the company should give “directly to the public” instead.

“This is what I will be doing,” he wrote in another reply four hours later. Then, overnight, he announced his plans to donate SpaceX stock.

There are currently more than 70 million children under the age of 18 in the United States, according to the Federal Interagency Forum on Child and Family Statistics. Musk owns around 849 million Class A common shares of SpaceX, and more than 5.5 billion Class B supervoting shares. He stands to earn many more.

Musk’s philanthropic giving to date has been almost exclusively done through his own Musk Foundation. Despite his negative opinions about philanthropy, it’s the fifth-largest private charitable foundation in the U.S. A recent review by The Economist showed that a majority of the total money laid out by the Musk Foundation over the years has gone to entities tied to Musk in some way. Nearly 60% has gone to another charity, called The Foundation, run by his money manager, Jared Birchall.

Tech.title: Khosla Ventures doubles down on Even Healthcare to challenge India’s hospital economics
Tech.content:
Even Healthcare has raised $50 million in a funding round led by Khosla Ventures, as the Indian startup seeks to change how hospitals in the world’s most populous country make money and how doctors are rewarded.

The all-equity Series B round also saw participation from Alpha Wave and valued it at $300 million, triple its valuation 18 months ago, according to Even. The latest funding brings Even’s total capital raised to more than $120 million.

Hospitals in India typically earn more when patients undergo additional tests, procedures, or longer stays, even when they may not need them. Even wants to change that by focusing on patient care rather than pushing unnecessary treatments that drive up medical bills.

That approach has continued to appeal to Khosla Ventures, which has invested in Even since its seed round in 2021. The Silicon Valley venture firm is doubling down as Even moves to build and operate hospitals of its own, giving it greater control over patient care and costs.

Vinod Khosla, founder of Khosla Ventures, said Even’s approach goes beyond fixing individual parts of a fragmented healthcare system by bringing financing, technology, and care delivery together. The goal, he said in a prepared statement, is to reward better health outcomes rather than greater use of healthcare services.

“The clinical and economic results so far give us conviction that this can become an important new model for healthcare in India and beyond,” Khosla said.

Initially, Even relied on partner hospitals to treat its members, but Mayank Banerjee, who founded the startup in 2021 with Matilde Giglio and Alessandro Ialongo, said in an interview that the startup began questioning that model after finding that patients had undergone tests or been recommended surgeries it considered unnecessary.

“We think patients are getting not only a bad experience, but insurers are getting a bad economic deal. And as a result, we decided to fix it by building our own hospitals,” Banerjee told TechCrunch.

Even has since opened two hospitals in Bengaluru, both of which reached operational profitability, excluding depreciation, within a year of opening, Banerjee stated. The startup plans to open five more hospitals in the southern Indian city over the next six months, funded by its latest round.

Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even leases hospital buildings on 20-year agreements and spends on fitting them out and buying medical equipment.

Unlike hospitals where doctors may have financial incentives to recommend more procedures, Even pays its doctors fixed salaries — not tying their compensation to the number of tests or surgeries they perform, though Banerjee said doctors can earn bonuses based on patient-reported clinical outcomes.

The same principle extends to hospital management, whose compensation is not linked to the number of procedures performed, Banerjee told TechCrunch. Managers, he said, receive salaries and company-wide incentives, while marketing teams focus on bringing in patients instead of the revenue those patients generate. Moreover, every employee, including doctors and other hospital staff, receives equity in Even. The idea is to give employees a stake in the startup’s long-term performance, not to reward them for generating more medical bills.

Most of Even’s revenue comes from patients paying for treatment, Banerjee said. The startup also generates revenue through its relationships with insurers. It is also working with insurer partners on a model that could compensate it for hospitalizations it helps prevent, not simply for providing more treatment.

Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even tracks how patients recover after treatment using established medical scoring systems. In the case of knee replacements, for instance, it uses the Oxford Knee Score to measure pain and mobility. The startup publishes results on its website, alongside figures from other healthcare systems for comparison.

Even says its hospitals have an unplanned readmission rate of less than 1%, compared with an industry benchmark of 8% to 15%. Furthermore, it claims patients spend 40% less time in the hospital and that its approach has saved insurers more than ₹500 million (about $5.27 million).

Jai Sajnani, a partner at Khosla Ventures, told TechCrunch that the early performance of Even’s hospitals was a key reason the firm led the round. “We look forward to helping the Even team put quality care within reach of every family in Bengaluru and across India,” he said.

Even is still losing money, though. The startup posted a net loss of ₹902 million (about $9.50 million) in fiscal 2025, nearly 25% more than the previous year, on revenue of ₹272 million (about $2.86 million), regulatory filings show.

In August, Even also laid off about 350 employees, according to Indian startup-news website Entrackr. Banerjee acknowledged the restructuring and called it a difficult decision. He said the affected employees received severance, extended health insurance, and accelerated equity vesting.

Even currently employs about 650 people, including around 300 doctors full-time. The startup has about 250,000 members and has recorded more than 750,000 patient interactions since its launch in 2021, including consultations, diagnostic tests, and surgeries, Banerjee said.

Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even could turn profitable within months if it stopped spending on expansion, but the startup is choosing to grow instead. He declined to say when the startup expects to become profitable.

“Right now, we’re investing in growth and serving more patients,” Banerjee said.

Tech.title: No agenda, no rush, no leaving San Francisco: Benchmark’s partners on investing in a frenzied market
Tech.content:
The players sometimes change. I sat down with four of Benchmark’s partners three years ago, and three of those individuals are no longer with the firm. The capital commitments have changed, too. This summer, Benchmark announced $2 billion across two funds, marking only the second time in its 31-year history that it has veered from raising a far smaller vehicle.

But at this week’s TechCrunch Disrupt, the venture firm’s five partners convincingly portrayed a close-knit team that’s not about to put the pedal to the metal, even as many of their rivals do exactly that. The world may be speeding up, but they’re investing at the pace Benchmark always has: just two or three new bets per year per partner. The world is drowning in information, yet their Monday partner meetings still have no agenda. And while economic indicators point to trouble ahead, they don’t seem too bothered, seeing many of the warning signs as products of X-fueled hysteria.

Here’s what Benchmark’s five general partners — gathered together on our stage — had to say at the show. Some of the comments below have been edited for length and clarity; you can watch the full interview at the end of the article.

Benchmark has evolved in some ways, including a bigger core fund and a new growth fund. How do you think about adapting without losing what makes you Benchmark?

Peter Fenton: The craft that hasn’t changed is the core fund: working closely with founders at the beginning. It’s usually a 10-to-15-year commitment, [working] shoulder to shoulder, and that doesn’t scale. There’s also been inflation. We held the core fund at $500 million for 20 years, and it has just inflated to be consistent with the existing economy, which we hadn’t done and that was probably a tactical error on our part.

[As for the growth fund] it’s an expansion of our mandate. In some ways, we get permission from the ecosystem to do more than just the core early-stage business. [Not having this previously] was a fork in our eye. A number of opportunities that came to Benchmark would have returned somewhere between 10 and 1,000x to Benchmark, and we were constricted by our early-stage focus.

Are you thinking to make handful of bets with that $1.25 billion growth fund?

Fenton: We all have different answers, which is the beauty of a partnership. I’d love for us to have, as that great J.P. Morgan paper puts it, the agony and ecstasy of a concentrated portfolio. If the fund is successful, one or two investments will generate 90% of the returns. So I think it’s four to six, maybe seven to eight.

Ev, you joined Benchmark late last year. You’ve worked at Founders Fund, Bond, and Kleiner Perkins. How does Benchmark differ?

Ev Randall: Every firm is ultimately a collection of the people within the firm and how they work together. Some are very hierarchical, with a 50- or 60-person investment team and investment processes that are federated into product groups. And then you have small partnerships. Very early in my career, I was drawn to small partnerships because they allow a higher level of throughput and fidelity in your conversations, where you don’t feel like you’re making decisions through some Byzantine corporate structure. You’re going out on the field together, like a sports team.

And then the other piece is: You have to find your people, You have to find people who you not only like but admire. With Benchmark, with the current crop of GPs, it was obvious that everyone liked each other and got along, but it went deeper than that. It’s a group that admires each other and learns from each other. That mix of attributes is very rare, and when I saw it, I immediately wanted to join, and I think Jack felt the same way also as a newcomer.

Jack, you joined in February, but it was just a year ago that you raised a second, $275 million fund for your own firm in what you told the Wall Street Journal took one week. You have a hugely popular podcast. Why join Benchmark?

Jack Altman: It’s funny. I did the podcast with these guys at the start of this year, and during that podcast, obviously we talked about the commitment to being a small fund, but more than that, what I heard was that they want to be the first people who founders call, they want to be concentrated, and they just care. So much in this industry gets tied up in money and status, and what I felt from the Benchmark team then, and ten times more as I’ve gotten to know them so well, is it’s a group that really cares about founders and helping companies. And I did enjoy being an individual investor. . .but in a market this crazy, I don’t know how I’d feel, figuring it out on my own. Having a group of people who are so smart and focused and driven to learn it with and from has been awesome. There’s no better place to learn.

I’m told you meet on Mondays with no agenda.

Chethan Puttagunta: Jack tried to make an agenda. [Laughs.]

Altman: I’ve got an agenda for next Monday.

Eric Vishria: It’s weirdly arbitrary, honestly. It’s an ongoing conversation. In a time of rapid change, you’re trying to figure out what’s becoming possible that wasn’t possible six months ago, and who’s bending light. We talk about what companies we’re meeting, what piqued our interest and why, what we’re seeing in board meetings. You can try to systematize it, but one of the beauties of five people is you don’t have to. It’s a decades-long conversation that only works if you’re small and actually enjoy spending time together. After this session, we’re having dinner with one of the very few entrepreneurs who has built a multi-hundred-billion-dollar company, someone we’re not invested in, just to stretch our thinking.

Puttagunta: Part of not having an agenda is you need space to be reactive. If a founder needs help landing an executive or a strategic partnership, the five of us can be at their disposal.

You’re an equal partnership. Can one person put the kibosh on a deal?

Puttagunta: Nobody knows. We don’t have rules around it.

Altman: I actually don’t know. I was waiting to see what someone else [said].

It’s never happened?

Altman: Because the firm is structured around a low volume of deals, you don’t actually want to have all of this rigor. If we invested in 100 or 200 companies a year, you’d want a CRM and a formal voting process. Because it’s so rare, the lack of structure is a huge asset.

Fenton: One of the differentiating aspects of our brand is we’re not so cocksure to come in and say ‘winner’ or ‘loser.’ It’s not Shark Tank. We sort of feel awe, for lack of a better term, at all the possibilities . . . The occasional case where someone comes in who’s polarizing — the entrepreneurs feel that. If someone in the room doesn’t like you, we’re not a great partner.

Companies are growing faster than ever. I’d think it’s easier to feel you’re missing out on opportunities if you don’t invest with greater frequency. Have you picked up the pace?

Puttagunta: I think the pace is consistent. I think part of the reality of venture capital in our business is that we are not going to be part of every successful company, and that’s okay. There are companies that we identify, we find that the entrepreneur has some great strength, and we want to amplify that strength. And it’s our job to find a way to work with that person. It kind of doesn’t matter how much capital they want to raise, or what structure, or where they are. You just have to work through all that stuff.

One thing that founders are interested in as a trend is VCs backing competing companies. Has that VC-founder pact changed because companies are growing so quickly and expanding into one another’s territory?

Vishria: One of the things we have an ethos around is, we are making a commitment to an entrepreneur, and through that commitment, we’re saying we’re going to work with you in this thing, and whatever that thing is, and we are working closely enough where it matters, and it should matter to them, and as it matters to us. The harsh reality of this world is every company is evolving very quickly, and so you do have companies that will naturally evolve from one thing to another, or pivot or change, and you are going to get conflicts. That’s just the reality of the of the kind of current dynamic. . .

Of course, we’re maintaining confidentiality and doing those things and fortunate to not end up in in that type of insane direct conflict [as happened recently with rival companies Factory and Cognition]. . . that commitment of exclusivity in that area is really important. But things are evolving. There’s no doubt about that.

Puttagunta: And I think people are ultra ambitious in this AI era. As the cost of coding new products effectively goes to zero, founders see a surface area and they want to attack the surface area, and so I think it’s probably going to happen more, where you start to run into each other. But there’s a way to be there’s a way to maintain that relationship and be respectful.

Jack, have you made an investment for Benchmark yet, and if so, did you feel a lot of pressure with that first deal?

Altman: I have, a few, and some are recent, so not all are disclosed. My background was software, but since joining, I’ve done chips, robotics and infra. Someone asked me when I joined, ‘How was the onboarding?’ And I was like, ‘It was perfect. There was no onboarding.’ Either Chethan or Eric told me early on, ‘Hey, you’re going to feel tight on your first one. Don’t. You’re going to make many investments while you’re here. This whole game includes crazy power laws. The odds of it being your first are low.’ . . . I trusted they understood what my shape was as a person, as an investor, and I was going to just try to stay as consistent to that as I could.

It really is a group dynamic on a lot of these. The investments I’ve made, I don’t think we would have won them if I didn’t have my partners. I don’t know that I would have been able to know how to get to a yes without them.

Eric, the AI chip company Cerebras was an unusual bet for Benchmark at the time it was made. What persuaded you to move forward with it?

Vishria: We invested in the spring of 2016, in the first round. We hadn’t made a hardware investment in 10 years. The founders seemed good, they had a very simple thesis, and I didn’t understand most of the rest. On the Sunday night before they came back to pitch the partnership, Peter told me it went against everything he’d learned in venture. Then, after the Monday pitch, he had flipped. A big part of it is understanding each other’s instincts. That began a journey of lots of ups and downs and many potential deaths of the company along the way, and it’s far from over. The romanticism of falling in love with a founder and an idea is why we do this.

Fenton: Andrew and his co-founders are heretics. What they were saying was unorthodox, and you see it today, with people dumping on the stock because it’s polarizing. That’s exactly where we have to be as investors. If it’s consensus, why is there a startup?

On that point, Cerebras priced at $185 when it went public earlier this year, jumped to $350, and is back near $185. Why?

Vishria: About six weeks before the IPO, I showed the company stock chart after stock chart: CoreWeave, Datadog, DoorDash, Amazon. Peak to trough, it’s insane how many of them move 500% in a year, up and down. So who knows? You control what you can control, and you update the public markets every 12 weeks. Being a public company takes a stomach of titanium, and the employees have to understand that.
